    Building a Computational Mind

    Learn to write Python from nothing. See, at every step, exactly what the machine is doing underneath — until the two become one picture in your head.

    • Build v6.0
    The keystone. The physical processor does not understand or execute Python. It executes CPython's own native machine instructions. Those instructions make CPython read your Python bytecode as data and carry out what it asks for. Everything in this book hangs off that one sentence.

    Front matterHow to read

    How to read this book

    Four depths, one ritual, and permission to stop early.

    This book teaches two subjects as one. Not Python and then, separately, how computers work — but a single chain of cause and effect that starts with what you meant and ends with a voltage changing somewhere.

    Four depths

    Every idea in this book exists at four depths. You do not have to reach the bottom to be allowed to continue. A ten-year-old should complete Levels 1 and 2 comfortably and dip into Level 3 when curious.

    Level 1

    Core model

    The smallest accurate picture you need to actually use the idea. Never a lie — just not the whole thing yet.

    Level 2

    Memory model

    Names, objects, references, frames. What exists in memory before and after each line you write.

    Level 3

    Runtime model

    The compiler, the bytecode, the interpreter loop, the allocator, and where the operating system joins in. Kept behind a + so it never blocks you.

    Level 4

    Expert microscope

    Implementation specifics, version differences, optimisations, edge cases. For the day you come back older.

    Levels 3 and 4 always live inside a panel you open by choice. If you skip them, nothing later breaks — that is a design rule of this book, not a hope.

    The one discipline

    Predict, run, reconcile. Before you run anything, write down what you think will happen. Then run it. Then explain the difference in words. The gap between your prediction and reality is the only place learning actually happens — reading correct code teaches you almost nothing, because nothing ever surprises you.

    What a mastery gate means

    Each chapter ends with a gate: a short list of things you must be able to do, from memory, without the book open. Not recognise. Do. If you cannot, the chapter tells you exactly which section to return to. Recognising a page you have read before feels like knowing and is not knowing.

    Front matterReference system

    The reference system

    Exactly which Python, which build, which machine — because half the interesting facts change when these change.

    A book that says "Python does X" without saying which Python is quietly guessing. Here is the machine every measurement and every disassembly in this book comes from.

    Language version
    Python 3.14 (language reference for the 3.14 series)
    Implementation
    CPython 3.14.6 — the interpreter you get from python.org. Other implementations exist (PyPy, MicroPython, GraalPy) and differ in almost everything marked CPython
    Build
    Standard build, with the global interpreter lock. The free-threaded build (python3.14t) became officially supported in 3.14 but is still opt-in and is not what this book measures
    Operating systems shown
    Windows 11 and Linux. Where they behave differently the text says so
    Representative processor
    A 64-bit x86-64 desktop CPU. Every timing or cache figure is an example from one machine, never a law of nature
    Pointer width
    64 bits, so a memory address is 8 bytes. On a 32-bit machine every diagram in this book still works; the numbers halve
    Most version-sensitive
    Bytecode instruction names, object sizes, and anything about the specialising interpreter. These changed in 3.11, 3.12, 3.13 and 3.14 and will change again
    CPythonHardware example

    Where the numbers in this book come from. Disassemblies and object sizes were produced on CPython running on a 64-bit machine and are reproduced with the exact commands shown, so you can run them yourself and compare. If your output differs, your version differs — and noticing that is a skill this book is trying to give you, not a failure.

    Verified against: docs.python.org 3.14 · dis module documentation · CPython 3.14 branch source · run locally 2026-07-31
    A habit worth building now

    When you read any programming fact anywhere, ask: is that the language promising, or this one program's way of doing it, or the operating system, or this particular chip? Most confusion in programming is one of those four wearing another's coat. The next section gives you the labels.

    Front matterTruth contract

    Five kinds of truth

    Every technical claim in this book wears a label saying what kind of thing it is.

    "Lists keep their order" and "small integers are shared" sound like the same sort of fact. They are not. One is a promise the language makes to you forever. The other is a trick one interpreter plays and could stop playing tomorrow.

    The five labels

    Python language

    A promise of the language itself

    True in every correct Python, on every machine, for as long as the language keeps its word. Example: assignment never copies the object.

    CPython

    How this one interpreter does it

    True of CPython, possibly only of this version. Example: reference counting, bytecode names, small-integer caching.

    OS-dependent

    The operating system decides

    Differs between Windows, Linux and macOS. Example: how a process is created, what a file handle is called, how the console behaves.

    Hardware example

    One machine's numbers

    A measurement from a particular chip. Useful for scale, never a universal fact. Example: cache line width, memory latency.

    Simplified model

    Deliberately incomplete, on purpose

    A reduced picture used to get you moving. Every one of these states what it explains correctly, what it leaves out, and exactly where the fuller version arrives.

    The rule this book holds itself to

    A disclaimer at the front is not enough. The label goes where the claim is.

    If you find a technical statement in this book with no badge and it is not obviously Level‑1 plain English, that is a defect in the book, not a subtlety you missed.

    Front matterThe spine

    The execution ladder

    Thirteen floors between what you meant and what the machine did. One diagram, used for the entire book.

    Most books about programming show you the top floor. Most books about computers show you the bottom. The thing that actually confuses people is the staircase. So this book uses one staircase, every time, and lights up only the floors that a particular line of code actually visits.

    The canonical ladderreference copy

    1. Human intention — what you wanted to happen
    2. Python source text — characters in a file, nothing more
    3. Tokens — the text chopped into meaningful pieces
    4. Syntax tree — the shape of the meaning
    5. Compiler — CPython's translator, written in C
    6. Code object and bytecode — the instruction list CPython will follow
    7. CPython runtime — the loop that reads that list
    8. Native machine instructions — the real instructions of CPython itself
    9. CPU control logic — fetch, decode, execute
    10. Registers and ALU — where arithmetic physically happens
    11. Caches and RAM — where the bytes actually live
    12. Operating-system services — only when the program needs the outside world
    13. Device, file, terminal, result — something you can see

    In real chapters, floors that a line of code does not touch are dimmed and marked not involved — because knowing what is not happening is half the model.

    The keystone — say this one out loud

    The physical CPU does not understand or directly execute Python bytecode. It executes CPython's native machine instructions. Those instructions make the CPython runtime inspect Python bytecode and perform the requested work.

    Floor 6 is data. Floor 8 is instructions. They are not the same kind of thing and they never become the same kind of thing. If you keep only one sentence from this whole book, keep that one.

    Front matterNotation

    The visual grammar

    Every shape means exactly one thing, everywhere in the book, forever.

    Diagrams here are instruments, not decoration. You are meant to draw them yourself with a pencil. That only works if the shapes never change meaning between chapters.

    Volume 0 · Chapter 1How a computer obeys

    Two states and a wire

    Bits, bytes, encoding, and the reason nothing in memory knows what it means

    Before any of the Python in this book will make real sense, you need one strange fact in your bones: a computer cannot store a letter. It cannot store a number either. It can only hold things in one of two states — and everything else is an agreement.

    Unit 0.1.1
    Problem

    Make sand remember something

    Something you can feel

    Here is a job. You have a wire and a torch bulb. Nothing else. You must use them to remember the answer to one question that your friend will ask you tomorrow.

    You cannot write on the wire. You cannot store a sentence in it. There is exactly one thing you can do to a wire: push electricity through it, or don't.

    So the wire can be in one of two states. On, or off. That is the entire vocabulary you have.

    Try it. The question your friend will ask is: "Did it rain today?"

    Now the wire can do the job perfectly. You and your friend agree, in advance: bulb lit means yes, bulb dark means no. You set the switch. Tomorrow your friend looks. The answer survived the night.

    The idea to keep

    The wire does not contain the word "yes". It contains electricity or no electricity. The meaning lives in the agreement, not in the wire.

    This is not a childish simplification you will grow out of. It is the actual situation inside every computer that has ever been built. Change the agreement and the same wire means something completely different.

    It is worth being clear about why two states rather than three or ten. Nothing forbids a wire from carrying several distinguishable voltages, and machines have been built that way. The difficulty is that distinguishing more levels requires measuring more precisely, and a real wire is never quite clean — voltages sag over distance, wobble with temperature, and pick up interference from their neighbours.

    With two states the margin for error is enormous: anything in the lower half is off and anything in the upper half is on, so a signal can be badly distorted and still be read correctly. With ten states the bands are a tenth as wide and the same distortion produces a wrong answer. Two states is not a limitation of the technology; it is a deliberate choice to trade capacity per wire for reliability, and it is why digital signals can be copied endlessly without degrading while analogue ones cannot.

    Hardware exampleSimplified model

    What "on" really is. Inside a real chip, "on" is not a torch bulb. It is a voltage above some threshold — often around 1 volt on a modern processor, compared with roughly 0 volts for "off". Memory chips store the state in tiny capacitors that leak, which is why RAM has to be refreshed thousands of times a second.

    What this model gets right: two distinguishable states, and meaning by agreement. What it leaves out: voltages, timing, refresh, and the fact that a stored charge is never exactly full or exactly empty. You get the fuller version when we reach RAM in Chapter 0.2 and again in Volume III.

    Category: hardware example. Figures vary by chip generation and are not a rule of nature.
    The formal word

    One of these two-state things is called a bit. The word is squashed from binary digit. "Binary" just means two-valued. A bit is the smallest amount of information there is: enough to answer exactly one yes-or-no question.

    Unit 0.1.2
    Problem

    One wire is not enough

    Counting with switches

    One bit answers one yes/no question. But you want to remember how many biscuits are left, and that is not a yes/no question.

    So use more wires. With two wires you have four possible combinations: off-off, off-on, on-off, on-on. With three wires, eight. Every wire you add doubles the number of patterns, because each old pattern can now be followed by an on or an off.

    The growth here is the important part and it is worth pausing on, because the same arithmetic governs a great deal of what follows. Each wire you add does not add to the number of patterns — it doubles it. One wire gives two patterns, two give four, three give eight, ten give 1,024. Sixteen wires give over sixty-five thousand.

    That doubling is what makes computers possible at scale. A modest number of wires distinguishes an enormous number of things, so representing a large quantity does not require a large amount of hardware. It is also what makes the byte a sensible unit, as the unit on bytes explains, and it is the same relationship that Chapter II.8 meets from the opposite direction, where halving a problem repeatedly reaches the answer in very few steps.

    Now you need an agreement about which pattern means which number. The one the whole world uses is the same trick you already use for ordinary numbers — you just do not notice you use it.

    You already know how this works

    Write the number 407. What does the 4 mean? Not four. It means four hundreds, because of where it sits. Each position is worth ten times the position to its right: hundreds, tens, ones.

    Binary does exactly the same thing, but each position is worth two times the one to its right: eight, four, two, one.

    Predict — write it down before reading on

    What number is the pattern 1100? Work it out with the columns: eight, four, two, one. Write your answer on paper. Then: what pattern would you need for the number 5?

    Answers, once you have written yours: 1100 is 8 + 4 = 12. And 5 is 4 + 1, so 0101.

    New Python — the prompt, and one function

    Everything you type in this book starts at the prompt, which looks like >>>. You type something and press Enter, and Python answers on the next line. That is the whole ritual for now.

    You also meet your first function: bin. A function is a named machine you hand something to, using brackets. bin(12) means "hand 12 to the bin machine". It hands back the binary pattern as text. The 0b on the front is Python's way of saying "the rest of this is binary, not ordinary digits".

    Python language

    Whole numbers in Python have no size limit. Most programming languages give you a fixed number of bits per number and break loudly when you exceed them. Python promises that an int is as big as it needs to be; 2 ** 1000 is an ordinary answer, not an error. This is a promise of the language, not a trick of one interpreter.

    Underneath, CPython achieves it by storing a big number as several chunks with a length — which is why it is slower and larger than a fixed-size number. You get that machinery in Volume II.

    Source: Python language reference, numeric types — int has arbitrary precision.
    Unit 0.1.3
    Problem

    How many wires should we group together?

    The byte

    Machines do not deal with bits one at a time, any more than you buy eggs one at a time. They deal in a standard bundle. That bundle is eight bits, and it is called a byte.

    Eight bits gives you 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 256 different patterns. Counting from zero, that is 0 to 255.

    Why eight and not seven or ten? Partly history: 256 patterns was enough for every letter, digit and punctuation mark anyone in 1960s America wanted, with room left over. Partly convenience: eight is a power of two, so bytes split neatly in half and in half again. It is a convention that hardened into a standard, not a law of physics.

    Numbers worth knowing by heart

    1 bit → 2 patterns. 8 bits (one byte) → 256 patterns. Every extra bit doubles it.

    Doubling is violent. Sixteen bits is 65,536 patterns. Thirty-two bits is over four billion. Sixty-four bits — the size of one address on the machine this book uses — is about 18 quintillion. That is why your computer can give every byte of memory its own number and never run out.

    Unit 0.1.4
    Break

    The mistake almost everyone makes

    Deliberate misconception

    The comfortable wrong idea

    "Memory stores letters and numbers. A letter is stored as a letter, and a number is stored as a number, and the computer keeps track of which is which."

    It is a reasonable guess. It is also wrong in a way that causes real bugs for the rest of your life if you do not fix it now.

    Take the byte 01000001. In the column trick, that is 64 + 1 = 65.

    But under the agreement called ASCII, pattern 65 means the letter A. Under an agreement about screen brightness, it might mean a fairly dark grey. Inside a program's instruction list, it might be part of a machine instruction.

    Nothing about the byte itself says which. There is no little tag. The eight switches are in exactly the same positions in every case.

    This is the most important sentence in the chapter and it is worth resisting the urge to read past it. There is no hidden field, no tag, no extra bit recording what a byte is for. Memory holds patterns, and patterns alone. The meaning lives entirely in whatever the program does with them.

    Two consequences run through the rest of this book. The first is that the same bytes genuinely can be several things at once, depending only on who is reading — which is why Chapter III.1 can read one file as text or as bytes, and why reading it under the wrong agreement produces plausible nonsense rather than an error. The second is that any system wanting values to know what they are must build that knowledge itself, storing the description alongside the data. Chapter I.2 shows Python doing exactly that, and the twenty-eight bytes it spends on a small integer are the price of the tag this chapter shows to be absent.

    New Python — two more functions

    chr(n) hands you the character that agreement number n stands for. ord(c) does the reverse: hand it a character, get the number back. The quotation marks around 'A' tell Python "this is text, not a name".

    Python languageSimplified model

    Careful — Python text is not ASCII. Python strings hold Unicode characters, which covers every writing system, not the 128 symbols of ASCII. ord('漢') is 28450. ASCII survives as the first 128 numbers of Unicode, which is why ord('A') is still 65.

    What this model gets right: characters are numbers under an agreement. What it leaves out: how those numbers become bytes on disk, which is a separate agreement called an encoding (UTF-8 and friends). You get the fuller version in Volume I, "Text, properly", and again in Volume III.

    Source: Python language reference, string type; Unicode standard code point assignments.
    Become the machine

    You are the memory chip

    First person

    Trace · a byte's point of view

    1. meI am eight tiny stores of charge. Right now I am 0 1 0 0 0 0 0 1. I have been this way for four milliseconds.
    2. meI do not know what I mean. I have no field for that. I am charge levels.
    3. readSomething asks for my contents. I hand over all eight states. I am not asked why.
    4. elsewhereWhatever received me decides. If it was a text program, it draws an A. If it was doing arithmetic, it adds 65.
    5. meI am unchanged either way. Reading me does not alter me.

    Ladder · storing one bytefloors involved

    1. Human intention
    2. Python source text
    3. Tokens
    4. Syntax tree
    5. Compiler
    6. Code object and bytecode

    You have met one floor. The other twelve are still dark, honestly, because you have not built them yet. By the end of Volume 0, floors 9 to 13 will light up. Volume I lights the top.

    Retrieval lock

    Reconstruct it without looking

    Close the book

    1. Redraw. From memory, draw one byte as eight boxes with the column values above them. Fill in the pattern for the number 100. Then check with bin(100).
    2. Explain. In your own words, to a person who has not read this: why can the same byte be a letter and a number at the same time?
    3. Modify. Predict chr(97) before running it. Then predict chr(ord('a') + 1). Run both.
    4. Transfer. A friend says "the file is corrupted — it opened as nonsense symbols". Using this chapter, explain what most likely happened to the bytes. (Hint: probably nothing at all happened to them.)
    5. Stretch. How many bits do you need to give every person alive today their own unique pattern? Start doubling from 8 and count.
    Mastery gate — Chapter 0.1
    • You can convert a four-bit pattern to a number, and a number under 16 to a four-bit pattern, on paper, without help.
    • You can say how many different patterns one byte has, and why.
    • You can explain, in one sentence, why memory does not know whether it holds a letter or a number.
    • You can name the difference between the state of a bit and the meaning of a bit.

    If any of these is shaky, return to Unit 0.1.2 and redo the prediction exercise with three fresh numbers before continuing. Chapter 0.2 assumes all four, and will not re-teach them.

    Volume 0 · Chapter 2How a computer obeys

    The wall of boxes

    Memory locations, addresses, reading and writing — and the first three stages of the toy processor

    A byte on its own is useless. You need billions of them, and you need to be able to find the one you want without searching. The solution is so simple it is almost disappointing: give every box a number and never move it.

    Unit 0.2.1
    Problem

    Sixteen billion boxes and no labels

    Something you can feel

    Imagine a wall of post boxes that goes on further than you can see. Each box holds exactly one byte. A modern computer has about sixteen billion of them.

    You need the byte you stored a moment ago. How do you find it?

    You could search from the left. Sixteen billion boxes at one per second is over five hundred years. That is not a plan.

    You could write a label on each box saying what is inside. But labels are made of bytes, so now you need boxes for the labels, and boxes for their labels. That is not a plan either.

    The answer used by every computer ever built: number the boxes. Left to right, starting at zero, never changing. The number of a box is called its address.

    What makes numbering work, where the other two ideas failed, is that it requires no storage at all. A label written on a box takes room and must be searched. A position counted from the left takes no room but must be walked to. A number that is the position is known without being kept anywhere and reached without travelling — the machine calculates where to look and looks there.

    That is the whole reason the scheme scales. Sixteen billion boxes need sixteen billion numbers, and not one of those numbers is stored: they exist as a way of talking about positions rather than as data. Everything else in this volume — the program counter of Chapter 0.3, the address spaces of Chapter 0.4, the references in every Python object — depends on a position being something you can compute rather than something you must look up.

    An address is not stored anywhere. It is not written on the box. It is simply which box you mean — the way house number 12 is not painted inside the house, it is a position on the street. And because the boxes never move, the address never goes stale.

    The idea to keep

    The address is where. The contents are what. They are two completely different things, and the whole of memory works on keeping them apart.

    Getting these confused is the single most common source of muddle for beginners — and, in languages with pointers, the single most common source of catastrophic bugs.

    Hardware example

    How many boxes can you number? On the 64-bit machine this book uses, an address is 64 bits wide, which is enough to number about 18 quintillion boxes. No computer has anywhere near that much memory; the width is generous on purpose. On an older 32-bit machine an address was 32 bits, which numbers about 4.29 billion boxes — which is exactly why 32-bit computers could not use more than 4 GB of RAM. That famous limit was never a rule about memory. It was a rule about how many digits the address had.

    Category: hardware example. Address width is a property of the processor architecture, not of Python.
    Unit 0.2.2
    Break

    Put 300 in a box

    Deliberate failure

    Go on. Box 5 is empty. Put the number 300 in it.

    You cannot. One box is one byte. One byte has 256 patterns, numbered 0 to 255. There is no pattern for 300. The box is not too small in the way a shoe is too small — there is simply no arrangement of eight switches that anyone has agreed means 300.

    Descend

    What the machine actually does

    Earned by the failure

    The machine uses two boxes side by side and a new agreement: read them as one 16-bit number. 300 is 1 × 256 + 44, so box 5 holds 1 and box 6 holds 44.

    This is why you keep hearing "16-bit", "32-bit", "64-bit". They are not different kinds of memory. They are agreements about how many boxes in a row to read as one value. And now a genuinely useful piece of knowledge falls out for free: if a value spans several boxes, some machines store the big end first and some store the small end first. That disagreement has a name — endianness — and it is why files written on one machine sometimes open as gibberish on another. You will meet it properly in Volume III.

    CPython

    Python hides all of this from you, and it costs something. A Python int is never a bare byte in a box. It is an object with a header, a sign, a length, and its digits in chunks — which is how it can grow without limit. That is why one small Python integer occupies far more memory than the single byte the value would need. You measure this yourself in the pilot chapter of Volume I.

    Category: CPython implementation. Other Pythons store integers differently.
    Unit 0.2.3
    Tool

    The only two things you can do to memory

    Read and write

    There are exactly two operations. Both are more surprising than they sound.

    Reading is copying

    When the machine reads box 5, the box still holds 200 afterwards. Nothing is removed. Reading takes a copy of the contents and leaves the original alone. You can read the same box a million times and it never wears out or empties.

    Writing destroys

    When the machine writes 7 into box 5, the 200 is gone. Not moved to a bin. Not recoverable. The switches are simply in new positions, and no record exists that they used to be somewhere else.

    This asymmetry is the source of an entire family of bugs, and it is worth saying out loud in a slightly dramatic voice: memory has no undo. Anything that looks like undo — in a text editor, in a game, in Python — is a program that deliberately kept a copy first.

    Sit with the asymmetry, because it is unlike anything in ordinary experience. Reading a book leaves the book unchanged, and so does reading a box; that much is familiar. But writing has no counterpart in the physical world worth trusting: putting a new object in a drawer means removing the old one and having it in your hand, whereas writing to a box means the previous contents are simply gone, not moved, not displaced, not recoverable by any means whatever.

    Every mechanism in computing for not losing things is built on top of this, precisely because the hardware offers no help. Chapter I.7's copying, Chapter II.11's reference counts, Chapter III.9's atomic rename all exist because the underlying operation destroys, and anything wishing to preserve must arrange to have written the old value somewhere else first.

    Unit 0.2.4 · Toy processor stage 1
    Build

    You are the processor

    No computer required

    Get a pencil and paper. You are about to be a processor, and you will discover that being one is duller than you imagined — which is exactly the point.

    Draw eight boxes in a row. Number them 0 to 7 above the line. Write these starting contents inside:

    Box 0 – 3
    Empty. Write 0 in each.
    Box 4
    6
    Box 5
    9
    Box 6 – 7
    Empty. Write 0 in each.

    Now here is your instruction sheet. Obey it exactly, in order, one line at a time. Do not read ahead. Do not skip. Do not improve anything.

    Predict — before you start

    Write down: (a) what number ends up in box 6, and (b) which line you will be standing on when you stop. Then run the sheet by hand.

    You should have said "15" and stopped at line 6. If not, run it again more slowly — the discipline of not skipping is the skill being trained here.

    Descend

    What you just were

    Naming what you did

    Every part of that exercise has a real name, and you now have the experience to attach the names to.

    Your boxes

    Memory

    Numbered locations, each holding one value, which stay put.

    Your HAND

    A register

    One tiny working space inside the processor. Fast, and there is almost no space in it.

    Your finger on the line

    The program counter

    The thing that remembers which instruction is next. Line 4 could move it.

    The sheet itself

    The program

    Instructions in order. Notice they lived somewhere too — on paper.

    "Add what you see"

    The ALU

    The arithmetic unit. The one place a sum can physically happen.

    "If it is zero, go to"

    A conditional jump

    The only reason a machine can appear to make decisions.

    What you should have noticed

    You never once decided anything. You never guessed. You never wondered what the numbers were for. Line 4 felt like a decision, but you did not choose — you compared to zero and followed the rule. That is exactly, precisely, all a processor ever does, three billion times a second, without ever getting bored or curious.

    That sentence is the point of the whole exercise and worth defending, because it will feel untrue. You were conscious throughout, you understood what you were doing, and it seemed at moments as though you were choosing. But look back at the instruction sheet: at every step exactly one action was permitted, determined entirely by the sheet and the numbers already written. At no point were two continuations available.

    That is what "the machine never guesses" means, and it is the property that makes computers trustworthy rather than clever. A processor executing a billion instructions a second is doing precisely what you just did, with the same absence of judgement, which is why a program that behaves correctly today behaves identically tomorrow — and why every surprising thing in this book turns out to be the machine obeying an instruction somebody did not realise they had given.

    Unit 0.2.5 · Toy processor stages 2 and 3
    Tool

    Moving the wall of boxes into Python

    Your first data structure

    Paper is fine for eight boxes. It is hopeless for a thousand. So we move the wall into Python — and to do that you need exactly three new pieces of Python, no more.

    New Python — three pieces, taught here because the simulator needs them now

    1. A list. Square brackets with values separated by commas make a row of slots: [0, 0, 65, 12]. That is our wall of boxes.

    2. Indexing. Put a number in square brackets after the list to reach one slot: memory[2] is the slot at position 2. Counting starts at zero, exactly like addresses — this is not a coincidence, it is the same idea.

    3. A name. memory = [0, 0, 65, 12] attaches the name memory to that list so you can refer to it again. For now, treat a name as a label you stick on something. The full, honest, diagram-by-diagram treatment of what assignment really does is the pilot chapter of Volume I, and it is more interesting than you would expect.

    Simplified model

    A Python list is not really a row of bytes. What this model gets right: numbered slots starting at zero, reachable instantly by number, that you can read and overwrite. That is genuinely how both work. What it leaves out: a Python list holds references to objects scattered around memory, not raw bytes packed side by side; each slot on a 64-bit machine holds an 8-byte address, not a value. You get the fuller version in the Volume I pilot chapter, and the complete machinery in Volume II under dynamic arrays.

    Category: simplified teaching model. Declared here so it can be corrected later without anything you learned turning out to be a lie.
    Predict, run, reconcile

    Before running each one, write down what you expect: memory[8] — then memory[-1] — then memory[6] = memory[6] + 1 followed by memory.

    One of those three does something you probably did not predict, and one of them fails outright. Both are worth the surprise.

    memory[8] raises IndexError: there is no box 8 when there are eight boxes numbered 0 to 7. memory[-1] gives you the last box — a Python convenience that real memory does not have. And the third line reads box 6, adds one, and writes the result back over the top, destroying the old value. Read, compute, write: the loop the whole machine is built from.

    Ladder · memory[6] = memory[4] + memory[5]floors involved

    1. Human intention — store the total in box 6
    2. Python source text
    3. Tokens
    4. Syntax tree
    5. Compiler
    6. Code object and bytecode
    7. CPython runtime
    8. Native machine instructions
    9. CPU control logic
    10. Registers and ALU — the actual addition
    11. Caches and RAM
    12. Operating-system services
    13. Device, file, terminal, result

    Floors 12 and 13 are dark and that matters. Adding two numbers and storing the result never asks the operating system for anything. The program does it entirely inside its own memory. The OS only appears when the program needs something it does not own — the screen, a file, the network. If you remember one thing about the OS, make it that.

    Retrieval lock

    Reconstruct it without looking

    Close the book

    1. Redraw. Draw eight boxes with addresses above. Show the state after memory[2] = 40 and then memory[3] = memory[2]. Mark clearly which box changed and which did not.
    2. Explain. Why does reading a box a thousand times not empty it, while writing to it once loses the old value forever?
    3. Modify. Rewrite the paper instruction sheet so that it puts the difference between boxes 4 and 5 into box 6, and reports "nothing to report" when they are equal. Test it by hand with 6 and 9, then with 9 and 9.
    4. Transfer. Your friend says their game "remembers" their score after they close it. Explain why memory boxes alone cannot do that, and what must be involved instead. (You do not have the full answer yet — say what you can and note what you are missing.)
    5. Stretch. If one box holds 0 to 255, what is the largest number three boxes side by side can hold? Show your working, not just the answer.
    Mastery gate — Chapter 0.2
    • You can state the difference between an address and its contents, and give an example where they are different numbers.
    • You can explain why reading is repeatable and writing is destructive.
    • You can execute a short instruction sheet by hand without skipping or improvising.
    • You can name, from memory, the real component that each part of the paper exercise stood for: memory, register, program counter, ALU, conditional jump.
    • You can build a list in Python, read one slot, and overwrite one slot.

    The fourth item is the one that matters most. Chapter 0.3 builds every one of those components properly, and it assumes you already have a physical memory of having been them.

    Volume 0 · Chapter 3How a computer obeys

    The machine that never guesses

    Registers, the ALU, the program counter, the instruction register, the decoder, and the fetch–decode–execute loop — built one part at a time

    In Chapter 0.2 you were a processor for eight lines. Now you build one. Not a metaphor for one — a working processor, in Python, assembled one component at a time, where you can stop it mid-instruction and look inside.

    How this chapter is built

    Nine stages. Each adds exactly one component and exactly as much Python as that component needs. Nothing appears fully formed. If you find yourself reading a line of Python you have never met, that is a defect in this chapter — every construct is introduced in a green box immediately before its first use.

    Stage 4
    Problem

    Why does the processor need pockets?

    Registers

    Your paper exercise had a HAND: one scrap holding one number. That was not a teaching trick. Real processors work the same way, and the reason is distance.

    RAM sits on the motherboard, centimetres from the processor. That sounds close. It is not. Electricity travels fast, but a processor executes an instruction in well under a nanosecond, and in one nanosecond light itself travels only about thirty centimetres. Fetching a value from RAM can cost the processor hundreds of wasted steps while it waits.

    So the processor keeps a handful of storage places inside itself, next to the arithmetic. These are registers. They are absurdly fast and absurdly few.

    The obvious question is why there are so few, when memory is measured in billions. The answer is the same physics as Chapter II.12's hierarchy: a storage place can be fast or numerous, not both. Fast means physically close to the circuitry that uses it, and only a small number of things can be close to any one place. Registers are few precisely because they are instant, and RAM is slow precisely because it is vast.

    That constraint shapes everything above it. A processor with sixteen registers can hold sixteen values in its hands, so a calculation involving more must shuttle values back and forth to memory — which is why instruction sets have load and store at all, and why Chapter IV.3's decision about where to keep intermediate values is a real design question rather than an arbitrary one.

    Hardware example

    On one representative 64-bit x86-64 desktop processor: sixteen general-purpose registers, each 64 bits wide. That is 128 bytes of general-purpose register space in total — against perhaps sixteen billion bytes of RAM. Reading a register takes effectively no time; reaching main memory can take on the order of a hundred processor cycles.

    Different processors differ enormously. An ARM chip in a phone has a different count and different names. These numbers give you the scale of the gap, not a universal fact.

    Category: hardware example. Register counts and latencies are architecture-specific.

    Our toy processor gets three registers, and you have already met all three by doing them with a pencil:

    A — the accumulator
    The working scrap. Your HAND. Nearly every instruction reads it or writes it.
    PC — program counter
    The address of the next instruction. Your finger on the line.
    IR — instruction register
    The instruction currently being carried out. The line you are reading right now.
    Stage 5
    Descend

    Where the plus sign actually happens

    The ALU

    In A = A + memory[5] the interesting character is +. It looks free. It is not.

    Inside the processor there is a lump of circuitry called the arithmetic and logic unit, or ALU. It has two inputs, one output, and a control signal telling it which operation to perform. It cannot store anything. It cannot decide anything. Values go in, an answer comes out, and it forgets immediately.

    The addition itself is done with switches, column by column, exactly like the addition you do on paper — carry and all. Nobody taught the circuit what addition means. It is wired so that the output switches land in the right positions.

    The trick that makes decisions possible

    To compare two numbers, a machine subtracts them and looks at whether the answer is zero.

    That is the entire mechanism. "Are these equal?" becomes "is A minus B zero?" A processor has no equals-detector; it has a subtractor and a zero-detector. Every if you will ever write in Python eventually rests on this.

    Simplified model

    Our COMPARE will leave its answer in A. What this gets right: comparison is subtraction, and the decision is a zero test. What it leaves out: a real processor keeps a separate flags register whose bits record zero, negative, carry and overflow, so that comparing does not destroy your working value. The fuller version arrives in Volume IV when we read real machine code.

    Category: simplified teaching model, declared at the point of use.
    Stage 6
    Problem

    How does it know what comes next?

    The program counter

    So far you have typed each instruction yourself. The machine has to work out its own next move — and it must be able to do so with no cleverness whatsoever.

    The answer: keep the program in memory too, and keep one register holding the address of the next instruction. That register is the program counter.

    It is difficult now to see how radical this is, because every computer you have used works this way. But consider what it means: instructions and data occupy the same memory, in the same kind of boxes, distinguishable only by what the machine happens to do with them. A number can be executed. An instruction can be added to. Nothing in the hardware objects, because Chapter 0.1 established there is no tag saying which is which.

    That single decision is why a computer is general-purpose rather than a machine for one job. A program can be loaded like data, because it is data; it can be written by another program, transmitted, stored in a file. Chapter 0.5's keystone depends entirely on this — Python bytecode is data to the processor, inspected by CPython's instructions — and so does every compiler, interpreter and operating system in existence.

    This is the idea that made general-purpose computers possible: instructions live in memory, alongside data, and are just numbers. Change the numbers and you have a different program. You do not rewire anything.

    Our instructions are two boxes wide: an opcode saying what to do, then an operand saying what to do it to. Fixed width, always two, even when the operand is unused — because a machine that has to work out how wide each instruction is has to think, and we are trying very hard not to make it think.

    1 — LOAD n
    Copy the contents of box n into A
    2 — STORE n
    Copy A into box n
    3 — ADD n
    Add the contents of box n to A
    4 — SUB n
    Subtract the contents of box n from A
    5 — COMPARE n
    Subtract box n from A, leaving the answer in A. Zero means they were equal
    6 — JUMP n
    Set the program counter to n
    7 — JUMP_IF_ZERO n
    Set the program counter to n, but only if A is zero
    8 — PRINT
    Show the value in A. Operand ignored
    9 — HALT
    Stop. Operand ignored

    Now write the paper program from Chapter 0.2 as numbers. Boxes 30 and 31 hold the two values; the answer goes in box 32.

    New Python — making a long list quickly

    [0] * 40 builds a list of forty zeros. Multiplying a list by a whole number makes that many copies of its contents joined together. It saves typing forty zeros; it does nothing else clever.

    Stage 7
    Tool

    Holding the instruction still while you obey it

    The instruction register

    Here is a subtlety worth its own stage. The instruction is in memory. Carrying it out may involve reading other memory. So the machine first copies the instruction out of memory into its own register, where it will sit undisturbed, and only then acts on it.

    That register is the instruction register. Our version needs two parts, because our instructions have two parts:

    Stage 8
    Tool

    Working out which instruction this is

    The decoder

    The machine now holds the number 1 in its instruction register. It must do the LOAD thing rather than the ADD thing. Choosing between behaviours based on a value is called decoding, and in a real processor it is a lump of circuitry that turns an opcode into control signals — the wires that tell the ALU which operation to run and tell the registers when to accept a new value.

    New Python — asking a question and acting on the answer

    if runs a block of code only when something is true. elif means "otherwise, if this instead". else means "otherwise, in every remaining case". The lines belonging to each branch are indented by four spaces — in Python the indentation is not decoration, it is how the language knows which lines belong to which branch.

    == asks "are these equal?" and gives back True or False. One equals sign assigns; two equals signs ask. Confusing them is the most common typing mistake in programming, and Python will catch it for you.

    Stage 9
    Build

    Doing it forever

    The control unit

    Fetch, decode, execute. Then again. Then again. The control unit is the part that never stops driving that cycle — and "never stops" is meant literally. A powered processor is always in the middle of this loop. There is no idle state where it sits and waits for something interesting; when your computer looks idle, it is executing instructions whose job is to do nothing.

    New Python — repeating, and escaping

    while True: repeats the indented block forever. break jumps out of the loop immediately — it is how our HALT instruction will stop the machine.

    Stage 10
    Build

    The complete processor

    Every line already explained

    Here is the whole machine. Read it slowly and check the claim this chapter made at the start: there is nothing in it you have not been taught.

    Become the machine

    One trip round the loop

    First person

    Trace · the control unit's point of view, first instruction

    1. fetchMy PC says 0. I read box 0. It contains 1. I put that in my IR opcode.
    2. fetchI read box 1. It contains 30. That is my operand.
    3. fetchI set PC to 2. I do this now, before I know what the instruction is.
    4. decodeOpcode 1. I check my branches in order. The first matches. It is LOAD.
    5. executeLOAD means: read box 30, put it in A. Box 30 holds 6. A is now 6.
    6. loopNothing halted me. Back to the top. PC says 2. I have no memory of what I just did.
    Stage 11
    Break

    Six ways to destroy it

    Failure experiments

    You do not understand a machine until you have broken it on purpose. Do all six. Predict each outcome before running it, and write your prediction down.

    The failures are worth attempting rather than reading about, because each teaches something different about what the machine is not doing. An invalid opcode does not produce a helpful message: the decoder finds no matching case and whatever happens next was never designed. A jump into data executes numbers that were never meant as instructions, and they will be decoded as something, because every number is a valid pattern.

    The missing halt is the most instructive of all. Nothing stops the program counter walking off the end of your program into whatever follows, which the machine executes with exactly the same confidence it executed your instructions. There is no boundary, no marker, and no notion of "the end" — only a counter that keeps increasing. Chapter 0.4's address spaces exist largely to contain the consequences.

    1. Infinite loop. Change the PRINT instruction to memory[6] = 6; memory[7] = 0 — a JUMP back to address 0. Predict what happens, then run it and stop it with Ctrl+C. Nothing is wrong with the processor. It is obeying perfectly. That is the horror of it.
    2. Invalid opcode. Set memory[6] = 77. Which branch catches it? What would a real processor do? (Real answer: it raises an illegal-instruction fault and the operating system usually kills the program — you will meet that mechanism in Volume III.)
    3. Jump into data. Set memory[6] = 6; memory[7] = 30 so the machine jumps to address 30, where your data lives. Box 30 holds 6, so it will be decoded as a JUMP instruction. Trace by hand where it goes. This is not a hypothetical bug — it is the foundation of a whole family of real security attacks.
    4. Not enough registers. Write a program that adds three numbers, using only A. You will find you must keep storing partial results back to memory. Count the extra instructions. Now you know exactly why processors have sixteen registers and not one.
    5. Accidental overwrite. Change STORE's target to memory[5] = 4, so the program stores its answer into address 4 — part of the program itself. Predict, then run. It still prints 15, and that is the interesting part: the instruction at address 4 had already been fetched before it was overwritten. Now change it to memory[5] = 6 instead, so it overwrites the PRINT instruction that has not run yet. You get unknown opcode 15 at 6. You have just watched a program edit itself mid-flight, and discovered that fetching before executing decides whether it matters.
    6. No HALT. Delete the HALT instruction (set both boxes to 0). Opcode 0 is not in the table. Which branch fires? Explain why a machine that ran off the end of its program would otherwise keep executing whatever numbers happened to be lying in memory next.
    What all six have in common

    In every case the processor did exactly what it was told, at full speed, without hesitation. There is no sense in which it "went wrong". A processor cannot go wrong in that way; it can only be wrong-instructed. Every bug you ever write will be an instance of this.

    Stage 12
    Rebuild

    What you have really built

    The bridge to CPython

    Now for the part that rearranges your head.

    Your toy processor executes toy instructions: 1 means LOAD, 3 means ADD. Those numbers mean something only because your if/elif chain gives them meaning.

    But your toy processor is a Python program. So something must be executing it. That something is CPython — a large program written in C, compiled into real machine instructions for your actual processor.

    And CPython works exactly like your toy. It holds a list of Python bytecode instructions. It has a counter saying which one is next. It fetches, decodes and executes them in a loop, and it decides what each one means with a large branch on the opcode number.

    Which leaves the real processor at the bottom, executing CPython's native instructions, and knowing nothing whatsoever about Python.

    The keystone, now earned

    The physical CPU does not understand or directly execute Python bytecode. It executes CPython's native machine instructions. Those instructions make the CPython runtime inspect Python bytecode and perform the requested work.

    You have just written the small version of CPython's evaluation loop. Your opcodes are data to Python, exactly as Python's opcodes are data to the real processor. Three floors of the same trick, stacked.

    Ladder · running your toy CPUall three machines at once

    1. Human intention — add two numbers with a machine you built
    2. Python source text — toy_cpu.py
    3. Tokens
    4. Syntax tree
    5. Compiler
    6. Code object and bytecode — your loop, as data
    7. CPython runtime — fetching and decoding that bytecode
    8. Native machine instructions — CPython's own code
    9. CPU control logic — the real fetch–decode–execute
    10. Registers and ALU
    11. Caches and RAM — where your memory list actually lives
    12. Operating-system services
    13. Device, file, terminal, result — the 15 on your screen

    Floor 12 is dark for the arithmetic but would light up for the print — putting characters on a terminal is the one thing in this program the process cannot do by itself. Volume III is about that single fact.

    CPython

    How close is the toy to the real thing? Genuinely close in shape, and much simpler in detail. CPython's evaluation loop lives in Python/ceval.c and is a computed-goto dispatch over well over a hundred opcodes, with a stack of values rather than a single accumulator, plus a specialising mechanism that rewrites hot instructions into faster variants at runtime. But the skeleton — fetch the next opcode, decode it, do the thing, advance the counter — is what you just wrote.

    Category: CPython implementation detail, version-sensitive. Specialisation was introduced in 3.11 and has changed in every release since.
    Level 3 Why a stack instead of an accumulator?

    Your toy has one working register, so a + b * c would need careful ordering and several trips to memory. CPython instead keeps a stack of values: LOAD b, LOAD c, MULTIPLY (pops two, pushes one), LOAD a, ADD. Nested expressions of any depth work with no register allocation at all, which matters enormously for a compiler that must handle arbitrary source code.

    Real processors went the other way: registers, with a compiler that works hard to allocate them. Stack machines are easy to compile for and slower to run; register machines are the reverse. CPython chose easy-to-compile because the interpreter overhead dominates anyway.

    You build the stack version yourself in Volume IV.

    Retrieval lock

    Reconstruct it without looking

    Close the book

    1. Redraw. From memory, draw the processor: the box for the CPU, three registers inside it labelled, the ALU, and RAM outside. Add arrows for fetch and for store.
    2. Explain. Say out loud, in order, what happens in one trip round the fetch–decode–execute cycle. Include when the program counter changes and why it changes then.
    3. Modify. Write a toy program that counts down from 5 to 0, printing each number. You will need JUMP_IF_ZERO, SUB and a box holding the constant 1. Predict its output, then run it.
    4. Transfer. Explain to someone else why a processor cannot tell the difference between your program and your data, using the jump-into-data experiment as your example.
    5. Stretch. Add a tenth instruction, 10 — JUMP_IF_NEGATIVE. Where does it go in the chain? What does it need from the ALU that our COMPARE currently throws away?
    Mastery gate — Chapter 0.3 and Volume 0 so far
    • You can name the three registers in the toy machine and say what each holds.
    • You can describe the fetch–decode–execute cycle from memory, including when the program counter advances.
    • You can explain how a machine makes a decision using only subtraction and a zero test.
    • You can explain why instructions and data are indistinguishable in memory, and give one consequence.
    • You can write a short toy program with a loop in it, predict its output, and be right.
    • You can state the keystone sentence in your own words without looking at it.

    The last one is the gate for the whole of Volume 0. If you cannot say it in your own words, reread Stage 12 and Figure F.1 together — everything in Volume I assumes it.

    Back · Chapter 0.2The wall of boxes Next · Volume I pilotNaming things
    Volume 0 · Chapter 4How a computer obeys

    The room the program lives in

    Processes, address spaces, the privilege boundary, system calls, scheduling and virtual memory

    Your toy processor owned the whole machine. Real programs do not. Every program you run is locked in a room, believing it owns everything, while a much more powerful program quietly decides what it may touch and when it may move.

    Prerequisites

    Chapter 0.2 (addresses and contents) and Chapter 0.3 (the fetch–decode–execute cycle). This chapter is where floor 12 of the ladder — the operating system — stops being a dark row and becomes the subject.

    Unit 0.4.1
    Problem

    Two programs, one processor

    Something you can feel

    Right now your machine is running a browser, a music player, a clock and about two hundred other things. Your processor has perhaps eight cores. The arithmetic does not work.

    Worse. Your toy CPU used address 30 for its data. So does every other program ever written — address 30 is a perfectly ordinary address. If your game writes to address 30 and your browser writes to address 30, one of them destroys the other's data.

    And worse again. Nothing in Chapter 0.3 stopped a program from writing anywhere. Your toy processor would happily store into address 4 — its own instructions. What stops a program storing into another program's instructions? Or into the code that checks your password?

    The three problems this chapter solves

    Sharing one processor. Stopping programs from standing on each other's memory. Stopping programs from doing whatever they like.

    All three are solved by the same thing: one program with special powers, which is always in charge. It is called the operating system — Windows, Linux, macOS, Android.

    Notice that the three problems are not really three. Each is a case of one program being able to reach something that belongs to another, and each is solved not by asking programs to behave but by making the reaching impossible. That distinction matters: a rule that programs must respect can be broken by a mistake, whereas an arrangement in which the addresses simply do not lead anywhere cannot be broken at all.

    Unit 0.4.2
    Tool

    Every program gets its own room

    The process

    When you start a program, the operating system creates a process: a running program plus everything it owns. The most important thing it owns is its address space — its private wall of numbered boxes.

    Here is the trick that makes it all work, and it is genuinely startling the first time:

    OS-dependentHardware example

    Every process sees address 0. They are not the same address 0. Each process gets its own numbering that starts at zero and runs to the top. Two processes can both hold a value at "address 30" and never collide, because those two addresses are translated to completely different physical locations in the actual RAM chips.

    This requires hardware help: a unit inside the processor called the memory management unit performs the translation on every single memory access. Windows, Linux and macOS all use it; the details of how they lay out the space differ.

    It is worth seeing why this must be hardware rather than software. The translation happens on every memory access — every instruction fetched, every value loaded or stored — which is several times per instruction, billions of times a second. Anything performing that in software would be slower than the memory it was protecting. Only dedicated circuitry can do it in the time available, which is why memory protection is a property of processors rather than a feature an operating system could simply provide.

    Category: operating-system dependent, with hardware support. Layout differs per OS and per architecture.

    The room is not one undivided space. It has four regions, and knowing them explains a great deal of Python behaviour later.

    New Python — asking the operating system who you are

    import os loads a toolbox of operating-system functions. os.getpid() asks for this process's identity number. Every running process on your machine has one, and the operating system uses it to keep them apart.

    Unit 0.4.3
    Problem

    Who stops a program misbehaving?

    The privilege boundary

    Locking each program in a room raises an obvious question: who built the rooms, and what stops a program simply walking out?

    The question is sharper than it first appears. If a program cannot reach outside its own room, it cannot reach the screen either — the screen is not in its room. Nor the keyboard, nor a file, nor a network. The isolation that protects everything from your program also cuts your program off from everything, and a program that cannot affect anything outside itself is of no use whatever.

    So the arrangement needs one carefully controlled exception: a way for a program to ask for something it cannot do itself. Everything in the rest of this chapter is that exception and its consequences, and the reason it is designed so elaborately is that it is the single point at which the isolation is deliberately crossed.

    The answer is built into the processor itself. It runs in one of two modes.

    User mode

    Where your program lives

    Ordinary instructions work. Anything that could affect other programs or the hardware directly is forbidden. Your Python always runs here.

    Kernel mode

    Where the operating system lives

    Every instruction is permitted. Memory mappings, devices, the timer, other processes — all reachable.

    The processor knows which mode it is in and checks every instruction against it. A user-mode program that attempts a privileged instruction does not succeed and then get told off — the instruction fails at the hardware level, and control jumps to the operating system.

    The core of the kernel is just a program. What makes it powerful is not clever code; it is that the processor is running it in kernel mode.

    Unit 0.4.4
    Tool

    Asking for something you do not own

    The system call

    Your program cannot touch the screen. It cannot open a file. It cannot send a packet. All of those are hardware, and hardware belongs to the kernel.

    So it asks. A system call is a program deliberately handing control to the kernel and saying: please do this on my behalf. It is the only door out of the room, and it is guarded.

    OS-dependent

    The same Python, different doors. When your Python writes to the screen, on Linux the call is named write; on Windows the path runs through the Win32 API to WriteFile and the console subsystem. Your Python source is identical. Everything below floor 12 differs.

    This is exactly why print is not a simple operation, and why writing a million lines one at a time is dramatically slower than writing them in one block. You are paying for a million door-crossings instead of one.

    Category: operating-system dependent. Volume III covers buffering, which exists entirely to reduce these crossings.
    Unit 0.4.5
    Descend

    How two hundred programs share eight cores

    Scheduling

    They do not run at the same time. They take turns, extremely fast.

    The illusion is worth appreciating rather than merely noting, because it is one of the more audacious tricks in the machine. Each program is written as though it owns the processor and runs continuously; in reality it is stopped thousands of times a second, has its entire state put aside, and is later restored so precisely that it cannot tell. Nothing in a program can detect that it was interrupted, because everything it could examine — its registers, its memory, its program counter — is put back exactly as it was.

    That is why the same mechanism serves two quite different purposes at once. It lets more programs run than there are processors, which is the obvious use, and it lets a program that is merely waiting cost nothing, since the kernel simply does not schedule it. Chapter III.6 depends on the second of those and Chapter III.7 builds an entire model of concurrency on it.

    The kernel lets a process run for a few milliseconds, then a hardware timer fires, control jumps to the kernel, and the kernel may hand the processor to somebody else. Choosing who goes next is scheduling. Swapping one process out and another in is a context switch.

    A context switch means saving every register — including the program counter, so the process can be resumed on precisely the instruction it was about to run — and loading somebody else's saved registers instead. The paused process notices nothing. It has no way to notice. Its next instruction simply happens later than it expected.

    The illusion, named

    "Running at the same time" almost always means "taking turns so fast you cannot see the joins".

    With eight cores, eight processes really do run simultaneously. The other two hundred are interleaved. When you meet threads and async in Volume III, this is the distinction that will keep you sane.

    Unit 0.4.6
    Break

    Two programs, one address, no collision

    Deliberate puzzle

    Predict — think before reading on

    Two Python processes are running. Each stores a value at what it calls address 30,000. Neither crashes and neither sees the other's value. But there is only one set of RAM chips in the machine. Where did the second value actually go?

    Descend

    The addresses were never real

    Virtual memory

    The addresses your program uses are virtual addresses. They are not positions in the RAM chips. They are positions in an imaginary wall of boxes that exists only for this process.

    The operating system keeps a table for each process saying which imaginary regions map to which real ones. The processor consults that mapping on every access. Process one's address 30,000 might land at real location 4,182,016; process two's might land at 9,771,264. Neither program can tell, and neither can reach the other's, because there is no entry in its table that leads there.

    Hardware exampleSimplified model

    The mapping is not per byte — that would need a table bigger than the memory it describes. It works in blocks called pages, commonly 4,096 bytes on x86-64. What this model gets right: addresses are translated, per process, by hardware. What it leaves out: multi-level page tables, the translation cache, page faults, and swapping to disk. The fuller version is Volume III.

    Category: hardware example. Page size and table structure are architecture-specific.
    What this buys you

    Three things at once, from one mechanism. Programs cannot corrupt each other. Programs cannot read each other's secrets. And a program can be given a tidy address space that starts at zero even though the real memory it ends up using is scattered in fragments all over the chips.

    Become the machine

    Being interrupted

    First person

    Trace · a process being switched out mid-loop

    1. meI am adding numbers. My program counter says 4,120. My accumulator holds 71. I expect to continue.
    2. hardwareA timer fires. I am not asked. Control leaves me instantly, between two instructions.
    3. kernelThe kernel saves every one of my registers — including the program counter — into its record of me.
    4. kernelIt loads another process's saved registers and switches the memory mapping to that process's table.
    5. elsewhereSomebody else runs for a few milliseconds. I do not exist as far as the processor is concerned.
    6. kernelMy turn again. My registers are restored exactly. Program counter 4,120. Accumulator 71.
    7. meI add the next number. I have no idea any of that happened. I cannot have any idea.
