    Volume 0 · Chapter 5How a computer obeys

    Where Python fits

    python.exe as an ordinary process, source text becoming bytecode, and the sentence the rest of this book rests on

    You have built a processor and you have seen the room a program lives in. Now the two halves of this book meet. We put Python itself into the picture, and the answer to the innocent question "what kind of thing is Python?" turns out to reorganise everything you thought you knew about running a program.

    Prerequisites

    All of Volume 0 so far: bits and bytes from Chapter 0.1, addresses and memory from 0.2, the fetch–decode–execute loop you built by hand in 0.3, and processes, the kernel boundary and system calls from 0.4. This chapter uses every one of them, which is why it comes last.

    Unit 0.5.1
    Problem

    What kind of thing is Python?

    A question that sounds simple

    Ask most people what Python is and they will say "a programming language". That is true, and it is not the answer you need, because it does not tell you what is on your computer or what happens when you use it.

    Try a different question, which has a sharper answer. When you type python and press Enter, what runs? Something must. Chapter 0.4 established that a program is a process, and a process is created from something that exists on a disk. So there is a file somewhere. What is in it?

    The confusion is worth taking seriously rather than clearing up in a sentence, because the same word is doing three different jobs and mixing them up causes real muddles later.

    Python, the language
    A set of rules about what programs mean. Rules are not a thing you can run. They are written down in a document, and they exist in the same way the rules of chess exist
    CPython, the program
    An actual file on your disk — about eight megabytes of it on the machine these words were checked on — that knows those rules and can carry them out. This is what runs
    Your program
    The text you wrote. Also not a thing that runs. It is something CPython reads

    The middle one is the surprise, and this whole chapter is about taking it seriously. There is a program on your machine called CPython. It was written by people, mostly in a language called C, and then turned into machine instructions of the kind Chapter 0.3 described. It is the thing your processor actually executes.

    Other programs that know Python's rules exist, and they are different programs. That is why this book keeps saying "CPython" where it might have said "Python" — not pedantry, but the difference between a rule and a thing that obeys the rule.

    Unit 0.5.2
    Tool

    An entirely ordinary program

    CPython has no special powers

    Here is the claim, and then the reasons to believe it. CPython is an ordinary program. Every single thing Chapter 0.4 said about processes applies to it, unchanged and without exception.

    It runs in user mode. It cannot touch the screen, or a file, or the network, without asking the kernel — which is why print will turn out to be so much more expensive than arithmetic. It gets an address space of its own, with the four regions of Figure 0.4.1. Its addresses are virtual and translated by hardware. It can be interrupted by the timer at any moment and have the processor taken away, and it cannot tell that this happened. It has a process identity number, like everything else.

    None of that is special treatment. Your game, your browser and your calculator are in exactly the same position, and if you ran two Pythons at once they would be two entirely separate processes that share nothing — which is the experiment Chapter 0.4 had you perform with two terminals.

    The reframe

    Python is a language. CPython is a program that reads that language. Your program is data that CPython reads.

    Read that last part again, because it is the one that does the work. Your program is data. The processor is running CPython; it is not running your program. Your program is the thing CPython is looking at — exactly as, in Chapter 0.3, your processor was running and the toy program was the numbers it was looking at.

    Unit 0.5.3
    Become the machine

    What happens when you type python

    Start to finish

    Follow it through, using everything Chapter 0.4 built. Nothing here is new machinery; it is the old machinery doing a new job.

    Trace · from keystroke to prompt

    1. shellYou type python and press Enter. The shell is itself a process, waiting for you. It searches a list of folders for a file with that name.
    2. syscallThe shell asks the kernel to create a new process. Floor 12 — the shell cannot make a process by itself, because processes are the kernel's business.
    3. kernelThe kernel builds a fresh address space, arranges for CPython's machine instructions to be available in its code region, and sets the program counter to the first one.
    4. cpythonCPython starts, and does a surprising amount before you see anything. It builds its type system, its built-in names, its module table. On the machine these words were checked on, forty-five modules are already loaded before your first line runs.
    5. cpythonOnly then does it print >>> and wait.
    6. youYou type 2 + 2. Those five characters are read from the terminal — another floor-12 crossing, because the keyboard is not yours either.
    7. cpythonCPython turns that text into something it can act on, acts on it, and prints 4 — one more crossing, to reach the screen.
    8. loopBack to the prompt. Read, act, print, repeat: a fetch–decode–execute cycle with a human being in the fetch stage.

    Step four explains something you may have noticed and put down to your computer being slow. A tiny Python program takes a surprisingly long time to start — a good fraction of a second — and almost none of that is your program. It is forty-five modules being located on disk, read, and executed, before anything of yours happens at all. Chapter 0.4's point about the cost of crossing to the kernel, arriving in the least expected place: starting up is expensive because starting up is mostly file access.

    Unit 0.5.4
    Descend

    Why text cannot simply be obeyed

    The four stages, and the reason for each

    Step seven of that trace hid the interesting part. What does it mean to "turn text into something it can act on"?

    Start with why the text will not do as it stands. Chapter 0.3's processor obeyed a list of numbers, one after another, where each number meant an operation. The text x = 2 + 3 is not a list of operations. It is nine characters, and characters are not operations — there is no character that means "add". Worse, the operations you would want are not in the order they must happen: the addition must happen before the assignment, but the = comes first in the text.

    So something must convert. CPython does it in four steps, and each step exists because it solves one problem and hands on something simpler to the next.

    Stage one, the tokenizer, answers a question about characters: which of them belong together? It decides that x is one name rather than one letter, that a space separates things without being a thing, and hands on a list of meaningful units instead of a list of characters. After this stage nothing ever has to look at a character again.

    Stage two, the parser, answers a question about arrangement: what belongs to what? The tokens are still in a straight line, and a straight line cannot say that the addition happens before the assignment. So the parser builds a shape — the tree in the figure — in which one thing being inside another means it must happen first. The Add sits inside the Assign, which is the whole of "work out the sum before storing it".

    Stage three, the compiler, answers a question about order: the processor needs a straight line again, but this time in the order things must be done rather than the order they were typed. So it walks the tree and flattens it, deepest parts first. And it takes the opportunity to notice things it can settle in advance.

    Stage four is the result: a short flat list of simple instructions called bytecode, which looks a great deal like the toy machine code you wrote in Chapter 0.3, because it is the same kind of thing for the same reason.

    New Python — looking at the bytecode

    import dis loads a tool called the disassembler, whose job is to show bytecode in a readable form. dis.dis("x = 2 + 3") shows the bytecode for that source. You are not expected to write bytecode or to memorise any of it. You are expected to see that it exists, that it is short, and that it is flat.

    Look at what the constant is. It is 5. Not 2, not 3, and there is no addition instruction anywhere. The compiler noticed that 2 + 3 contains nothing that could change while the program runs, worked it out at stage three, and stored the answer. Your program, when it runs, does no arithmetic at all — it loads a five and stores it.

    This is called constant folding, and it is worth pausing on because it is the first evidence you have seen that the four stages are not merely translating. They are reasoning about your program. Compare a version where the compiler cannot know the answer:

    CPython

    None of these four stages is required by the Python language. The language says what programs mean, not how an implementation should get there. Tokens, syntax trees, bytecode, and the .pyc files in which CPython caches its bytecode so it need not recompile unchanged files, are all CPython's chosen route. Another implementation may translate straight to machine instructions, and some do.

    The instruction names above are CPython's too, and they change between versions — BINARY_OP replaced a family of separate instructions in 3.11. Run dis on your own Python rather than trusting a printed listing, including this one.

    Category: CPython implementation. The bytecode format is explicitly unstable between releases.
    Unit 0.5.5
    Rebuild

    You have already written this

    Side by side

    Something must now read that bytecode and act on it. Here is CPython's loop for doing so, beside the one you wrote in Chapter 0.3.

    The differences are worth naming, because knowing which are superficial is as useful as knowing what is shared. CPython has more opcodes, so more can be done per instruction. It uses a stack rather than a single accumulator, because a single accumulator cannot hold the several partial results a nested expression needs. And it is written in C, so it is compiled to machine instructions rather than being interpreted itself.

    That last difference is the important one, and it produces the strange and beautiful arrangement this chapter exists to explain.

    Three interpreters, stacked

    Your toy program was data to your toy CPU. Your toy CPU was a Python program, which is data to CPython. CPython is machine instructions, which the processor executes. Only the bottom layer is ever really run.

    Every layer above the bottom is a program pretending to be a machine, by looking at numbers and deciding what they mean.

    Unit 0.5.6
    Rebuild

    The keystone, and three ways of getting it wrong

    The sentence the rest of this book rests on

    Everything in this chapter can be compressed into one sentence, and it is worth learning properly because the rest of the book leans on it constantly.

    The keystone

    The physical CPU does not understand or directly execute Python bytecode. It executes CPython's native machine instructions. Those instructions make the CPython runtime inspect Python bytecode and perform the requested work.

    Three natural misunderstandings cluster around it, and each is worth meeting now rather than carrying.

    "The CPU runs my Python." It does not, and the reason is not a technicality. The processor's instruction set is fixed in silicon; it was designed years before your program existed and it contains no instruction that means LOAD_CONST. Nothing anywhere converts your bytecode into machine instructions. What happens instead is that CPython's machine instructions — which the processor does execute — look at your bytecode as data, one number at a time, and do whatever each number calls for. The relationship between your program and the processor is the relationship between a recipe and a cook, not between a key and a lock.

    "Python is interpreted, not compiled." This sounds like a fact and is really a muddle, because both words are being used loosely. Python is compiled: stages one to three are a compiler, and they produce bytecode. What Python does not do is compile all the way down to machine instructions. So the honest description is that Python is compiled to bytecode and the bytecode is interpreted — and the same is true of several languages usually described as compiled. "Interpreted" and "compiled" are not two kinds of language; they are two things an implementation can do, and most real implementations do some of each.

    "Bytecode is machine code for a pretend machine." This one is nearly right, which makes it the most useful to sharpen. Bytecode is indeed a set of instructions for a machine that does not physically exist, and Chapter 0.3's toy processor is the same idea. The thing to keep hold of is that the pretend machine is made of a program. There is no hardware anywhere that is waiting for bytecode. The "machine" is a loop, in C, doing exactly what the loop you wrote in Chapter 0.3 was doing — and if that loop stopped, the bytecode would be inert numbers again.

    Unit 0.5.7
    Assemble

    The whole ladder, one statement

    All thirteen floors

    You now have every floor. Here is print(2 + 3), top to bottom, with nothing skipped and nothing waved at.

    Ladder · print(2 + 3)the complete walk

    1. Human intention — show me the answer
    2. Python source text — thirteen characters
    3. Tokens — NAME, bracket, number, plus, number, bracket

    Thirteen floors lit at once, which is rare. Most statements light far fewer — and from here on, the interesting question in every chapter is which floors this one does not need. That question is the whole method of the rest of the book, so it is worth noticing that you now have a way of asking it precisely.

    One thing that ladder makes visible deserves saying plainly. The arithmetic — the actual adding of 2 and 3 — does not appear on it, because the compiler did it at floor 5 and nothing at run time added anything. Meanwhile floor 12, which exists only because the screen belongs to the kernel, will turn out to cost roughly a thousand times what an addition costs. The expensive part of that line is not the sum. It is the speaking.

    • You can distinguish the language, the implementation and your program, and say which of them runs.
    • You can explain that CPython is an ordinary user-mode program, and name three consequences from Chapter 0.4.
    • You can name the four stages from source text to bytecode and say what problem each one solves.
    • You can say which of those stages are CPython's choice rather than the language's requirement.
    • You can identify constant folding in a disassembly and explain why it is possible.

    This is the gate for the entire volume, and every chapter of Volume I assumes all eight. If any is shaky, the return path is: items 1–2 → Units 0.5.1 and 0.5.2; items 3–5 → Unit 0.5.4 with Figure 0.5.2 open; item 6 → Unit 0.5.5 beside Chapter 0.3 Stage 10; items 7–8 → this chapter's ladder and Unit 0.5.6.

    What Volume 0 was for

    You have built a processor from nothing, learned what a program is to an operating system, and placed Python inside that picture. From here, every Python idea in this book arrives with a place to stand: a name is a thing in memory, a loop is a jump, an error is a search through frames, and a print is a request to somebody with more privileges than you.

    That is the point of having done it in this order. Volume I could have started on page one, and you would have learned the same syntax with nowhere to put it.

    Back · Chapter 0.4The room the program lives in Next · Volume IThe conversation
    Volume I · Chapter 1Python foundations

    The conversation

    The interactive prompt, expressions versus statements, and why showing you an answer is the most expensive thing on the page

    Volume 0 built a machine and put Python inside it. Now you talk to it. The interactive prompt is the friendliest thing in this book and it is also, once you look, a small demonstration of everything Volume 0 established — a compiler running on every line you type, and a system call for every character you see.

    Prerequisites

    All of Volume 0, and Chapter 0.5 in particular: that CPython is an ordinary program, that your source is data to it, and that the screen belongs to the kernel. This chapter uses all three within its first two pages.

    Unit I.1.1
    Problem

    How do you talk to something that cannot listen?

    Something you can feel

    A processor does not take questions. Chapter 0.3 built one, and its entire behaviour was: fetch, decode, execute, repeat. There is no step in that loop where somebody types something.

    Yet you can type 2 + 2 and get 4. Something is bridging the gap, and knowing what it is prevents a misconception that otherwise persists for years — that the prompt is somehow a simpler or more direct route to the machine than a program is.

    It is the opposite. The prompt is a program — CPython — running the loop from Chapter 0.5's trace: read a line, compile it, run it, show the result, wait for the next. Everything Volume 0 described happens on every line you type, including all four stages of Figure 0.5.2. Your line is tokenized, parsed into a tree, compiled into bytecode, and executed by the evaluation loop, and then the whole apparatus goes back to waiting. The prompt is not less machinery than a script; it is the same machinery, invoked one line at a time.

    Seeing it that way settles a question people otherwise carry for a long time: why code that works at the prompt sometimes behaves differently in a file. The answer is that the prompt is not a neutral window onto Python. It is a program with its own behaviour, and two of its conveniences — displaying values automatically, and keeping every name you have defined available — are things a script does not do. Both are helpful and both mean the prompt is a slightly different environment rather than a smaller one.

    There is also a genuine difference in what gets compiled. A script is compiled once, in its entirety, before any of it runs; the prompt compiles each line as it arrives, which is why a syntax error on line ten of a file prevents line one from running, and a syntax error at the prompt affects only the line you just typed. That is not a rule to memorise separately — it follows from when compilation happens, which follows from Figure 0.5.2.

    New Python — the prompt

    Typing python at a terminal starts the interactive interpreter, which shows >>> and waits. This is also called the REPL: read, evaluate, print, loop. Everything in Volume I can be tried there, and should be.

    Unit I.1.2
    Descend

    Two kinds of line

    A distinction the prompt hides

    Type two things and watch the difference in what comes back.

    This is the difference between an expression, which has a value, and a statement, which performs an action. 2 + 2 is an expression: it means 4, and could be substituted anywhere a 4 could appear — inside a larger sum, as an argument, as an item in a list. x = 2 + 2 is a statement: it binds a name, and is not itself worth anything, so there is nowhere it could be substituted.

    The test worth carrying is whether the thing could sensibly be put inside brackets and used. (2 + 2) * 3 is fine because the bracketed part has a value. (x = 2) * 3 is meaningless, because assignment produces nothing to multiply. Every construct in Python is one or the other, and knowing which is what tells you where it may appear.

    The distinction is not merely terminological, because Python enforces it in the grammar rather than treating it as a convention. That is a design decision with consequences in both directions, and it is worth seeing both.

    Python enforces the distinction rather than blurring it, and the enforcement is visible.

    The cost of that strictness is real and worth acknowledging. Languages permitting assignment inside expressions can write compact things Python cannot, such as reading a value and testing it in a single condition — which is common enough that Python eventually added a separate operator for exactly that case, deliberately spelled differently so it cannot be typed by accident. The benefit is that one entire family of bugs, in which = is written where == was meant and the program compiles and runs and is quietly wrong, does not exist in Python at all. Given how often that bug is written, the trade looks favourable; but it is a trade, and pretending otherwise would misrepresent the design.

    The prompt hides the distinction by showing you the value of anything that has one, which is convenient and slightly misleading. In a script, an expression on a line by itself computes its value and throws it away, so 2 + 2 in a file does nothing whatsoever. That is not the compiler being clever; it is the ordinary meaning of an expression statement. What is clever is that the compiler notices there was nothing to do and emits nothing at all.

    Unit I.1.3
    Tool

    Saying something out loud

    print, and what it costs

    Since a script shows nothing by itself, a program that wants to communicate must say so.

    Now the part that matters, and that Chapter 0.5's ladder set up. Printing crosses to floor 12: the terminal belongs to the kernel, so showing a character requires a system call, and Chapter 0.4 established that crossing that boundary is expensive.

    It is worth being precise about how expensive, because the usual telling overstates it and the true picture is more interesting.

    Two different comparisons, often confused

    Measured against a hardware addition, which takes well under a nanosecond, a system call really is on the order of a thousand times more expensive. Measured against a Python addition, which takes tens of nanoseconds because it is interpreted, the same system call is only a few times more expensive.

    Both are true. The first is a fact about processors and the second is a fact about interpreters, and which one applies depends on what you are comparing. Chapter II.8 finds the same thing from the other direction: in Python, the dominant cost is usually interpretation rather than the operation being performed.

    The reason printing costs more than the system call underneath it deserves unpacking, because it is a pattern that recurs throughout the book. print must convert each argument to text, which for a number means generating digits; it must join the arguments with separators; it must append a line ending; and it must place the result in a buffer, checking whether that buffer is now full. All of that is work done in compiled C on your behalf, and all of it happens before any question of the kernel arises. The system call is the last and smallest step.

    The practical consequence survives either comparison: a print inside a loop running a hundred thousand times will dominate whatever the loop computes, not because printing is badly built but because it is doing far more than the arithmetic beside it. The remedy is the one Chapter II.13 will generalise — do less of the expensive thing rather than making it faster. Collecting results and printing once at the end changes the number of expensive operations from a hundred thousand to one, which no amount of optimising a single print could achieve.

    Chapter III.2 explains the buffering that keeps it as cheap as it is, and it is worth knowing now that the buffering is why the measured cost is seventeen times rather than hundreds: many print calls share one crossing to the kernel. Turn the buffering off and the picture changes considerably.

    Unit I.1.4
    Break

    Two characters that change everything

    Deliberate failure — quotation marks

    Predict

    What is the difference between 2 + 2 and '2 + 2'?

    The reason the quotes are so decisive is that they act at the very first stage of Figure 0.5.2. The tokenizer — which Chapter IV.1 builds — treats an opening quote as a signal to stop looking for meaning and to swallow everything up to the closing quote as one unit. The + inside never becomes an operator token, because it never becomes a token at all.

    So the arithmetic is not merely skipped. It was never seen. By the time any part of Python could have added anything, the characters had already been sealed into a single value, and no later stage has any way to notice what they spell. This is why you cannot persuade Python to evaluate a quoted sum by asking politely elsewhere in the program: the decision was made at stage one, and stages two through four receive a value with no internal structure to examine.

    It also explains something that will matter throughout Volume I. Quotation marks are not a way of labelling something as text; they are a way of preventing it from being read as code. The difference shows up whenever the two are confused — a number in quotes is not a number that has been marked as text, it is a piece of text that happens to contain a digit, and Chapter I.2 will show that adding it to another number fails rather than converting.

    One detail in that transcript is deliberately unexplained and worth flagging so you can watch for it: the prompt showed '2 + 2' with quotes, while print showed it without. That is two different ways of displaying a value — one meant for you to read, one meant to be unambiguous about what the value is. Chapter I.9 explains why both exist and when each is used.

    Ladder · print(2 + 2) at the promptevery floor, for one short line

    1. Human intention — show me the answer
    2. Python source text — the characters you typed
    3. Tokens — where the quotes would have acted
    4. Syntax tree — a call wrapping an addition
    5. Compiler — folds 2 + 2 to 4 before the program runs
    6. Code object and bytecode — load print, load 4, call
    7. CPython runtime — formats the value and fills a buffer
    8. Native machine instructions
    9. CPU control logic
    10. Registers and ALU — barely used: the sum was done at floor 5
    11. Caches and RAM
    12. Operating-system services — a write call, because the terminal is not yours
    13. Device, file, terminal, result — a 4 appears

    Thirteen floors for four characters of arithmetic, and the arithmetic is the one thing that does not happen at run time. This is the shape of nearly every line in this book: a small amount of computing surrounded by a large amount of arranging, and the interesting question in each chapter is which floors a given statement actually needs.

    Retrieval lock

    Close the book

    1. Explain. Why is the prompt not a more direct route to the machine than a script? Say what happens to every line you type.
    2. Explain. Distinguish an expression from a statement, and give one of each. Then say what a script does with a bare expression.
    3. Modify. Try x = (y = 3) and read the error. Then explain what class of bug Python's refusal prevents.
    4. Redraw. Draw what happens to '2 + 2' at stage one of Figure 0.5.2, and say why no later stage can recover the arithmetic.
    5. Explain. Give both comparisons for the cost of printing — against a hardware addition and against a Python one — and say why they differ so much.
    6. Transfer. A friend's program prints a status line inside a loop running a hundred thousand times and is slow. Explain which floors are responsible and suggest a change that does not alter what the loop computes.
    7. Stretch. Compile 2 + 2 both ways with dis and compare. Explain why one version contains no addition and the other contains a print instruction you never wrote.

    • You can tell an expression from a statement and predict which the prompt will display.
    • You can say why a bare expression in a script does nothing.
    • You can explain what quotation marks do, and at which stage they act.
    • You can say why print is expensive, and what most of the expense actually is.
    • You can distinguish the hardware comparison from the interpreted one.
    • You can walk print(2 + 2) down all thirteen floors.

    If item four is shaky, everything in Volume I about strings will be harder than it should be. The rule is worth over-learning: quotes act first, before anything can mean anything.

    Volume I · Chapter 2First contact

    Making values

    Types, objects, and the type tag that raw memory does not have

    In Chapter 0.1 you learned that memory cannot tell a letter from a number. In this chapter Python appears to do exactly that — and the way it manages the trick explains almost everything about how Python works.

    Prerequisites

    Chapter 0.1 (bits, bytes, interpretation), Chapter 0.2 (addresses), Chapter 0.5 (CPython as a program), Chapter I.1 (expressions). The central idea of this chapter is a direct contradiction of something you were taught in 0.1, and resolving it is the point.

    Unit I.2.1
    Problem

    The same plus sign does two different jobs

    Something you can feel

    Type 5 + 5 and Python says 10. Type '5' + '5' and Python says 55. Same operator. Completely different behaviour.

    Something decided. And since Chapter 0.1 told you that memory has no idea what it holds, the obvious question is: decided using what?

    Unit I.2.2
    Tool

    Four kinds of value you will use every day

    Types

    Every value in Python is of some type. The type is what says which behaviours a value has. Four cover almost everything at first.

    int
    A whole number: 5, -40, 1000000. No size limit, as you saw in Chapter 0.1
    float
    A number with a decimal point: 2.5, -0.001. Fast, and not exact — see Unit I.2.5
    str
    Text, in quotes: 'hello', '5'. Short for string, meaning a string of characters
    bool
    One of exactly two values: True or False. Capital letters, no quotes
    New Python — asking what something is

    type(x) hands back the type of a value. It is the single most useful debugging tool in the language, and you should reach for it every time Python surprises you.

    Unit I.2.3
    Descend

    Resolving the contradiction

    The type tag

    Chapter 0.1 was completely true: a raw byte in memory carries no information about what it means. That has not changed.

    What CPython does is build the tag itself. It never stores a bare number in memory. It stores an object: a small block containing the value and a pointer to the type, side by side.

    The resolution — hold both halves at once

    Memory still has no type tag. Python objects have one, because CPython puts it there and pays for it in bytes.

    This is not the language cheating physics. It is a program spending memory to buy knowledge — and it is exactly why sys.getsizeof(7) came out at twenty-eight bytes in the pilot chapter, for a value that needs three bits.

    The trade is worth naming, because it is the single decision from which most of Python's character follows. Carrying a type on every object costs memory — the pilot chapter measured a small integer at twenty-eight bytes, most of which is machinery — and costs time, since every operation must consult the tag before it can act. What it buys is that a value is self-describing: it can be passed anywhere, stored in any container, and asked what it is, without anybody having declared anything in advance.

    A language that puts the type in the source rather than in the object makes the opposite trade. It knows at compile time that a particular location holds an integer, so the addition it emits needs no tag and no lookup, and the value in memory can be four bare bytes. It is faster and smaller, and it requires you to tell it things Python works out for itself. Neither arrangement is the correct one; they are different answers to where the knowledge should live, and the rest of this book is largely about the consequences of Python's answer.

    Unit I.2.4
    Break

    Mixing them

    Deliberate failure

    Predict — write it down

    What does '5' + 5 do? Add them to get 10? Join them to get '55'? Something else?

    Descend

    Why the two messages differ

    Earned by the failure

    When CPython meets +, it follows the type pointer of the value on the left and asks that type: can you add this thing on the right?

    In '5' + 5, it asks str, which knows how to join text to text and refuses anything else — hence a message about concatenation. In 5 + '5', it asks int, which knows about numbers, and then gives the right-hand type a chance to answer too. Both decline, so the message is the more general one about unsupported operands.

    Python could have guessed. Some languages do: they would silently turn 5 into '5', join them, and hand you '55'. Python's designers decided that quietly guessing what you meant produces bugs you find months later, on a Friday. Refusing is a design decision, not a limitation.

    The word for the difference is worth having precisely. A language is strongly typed when it refuses operations whose meaning is not defined for the values involved, and weakly typed when it converts something to make the operation work. That is a separate question from whether types are checked before the program runs or while it runs, and the two get confused constantly. Python is strongly typed and checks at run time; some languages are weakly typed and check at compile time; every combination exists.

    Being strong about it is a deliberate cost. It means more errors, and it means those errors arrive while the program is running rather than before. What it buys is that when an operation does succeed, it meant something — whereas in a language that silently converts, '5' + 5 produces an answer that is either 10 or '55' depending on rules nobody remembers, and the program continues carrying that value into everything downstream.

    Python language

    Python is strongly typed and dynamically typed. Dynamically: a name can be bound to any type, and types are checked while the program runs, not before. Strongly: it will not silently convert one type into another to make an operation work. Both halves are language guarantees, not CPython behaviour.

    You convert explicitly when you want to: int('12') gives the number 12; str(12) gives the text '12'.

    Source: Python language reference, data model and binary arithmetic operations.

    Ladder · 5 + 5 against '5' + '5'where the two part company

    1. Human intention — combine these two things
    2. Python source text — identical but for two pairs of quotes
    3. Tokens — NUMBER, PLUS, NUMBER against STRING, PLUS, STRING
    4. Syntax tree — the same shape: an Add node either way
    5. Compiler — emits the same instruction either way
    6. Code object and bytecode — one BINARY_OP, not two different ones
    7. CPython runtime — here, and only here: follow the left value's type pointer and ask that type how to add
    8. Native machine instructions — int addition, or allocate-and-copy for text
    9. CPU control logic
    10. Registers and ALU — a real addition, or address arithmetic and byte copying
    11. Caches and RAM — the joined text needs a brand-new object; the sum may reuse a cached one
    12. Operating-system services
    13. Device, file, terminal, result

    Floors 1 to 6 are indistinguishable. The entire difference in behaviour is decided at floor 7, by following one pointer — which is exactly why the type tag has to be stored on the object rather than in the instruction.

    Unit I.2.5
    Break

    The one that shakes people

    Second deliberate failure

    Predict — be honest with yourself

    What is 0.1 + 0.2?

    Descend

    Chapter 0.1, collected with interest

    Binary fractions

    In Chapter 0.1 you built numbers from columns worth 8, 4, 2, 1. Fractions continue the same pattern to the right of the point: a half, a quarter, an eighth, a sixteenth.

    Now try to make one tenth from halves, quarters, eighths and sixteenths. You cannot. There is no combination that lands exactly on 0.1 — the way there is no combination of thirds that lands exactly on 0.1 in ordinary decimal, which is why one third is 0.3333 forever.

    So the machine stores the closest pattern it can. Add two "closest patterns" together and the tiny errors add up too, and occasionally they become visible.

    It is worth being exact about which numbers suffer, because "floats are inaccurate" leaves people unable to predict anything. A binary fraction can represent exactly those values expressible as a sum of halves, quarters, eighths and so on — so one half, three quarters and 0.375 are all stored perfectly, and arithmetic on them is exact. One tenth is not among them, for the same reason one third has no exact decimal expansion: the digits recur forever and must be cut off.

    So the trouble is not random and it is not everywhere. It appears exactly when a value that looks tidy in decimal is untidy in binary, which is most of the numbers people actually type — prices, percentages, measurements. That is why the effect feels arbitrary in practice while being entirely determined underneath, and why a program can handle 0.5 and 0.25 flawlessly for months and then be wrong about 0.1.

    Hardware examplePython language

    This lives below Python entirely. A Python float is a double-precision binary floating-point number as defined by the IEEE 754 standard, handled by dedicated circuitry in the processor. Java, C, JavaScript and your spreadsheet all give the same answer for 0.1 + 0.2 for the same reason.

    The practical rule, which you will use for the rest of your life: never compare floats with ==. Ask whether the difference is small enough instead. For money, use exact whole numbers of pennies, or the decimal module.

    Category: hardware standard (IEEE 754), surfaced through the language. Not a CPython choice.
    Level 4 Expert microscope — what those 28 bytes are doing

    In the pilot chapter you measured sys.getsizeof(7) as 28 bytes on a 64-bit build. Here is roughly where they go:

    8 bytes
    reference count — how many references point at this object
    8 bytes
    type pointer — the arrow in Figure I.2.1
    8 bytes
    size/sign field — how many digit-chunks, and whether negative
    4 bytes
    the digits themselves — one chunk is enough for 7

    Two-thirds of the object is machinery. That machinery is what buys you integers that never overflow, objects that can be shared safely, and a + that behaves differently for different types.

    CPythonHardware example

    Exact sizes are specific to CPython on a 64-bit build and have changed between versions. The breakdown above is the shape of the object, not a promise about its bytes. Measure on your own machine.

    Category: CPython on 64-bit. Verify with sys.getsizeof.

    Item three is the hinge of this chapter. If it is shaky, reread Unit I.2.3 with Figure 0.1.3 open beside it — the two figures are designed to be read together.

    Volume I · Chapter 3Gold-standard pilot

    Naming things

    Binding, references, object identity and the difference between rebinding a name and mutating an object

    This is the chapter where most people quietly acquire a wrong idea that costs them years. The wrong idea is comfortable, it works for a while, and then it produces a bug that looks like the computer lying to you. Let us not do that.

    Prerequisites — checked, not assumed

    You need Volume 0 in full: bytes, addresses, read versus write, and the fetch–decode–execute cycle. From Volume I you need Chapter 2, values and types. If the phrase "the address is where, the contents are what" does not feel obvious, go back to Chapter 0.2 first. This chapter leans on it constantly.

    Unit I.3.1
    Problem

    You worked it out and then it was gone

    Something you can feel

    Type 17 * 23 at the prompt. Python answers 391. Now use that answer in your next sum.

    You cannot. It has gone. Python computed it, showed it to you, and threw it away — because nothing was holding on to it.

    This is not Python being unhelpful. Look back at your toy processor: the value in A survived only until the next instruction overwrote it. Anything you want to keep, you must deliberately keep.

    Model

    A luggage label, not a box

    Before any syntax

    Picture a suitcase on an airport belt. You tie a paper label to the handle: SUITCASE FOR MADRID.

    Now — is the suitcase inside the label? Obviously not. The label is tied to the suitcase. Two things exist: a suitcase, and a label pointing at it. You can tie a second label to the same suitcase. You can untie a label and tie it to a different suitcase. None of that touches what is inside the suitcase.

    The idea to keep — the whole chapter is this

    In Python, a name is a label tied to an object. It is not a box holding a value.

    Everything surprising later in this chapter follows from taking that sentence completely literally.

    It is worth saying what the label model is for, since a reader who has never been confused by variables may wonder why a chapter is spent on it. It is not a more accurate way of describing something you already understand. It makes different predictions from the model most people arrive with, and the two disagree in exactly the cases that cause real defects — copying a list, passing one to a function, storing one in two places.

    So the test of the model is not whether it sounds reasonable but whether it predicts correctly, and this chapter is arranged to make you check. Each experiment below is one where the two models give different answers, which is the only kind of experiment worth doing: Chapter II.2 makes the same argument about tests, and Chapter II.3 about debugging.

    Unit I.3.2
    Tool

    The smallest possible Python

    One line

    The = is called assignment, and the more precise word for what it does is binding. It is not the equals of mathematics. score = 7 is an instruction, not a statement of fact — which is why score = score + 1 is perfectly sensible in Python and nonsense in algebra.

    Predict — write both answers down before running anything

    (a) score = 7 then score = score + 3 then score — what appears?

    (b) a = 7 then b = a then a = 100 then b — what appears?

    Most people get (a) right and (b) right for the wrong reason. Keep your reasoning, not just your answer — we come back to it.

    Being right for the wrong reason is worth taking seriously rather than treating as a near miss, because it is the most dangerous state to be in. A wrong model that produces correct answers is invisible — nothing prompts you to revise it, and confidence grows with each success. It fails only later, on a case that happens to distinguish the models, and by then the belief is well established and the failure looks inexplicable.

    That is precisely what happens with the box model. It handles numbers and strings flawlessly, which is most of what a beginner writes, so it can survive months of successful programming before meeting a list and producing a result that seems impossible.

    Python language

    The rule, precisely. Assignment binds a name to an object. It never copies the object, and it never changes the object that was previously bound. b = a makes b a second label on the object a currently labels. Rebinding a afterwards moves only a's label; every other name is untouched.

    This is a promise of the Python language itself. It is true in CPython, PyPy, MicroPython, and any correct implementation, on every operating system, on every processor.

    Source: Python language reference, section 7.2 — assignment statements bind names to objects.
    Unit I.3.3
    Look inside

    What exists in memory, before and after

    Level 2

    Ladder

    What the machine does for score = 7

    All thirteen floors

    Ladder · score = 7 at the promptfloors involved

    1. Human intention — keep this number for later
    2. Python source text — the eleven characters you typed
    3. Tokens — NAME “score”, EQUAL, NUMBER “7”
    4. Syntax tree — an Assign node: target score, value 7
    5. Compiler — CPython's compiler, written in C
    6. Code object and bytecode — LOAD_CONST 7, STORE_NAME score
    7. CPython runtime — fetches each opcode and does the work
    8. Native machine instructions — the C code of CPython, compiled
    9. CPU control logic — ordinary fetch–decode–execute
    10. Registers and ALU — address arithmetic and the dictionary hash
    11. Caches and RAM — where the int object and the namespace live
    12. Operating-system services
    13. Device, file, terminal, result

    Floor 12 is dark, and that is the point. Binding a name involves no system call, no kernel, no permission check, nothing outside the process. The program does it entirely inside memory it already owns. The operating system would only appear if the process needed more memory than it currently holds — and even then it asks in large blocks, rarely, not per assignment. Floor 13 stays dark too: nothing was displayed, because the prompt echoing a value is a separate action.

    Become the machine · CPython executing score = 7

    1. compileI see an Assign node. I emit two instructions: push the constant 7, then store it under the name score.
    2. evalMy instruction pointer reads LOAD_CONST 0. I look up slot 0 of this code object's constants table. It holds a ready-made int object for 7.
    3. evalI push a reference to that object onto my value stack. I did not copy the 7. I copied an address.
    4. evalNext opcode: STORE_NAME 0. Name slot 0 is the text "score".
    5. runtimeI pop the reference and write it into this module's namespace dictionary under the key "score". I increase the object's reference count, because one more thing now points at it.
    6. cpuUnderneath, my C code became machine instructions: hash a string, index into a table, write eight bytes, increment a counter. The processor did that without any idea that a “name” was involved.
    7. osI did not speak to the kernel once.
    Unit I.3.4
    Break

    The comfortable idea now fails

    Deliberate misconception

    The wrong model you may still be carrying

    "A variable is a box. b = a copies what is in box a into box b. That is why changing a afterwards did not change b."

    That model predicted the right answer a moment ago. Here is where it dies.

    Predict — write it down, this one matters

    shopping = ['milk', 'eggs'], then backup = shopping, then shopping.append('bread'), then look at backup.

    What is in backup? The box model says two items. Write down your answer and which model you used.

    Descend

    Why the label model survives and the box model does not

    Earned by the failure

    Draw it with labels and there is no mystery at all. backup = shopping tied a second label to the one existing list object. shopping.append('bread') did not rebind anything — it reached through the label and changed the object itself. One object, two labels, so both labels show the change.

    This is the distinction the whole chapter has been building towards, and it has two names worth learning properly:

    Two things make this pair worth memorising as a pair. First, the difference is invisible in the syntax: x = ... rebinds and x.append(...) mutates, and nothing about their appearance announces that one affects only this name and the other affects every name. Second, whether an operation can mutate is a property of the object rather than of the name, so the same line of code is safe with a tuple and dangerous with a list.

    Between them, those two rules settle every question in the rest of Volume I. Chapter I.6's slots, Chapter I.7's copies and aliases, Chapter I.8's argument passing, and Chapter I.10's requirement that keys be immutable are all consequences, and none of them needs a further rule.

    Rebinding

    name = something

    Moves this one label to a different object. Affects no other name. Never changes any object.

    Mutation

    name.append(...), name[0] = ...

    Changes the object itself. Every name tied to that object sees it, because there is only one object.

    Python language

    Why a = 100 looked like the box model was working. Integers are immutable: there is no operation that changes an int object into a different number. So the only thing that can ever happen to an int name is rebinding, and rebinding behaves identically under both models. Lists are mutable, so the models finally disagree — and the box model loses.

    Immutable in Python: int, float, str, tuple, bool, frozenset. Mutable: list, dict, set, and most objects you will write yourself.

    Source: Python language reference, data model — objects have an identity, a type and a value; the value of an immutable object cannot change.
    Unit I.3.5
    Evidence

    Prove all of it yourself

    Instruments

    Do not take any of this on trust. Python ships with tools that let you see identity directly.

    New Python — three instruments

    id(x) gives a number that is unique to that object for as long as it exists. Two names with the same id are tied to the same object.

    x is y asks "are these the very same object?" — identity. x == y asks "do these have the same value?" — equality. Two different lists can be equal without being identical.

    import sys then sys.getsizeof(x) reports how many bytes that object occupies.

    CPythonHardware example

    How big is the number 7? On the reference build, sys.getsizeof(7) reports 28 bytes. Twenty-eight bytes to hold a value that needs three bits. The extra is object machinery: a reference count, a pointer to the type, a digit count, and the digits themselves — the price of integers that never overflow and objects that can be shared safely.

    This number is specific to CPython on a 64-bit build. On a 32-bit build it is smaller; on another implementation the question may not even be meaningful.

    Category: CPython implementation on a 64-bit build. Measured with sys.getsizeof; verify on your own machine.
    Level 3 Runtime model — where the name is actually written

    A name is not stored next to the object. It is stored in a namespace, and CPython uses two quite different mechanisms depending on where you are.

    At module level or in the prompt: a dictionary

    The compiler emits STORE_NAME. At run time CPython hashes the text "score" and writes the reference into the module's namespace dictionary. Looking it up later means hashing again and probing a table.

    Inside a function: an array slot

    The compiler knows every local name when it compiles the function, so it assigns each one a numbered slot and emits STORE_FAST 0 instead. At run time that is an array write at a known offset — no hashing, no text, no lookup. This is a large part of why code inside a function runs faster than the same code at module level.

    CPython

    Bytecode instruction names are not part of the Python language and carry no compatibility promise. They changed in 3.11, 3.12, 3.13 and again in 3.14. Never write a program that depends on them.

    Source: CPython dis module documentation, 3.14; CPython 3.14 branch, Lib/dis.py.
    Level 4 Expert microscope — shared objects, reference counts, and a trap

    Try this at the interactive prompt, one line at a time:

    Mechanism one — the small-integer cache. CPython pre-builds one object for every integer from −5 to 256 when it starts, and hands out the same object every time. That is why 256 is shared everywhere, in any context. It is an optimisation, not a rule: small integers are extremely common, and making a fresh object for each would be wasteful.

    Mechanism two — constant sharing within one code object. When the compiler compiles a whole file, it builds one constants table for it, and both 257 literals become the same entry. So both names end up pointing at one object — not because 257 is cached, but because it appeared once in that table. At the prompt each line is compiled separately, so each gets its own table and its own 257.

    CPython

    Both mechanisms are implementation details with no promise attached. The practical rule that is a language-level promise: use == to compare values and reserve is for None, True, False and deliberate identity checks. Code that relies on is for numbers is broken code that happens to work.

    Category: CPython implementation. Range verified empirically; both mechanisms are longstanding but unguaranteed.

    How Python knows when to reclaim an object

    Every CPython object carries a reference count: how many references currently point at it. b = a increments it. Rebinding a decrements the old object's count. When it reaches zero the object is freed immediately — which is why in CPython you can often predict exactly when memory is released, and why that prediction does not hold on other implementations.

    Reference counting alone cannot free objects that point at each other in a cycle, so CPython also runs a cycle collector. Volume II builds both.

    And a note on the free-threaded build

    In the free-threaded build of 3.14 — officially supported since PEP 779, but not the default — reference counting works differently, using biased reference counting and per-object locking so that multiple threads can update counts without one global lock. Nothing in this chapter's Python-language content changes; the CPython details in this panel do.

    OS-dependent

    When a process does eventually need more memory for new objects, CPython asks its allocator, which asks the operating system in large blocks — VirtualAlloc on Windows, mmap or brk on Linux. That is a genuine kernel crossing, and it is rare. It is not what happens when you bind a name.

    Category: operating-system dependent. Volume III covers this properly.
    Unit I.3.6
    Rebuild

    The model you leave with

    Replacing the old one

    Four sentences to keep for good

    Objects live in memory. Names are labels tied to objects. Assignment moves a label and never copies an object. Mutation changes an object and is seen by every label tied to it.

    If you can apply those four sentences to a piece of code and predict what happens, you have the model this chapter exists to give you — and you have it more securely than most working programmers.

    Retrieval lock

    Reconstruct it without looking

    Close the book

    1. Redraw. Without looking at Figure I.3.2, draw the memory state after x = [1, 2], y = x, y = [9]. How many objects exist? What does x show? Then check by running it.
    2. Explain. In your own words: why does backup = shopping not make a backup, and what would?
    3. Modify. Change the shopping-list experiment so backup really is independent. Prove it with is and with an append.
    4. Transfer. A friend writes a function that takes a list and sorts it with items.sort(). They are astonished that the caller's list changed too. Explain it with labels, and give them two ways to fix it.
    5. Predict harder. t = ([1, 2], 3) — a tuple, which is immutable. Predict whether t[0].append(9) raises an error. Run it. Then explain the result using only this chapter's four sentences. (This one is genuinely subtle. Take your time.)

    • You can state what assignment does in one sentence, without using the word "box".
    • You can distinguish rebinding from mutation, and predict which names are affected by each.
    • You can say which floors of the execution ladder a plain assignment uses, and explain why floor 12 is dark.
    • You can explain the difference between is and ==, and say which one you should almost always use.
    • You can name one thing in this chapter that is a Python-language promise and one that is a CPython detail.

    If the last item is hard, reread the badges rather than the prose — the labels exist precisely so this question has an easy answer. The next chapter, Asking questions, assumes every item above.

    Back · Chapter 0.3The machine that never guesses Next · Chapter I.4Asking questions
    Volume I · Chapter 4Python foundations

    Asking questions

    Booleans, comparison operators, if and elif, truthiness — and the conditional jump that every decision compiles into

    A program that always does the same thing is an expensive way to have a fixed answer. Everything interesting begins when a program can look at something and choose. This chapter builds that — and then shows that the choosing, at the bottom, is the instruction you already wrote by hand in Chapter 0.3.

    Prerequisites

    Chapter I.2 (types, and that a value knows what it is), Chapter I.3 (names), Chapter 0.3 Stages 5–7 (the ALU, the program counter, and the conditional jump — this chapter is where that opcode reappears), Chapter 0.5 (bytecode, and dis).

    Unit I.4.1
    Problem

    A program that always does the same thing is a very long calculator

    Something you can feel

    Everything so far has run straight through: every line, in order, every time. Such a program is entirely predictable, which sounds like a virtue and is in fact its limitation — if the outcome never depends on anything, you could have written down the answer instead.

    What is needed is for the program to look at a value it did not know in advance and take a different route depending on what it finds. That requires two things, and it is worth separating them at the outset because they are genuinely separate mechanisms that people habitually run together.

    The first is a way to ask a question and receive an answer — to compare two things and obtain something that records how the comparison came out. The second is a way to act on that answer, running one piece of code rather than another. Keeping them apart matters because the answer to a question is an ordinary value that can be stored, passed to a function, or printed, entirely independently of whether anybody branches on it. A great deal of confusion about conditions dissolves once you see that the question and the choosing are two operations rather than one.

    There is also a reason to be interested in how the choosing happens, beyond curiosity. Chapter 0.3 built a processor whose only decision-making instruction jumped when a register held zero, and nothing was said at the time about how that meagre facility could support the kind of branching a real language offers. Unit I.4.4 answers that, and the answer — that it needs nothing more — is one of the more satisfying moments available this early in the book.

    Unit I.4.2
    Tool

    Questions have answers, and the answers are values

    Booleans and comparison

    Python's comparison operators are expressions in the sense of Chapter I.1: they produce a value, and that value can be stored, printed or passed around like any other.

    That the result is a value rather than an event is the point of the unit, and it has consequences that are easy to miss. A comparison can be given a name, kept in a list, returned from a function, or handed to another function as an argument — all without any branching happening anywhere. Chapter II.10 relies on precisely this when it passes a comparison-producing function to a sort; Chapter I.6 relies on it when filtering. If comparisons were a special kind of syntax that only made sense inside an if, none of that would be possible.

    The operators are == for equal, != for not equal, and <, >, <=, >=. The doubled equals sign is worth dwelling on, because confusing it with assignment is the most common early error in every language that has both, and the reason it is so common is that the two operations are conceptually adjacent — "make this equal to that" and "is this equal to that" differ by one word in English and one character in code.

    Chapter I.1 showed why Python catches the confusion rather than letting it through. Assignment is a statement, and a statement produces no value, so it cannot appear where a value is required. Writing if x = 3: is therefore a syntax error reported before the program starts, rather than an assignment that quietly succeeds and yields a value the condition then tests. Languages that allow assignment inside a condition have a well-documented family of bugs that Python simply does not have, and the cost of that immunity is that you occasionally cannot write something compact that would have been legal elsewhere. It is a trade, and this book's position is that stating the trade is more useful than presenting the outcome as obviously right.

    Comparison is not restricted to numbers, and the results reward a moment's attention.

    Both results in that transcript repay a moment. Text comparison is defined by the numeric code point of each character in turn, which is Chapter I.9's subject arriving early; it means the ordering is precise and well-defined and is not the ordering a person would call alphabetical. Every capital letter has a lower code point than every lower-case letter, so Zebra precedes apple in any naive sort, and a program that sorts names without addressing this will produce output that looks broken to anybody who reads it.

    And True == 1 being true is not a quirk of the comparison but a fact about the type: Python's booleans are a subtype of integer, so True genuinely is one and False is zero. That occasionally does useful work — summing a list of comparisons counts how many were true — and occasionally explains something baffling, such as a dictionary in which the key 1 and the key True turn out to be the same key. Chapter I.10's rule that equal keys are the same key is doing exactly what it says; it is the equality that is surprising.

    Unit I.4.3
    Tool

    Taking a different path

    if, elif, else

    New Python — the if statement

    if condition: followed by an indented block runs that block only when the condition is true. elif offers another condition to try; else catches everything remaining. The indentation is not decoration — it is how Python knows which lines belong to the block, which is why Chapter IV.1's tokenizer has to track it.

    The ordering of the conditions is doing real work, and it is worth being explicit about what work, because this is a defect people write repeatedly. Each elif is tested only if every condition above it failed, which means each one may quietly assume the failure of all its predecessors. The second branch reads as "at least seventy", and what it actually means is "at least seventy and less than ninety" — the upper bound is supplied by the branch above rather than being written anywhere. Rearrange the branches into ascending order and every score above fifty matches the first test, and the chain reports a pass for everything.

    The same behaviour explains a second common defect. Writing separate if statements rather than an elif chain means every condition is tested independently and every matching branch runs, so a score of 72 would print both good and a pass. The two versions differ by two characters and mean quite different things: a chain chooses one branch, and a sequence of separate if statements runs all the branches that apply. Neither is wrong in general; they answer different questions, and the defect is using one while thinking of the other.

    A word about the indentation, since it is doing structural work that other languages give to punctuation. The indented lines beneath an if are a block, and their indentation is the only thing marking them as belonging to it. That has a consequence Chapter IV.1 will make precise: Python's tokenizer cannot discard whitespace as our own tiny language's tokenizer does, because in Python a change of indentation is a token. It also explains why mixing tabs and spaces is an error rather than a matter of preference — two lines that look identically indented may not be, and the language forbids the ambiguity rather than guessing.

    Unit I.4.4
    Descend

    It is still subtract-and-check-for-zero

    What a decision compiles into

    Chapter 0.3 gave your toy processor an opcode that jumped only if the accumulator held zero, and at the time it may have seemed a meagre basis for decision-making. Disassemble an if and see what Python's decisions are made of.

    Follow the instructions once through, for each outcome, because the mechanism is simpler than the diagram suggests. The two loads put x and 3 where the comparison can reach them. COMPARE_OP removes both, works out whether the first exceeds the second, and leaves a single True or False in their place — which is Unit I.4.2's claim that a comparison produces a value, visible as an instruction. Then POP_JUMP_IF_FALSE removes that value and inspects it. If it is true, nothing happens at all and execution simply continues into the next instruction, which is the first line of the true branch. If it is false, the instruction writes a new address into the program counter, and the next fetch therefore comes from a different place.

    Notice what is not in that listing. There is no instruction meaning "begin a block", none meaning "this is an else", and no record anywhere of which lines were indented. The block structure you wrote was consumed entirely by the compiler at floor 5 and converted into a single number — the address to jump to — in exactly the way Chapter IV.3 will show brackets being converted into instruction order. Everything about how the source was arranged is gone by floor 6, and what remains is where to go.

    There is no such thing as branching

    At floor 9 there are no conditions, no if, and no blocks. There is a counter holding the address of the next instruction, and instructions that can write to it. Every decision in every program you will ever write reduces to that.

    Chapter I.5 will show that loops are the same instruction pointing backwards instead of forwards, and Chapter IV.6 will show that even exceptions — which feel like the most magical control flow in Python — end in an assignment to a program counter.

    Unit I.4.5
    Break

    A comparison that lies

    Deliberate failure

    Predict

    Is 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 true?

    It is worth being exact about the cause, because "floats are inaccurate" is a slogan that leaves people unable to predict when trouble will arrive. A float stores a number as a fixed quantity of binary digits, so the numbers it can represent exactly are those expressible as a sum of powers of two. One half, one quarter and three eighths are all exact. One tenth is not, for precisely the reason one third is not exact in decimal: the expansion recurs forever and must be cut off somewhere. So 0.1 is not one tenth — it is the closest representable number to one tenth, and it has been ever since it was typed.

    Two such approximations added together produce a third approximation, and there is no reason for it to coincide with the stored approximation of 0.3. Nothing went wrong in the addition; the inputs were already slightly not what they appeared to be. This also explains why the trouble is unpredictable in practice: 0.5 + 0.25 == 0.75 is perfectly true, because all three of those are exactly representable, so a program can pass every test its author tries and fail on a tenth.

    So exact equality between floats asks a question that is almost never the one you mean. The repair is to ask whether they are close enough for the purpose.

    Unit I.4.6
    Descend

    What counts as true when it is not a comparison?

    Truthiness

    An if does not require a comparison. It accepts any value at all, and asks that value whether it considers itself true.

    This lets if items: mean "if there are any", which reads well and is idiomatic. It also has a sharp edge worth meeting deliberately: 0 and None and '' are all false, so a check meaning "was a value supplied?" will treat a supplied zero as if nothing had been supplied. When the difference matters, ask precisely — if count is not None: rather than if count:.

    The reason this rule exists is worth stating rather than accepting, because it is a deliberate design choice with a cost. Allowing any value in a condition makes a great deal of ordinary code shorter and more readable: if items: says "if there are any" more clearly than if len(items) > 0: does, and it works for every container without knowing which one it has. That generality comes from Chapter II.7's protocol idea — the value is asked whether it is true, and each type answers for itself.

    The cost is that several genuinely different situations collapse into the same answer. Zero, the empty string, the empty list and None are all false, so a check written to mean "did the caller supply a value?" will treat a supplied zero exactly as if nothing had been supplied. That is a real defect and a quiet one, because it appears only when the value legitimately happens to be zero or empty — which may be rare in testing and common in production. When the distinction matters, ask the precise question: if count is not None: tests what you actually mean, and costs one extra clause.

    The same rule governs and and or, which do something more interesting than they appear to.

    Ladder · if score >= 70:where a decision actually happens

    1. Human intention — behave differently depending
    2. Python source text — a condition and an indented block
    3. Tokens — indentation becomes structure here
    4. Syntax tree — a test with two bodies
    5. Compiler — lays both branches out and computes the jump target
    6. Code object and bytecode — COMPARE_OP, then a conditional jump
    7. CPython runtime — evaluates the comparison, then may set the counter
    8. Native machine instructions
    9. CPU control logic — the counter is written; nothing here knows what a condition is
    10. Registers and ALU — the comparison itself, as a subtraction
    11. Caches and RAM
    12. Operating-system services — dark: deciding needs nobody's permission
    13. Device, file, terminal, result

    Floors 12 and 13 dark is worth noticing, because it is the common case that Chapter I.1's print was not. A decision happens entirely inside your process, at full speed, needing nothing from anybody. Most of what a program does looks like this, and the chapters where floor 12 lights up are the ones where the interesting costs live.

    Reconstruct it without looking

    Close the book

    1. Explain. Why is a comparison an expression rather than a statement? Say what follows from that.
    2. Modify. Write a grading chain with elif, then rewrite it with separate if statements and find an input where they differ. Explain why.
    3. Redraw. Draw the two instruction sequences for an if/else, marking the jump and its target. Say what the program counter holds at each step for a true and a false condition.
    4. Explain. Why is 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 false? Answer using Chapter I.2, and say what you would write instead.
    5. Explain. State the truthiness rule in one sentence, then give an input where if count: and if count is not None: differ.
    6. Modify. Demonstrate short-circuiting with a function that prints. Then write a condition that would raise an error if and did not short-circuit.
    7. Transfer. A colleague's sort puts all capitalised names before all lower-case ones. Explain why, using Chapter I.9's code points.
    8. Stretch. Disassemble an if/elif/else chain with three branches. Count the jumps and explain where each one goes.
    Mastery gate — Chapter I.4
    • You can write comparisons and predict their values.
    • You can write if/elif/else and say why only one branch runs.
    • You can explain what a decision compiles into, naming both instructions.
    • You can connect that to Chapter 0.3's conditional jump.
    • You can explain why float equality is unreliable and what to write instead.
    • You can state the truthiness rule and identify where it is dangerous.
    • You can explain short-circuiting and give a case where it prevents an error.

    If item three is shaky, disassemble one if and find the two instructions. Every loop in Chapter I.5, every function return, and every exception in Chapter I.11 rests on the same mechanism — a number written into a counter.
