    Volume I · Chapter 5Doing work

    Doing it again

    while, for, and the backward jump that every loop in every language compiles into

    A processor can only move forwards through instructions or jump somewhere else. There is no repeat instruction, in any machine, anywhere. Loops exist because you can jump backwards — and you already built that in Chapter 0.3.

    Prerequisites

    Chapter 0.3 (the program counter, JUMP, JUMP_IF_ZERO, and failure experiment 1), Chapter I.3 (rebinding), Chapter I.4 (comparison and conditional jumps). This chapter is I.4 plus one arrow pointing upwards.

    Unit I.5.1
    Problem

    Print the numbers 1 to 100

    Something you can feel

    Go on. With only what you know so far, you would write one hundred lines of print. Then someone asks for 1 to 10,000.

    The problem is not the typing. It is that the number 100 is now baked into the shape of your program. To change it you must rewrite the program. That is not a program; that is a very long receipt.

    What you want is to describe the work once and say how many times.

    That sentence contains the whole idea, and its two halves correspond to the two loops this chapter teaches. Describing the work once is common to both. Saying how often is where they differ: sometimes you know the number in advance, or can derive it from something you already have, and sometimes you do not and must continue until a condition changes.

    The distinction matters more than it appears to, because it decides which loop is honest about your intention. A loop over a known collection announces that it will finish; a loop on a condition announces that it might not. Choosing the wrong one is not merely stylistic — it misrepresents to every future reader what the code is capable of doing.

    Unit I.5.2
    Tool

    Keep going while something is true

    while

    New Python — the while loop and +=

    while takes a condition and a block, exactly like if — colon, then indented lines. The difference is what happens at the bottom of the block: instead of carrying on, Python goes back and tests the condition again.

    count += 1 is shorthand for count = count + 1. Read it as "add one to what count is bound to, then rebind count to the result". It is read-modify-write, exactly as in Chapter 0.2.

    Predict — write down what each prints

    (a) The loop above, but with count = 1 changed to count = 6.
    (b) The loop above with the line count += 1 deleted.

    Run (a). Do not run (b) yet — predict it first, then run it, and be ready to stop it with Ctrl+C.

    (a) prints nothing at all. The condition is tested before the first pass, not after, so a loop can run zero times — which is usually what you want and occasionally a nasty surprise.

    (b) prints 1 forever. And you have met this before: it is failure experiment 1 from Chapter 0.3, where your toy machine jumped back to address 0 and never stopped. Nothing is broken. The machine is obeying perfectly, which remains the horror of it.

    Unit I.5.3
    Descend

    There is no repeat instruction

    The backward jump

    Disassemble the loop and the whole illusion comes apart.

    The thing to actually take away

    A loop is a conditional jump that leaves, plus an unconditional jump that goes back. Nothing repeats. The counter simply gets set to a smaller number.

    Your toy machine had both instructions: 7 JUMP_IF_ZERO to leave, and 6 JUMP to go back. You had everything you needed for a loop in Chapter 0.3 — and in the retrieval lock you wrote one, counting down from five.

    Look at what that means for the concept of a loop. There is no loop instruction, no notion of a body, and nothing in the machine that repeats anything. There is a jump whose target address is lower than the address of the jump itself, so the counter goes backwards and the same instructions are fetched again. Repetition is not a feature the processor provides; it is a consequence of being allowed to move the counter in either direction.

    The two loops in this chapter therefore compile into the same shape, and so does everything else that repeats: the comprehensions of Chapter II.1, the iteration of Chapter II.5, the evaluation loop of Chapter IV.4 that runs your entire program. Each is a conditional jump forward to leave, and an unconditional jump backward to go round again.

    Unit I.5.4
    Tool

    When you know how many times

    for and range

    The counter pattern — set up, test, increase — is so common that writing it by hand three times a day invites the same three mistakes. So Python has a loop for it.

    New Python — for and range

    range(5) produces the numbers 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 — five numbers, starting at zero, stopping before five. for i in range(5): runs its block once for each, with i bound to the current one.

    Starting at zero and stopping before the end is the same convention as list indexing and memory addresses, and it is not an accident. range(2, 6) gives 2, 3, 4, 5.

    Use for

    When you know the collection

    Counting a fixed number of times, or working through every item in a list. Most loops you write should be this one.

    Use while

    When you know only the condition

    "Until the player quits", "until the answer is close enough". You cannot say in advance how many passes it takes.

    Unit I.5.5
    Tool

    Leaving early and skipping ahead

    break and continue

    break
    Leave the loop immediately. You met it in Chapter 0.3, where it stopped your toy processor at HALT
    continue
    Abandon this pass only, and go straight back to the top for the next one

    Ladder · a loop that only countsfloors involved

    1. Human intention — do this many times
    2. Python source text
    3. Tokens — including INDENT and DEDENT
    4. Syntax tree — a While or For node holding a body
    5. Compiler — flattens the body and computes the jump distances
    6. Code object and bytecode — POP_JUMP_IF_FALSE out, JUMP_BACKWARD round
    7. CPython runtime — the same eval loop, going round your loop
    8. Native machine instructions
    9. CPU control logic — the program counter moving backwards
    10. Registers and ALU — the comparison, every single pass
    11. Caches and RAM
    12. Operating-system services
    13. Device, file, terminal, result

    A loop of a billion passes crosses to the kernel zero times — unless you print inside it. That single fact explains why a silent loop finishes in seconds and the same loop with a print in it takes minutes. The loop is not the slow part.

    Level 3 Runtime model — why for is not just a tidier while

    A while loop tests a condition. A for loop does something quite different: it asks an object for an iterator and then repeatedly asks that iterator for the next item, until the iterator says it has run out.

    The mechanism underneath deserves a sentence now and gets a chapter later. A for loop knows nothing about lists, strings or files. It asks the object for an iterator, then repeatedly asks that iterator for the next item until it reports there are none. Everything specific to being a list lives in the list's iterator rather than in the loop.

    That is why one statement works unchanged over things with nothing physically in common — a list in memory, the characters of a string, the lines of a file arriving from a disk, a range that computes its numbers rather than storing them. They agree only on how to be asked for the next thing, and the loop needs nothing else. Chapter II.5 builds one from scratch, and Chapter III.1 depends on the file version to read a file larger than the machine's memory.

    This is why for works unchanged over a list, a string, a dictionary, a file or a stream of results from a database: none of those has a "count" that Python needs to know in advance. They all answer the same two questions — give me an iterator, and give me the next item.

    You build an iterator yourself in Volume II, and it turns out to be one of the most reusable ideas in the language.

    CPython

    CPython's compiler also duplicates a while loop's test — once before the loop and once at the bottom — so that each pass costs one conditional jump instead of two. You may see the same comparison twice in a disassembly. That is an optimisation, not a mistake, and its exact form varies between versions.

    Category: CPython implementation. Verify with dis on your own build.
    Unit I.5.6
    Break

    The loop that runs one time too few

    Deliberate failure

    Predict

    How many numbers does for i in range(1, 5): print? And what is the last one?

    Four numbers: 1, 2, 3, 4. Not five, and the last is 4, not 5. range stops before its end value.

    This is the off-by-one error, and it is so common it has its own name and its own jokes. It is not carelessness — it is a genuine consequence of a real design choice, and the choice is a good one. Because range(n) gives exactly n values starting at 0, it lines up perfectly with list positions and memory addresses, which also start at zero. You met that in Chapter 0.2, where the eighth box had address 7.

    The habit that fixes it permanently

    Stop asking "where does it stop?" and start asking "how many does it give me?" range(5) gives five. range(1, 5) gives four — five minus one. Counting how many, rather than checking the last one, makes off-by-one errors nearly impossible.

    Reconstruct it without looking

    Close the book

    1. Redraw. Draw a loop as instructions in memory, with the two jumps marked. Label which one leaves and which one goes back.
    2. Explain. Why is there no repeat instruction in any processor, and what does the machine do instead?
    3. Modify. Write a loop that prints the five times table up to 5 × 12. Then rewrite it the other way — if you used for, use while, and vice versa. Check both give identical output.
    4. Transfer. A friend's program is stuck printing the same line forever. Using this chapter and Chapter 0.3, give them the two things to check first, and say why the machine is not at fault.
    5. Stretch. Write a loop that counts down from 10 to 1. Then work out which of your toy machine's nine opcodes you would need to do the same thing, and in what order.

    • You can write a for loop over range, and say how many passes it will make before running it.
    • You can explain why a loop can run zero times.
    • You can name the two bytecode instructions that make a loop, and the toy-machine instructions they correspond to.
    • You can explain the cause of an infinite loop and connect it to Chapter 0.3's first failure experiment.
    • You can say which floors of the ladder a silent loop uses, and why adding print changes the cost so dramatically.

    If item four is shaky, reread Unit I.5.3 with Figure I.4.1 beside it. Chapter I.6 puts loops and lists together and assumes both are solid.

    Volume I · Chapter 6Doing work

    Rows of things

    Lists, indexing, slicing, and what a list actually holds — correcting the model you were given in Chapter 0.2

    In Chapter 0.2 you were told a Python list is a row of boxes, and warned that the model was deliberately incomplete. This is the chapter where the promise is kept and the model is repaired.

    Prerequisites

    Chapter 0.2 (addresses, indexing from zero, the declared simplification), Chapter I.3 (names, references, rebinding versus mutation), Chapter I.5 (loops). This chapter is where I.3's model earns its keep.

    Unit I.6.1
    Problem

    A hundred scores and a hundred names

    Something you can feel

    Thirty children each have a test score. Give each one its own name and you have thirty names, thirty assignments, and no way to write "add up all of them" without naming all thirty again.

    The worst part is not the typing. It is that you cannot loop over names. A loop needs something to count through, and a pile of individually named values is not a something.

    What you want is one name for the whole row, and a number to pick out any member of it. You already know exactly what that looks like: it is Chapter 0.2's wall of boxes.

    Two separate wants are hidden in that sentence, and both are worth making explicit because different structures satisfy them differently. The first is collection: one name for many things, so they can be passed, stored and looped over as a unit. The second is selection by position: a way to say "the third one" and get it immediately, without examining the first two.

    A list provides both, and the second is the one that costs something to provide. Getting the third item instantly requires knowing where the third item is without looking, which requires the slots to be a fixed size and laid out in order — and that requirement is exactly what Unit I.6.4 shows a list paying for, and what Chapter II.9 explains in full.

    And now a loop has something to work with:

    Unit I.6.2
    Rebuild

    Keeping the promise from Chapter 0.2

    Correcting simplification S-03

    Simplified model

    What you were told in Chapter 0.2: a Python list is a row of boxes holding values. What was correct about it: numbered slots starting at zero, reachable instantly by number, that you can read and overwrite. All of that is true and none of it is being withdrawn. What it left out is what the slots contain.

    Declared simplification S-03. Corrected below, as promised.

    A list slot does not contain a value. It contains a reference — an address, pointing at an object that lives somewhere else entirely.

    This corrects Chapter 0.2's picture, and it is worth saying why the earlier version was offered rather than treating it as an error. There you saw a row of boxes containing numbers, which is exactly how an array works in a language where the type is known in advance and every element has the same size. It is a true picture of a great many computers, and a true picture of what Chapter II.12's array module gives you. It is not a picture of a Python list.

    The reason follows directly from Chapter I.2. If every value is an object carrying its own type, then values have different sizes — an integer, a string and a list will not fit interchangeably in a fixed-width slot. The one thing that is a fixed size is an address. So the slots hold addresses, and that single decision is what lets a list hold anything at all, mixed freely, which the row-of-numbers version cannot do.

    This follows inevitably from Chapter I.3. If a name is a label tied to an object, and a list is a row of positions that behave like names, then each position is a label too. Same rule, thirty times over.

    Unit I.6.3
    Break

    Three rows that are secretly one row

    Deliberate failure

    You want a grid: three rows, each holding a single zero. Chapter 0.2 taught you that [0] * 3 makes three copies. So this looks reasonable.

    Predict — this one catches nearly everybody

    grid = [[0]] * 3, then grid[0][0] = 9, then look at grid. What do you expect?

    Descend

    Multiplying copied the addresses

    Earned by the failure

    Draw it with references and the mystery evaporates in about four seconds.

    [[0]] * 3 makes a list with three slots. Into each slot it copies the reference that was in the original — not the object it points at. So all three slots hold the same address. There is one inner list, with three labels on it, and Chapter I.3 already told you exactly what happens next: mutate the object and every label sees it.

    The fix is to build three separate objects instead of copying one address three times.

    Python language

    The rule, stated once so you never have to rediscover it. Multiplying a list repeats its references. If the items are immutable — numbers, text, tuples — sharing is invisible and harmless, because nothing can change them. If the items are mutable — lists, dictionaries, sets — sharing is very visible indeed.

    The rule is not a special case about multiplication. It is the ordinary behaviour of references, appearing where people do not expect it: multiplying a list copies its slots, and a slot holds an address, so what is duplicated is the address rather than the thing at the far end of it. Nothing was copied that anybody would call a value.

    The same reasoning covers three further situations you will meet, and recognising the shared shape is worth more than the individual rules. Assigning a list to a second name gives two names for one object. Putting a list inside another list stores an address, not a copy. Passing a list to a function hands over an address, which is why a function can modify its caller's list. All four are the same fact, and Chapter I.7 is devoted to its consequences.

    This is why [0] * 3 in Chapter 0.2 was perfectly safe and [[0]] * 3 here is not. Same operation; the difference is entirely in what is being shared.

    Source: Python language reference, sequence types — repetition does not copy elements.
    Unit I.6.4
    Tool

    Taking a piece, and taking a copy

    Slicing

    New Python — slices

    L[1:3] gives a new list holding positions 1 and 2 — starting at the first number, stopping before the second, exactly like range. L[:2] means from the start; L[2:] means to the end; L[:] means the whole thing.

    How far does the copy go?

    L[:] makes a new row of slots and copies the addresses into it. The objects are still shared. For a list of numbers that is a complete copy in every way that matters. For a list of lists, the outer list is new and the inner ones are not — which is called a shallow copy, and it is the subject of the next chapter.

    Unit I.6.5
    Tool

    Growing and shrinking

    Changing a list in place

    L.append(x)
    Add one item to the end
    L[2] = x
    Overwrite the reference at position 2
    L.remove(x)
    Delete the first item equal to x
    L.pop()
    Remove the last item and hand it back
    L.sort()
    Reorder this list. Returns nothing — a deliberate warning that it changed the original

    Every one of those mutates. None of them rebinds. So every name tied to that list sees the change — which is exactly the distinction from Chapter I.3, now with five ways to trigger it.

    The mistake this causes

    L = L.sort() looks sensible and destroys your data. sort reorders the list and returns None, so you have just rebound L to nothing. Write L.sort() on its own line, or use sorted(L), which leaves the original alone and returns a new list.

    Level 3 Runtime model — what a list object actually is

    A CPython list is three things: an object header, a pointer to a block of memory holding the references, and two numbers — how many slots are used, and how many have been allocated.

    Those two numbers are different on purpose. If the block were exactly the right size, every single append would need a bigger block and a copy of everything into it. So CPython asks for more room than it needs and remembers the spare.

    When the spare room runs out, CPython asks for a larger block, copies all the addresses across, and frees the old one. That one append is expensive — but it happens rarely, and rarely enough that the average cost of appending stays tiny. That argument has a name, amortised analysis, and you build it properly in Volume II.

    Two things follow immediately and are worth knowing now. Appending to the end of a list is cheap. Inserting at the front is not, because every existing address has to shuffle up one slot.

    CPythonHardware example

    The exact sizes and the growth pattern are CPython's choices on a 64-bit build and have changed between versions. The shape — grow in jumps, keep spare room — is common to dynamic arrays in every language. Measure your own.

    Category: CPython on 64-bit. Verified with sys.getsizeof.

    1. Human intention — give me the third score
    2. Python source text

    5. Compiler
    6. Code object and bytecode — load the list, load 2, BINARY_SUBSCR

    Floor 10 is why indexing is instant no matter how long the list is. The machine does not search — it calculates where slot 2 must be and goes straight there. Position 2 of a four-item list and position 900,000 of a million-item list cost the same.

    Two labels, one thing

    Aliasing, shallow and deep copies, mutating a collection while looping over it, and what immutability actually buys you

    Chapter I.3 gave you the model. Chapter I.6 gave you a structure with references inside references. This chapter is where the two meet, and where the model either holds up under pressure or you find out it was never really yours.

    Prerequisites

    Chapter I.3 (rebinding versus mutation, is versus ==), Chapter I.5 (loops), Chapter I.6 (list slots hold references; slicing makes a new list). Every surprise in this chapter is predictable from those three. That is the test.

    Unit I.7.1
    Problem

    You made a copy and it was not a copy

    Something you can feel

    In Chapter I.6 you learned the fix for the pilot chapter's fake backup: M = L[:] builds a genuinely new list. Problem solved, apparently.

    Predict — use the model, not your instinct

    original = [[1, 2], [3, 4]], then backup = original[:], then backup[0].append(99).

    What is in original now?

    Unit I.7.2
    Descend

    How far a copy goes

    Shallow and deep

    A slice makes a new row of slots and copies the addresses into it. That is all it can do — a slot holds an address, so copying a slot copies an address. The objects those addresses point at are not touched, not examined, and certainly not duplicated.

    That is a shallow copy: one new object, everything inside it still shared.

    The word shallow does precise work and is worth unpacking rather than accepting as jargon. Any copy must decide how far down to go. Copying the outer list means making a new row of slots; the question is what to put in them, and the cheap answer — the same addresses — produces a genuinely new outer object whose contents are shared with the original.

    That is neither a bug nor a compromise; it is usually what you want. Copying only the top level is fast, costs memory proportional to the number of items rather than to their size, and is entirely safe when the items cannot be modified. Trouble arrives only when the shared things are mutable, because a change made by one route then shows up by the other — invisible in the code, and obvious in the diagram.

    Python language

    All three ways of copying a list are shallow. L[:], list(L) and L.copy() do the same job and share the inner objects identically. There is no accidental deep copy in Python — if you want one, you must ask for it explicitly.

    Source: Python language reference; copy module documentation, which states this distinction directly.
    New Python — the copying toolbox

    import copy loads the standard toolbox for copying. copy.deepcopy(x) walks through x and everything reachable from it, rebuilding every mutable object it finds, so that nothing in the result is shared with the original. (copy.copy(x) also exists and is shallow — the same one-level copy as a slice.)

    Which one do you actually want?

    Almost always the shallow one. If your list holds numbers or text — immutable things — a shallow copy is a complete copy in every way you can observe, because nothing shared can ever change. Reach for deepcopy only when you have mutable objects nested inside and you genuinely need to change one copy without the other.

    Unit I.7.3
    Break

    Changing a list while you are walking through it

    Deliberate failure

    Predict — be specific about which numbers appear

    Loop over [1, 2, 3, 4]. Print each item. When you see 1, remove it from the list. Which numbers get printed?

    Descend

    The loop counts positions, not items

    Earned by the failure

    Chapter I.5 Level 3 told you that for asks for an iterator and then repeatedly asks it for the next item. A list iterator keeps one number: which position am I up to.

    1. Position 0. The item there is 1. Print it. Remove 1 — everything shuffles down, so the list is now [2, 3, 4].
    2. Position 1. The item there is now 3, because 2 slid into position 0 while the iterator was not looking.
    3. Position 2 gives 4. Position 3 is past the end, so the loop stops.

    The iterator did nothing wrong. It advanced from 0 to 1 exactly as it should. The list moved underneath it.

    The general principle is worth stating beyond this example, because the same shape appears with dictionaries, sets and files. An iterator holds a position in a collection, and it holds that position as a number rather than as a grip on a particular item. Change the collection's shape while it is looking and the number now refers to somewhere else — not because anything failed, but because the meaning of the position changed underneath it.

    Python could have prevented this by copying the collection when iteration begins, and chose not to, because that would make every loop over a large list expensive to protect against a mistake most loops never make. Instead it makes the copy available when you want it — four characters — and, for dictionaries and sets, raises an error rather than quietly skipping. That the list version fails silently and the dictionary version complains is worth noticing: the same mistake, and two different judgements about how much protection is worth its cost.

    The rule, and the fix

    Never add to or remove from a collection while you are looping over it. Loop over a copy, or build a new list instead.

    for v in L[:]: — four characters — makes the loop walk a snapshot while you edit the original. Every item gets visited, and the removals still happen.

    Unit I.7.4
    Tool

    Things that cannot change

    Immutability, and one subtlety

    Every problem in this chapter comes from mutation. So there is an obvious defence: use objects that cannot be mutated.

    A tuple is a row of items, like a list, written with round brackets instead of square ones — and once built, its slots can never be changed.

    New Python — the tuple

    (3, 4) builds a tuple. Indexing, slicing, len and looping all work exactly as they do for lists. What does not exist is any way to change a slot: no item assignment, no append, no remove. One oddity worth knowing now: a one-item tuple is written (3,) with a trailing comma, because (3) is just the number 3 in brackets.

    Predict — the stretch question from Chapter I.3, now answered

    t = ([1, 2], 3) is a tuple, and tuples are immutable. Does t[0].append(9) raise an error?

    Read it with the model and it is not even strange. The tuple's slots hold two addresses. Those addresses are still exactly what they were: the same list object, the same int. Nothing about the tuple changed. What changed is the object at the far end of one of its arrows — and the tuple has no say over that whatsoever.

    Python language

    Immutability is shallow too. A tuple guarantees that its own slots never change. It guarantees nothing about the objects those slots point at. A tuple of numbers and strings is genuinely unchangeable; a tuple containing a list is not, in any way that matters to you.

    The guarantee is narrower than the word suggests, and stating it exactly prevents a family of misunderstandings. A tuple promises that its own slots will never be reassigned: the addresses it holds are fixed for its lifetime. It promises nothing at all about the objects at those addresses, because they are not part of the tuple — the tuple merely knows where they are.

    Read that beside the shallow copy above and the two are visibly one idea seen from opposite sides. A shallow copy duplicates the slots and shares what they point at; a tuple freezes the slots and leaves what they point at free to change. Both follow from the single fact that a slot holds an address, and neither is surprising once the diagram is in front of you — which is the argument for drawing it rather than reasoning about it in prose.

    The practical version: a tuple is only safely immutable if everything inside it is immutable as well.

    Source: Python language reference, data model — the value of an immutable object cannot change, but the objects it references may.
    Level 3 Runtime model — why sharing immutable objects is safe

    Now the pilot chapter's small-integer cache makes complete sense rather than being a curiosity.

    CPython hands out the same int object for 7 to every name that asks for it, and this causes no problems at all — because there is no operation anywhere in Python that can turn that object into an 8. Sharing is invisible when nothing can change.

    Try the same trick with lists and it would be a catastrophe. If every [] handed back one shared empty list, appending in one place would appear everywhere. Which is precisely the [[0]] * 3 trap from Chapter I.6, and precisely why CPython builds a fresh list object every time.

    Immutable
    Safe to share, cache and reuse. CPython does all three, aggressively, and you never notice
    Mutable
    Never shared behind your back. Every literal builds a new object, every time

    This is also why only immutable objects may be dictionary keys — a rule you meet in Chapter I.10 and which will then look inevitable rather than arbitrary.

    CPython

    Which immutable objects get cached, and when, is a CPython choice that varies by version and by context: small ints, short strings that look like identifiers, and the empty tuple are all commonly shared. Never write code that depends on it — use ==, as Chapter I.3 said.

    Category: CPython implementation. Verify with id() on your own build.

    Volume I · Chapter 8Doing work

    Machines of your own

    Defining and calling functions, frames on the stack, how arguments are really passed, and the scope rules that follow

    You have been calling functions since page one — print, len, bin. Now you build your own, and three seeds planted in earlier chapters get cashed in at once: the stack region of Figure 0.4.1, the pilot chapter's numbered slots, and the label model — which is about to dissolve one of programming's oldest arguments.

    Prerequisites

    Chapter 0.4 (the stack region of the address space), Chapter I.3 (names as labels; the Level-3 panel on STORE_FAST), Chapter I.6 (lists), Chapter I.7 (mutation seen through every label). Every "surprise" in this chapter is a straight consequence of those four.

    Unit I.8.1
    Problem

    The same six lines, four times

    Something you can feel

    Your program greets a player, and later greets another, and later two more. Four copies of the same lines, each with one word different. Then you improve the greeting — and must remember to improve it in four places, and you remember three.

    Copying code is not a typing problem. It is a truth problem: the same fact now lives in four places, and nothing keeps them agreeing.

    Spell out what goes wrong, because "keep it in one place" is advice everyone has heard and few can justify. Three copies of a piece of logic are three separate statements of the same belief. When the belief changes — a rule is corrected, a format is adjusted — all three must change together, and nothing whatever enforces that. Nothing lists them, nothing checks them, and nothing fails if two are updated and one is missed.

    What follows is the worst kind of defect: a program in which two parts genuinely disagree about the same rule, each looking correct in isolation. Chapter II.2 finds exactly that defect in Chapter I.12's program, and the repair there is the repair here — not to fix both copies, but to remove one so there is only ever a single answer.

    What you want is your paper instruction sheet from Chapter 0.2 back: a set of steps written once, with a blank where the changing part goes, that you can run on demand.

    Unit I.8.2
    Tool

    Build the machine, then press its button

    def, parameters, return

    New Python — defining a function

    def greet(name): builds a function. def means "define", greet is the name you are binding it to, and name is a parameter — a blank to be filled in at each call. The indented block is the machine's instruction sheet. Nothing in the block runs when you define it; it runs when you call it, with brackets: greet('Ada'). The value you put in the brackets is the argument.

    return hands a value back to whoever called, and ends the function immediately.

    Predict — write both down

    (a) result = greet('Ada') then print(result) — what appears, in total?
    (b) What is the difference between greet and greet('Ada') — not in effect, but in kind?

    Unit I.8.3
    Look inside

    Where the function's names live

    Frames on the stack

    When a call happens, CPython builds a frame: a workspace holding the function's local names — its parameters and anything it binds inside. Frames live in the stack region of Figure 0.4.1, and now you know why that region exists and why it grows and shrinks.

    The reason a frame is necessary at all is worth stating, because it is easy to imagine a simpler arrangement in which a function's variables just live somewhere fixed. That arrangement fails the moment a function calls itself, or calls something that calls it back, because the second call would overwrite the first call's values while the first is still using them. Chapter II.6's recursion is entirely built on frames being per-call rather than per-function.

    It also explains why the frames form a stack rather than any other structure. Calls finish in the reverse of the order they start — whatever you called most recently must finish before you can carry on — and that ordering is precisely what a stack captures. The shape is not a design choice; it is a consequence of what calling means.

    Call a function: a frame is pushed on top. It returns: the frame is popped off and destroyed, local names and all. Call a function from inside a function and a second frame stacks on the first — which is how each call keeps its own n without them colliding.

    Unit I.8.4
    Break

    You changed it inside, and outside nothing happened

    Deliberate failure

    Predict — the model decides, not intuition

    (a) def add_one(n): n = n + 1 — call it with x = 7. Is x now 8?
    (b) def stamp(items): items.append('seen') — call it with L = ['a']. Is L now changed?

    If your answers are "no and no" or "yes and yes", the model is not driving yet. Draw both before running.

    Descend

    The old argument, dissolved

    Earned by the failure

    Programmers have argued for fifty years about whether languages pass arguments "by value" (the function gets a copy) or "by reference" (the function gets the caller's variable itself). People ask which one Python is, and both answers are wrong.

    The argument persists because both descriptions capture something real and neither captures all of it. Reassigning a parameter does not affect the caller, which looks like the first camp is right. Mutating what a parameter refers to does affect the caller, which looks like the second is. Any single label has to misrepresent one of those.

    This book's position is that the vocabulary is the problem rather than the behaviour. You already have two rules from Chapter I.3 — rebinding moves a label, mutation changes an object — and those two rules predict every case correctly without needing a name for the scheme. Learning the label teaches you a word; learning the rules teaches you what will happen, which is the thing you actually needed.

    Look at the middle snapshot of Figure I.8.1. Calling a function binds the parameter name, in the new frame, to the same object the argument names. That is all. It is assignment across a frame boundary — the exact operation from Chapter I.3, wearing a different hat.

    So the two rules you already own settle every case forever:

    Rebind the parameter

    n = n + 1

    Moves this frame's label to a new object. The caller's label never moved. When the frame pops, nothing remains.

    Mutate the object

    items.append(...)

    Changes the one shared object. The caller's label points at that object, so the caller sees it — there is nothing else to see.

    Python language

    The rule, stated once. A call binds each parameter name to the argument's object — no copy of the object is made, and no access to the caller's name is granted. A function can therefore never rebind its caller's names, and can always mutate any mutable object it is handed. Both halves are language guarantees.

    The pilot chapter's exercise 4 — the friend whose function sorted the caller's list — is this rule. You solved it before you had the vocabulary.

    Source: Python language reference, calls — arguments are bound to parameter names in the function's namespace.

    Ladder · add_one(x)floors involved

    1. Human intention — run the machine on this value
    2. Python source text
    3. Tokens
    4. Syntax tree — a Call node: which machine, which arguments
    5. Compiler — the body was compiled once, at def, not per call
    6. Code object and bytecode — CALL, then the body's own bytecode, then RETURN_VALUE
    7. CPython runtime — builds the frame, binds arguments into slots, runs, pops
    8. Native machine instructions
    9. CPU control logic
    10. Registers and ALU
    11. Caches and RAM — the frame lives here, in the stack region
    12. Operating-system services
    13. Device, file, terminal, result

    Floor 5 is worth a pause: the body compiles once, when def runs. A million calls reuse one code object. Calling is cheap precisely because defining already did the expensive part.

    Become the machine

    One call, start to finish

    First person

    Trace · CPython executing result = add_one(x)

    1. evalLOAD_NAME add_one — I look up the name and push a reference to the function object.
    2. evalLOAD_NAME x — I push a reference to the int 7. Not a copy of 7. A reference.
    3. evalCALL 1 — one argument. I build a fresh frame for add_one and write the reference into local slot 0, the slot the compiler assigned to n.
    4. evalI start executing the function's code object. Slot 0 holds 7; I add 1, get a reference to 8, and write it back into slot 0. The caller's namespace was never touched.
    5. evalRETURN_VALUE — I pop the frame. Slot 0 ceases to exist; the 8 it pointed at survives only because I am handing a reference to it back.
    6. evalBack in the caller's frame, STORE_NAME result binds the returned reference.
    7. osNo system call anywhere. Calling your own functions is thinking, not speaking.
    Unit I.8.5
    Tool

    Who can see what

    Scope

    Names bound inside a function are local: they live in the frame and die with it. Names bound at the top of the file are global to it. The rules connecting them are short, and the second one has a famous sting.

    Rule one: reading looks outward. A function that only reads a name will find the global one if no local exists. That is why every function you write can use print and len without ceremony.

    Rule two: assignment makes it local — everywhere in the function. The compiler reads the whole body at def time, and any name assigned anywhere in it becomes local throughout it, including on lines above the assignment.

    Predict — the sting

    x = 5 at the top. Then a function whose body is: print(x) on the first line, x = 1 on the second. What happens when you call it?

    The error message is unusually honest: a local variable not yet associated with a value. Slot allocated at compile time, empty at run time. The practical rule: a function should either read a global or have its own local of that name — wanting both is nearly always a design smell, and the cure is to pass the value in as a parameter and hand the new one back with return. (A global declaration exists for the rare genuine need; this book will barely use it.)

    Unit I.8.6
    Break

    The default that remembered

    Second deliberate failure

    New Python — default values

    def greet(name, mark='!'): gives mark a default: call greet('Ada') and mark is '!'; call greet('Ada', '?') and it is '?'. Defaults make arguments optional.

    Predict — nearly everyone gets this wrong once

    def stash(item, box=[]): with body box.append(item) then return box. Call stash(1), then stash(2). What does the second call return?

    Descend

    Defaults are built once, at def

    Earned by the failure

    The expression [] is evaluated when def runs — once — and the resulting list object is stored on the function object. Every call that omits the argument binds box to that same stored object. One object, a new label per call: Chapter I.7 in miniature, and just as with [[0]] * 3, the danger exists only because the shared thing is mutable. mark='!' shares a string across calls too, harmlessly, because nothing can change it.

    The standard cure, used across the entire Python world: default to None, and build the fresh object inside the call.

    Level 3 Runtime model — the pilot's promise about slots, kept

    The pilot chapter's Level-3 panel showed that names inside a function compile to numbered slots — STORE_FAST 0 — instead of dictionary entries. Now you can see the whole picture.

    At def time the compiler reads the entire body, lists every local name (parameters first), and assigns each a slot number for good. The frame built at call time is little more than that array of slots plus a value stack and a position in the bytecode. Binding an argument is one array write. Reading a local is one array read. No text, no hashing, ever.

    This is also the machinery behind the UnboundLocalError sting: the slot for x exists from the first instruction of the function — the compiler put it there — but holds nothing until the assignment runs. Reading an empty slot raises precisely that error.

    CPython

    Frames were once heap-allocated Python objects, one per call; modern CPython lays frame data out in a contiguous internal stack and creates a full frame object only if something asks for it (a debugger, a traceback). Function calls got dramatically cheaper in 3.11 partly through this change. The slot model above is stable; the storage behind it is version-sensitive.

    Category: CPython implementation; internal frame layout changed in 3.11 and since.

    Reconstruct it without looking

    Close the book

    1. Redraw. Draw the three snapshots of Figure I.8.1 for stamp(L) instead of add_one(x) — and show why, this time, the change survives the frame being destroyed.
    2. Explain. To someone who asks "is Python pass-by-value or pass-by-reference?": give the two-sentence answer that makes the question dissolve.
    3. Modify. Write biggest(numbers) returning the largest item of a list without using max (you built the loop in I.6). Then write double_all(numbers) twice: once mutating the caller's list in place, once returning a new list and leaving the original alone. Prove the difference with is.
    4. Transfer. A friend writes def reset(score): score = 0 and cannot understand why scores never reset. Explain with frames and labels, then give them the working version.
    5. Stretch. def f(): return g() and def g(): return f() — each calls the other. Using Figure I.8.1, predict what must eventually happen to the stack region, then call f() and read the error Python gives you. You have just met the limit of Figure 0.4.1's downward arrow.

    Text, properly

    Strings as frozen sequences, methods that build rather than change, f-strings, and the full truth about characters and bytes — keeping the promise from Chapter 0.1

    Text has been in every chapter since 'hello'. This chapter makes it precise — and settles a debt: Chapter 0.1 told you letters are numbers under an agreement, and admitted the agreement it showed you was a simplified one. Here is the real agreement, and it covers every alphabet on Earth.

    Prerequisites

    Chapter 0.1 (bits, bytes, ord and chr, declared simplification S-02), Chapter I.6 (indexing and slicing), Chapter I.7 (immutability and why sharing it is safe). Strings will turn out to be a sequence like a list and frozen like a tuple — you own both halves already.

    Unit I.9.1
    Problem

    Text you have to work on, not just show

    Something you can feel

    So far text has gone in one direction: out of a print. Real programs take text apart — the first letter of a name, the bit before the comma, whether it is shouting — and build new text from pieces: Ada scored 5, where the 5 came from arithmetic a moment ago.

    To do either, you need to know what a string actually is. And the honest answer is: something you already know, twice over.

    Unit I.9.2
    Tool

    A row you can read like a list

    Strings are sequences

    And a for loop walks it exactly as it walks a list — one character at a time — because, as Chapter I.5's Level 3 promised, for only ever asks "give me an iterator, give me the next item", and strings answer.

    Unit I.9.3
    Break

    Fix one letter

    Deliberate failure

    Predict

    s = 'hello'. You want a capital H. Does s[0] = 'H' work? Lists allowed exactly this.

    Descend

    Why text is frozen on purpose

    Earned by the failure

    Chapter I.7 gave you the reasoning, and it lands harder here than anywhere: what cannot change is safe to share. Programs pass text around constantly — names, messages, file paths — and every hand-over is just another label on one object. If strings were mutable, any function you passed a name to could quietly rewrite it, and every label everywhere would see the vandalism. Because they are frozen, handing text to anything is always safe, no defensive copies needed, ever.

    It is worth asking why a string is frozen when a list is not, because the answer is a design decision rather than a technical necessity. Strings are used as dictionary keys constantly — every attribute name, every word in Chapter I.12's tally — and Chapter I.10 shows that a key must not change after filing. Making text immutable puts every string in the safe category permanently, rather than requiring you to remember which ones are safe to file.

    The second reason is sharing. If a string can never change, any number of names may point at one object with no possibility of interference, so Python is free to reuse a single object wherever the same text appears. That is why Chapter I.3's identity experiments behave as they do with text, and it would be impossible if any holder could modify what the others were looking at.

    So how do you get your capital H? You do not fix the old string. You build a new one.

    Unit I.9.4
    Tool

    Methods that build, never change

    The string toolkit

    New Python — string methods

    A method is a function that lives on a value and is called through the dot, as append lives on lists: s.upper(). Every string method that transforms text hands back a new string and leaves the original untouched — it has no other choice.

    The comfortable wrong idea

    "s.upper() converted my string and it did not stick, so the method is broken."

    Nothing converts. upper reads the frozen original, builds a fresh uppercase string, and returns it. Writing s.upper() on its own line computes a value and throws it away — the very fate Chapter I.1 warned about for a bare 2 + 2 in a script. Compare lists: L.sort() mutates and returns None; s.upper() mutates nothing and returns everything. The two designs are opposite, and each is forced by whether the object can change.

    Unit I.9.5
    Tool

    Building text from pieces

    f-strings

    New Python — the f-string

    Put an f before the opening quote and curly brackets become windows: f'{name} scored {score}'. Inside each window you may put any expression; Python evaluates it, turns the result into text, and splices it in. This is the standard way to assemble text in modern Python.

    Ladder · msg = f'{name} scored {2 + 3}'floors involved

    1. Human intention — assemble the message
    2. Python source text
    3. Tokens — the f-prefix makes the windows into real tokens
    4. Syntax tree — a JoinedStr node holding text pieces and expressions
    5. Compiler — folds 2 + 3 to 5, as ever
    6. Code object and bytecode — evaluate each window, convert, join
    7. CPython runtime — builds one new string object in the heap
    8. Native machine instructions
    9. CPU control logic
    10. Registers and ALU — copying characters is arithmetic on addresses
    11. Caches and RAM
    12. Operating-system services
    13. Device, file, terminal, result

    Building text is thinking; floor 12 stays dark until a print speaks it. One statement, one new object, no kernel.

    Unit I.9.6
    Tool

    Two ways to show the same value

    Paying a debt from Chapter I.1

    Chapter I.1 left you with a puzzle. The prompt showed 'hello' with quotation marks; print showed hello without them. Same value, two displays — and the promise was that this chapter would explain it.

    Python keeps two ways of turning any value into text, for two different audiences.

    For a person

    str — what it looks like

    What print uses. The characters themselves, plainly, with nothing added. Meant to be read.

    For a programmer

    repr — what it is

    What the prompt uses. An unambiguous form — text gets its quotes back — so you can tell one kind of value from another. Meant to be inspected.

    This is not a curiosity. 'ada ' and 'ada' are different words to Python, will hash to different slots, and will never match — and printed side by side they look the same. repr makes the invisible visible, which is why it becomes an instrument in Chapter II.3.

    The general principle is worth extracting, because it applies well beyond strings. Two forms exist because they serve different readers. One is for a person reading the output of a finished program, where quotation marks and escapes would be noise. The other is for a person debugging, where the difference between a name and the same name with a trailing space is the entire question, and a form that hides it is useless.

    That is why the prompt shows the second form and print the first, which felt arbitrary in Chapter I.1 and is now explicable: the prompt exists for inspection, and printing exists for output. When a value looks correct and behaves incorrectly, asking for the unambiguous form is the first thing to try — Chapter II.3 makes it a standing technique.

    New Python — !r in an f-string

    Inside an f-string window, {name!r} asks for the repr form instead of the plain one. When you are printing something to inspect it rather than to read it, use !r — a habit that will save you hours later.

    Unit I.9.7
    Rebuild

    The real agreement

    Correcting simplification S-02

    Simplified model

    What you were told in Chapter 0.1: each character is a number under an agreement, one byte per character, ord and chr translating both ways. What was correct: all of it — for English letters, digits and common symbols. What it left out: the world has vastly more than 256 characters, and the modern agreement therefore has two layers, not one.

    Declared simplification S-02. Corrected below, as promised.

    Layer one: every character gets a number. The agreement is called Unicode, the numbers are called code points, and there are more than 150,000 assigned — Latin, Greek, Arabic, Chinese, emoji, all of it. ord and chr speak this layer, and a Python string is a sequence of code points. That is what len counts.

    Layer two: every number gets bytes. A code point like 28,450 does not fit in one byte, so a second agreement — an encoding — says how to pack code points into bytes for disks and networks. The one the world settled on is UTF-8.

    Python language

    Text and bytes are two different types, and Python keeps them apart on purpose. A str is a sequence of code points — meaning. A bytes value is a sequence of raw bytes — storage. .encode() goes from meaning to storage; .decode() comes back, and both need to know which encoding. Mixing the two types without converting is an error, for exactly the reason '5' + 5 was in Chapter I.2: Python refuses to guess.

    The rule of thumb for everything ahead: inside your program, text; at every edge — files, networks, disks — bytes. Volume III lives at those edges.

    Source: Python language reference — str holds Unicode code points; the codecs and bytes documentation.
    Level 3 Runtime model — why UTF-8 won, and what CPython does inside

    UTF-8's width varies: one byte for code points up to 127, two, three or four for the rest. The design has two properties that conquered the world. First, the one-byte characters are the old ASCII values unchanged — every plain-English file ever written was already valid UTF-8, which is why the Chapter 0.1 model worked and why 'A'.encode() is just b'A'. Second, the marker bits mean a reader dropped into the middle of a stream can always find where the next character starts.

    The cost of varying width: to find the millionth character of UTF-8 bytes you must walk from the start — there is no base-plus-offset shortcut, because characters are not all the same size. This is precisely why CPython does not store your strings as UTF-8 internally.

    The trade is one this book has met several times and will meet again. A fixed-width encoding would let you jump straight to the millionth character by multiplying, exactly as Chapter I.6's list finds its millionth slot — but it would spend four bytes on every character, quadrupling the size of ordinary English text. A variable-width encoding spends one byte on the common cases and gives up the ability to calculate a position.

    Which is the right trade depends entirely on what dominates: storage and transmission, or random access. UTF-8 chose storage, which is why it won for files and networks, where text is overwhelmingly read from the beginning and size matters at every step. CPython chose the other way for strings in memory, so indexing stays instant — and the two choices coexist because the conversion happens exactly at the boundary Chapter III.1 describes.

    CPythonHardware example

    CPython inspects a string when it is built and stores every character at the same fixed width — the smallest of 1, 2 or 4 bytes that fits the biggest code point present. Fixed width restores Chapter I.6's indexing trick: position i is base + i × width, one multiply and one add. The prices: a string's memory depends on its widest character (measure sys.getsizeof('a') against sys.getsizeof('漢') on your build — the header alone also differs between versions), and encoding to UTF-8 at the edges is real work done at the edges. CPython also quietly reuses ("interns") many small identifier-like strings — one more instance of Chapter I.7's rule that sharing immutables is free.

    Category: CPython implementation (PEP 393 flexible storage); sizes are version- and build-specific.
    Retrieval lock

    Reconstruct it without looking

    Close the book

    1. Redraw. Draw the two layers for the word hi: characters, code points (ord gives them), bytes under UTF-8. Then do the same for a word containing 漢, and mark where len of the string and len of the bytes disagree.
    2. Explain. Why does s.upper() return a value while L.sort() returns None? Answer from immutability, not from memory of the two facts.
    3. Modify. Using slicing and +, build a capitalised copy of 'hello' without upper or capitalize. Then check the original survived.
    4. Transfer. A friend's program reports the "length" of a user's message as 27 in one place and 31 in another, for the same message. Using the two layers, say what each number is counting and which one the program should almost certainly use for "how many characters did they type".
    5. Stretch. From Figure I.9.1's pattern, work out the largest code point that fits in the three-byte form (how many blank slots are there?). Then check yourself: ord of a character you choose, against len of its encoding.
    Mastery gate — Chapter I.9
    • You can index, slice and measure a string, and loop over its characters.
    • You can explain why s[0] = 'H' fails, and why that restriction is a feature.
    • You can use upper, replace and split, catching the results — and say what split hands back.
    • You can build text with an f-string, including an expression inside a window.
    • You can state the two layers — code points and encodings — and place ord, len, encode and UTF-8 on the correct layer.
    • You can explain why Chapter 0.1's one-byte model worked at all, using the ASCII property of UTF-8.
    • You can say what repr shows that print hides, and why that matters for two strings that look alike.

    Item five is the repair this chapter existed to make. If it is shaky, put Figure I.9.1 beside Figure 0.1.2 — they are the same diagram with a cleverer agreement. Chapter I.10 needs items one to three.

    Volume I · Chapter 10Doing work

    The filing cabinet

    Dictionaries, looking things up by name instead of by position, the hash trick that makes it instant, and why keys must be frozen

    Lists find things by position. But most questions in real life are not "what is in slot two?" — they are "what is Ada's score?". This chapter adds the second great container, and underneath it sits one of the cleverest tricks in all of computing.

    Prerequisites

    Chapter I.6 (lists hold references; base + index × 8 arithmetic), Chapter I.7 (immutability; the promise its Level 3 made about dictionary keys is honoured here), Chapter I.9 (strings). The reveal in Unit I.10.4 leans directly on I.6's indexing trick.

    Unit I.10.1
    Problem

    Two lists, secretly married

    Something you can feel

    Thirty children, thirty scores. With lists you keep names and scores and pray position 7 in one still matches position 7 in the other. Sort one and forget the other, or remove a child from one list only, and every answer after that is quietly wrong.

    And even when the pairing survives, answering "what did Ada get?" means searching: walk the names list, find 'ada', remember the position, read the other list. Thirty names, up to thirty looks. A million names, up to a million looks.

    Two separate problems are tangled there and it is worth pulling them apart, because a dictionary solves both and for different reasons. The first is that the pairing between a name and its score exists only in your head and in the matching of two positions — nothing in the data records that they belong together, so any operation that reorders one list silently destroys the association. The second is the cost of finding: even with the pairing intact, locating Ada means examining names until you meet hers.

    What you want is a single container that stores the pairing itself — this name goes with this score — and answers by name, instantly.

    Unit I.10.2
    Tool

    Filing under a name

    The dictionary

    New Python — the dictionary

    {'ada': 7, 'grace': 4} builds a dictionary (type dict): a container of key: value pairs in curly brackets. The key goes in the square brackets where a list would take a position: phone['ada'] reads, phone['zoe'] = 9 files a new pair, and the same syntax on an existing key replaces its value — keys are unique, so filing under a taken name overwrites. len counts pairs, and 'ada' in phone asks whether a key exists.

    Predict — before you run it

    scores['leo'] — Leo was never filed. What happens? And what should happen — is silence an option?

    Python language

    Three language guarantees. Keys are unique — filing under an existing key replaces its value. A missing key raises KeyError on reading, while assignment to a missing key creates the pair. And a dictionary remembers insertion order: loops and printing walk the pairs in the order they were first added. (That last one was once a CPython accident; since Python 3.7 it is a promise of the language.)

    Source: Python language reference, mapping types; the 3.7 release notes elevating insertion order to a guarantee.
    Unit I.10.3
    Tool

    Walking the cabinet

    Looping over pairs

    New Python — .items(), .values(), and unpacking a pair

    Looping over a dictionary gives its keys. .values() gives just the values; .items() gives each pair as a two-item tuple — and Python lets you unpack a pair straight into two names: for name, score in scores.items(): binds both at once, each pass. (Unpacking works anywhere: a, b = (1, 2) is the same move outside a loop.)

    Unit I.10.4
    Descend

    How it finds Ada without looking for her

    The hash trick

    Here is the puzzle this chapter has been saving. Chapter I.6 showed why list indexing is instant: position 2 is base + 2 × 8 — the machine calculates where to look. But 'ada' is not a position. Surely the dictionary must search?

    It does not. It turns the key into a position.

    That is the sentence to hold on to, and the difference between the two verbs is the whole chapter. Searching means examining candidates until one matches, so the work grows with how many there are. Computing a position means doing an arithmetic operation on the key itself and going straight there, so the work does not depend on how many are stored at all. A dictionary with ten items and one with ten million answer at the same speed, which is not an optimisation of searching but a refusal to search.

    A hash function takes any key and produces a number from it — the same key always giving the same number. Take that number, wrap it round the table size, and you have a slot index. Now the I.6 arithmetic works again: base plus slot times slot-width. The dictionary does not find Ada. It computes where Ada must be, and goes straight there — whether the cabinet holds three pairs or three million.

    Become the machine

    Filing Zoe

    First person

    Trace · CPython executing scores['zoe'] = 9

    1. evalI have references to the dict, the key 'zoe' and the value 9 on my stack. The opcode says store-by-subscript.
    2. evalI ask the key for its hash. Strings know how to answer: a number computed from their characters.
    3. aluWrap the hash round the table size — a masking operation, floor 10 arithmetic, a nanosecond.
    4. evalI go straight to that slot. Empty — good. I write two references into it: one to the key object, one to the value object. The dictionary stores references, exactly as lists do.
    5. evalIf the slot had been taken by a different key that happened to land there, I would step to another slot by a fixed rule — more on that in Level 3.
    6. osNo system call. Filing is thinking.
    Unit I.10.5
    Break

    The key that would not file

    Deliberate failure

    Predict — the model decides

    A list as a key: {[1, 2]: 'point'}. Given how lookup works — the key's content becomes the position — what could go wrong with a key that can change its content?

    Descend

    Why a changeable key is a lost key

    Earned by the failure

    Suppose Python allowed it. You file a value under the key [1, 2] — its content hashes to slot 5, so the pair lands in slot 5. Then you append: the key is now [1, 2, 3], whose content hashes to slot 41.

    The argument is worth following rather than accepting, because it shows the restriction is forced rather than chosen. The whole mechanism rests on one assumption: that hashing a key today gives the same answer as hashing it tomorrow. If that fails, the value is filed at one address and later sought at another, and the dictionary will report that a key it is certainly holding does not exist — the worst kind of failure, since the data is present and unreachable.

    A mutable object cannot make that promise. Its hash depends on its contents, and its contents can change after filing, so nothing prevents the address from moving out from under the stored value. Python therefore refuses at the moment of filing rather than allowing a corruption that would surface much later and look inexplicable. Chapter I.7's tuples are acceptable keys for exactly the complementary reason: their contents are fixed, so their hash is too.

    Now look it up. The dictionary hashes what you hand it, walks to slot 41 — empty. Your value still sits in slot 5, but nothing will ever compute 5 from the key again. The pair is not deleted; it is unfindable — filed under a name that no longer exists.

    The rule this earns — and honours Chapter I.7's promise

    A key must hash the same way forever, so a key must be unable to change. Dictionary keys must be immutable — not by decree, but because a mutable key would break the one trick the whole cabinet stands on.

    Strings, numbers and all-immutable tuples: keys. Lists, dictionaries, sets: values only. And values may be anything at all, because a value is only ever reached, never used to compute where to look.

    Ladder · scores['ada']floors involved

    1. Human intention — what did Ada get?
    2. Python source text
    3. Tokens
    4. Syntax tree — a Subscript node, same as a list's
    5. Compiler
    6. Code object and bytecode — load dict, load key, subscript
    7. CPython runtime — hash the key, mask, probe, compare, hand back the value reference
    8. Native machine instructions
    9. CPU control logic
    10. Registers and ALU — hashing and masking are pure arithmetic
    11. Caches and RAM — one slot read, wherever the arithmetic pointed
    12. Operating-system services
    13. Device, file, terminal, result

    Same dark floors as a list index, and nearly the same cost — a little arithmetic bought you lookup by meaning. That trade, computation for search, is the deepest idea in this chapter.

    Level 3 Runtime model — collisions, crowding, and the growing cabinet

    Two loose ends make the picture honest.

    Collisions. Different keys can hash to the same slot — with a small table it is unavoidable. When the slot a key computes is already held by a different key, CPython steps to another slot by a fixed, repeatable recipe, and keeps stepping until it finds the key or an empty slot. Lookups therefore sometimes take two or three looks instead of one. On average, with a sensibly sized table, the count stays tiny and does not grow with the cabinet.

    Crowding. Collisions multiply as the table fills, so CPython never lets it fill: when roughly two-thirds of the slots are taken, it builds a bigger table and re-files every pair into it (each key re-hashed, since the wrap-around size changed). One expensive rebuild, rarely — the same amortised bargain as the growing list in Chapter I.6's Level 3. An empty dict already spends 64 bytes on this build for exactly this headroom.

    CPython

    Modern CPython actually splits the structure in two — a compact table of entries in insertion order, plus a small index array of positions — which is how the memory stayed small and the ordering guarantee became cheap to keep. The probing recipe, the two-thirds threshold and the growth factors are implementation details that have changed between versions. One more, for later: hashes of strings are deliberately randomised each time Python starts, a security measure against attackers who could otherwise manufacture collisions on purpose — so never write down a string's hash and expect it tomorrow. Numbers hash predictably: hash(7) is 7.

    Category: CPython implementation — compact dicts, open addressing, hash randomisation. Verify thresholds against the CPython source for your version.
    Retrieval lock

    Reconstruct it without looking

    Close the book

    1. Redraw. Draw Figure I.10.1's lower panel for filing 'grace', inventing a slot. Then draw the lookup that finds her, and mark the exact step where a mutated key would have broken it.
    2. Explain. Why can a dictionary use a tuple as a key but not a list — and why does a list inside a tuple spoil it? Two sentences, using hash and Chapter I.7's shallow-immutability rule.
    3. Modify. Take the two married lists from Unit I.10.1 and write a loop that builds one dictionary from them (loop over positions with range). Then answer "what did Ada get?" both ways and count the looks each design needs.
    4. Transfer. A friend counts words in a story by keeping a list of words seen and a list of counts, searching the first list for every word. The program is fine on a page and crawls on a book. Diagnose with this chapter, and sketch the dictionary version — .get(word, 0) makes it three lines.
    5. Stretch. Values are references, and nothing stops two keys' values referencing one object. Build shared = [], then d = {'a': shared, 'b': shared}. Predict what d looks like after d['a'].append(1), check, and explain with a drawing. Chapter I.7, in a new costume.
    Mastery gate — Chapter I.10
    • You can build a dictionary, read, add, replace, and test membership with in.
    • You can say what happens on a missing key, and when .get with a fallback is the right tool instead.
    • You can loop over keys, values and pairs, unpacking pairs into two names.
    • You can explain the hash trick — content becomes position — and connect it to Chapter I.6's indexing arithmetic.
    • You can explain why keys must be immutable, from the trick rather than as a rule to memorise.
    • You can state the insertion-order guarantee and which Python made it official.

    Items four and five are one idea seen from two sides. If either is shaky, walk the "filing Zoe" trace with a mutable key and watch where it becomes nonsense. Chapter I.12 builds its program on this container.
