    Volume I · Chapter 11Python foundations

    When things go wrong

    Exceptions, reading a traceback as a map of the stack, catching with try, refusing with raise — and why the broad net is worse than the crash

    Programs meet things their authors did not arrange for. A file is missing, a user types a word where a number was wanted, a calculation divides by zero. Python's response is to stop, loudly, with a report — and that report turns out to be a picture of Chapter I.8's stack of frames, which makes it far more useful than it first appears.

    Prerequisites

    Chapter I.8 and Figure I.8.1 (frames, and the stack of them — a traceback is that stack, printed), Chapter I.4 (conditions), Chapter I.2 (types, since exceptions have types), Chapter I.10 (dictionaries, for KeyError). Chapter IV.6 builds this machinery from scratch and explains what it costs.

    Unit I.11.1
    Problem

    The user types "twelve"

    Something you can feel

    Your program asks for a number and receives the word twelve. It cannot proceed, because there is no sensible number to proceed with. What should it do?

    Enumerate the possibilities and the design becomes clear. It could carry on with some substitute — zero, perhaps — which is the worst option, because the program then produces confident, plausible, wrong output. Chapter II.2 will argue this point at length; here it is enough to notice that a wrong answer nobody questions is more expensive than a stop.

    It could return a special value meaning failure, and require every caller to check. That is a real design, used by real languages, and Chapter IV.6 gives it a fair hearing; its weakness is that forgetting the check is undetectable.

    Python's answer is to stop and say so, in a way that cannot be ignored by accident.

    An exception is an object describing a problem, and raising one abandons the current work and looks for somebody prepared to deal with it. If nobody is, the program stops and prints a report.

    Three properties of that arrangement are worth naming now, because everything else in the chapter follows from them. It abandons the remaining work, which is essential rather than merely tidy: if the rest of the function ran anyway it would run on the assumption that the failed step had succeeded. It searches, outwards through the callers, rather than reporting to the immediate caller and stopping — because the code able to do something sensible about a missing file is rarely the code that tried to open it. And it carries information, both a type and a message, so that the handler can tell what happened.

    The type deserves particular attention because it is the part a program can act on. A message is for a person; a type is a fact your code can test. That is why Python has dozens of specific exception types rather than one general one — ValueError, TypeError, KeyError, FileNotFoundError — and why choosing the right one when you raise, in Unit I.11.5, matters more than the wording of the message.

    Unit I.11.2
    Descend

    The traceback is a map of the stack

    Reading the report

    The report is called a traceback, and people learn to skip to the last line. That habit discards most of the information.

    The wording most recent call last is Python telling you the order explicitly, and it is worth trusting rather than guessing: the bottom line is where the exception was raised, and the lines above it are how execution arrived there.

    Both ends matter, for different questions. The bottom tells you what failed. The lines above tell you why that code was running at all — and when a function is called from several places, that is frequently the more useful fact. A KeyError in a lookup function tells you little, since the lookup function is presumably correct; knowing which of five callers passed the bad key tells you everything, and it is the third line from the bottom that says so.

    There is a reason the habit of skipping to the last line is so common, and it is worth naming so you can resist it. The last line is the only part that is reliably short and reliably readable, and the lines above are full of file paths and line numbers that look like noise. But those lines are the only record of a fact that exists nowhere else in the program: the particular sequence of calls that occurred on this occasion. The source code contains every call that could happen; the traceback tells you which ones did.

    A practical consequence follows for long tracebacks, which frequently pass through library code. The most useful line is usually the lowest one that belongs to your program, because that is the last point at which you decided something. Everything below it is a library doing what it was asked; everything above is how you arrived. Reading a fifty-line traceback becomes manageable once you look for that boundary rather than trying to follow all of it.

    The stack is not merely printed for your benefit; the exception object carries it, and you can walk it.

    Unit I.11.3
    Tool

    Meeting the error instead of dying

    try and except

    New Python — try / except

    Code in a try block runs normally. If an exception is raised inside it, and an except clause names that exception's type, the rest of the try block is abandoned and the handler runs instead. as e binds the exception object so you can inspect it.

    The placement of the try block is a decision rather than a formality, and the principle is to make it as small as the operation you are guarding. A handler is written with a particular failure in mind, and every additional line inside the try is another operation whose failures that handler will also absorb — including failures it was never designed for and cannot sensibly address. Unit I.11.4 shows what that costs when taken to its extreme, but the milder version is common: a try wrapped around ten lines because one of them might fail.

    Exception types form a hierarchy, and catching a type also catches everything beneath it. That is a useful fact and a dangerous one.

    Two further clauses complete the statement, and both earn their place.

    Unit I.11.4
    Break

    The net that catches too much

    Deliberate failure

    Since naming the type is fiddly, it is tempting to catch everything. Watch what that costs.

    Predict

    A function catches Exception and returns None. Inside the try, a variable name is misspelled — tekst instead of text. What does the function do?

    Why the broad net is worse than the crash

    An uncaught exception is a good outcome: it stops immediately, names the problem, and shows you exactly where. A handler that catches everything converts that into a wrong answer with no report — which is the worst outcome available.

    So the rule is: catch what you can actually handle, and name it. If a handler cannot state which failure it is for, it is not a handler; it is a way of hiding whatever goes wrong.

    It is worth being precise about why this is so much worse than an ordinary bug, because the instinct is to see it as a minor lapse in style. An uncaught NameError is nearly the best failure available: it stops at once, names the misspelled variable, and points at the exact line. The cost of finding it is seconds. Caught by a broad handler, the same defect produces a function that returns a plausible value for valid input, which may be wrong in a way that only shows up much later and much further away — in a report, in a stored record, in a decision made on the strength of it. The handler did not merely fail to help; it converted a trivially diagnosable failure into an expensive one.

    The same reasoning gives the test for whether a handler is legitimate. Ask what the handler does about the failure. If it can name the situation and take a considered action — substitute a default, retry, report to the user in terms they can act on — it is a handler. If it merely returns None, or logs and continues, for anything at all that might go wrong, it is not handling anything; it is suppressing the report. And a program that cannot report its failures is a program you cannot debug.

    There is one legitimate use for the broad net, and it has a distinctive shape: a long-running program that must not die, such as a server handling many independent requests. There, catching everything at the boundary of one request is right, because one bad request should not stop the others. Even then the handler must record what it caught, in full, including the traceback — the point is to contain the failure, not to conceal it. A broad handler that logs nothing is indefensible in every context.

    Unit I.11.5
    Tool

    Raising your own refusals

    raise, and saying why

    Exceptions are not only something that happens to you. When your own function is asked for something it cannot sensibly do, the right response is the same one int gave you.

    Choosing the type matters, because it is what a caller can act on. ValueError means the argument was of the right kind but an unusable one — a negative length, an empty list where one item was needed. TypeError means it was the wrong kind of thing entirely, such as a string where a number was required. KeyError and IndexError mean a lookup found nothing. Using an accurate type lets a caller catch precisely, which is exactly what Unit I.11.4 asked of them, and a function that raises a generic Exception makes precise catching impossible for everybody downstream.

    The message deserves care too, and the criterion is concrete: it should contain the information needed to understand the failure without reading the source. 'invalid input' satisfies nobody. f'average of an empty list is undefined' says what was attempted and why it could not be done, and including the offending value — as int does when it quotes back the text it could not convert — saves a debugging session. The rule of thumb is to imagine the message appearing in a log at three in the morning with no other context.

    When you catch one error and raise another, say where it came from.

    Ladder · an exception travellingwhere it is decided and where it ends

    1. Human intention — this cannot proceed
    2. Python source text — raise, or an operation that fails
    3. Tokens
    4. Syntax tree
    5. Compiler — records which instructions each handler protects, in a table
    6. Code object and bytecode — the handler's instructions, and the table beside them
    7. CPython runtime — frames are discarded one by one until a handler is found
    8. Native machine instructions
    9. CPU control logic — ultimately, a number written into the counter
    10. Registers and ALU
    11. Caches and RAM — the exception object, and the traceback built from the wreckage
    12. Operating-system services — dark, unless the traceback is printed
    13. Device, file, terminal, result

    Floor 5 is the surprise, and Chapter IV.6 makes it the centre of its argument: which instructions a handler protects is decided at compile time and written into a table. Entering a try block therefore executes no instructions at all — it costs nothing until something actually fails, which is why guarding code generously is free and why failing is not.

    Retrieval lock

    Reconstruct it without looking

    Close the book

    1. Explain. Give three things a function could do when asked for something impossible, and say what is wrong with the two Python did not choose.
    2. Redraw. Write a three-deep call chain that fails, run it, and label each traceback line with the frame it corresponds to.
    3. Explain. Why do the upper lines of a traceback matter? Give a case where the bottom line alone is not enough.
    4. Modify. Write a function that catches ValueError precisely. Then introduce a typo inside the try and confirm it is still reported. Then widen the handler to Exception and watch the typo vanish.
    5. Explain. Why is an uncaught exception a better outcome than a handler that catches everything?
    6. Modify. Write a function that raises for invalid input, choosing the type deliberately. Say what a caller can now do that a returned None would not permit.
    7. Modify. Use raise ... from e and read the resulting traceback. Say what each half tells you.
    8. Stretch. Write a try with all four clauses and a flag that decides whether it raises. Record which clauses run in each case, and explain the difference between else and putting the code at the end of the try.
    Mastery gate — Chapter I.11
    • You can read a traceback and say which line is the failure and which are the route to it.
    • You can relate a traceback to Figure I.8.1's stack of frames.
    • You can catch a specific exception type and explain why the type matters.
    • You can explain the exception hierarchy and what catching a parent type does.
    • You can say what else and finally each guarantee.
    • You can explain why catching Exception is usually wrong, with a concrete example.
    • You can raise an appropriate exception from your own function and justify the type.
    • You can use raise ... from and say what is lost without it.

    If item six is shaky, run the typo experiment. Watching a misspelled name become a plausible None is the most persuasive argument in this chapter, and it is a defect that can live in real code for years.

    Back · Chapter I.10Looking things up Next · Chapter I.12One complete program
    Volume I · Chapter 12Doing work

    One complete program

    Building a word tally from every chapter of this volume — and discovering what you have actually built

    Eleven chapters of parts. This one assembles them into a real program that answers a real question, fails in an instructive way halfway through, and ends with a small shock about what the finished thing is.

    Prerequisites

    All of Volume I. Every tool here has been taught: strings and methods (I.9), dictionaries and .get (I.10), loops (I.5), lists and slicing (I.6), functions with defaults (I.8), f-strings (I.9), raise (I.11). Nothing new arrives except three small conveniences, each boxed as usual.

    Unit I.12.1
    Problem

    What is this passage actually about?

    Something you can feel

    Hand someone a page of text and ask what it leans on. They will guess. Count the words instead and the answer stops being an opinion — the words a passage repeats are the words it is built from.

    Counting by hand is unbearable past a paragraph, and unreliable long before that. This is precisely the kind of dull, exact, repetitive work that Chapter 0.2's paper processor was invented for.

    It is worth being explicit about why this task closes Volume I, because it was not chosen for difficulty. It was chosen because it needs almost everything the volume built, and needs each piece for a visible reason. Text arrives as a string, so Chapter I.9's methods apply. Words must be separated, counted, and looked up by name, which is Chapter I.10's dictionary rather than a list. The counting is a loop, the reporting a sort, the guarding an exception — and the whole must be organised into functions, which is Chapter I.8.

    A second reason is that the task contains a genuine decision the language cannot make for you: what counts as the same word. That question has no technical answer, and the unit below shows what happens when it is answered by accident rather than deliberately.

    Here is our passage, deliberately tiny so you can check every answer by eye:

    Unit I.12.2
    Smallest working Python

    A tally in four lines

    And a prediction worth making

    Chapter I.10's transfer exercise sketched this: a dictionary from word to count, and .get(word, 0) to treat "never seen" as zero.

    Predict — write down two numbers before running

    After tallying all fourteen words: (a) what will tally['the'] be? (b) how many different words will the dictionary hold?

    Count them off the passage above. Both answers are checkable by eye, which is why the passage is this small.

    Unit I.12.3
    Break

    The dictionary is not wrong

    Deliberate failure, and what it teaches

    It is tempting to say the dictionary made a mistake. It did not. It did precisely what Chapter I.10 said it would, and the reason is worth sitting with.

    Sit with that, because it is the shape of most defects you will meet. Nothing malfunctioned. The dictionary applied its rule perfectly, the loop ran exactly as written, and every individual step was correct. The program is still wrong, because a rule its author held in their head — that The and the are one word — was never communicated to the program at all.

    A defect of that kind cannot be found by checking the code against itself, since the code is internally consistent. It can only be found by checking the code against an intention, which is why Chapter II.2 is about writing intentions down in a form the machine can check, and why Chapter II.3 insists the productive question is what you are assuming rather than where the mistake is.

    A key becomes a position by hashing its exact content. 'The' and 'the' are different content, so they hash to different slots — and a slot has no notion of two keys "really being the same word". Nor does 'sat.' resemble 'sat': one is four characters, one is three. The cabinet filed four distinct keys under four distinct names, flawlessly.

    The lesson, which outlives this program

    The machine compares content, exactly. "Same word" is a human idea, and if you want it, you must define it.

    Almost every real counting bug is this: two things a person would call identical, which the machine correctly sees as different. Capitals, punctuation, a stray space at the end.

    Rebuild

    Defining "same word" yourself

    One small function

    New Python — strip with characters

    word.strip('.,!?;:') returns a new string with any of those characters removed from both ends — not the middle, so "don't" keeps its apostrophe. Like every string method from Chapter I.9, it builds a new string and leaves the original frozen and untouched.

    Unit I.12.4
    Tool

    Putting the winners first

    Sorting by something other than the value

    A dictionary keeps insertion order, not rank. To report the most-used words you need them sorted by count — and that means sorting by something other than the items themselves.

    New Python — sort with a key function

    list(counts.items()) turns the pairs into a real list you can reorder. pairs.sort(key=by_count, reverse=True) sorts it: key takes a function, which Python calls on each item to decide what to sort by, and reverse=True puts the largest first. Note there are no brackets after by_count — you are handing over the machine, not its result. Chapter I.8's type(greet) line was the promise; this is where it pays.

    Unit I.12.5
    Tool

    Refusing nonsense at the door

    The guard

    What happens if someone hands count_words a number? It would reach text.split() and fail with a message about integers having no split — technically true, unhelpful, and pointing at a line that is not the mistake.

    New Python — isinstance

    isinstance(text, str) asks whether a value is of a given type, and answers True or False. It is type() from Chapter I.2 in a form you can put straight into an if.

    Unit I.12.6
    Assemble

    The finished program

    Every chapter, at once

    Ladder · running tally.pythe whole volume, one program

    1. Human intention — what does this passage lean on?
    2. Python source text — twenty-six lines on disk
    3. Tokens — including the INDENT and DEDENT that carry your blocks
    4. Syntax tree — five FunctionDef nodes and a call
    5. Compiler — one code object per function, locals assigned slot numbers
    6. Code object and bytecode — FOR_ITER, COMPARE_OP, JUMP_BACKWARD, CALL, subscripts
    7. CPython runtime — frames pushed and popped; strings, ints and dicts built in the heap
    8. Native machine instructions — CPython's own compiled C, all the way down
    9. CPU control logic — fetch, decode, execute, some millions of times
    10. Registers and ALU — hashing, masking, comparing, address arithmetic
    11. Caches and RAM — the stack region for frames, the heap for every object
    12. Operating-system services — only for the four print lines
    13. Device, file, terminal, result — four lines of text

    All thirteen lit, and floor 12 lit for four lines out of a program that does thousands of operations. Almost everything your program does, it does entirely inside its own room — which is the shape of nearly every program you will ever write.

    Unit I.12.7
    Descend

    What you have actually built

    The reveal

    Read the shape of your program, ignoring what it counts.

    The recognition is worth taking seriously rather than treating as a pleasing coincidence. You did not set out to write a tokenizer; you set out to count words, and arrived at that shape because the problem required it. That is evidence about the shape rather than about you — splitting a stream into meaningful units, discarding what carries no meaning, and normalising what remains is one of a small number of structures that recur throughout computing, and it recurs because a great many problems genuinely have that form.

    It takes a stream of characters. It breaks that stream into meaningful units, deciding where one ends and the next begins. It normalises each unit so that superficial differences stop mattering. It discards what is not meaningful. It files what remains in a hash table, keyed by exact content, and looks each one up instantly as it goes.

    Now look at Figure 0.5.2 again — the four stages from source text to bytecode. Stage one is called the tokenizer, and the description you just read is what a tokenizer does.

    Simplified model

    What this comparison gets right: the pipeline shape — stream in, units out, normalise, discard, look up — and the use of a hash table for names. What it leaves out: a real tokenizer tracks line and column numbers for error messages, handles quotes and brackets and nesting, and emits the INDENT and DEDENT tokens that carry Python's block structure — none of which split can do. The fuller version is Volume IV, where you build a real one and compare it with CPython's.

    Declared simplification, discharged in Volume IV.
    Retrieval lock

    Reconstruct it without looking

    Close the book

    1. Redraw. Without the listing in front of you, write the four functions' names and one sentence each saying what it does and what it hands back. Then check — if any needs two sentences, it is doing two jobs.
    2. Explain. Why did the naive tally report eleven different words instead of eight, and why was the dictionary not at fault? Use hash and exact content.
    3. Modify. Add a function unique_words(text) returning how many different words a passage uses, then report the rarest three instead of the commonest — one argument changes. Then make tidy keep apostrophes but strip quotation marks, and prove with don't that you broke nothing.
    4. Transfer. The program counts cat and cats as different words. Decide whether that is a bug, and say where the fix would go — then explain why that answer is a consequence of how you built it, not luck.
    5. Stretch. report calls count_words, which calls tidy, once per word. Draw the frame stack at the moment tidy is running on the last word. Then predict what a traceback would look like if tidy raised — how many lines, naming which functions — and test it by making tidy raise deliberately.
    Mastery gate — Chapter I.12, and the whole of Volume I
    • You can build a program from small functions that each do one nameable thing.
    • You can count occurrences with a dictionary and .get, and explain why exact content decides what counts as the same key.
    • You can sort by something other than the values themselves, by handing a function to key — and say why handing over by_count without brackets is what makes it work.
    • You can guard a function's input and raise a clear error, and say what a good error message must contain.
    • You can walk any statement of your own program down the thirteen floors, and say which floors each line uses.
    • You can explain what your tally has in common with a tokenizer, and where the comparison stops.

    This gate closes Volume I. Item five is the one that proves the volume worked: if you can take your own line of code and say what happens at every floor from intention to terminal, you have the integrated model this book exists to build. If it is shaky, the return path is Chapter 0.5's assembled ladder and this chapter's ladder, read one after the other.

    Where this goes next

    You can now write real programs, and explain them from the Python down to the transistors. What Volume II adds is cost: why one correct program takes a second and another takes a week, what a data structure really costs, and how to measure rather than guess. Every question there begins where this chapter ends — with a program that works, asking what it is actually doing.

    It is worth being precise about what this program does not yet have, since Volume II begins by supplying each. It has no tests, so nothing but your own reading confirms it works — and Chapter II.2 will find a real defect in it that is present right now and that neither you nor its author noticed. It cannot be reused from another file, which Chapter II.4 fixes. Its counting and membership choices have costs nobody has measured, which Chapters II.8 and II.9 make visible. And it is one file with everything at the top level, which is fine at this size and stops being fine quickly.

    None of that makes it a bad program. It is a correct-looking, readable, working piece of software of exactly the kind Volume I set out to teach. The point of Volume II is that correct-looking and working are different claims, and that the tools for telling them apart are worth having.

    Volume II · Chapter 1Structures, programs and cost

    Membership and making

    Sets as dictionaries without values, comprehensions as loops that build, and the first honest measurement of what a data structure is worth

    Volume I gave you lists and dictionaries and, quietly, two different answers to the question "is this in there?" — one of which is enormously more expensive than the other. This chapter makes that difference visible, introduces the structure built for exactly that question, and then introduces the notation Python uses for building one collection from another.

    Prerequisites

    Chapter I.6 (lists, and the in test), Chapter I.10 (dictionaries, hashing, and why keys must be immutable — a set is that machinery with one part removed), Chapter I.5 (loops), Chapter I.12 (the word tally, which this chapter's technique would simplify). Chapter II.8 gives the notation for the growth measured here; Chapter II.9 explains the mechanism.

    Unit II.1.1
    Problem

    Have I seen this before?

    Something you can feel

    It is among the most common questions a program asks. Have I processed this identifier already? Is this word in the list of words to ignore? Has this visitor been here before? With a list, the answer is available and the way it is obtained is worth looking at.

    A list keeps its items in order, one after another, and knows nothing about what they are. So the only way it can answer "is x in here?" is to look at each item and compare. If x is absent, that means comparing against every single item before it can say no.

    That is fine for ten items. The question is what happens as the collection grows, and the reason it matters is that the growth is not in the number of items but in the total work, which is the number of items multiplied by the number of questions asked.

    The reason a list has no choice deserves a sentence, because it is not a deficiency to be fixed. A list's promise is that item five is at a known place, which requires the slots to sit in order at a fixed width. Nothing in that arrangement says anything about what is in them. So a list can find a position instantly and can only find a value by looking, and those two facts are the same fact seen from either end.

    Make it concrete by counting rather than timing, which is the instrument Chapter II.8 will formalise. Removing duplicates from a list requires asking, for each item, whether it has been seen already.

    Unit II.1.2
    Descend

    You have already built this

    A set is a dictionary with the values removed

    Chapter I.10 gave you a structure that answers a membership question without searching. A dictionary finds a key by computing a number from it — a hash — and using that number to go straight to where the key would be if it were present. No scanning; one computation and one look.

    Now notice that when you are only asking "have I seen this?", the values are dead weight. You want the keys and nothing else.

    The saving comes from the same place as the dictionary's. Chapter I.10 showed that a hash turns the key into a position rather than searching for it, so the number of items already stored has no bearing on how long the answer takes. That property is what you want here and the values were never part of it, so removing them costs nothing and keeps everything.

    What a set is

    A set is that machinery with the values removed: a collection of unique items that can say whether something is present without looking at everything.

    Which means everything Chapter I.10 established about dictionary keys applies unchanged. Items must be hashable, therefore immutable. Duplicates are impossible, because two equal items would hash to the same place. And there is no order, because position is determined by hash rather than by arrival.

    One consequence catches people, and it is worth meeting deliberately: {} is an empty dictionary, not an empty set, because dictionaries claimed the notation first. An empty set is set().

    Unit II.1.3
    Rebuild

    The same program, a thousand times cheaper

    The measurement

    Run the same duplicate-removal with a set for the membership test, counting the same way.

    Two things are worth saying about that result, because a factor of a thousand invites the wrong conclusion.

    It is not that sets are fast and lists are slow. Both structures do exactly what they were built for. A list keeps things in order and lets you have the fifth item instantly; a set cannot do either, and has no order at all. The improvement came from matching the structure to the question, which is the recurring subject of this volume rather than a fact about two types.

    And the cost is not nothing. A set uses more memory than a list for the same items, since the hash table keeps empty space to make collisions rare. It requires items to be hashable, which rules out lists and dictionaries as members. Chapter II.9 shows exactly what is being bought and paid for; until then the trade is worth stating rather than presenting sets as strictly better.

    There is a subtler cost worth naming, because it catches people who reach for a set as a general improvement. A set discards duplicates and discards order, and those are not always dead weight — sometimes they are your data. Counting how many times each word appears needs the duplicates, so Chapter I.12 needed a dictionary. Reporting results in the order they arrived needs the order, so a set would silently lose it. Reaching for a set is only correct when you genuinely do not want either.

    The practical rule is short. If you are asking "is this in here?" more than a handful of times, and you do not need order or repeats, use a set. If you find yourself writing if x in some_list inside a loop, you have found a defect Chapter II.8 will teach you to recognise on sight.

    Unit II.1.4
    Tool

    A loop that hands back a collection

    Comprehensions

    The second subject of this chapter is notation rather than machinery, and it is worth having now because everything after this uses it.

    A very common shape of loop does nothing but build a collection: make an empty one, walk something, append a transformed item, sometimes skipping. Three lines of setup and bookkeeping around one line of actual intent.

    The construction works for the other structures too, and the choice of brackets decides which you get.

    One further variation is worth flagging now and is developed in Chapter II.5: change the square brackets to round ones and you get something that produces items on demand rather than building them all first. That distinction does not matter for six squares and matters enormously for six million, since one arrangement needs memory for every item at once and the other needs memory for one.

    The comfortable wrong idea

    "Comprehensions are faster, so I should convert my loops."

    They are modestly faster, because the appending is done by the interpreter rather than by a method call you make each time. That is not the reason to use them. The reason is that a comprehension says what it produces: seeing one, you know a collection is being built and nothing else is happening. A loop might be building a collection, or printing, or modifying something elsewhere, and you must read the body to find out.

    Which also gives the rule for when not to use one. If the body does more than produce items — if it prints, writes a file, or updates something outside — then a comprehension is actively misleading, because it claims to be building a collection when its real purpose is the side effect. And a comprehension spanning several lines with multiple conditions has given up the clarity that justified it. The plain loop is not a lesser form; it is the right form whenever the work is not simply making one thing from another.

    Chapter I.12's word tally has a line this notation improves, and it is worth going back to look. Anywhere a list is built by walking another collection, the shape applies — and Chapter II.5 will show that changing one bracket turns the whole thing lazy, producing items on demand rather than building them all at once.

    Ladder · x in collectionone line, two entirely different amounts of work

    1. Human intention — choosing the structure; the cost is decided here
    2. Python source text — identical either way
    3. Tokens
    4. Syntax tree
    5. Compiler
    6. Code object and bytecode — the same instruction in both cases
    7. CPython runtime — a scan, or a hash and one look: decided by the object's type
    8. Native machine instructions
    9. CPU control logic
    10. Registers and ALU
    11. Caches and RAM — a walk through many objects, or one jump
    12. Operating-system services
    13. Device, file, terminal, result

    Floor 6 is the striking one: the bytecode is identical for both versions, because the instruction means "ask this object whether it contains that". What happens next is decided at floor 7 by which type was asked — which is Chapter II.7's protocol idea, and the reason a thousandfold difference in work leaves no trace in the source or in the compiled instructions.

    Retrieval lock

    Reconstruct it without looking

    Close the book

    1. Explain. Why must a list compare against every item to answer a failed membership test? Say what it would need to know to avoid that.
    2. Explain. Describe a set in terms of Chapter I.10's dictionary, and derive three of its restrictions from that description.
    3. Modify. Count the steps for duplicate removal at four sizes with a list and with a set. Report both ratios and say which is which.
    4. Explain. Give two things a list can do that a set cannot, and two costs of a set.
    5. Modify. Rewrite three loops of your own as comprehensions. Then find one that should not be converted and say why.
    6. Transfer. A colleague's script slows dramatically as its input grows. They mention checking membership against a list of previously-seen identifiers. Diagnose it without seeing the code.
    7. Explain. Why is {} an empty dictionary rather than an empty set, and what is the empty set?
    8. Stretch. Time both versions as well as counting them. Explain why the time ratio and the step ratio differ, and which you would trust for predicting behaviour on ten times the data.
    Mastery gate — Chapter II.1
    • You can explain why membership in a list costs what it does.
    • You can describe a set as a dictionary without values, and derive its restrictions.
    • You can measure the difference by counting rather than timing.
    • You can state what a set costs as well as what it saves.
    • You can write list, set and dictionary comprehensions.
    • You can say why a comprehension is clearer, and when it is the wrong choice.
    • You can recognise if x in some_list inside a loop as a problem.
    • You can explain why the same source line can do wildly different amounts of work.

    If item seven is shaky, it is the single most valuable pattern-recognition in this volume. Chapter II.8 gives it a name and Chapter II.9 explains the mechanism, but the habit of noticing it is worth forming now.

    Back · Chapter I.12One complete program Next · Chapter II.2Proving it works
    Volume II · Chapter 2Structures, programs and cost

    Proving it works

    Assertions, tests as executable claims, choosing what to claim — and finding a genuine bug in the program you were proud of

    Chapter I.12 ended with a working program, and it does work, on the passage it was written for. This chapter asks a harder question: how would you know? The answer turns out to require deciding what your program promises, which is a more demanding exercise than it sounds — and doing it here uncovers a real defect that was present all along and that nobody noticed, including its author.

    Prerequisites

    Chapter I.12 (the word tally — this chapter tests that exact program, so keep it to hand), Chapter I.8 (functions), Chapter I.10 (dictionaries), Chapter I.11 (exceptions and raise), Chapter I.4 (conditions and comparison). Chapter II.3 will use what this chapter finds.

    Unit II.2.1
    Problem

    "It worked when I tried it"

    Something you can feel

    You ran the program. The right numbers appeared. That is evidence, and it is worth being precise about what it is evidence of: that the program produces the right answer for one input, on one machine, on one occasion, as judged by an author who already believed it was correct.

    Each of those qualifications hides a real failure. One input, because Chapter I.12's passage happens to contain nothing awkward. One occasion, because you have not run it since changing three other things. And the judgement is the weakest link of all — you looked at the output and it matched what you expected, but your expectation came from the same understanding that produced the code. If that understanding was wrong, the output looked right precisely because it was wrong in the way you expected.

    That last point deserves emphasis, because it is why "I checked the output" is so much weaker than it feels. Reading your own program's results is not an independent check. It is the same mind, marking its own work, using the same assumptions that produced the work.

    What is needed is a claim written down separately from the code that satisfies it, and checked by the machine rather than by you. Not "the output looks right" but "this specific input must give this specific result", recorded, and re-checked automatically every time anything changes.

    Unit II.2.2
    Tool

    A claim the program checks itself

    The assert statement

    New Python — assert

    assert condition does nothing at all when the condition is true, and raises AssertionError when it is false. assert condition, message attaches an explanation to the failure. It is a statement rather than a function, which is why there are no brackets.

    An assertion is a claim written in the language the machine can check. That makes it different from a comment in a way worth stating plainly: a comment saying "this list is always sorted here" is a claim that was true when somebody wrote it and may have been false for two years. An assertion saying the same thing is checked on every run, and stops being true loudly.

    The comfortable wrong idea

    "assert is how you validate input from users."

    It is not, and the reason is a property of Python most people meet the hard way. Assertions can be switched off entirely, by running Python with the -O flag, at which point the compiler removes them and they cost nothing because they are not there.

    Consider what that means for a check you were relying on.

    So the division of labour is: assert states what you believe must be true about your own code, and is a development tool. Anything that must hold when a stranger is supplying the input needs a real check and a real raise — which is exactly what Chapter I.12 did with its TypeError, and now you can see why it used raise there rather than assert.

    Unit II.2.3
    Descend

    Choosing what to claim

    The part that is actually difficult

    Writing an assertion is easy. Deciding which assertion is the skill, and it is worth being explicit about the criterion, because the natural instinct — write more tests — is not the useful one.

    The criterion

    A test is worth having in proportion to the wrong implementations it would catch. Not how many tests you have, but how many ways of being wrong each one rules out.

    Chapter IV.4 will give the sharpest illustration of this: a stack machine with its operands swapped passes every test of addition and multiplication perfectly, because those are commutative, and fails only on subtraction. Two tests of addition carry almost no information. One test of subtraction carries all of it.

    Applying that to the word tally, three kinds of claim earn their place.

    The behaviour you meant. Chapter I.12 decided that The and the are the same word and that trailing punctuation does not count. Those were choices, made in tidy, and they are exactly the sort of thing a later edit could silently reverse.

    The edges. What does an empty string do? A string of only spaces? A word that is entirely punctuation? These are the inputs nobody tries by hand and everybody eventually receives.

    The relationships that must hold. This is the most valuable kind and the least obvious. Rather than asserting a specific answer for a specific input, assert something that must be true for every input — a property connecting the parts of the program to each other. Such a claim can be checked against inputs you never thought of, and it tends to catch the defects that specific examples miss.

    Unit II.2.4
    Break

    The test that failed

    A genuine bug, found by the third kind of claim

    Now the relationship. Chapter I.12's report prints two numbers: how many words the passage contains, and how many different ones. The first comes from len(text.split()). The tally comes from count_words. Those are two separate routes to counting the same thing, so they must agree.

    Write that down as a claim: every word that split found is counted exactly once in the tally.

    Predict

    Now try 'Wait ... what?' — three tokens, one of which is only punctuation. Does the claim still hold?

    Descend

    Two definitions of "word", in one program

    Diagnosing it

    Follow the failing token. split divides on whitespace, so '...' is a token. Then tidy strips punctuation from its ends — and this token is punctuation from end to end, so what remains is the empty string. And count_words has a guard, if w:, which skips empty results, correctly, because an empty string is not a word.

    So every individual step is correct, and the program is still wrong. The defect is not in any function; it is in the relationship between two of them. report counts words one way and count_words counts them another, and nothing ever compared the two definitions because they lived in different functions written at different moments.

    Why this class of bug is the one worth fearing

    No line is wrong. Every function does exactly what its name says. The program produces plausible output that nobody queries, and it will keep doing so for as long as nobody feeds it a passage containing a standalone dash or ellipsis.

    Chapter I.12 called tidy "the one place same word is defined". That was true and it was not enough — because report quietly introduced a second definition by counting tokens instead of asking the tally. Two definitions of one concept, in one program, is a defect waiting for the right input.

    The fix follows directly from the diagnosis. Stop counting twice; ask the thing that already knows.

    Note what the fix did not do: it did not change tidy, or add special handling for ellipses, or patch the symptom. It removed a duplicate source of truth. That is nearly always the better repair when two things disagree, and Chapter II.3 will make the point again from the debugging side.

    Unit II.2.5
    Rebuild

    Running them all, every time

    From scattered claims to a suite

    Scattered assertions in a session are lost the moment the session ends. To be useful they must live in a file, run together, and report what happened — including carrying on after one fails, so that a single break does not hide the state of everything else.

    Two details of that runner are deliberate and worth adopting.

    The names are sentences. test_every_word_is_counted_once tells you what broke without your having to read the body — which matters most six months later, when the failure appears and you have forgotten everything. A test called test_3 tells you only that something is wrong.

    It exits with a status. SystemExit(1) when anything failed is Chapter III.5's exit-code convention, arriving early: zero means fine, non-zero means trouble. That is what allows the tests to be run by something other than a person — a script, or a system that refuses to publish code whose tests fail — because a machine can read a number and cannot read your satisfaction with the output.

    Python ships a fuller testing framework, and the wider world has larger ones still, with better failure reports and ways to select which tests run. They are worth learning. What they do not change is anything in this chapter: they run claims and tell you which failed, and every difficulty that remains is in deciding what to claim.

    Ladder · an assertionand the floor where it can vanish

    1. Human intention — this must always be true
    2. Python source text — assert total == expected
    3. Tokens
    4. Syntax tree
    5. Compiler — with -O, emits nothing at all: the claim is deleted here
    6. Code object and bytecode — a comparison and a conditional jump, or nothing
    7. CPython runtime — the comparison runs; the raise happens only on failure
    8. Native machine instructions
    9. CPU control logic
    10. Registers and ALU
    11. Caches and RAM
    12. Operating-system services — dark, until the failure is printed
    13. Device, file, terminal, result

    Floor 5 is the whole reason assert is a development tool rather than a safety mechanism. The check is not skipped at run time — it is never compiled, so there is nothing to skip. That is what makes assertions free when disabled, and what makes relying on one for real validation a mistake you cannot detect by reading the source.

    Retrieval lock

    Reconstruct it without looking

    Close the book

    1. Explain. Why is "I ran it and the output looked right" weaker evidence than it feels? Give three separate reasons.
    2. Explain. State the criterion for a test being worth having, then apply it: which is more valuable, a fourth test of case-insensitivity or a first test of an empty input?
    3. Redraw. Trace the token '...' through split, tidy and count_words, marking where it is lost and why each step was correct.
    4. Modify. Write three more tests for the tally: one about the behaviour you meant, one about an edge, one about a relationship. Say which wrong implementations each would catch.
    5. Modify. Apply the one-line fix, re-run the suite, and confirm all four pass. Then break tidy deliberately — remove the .lower() — and note which tests catch it and which do not.
    6. Transfer. A colleague validates a password length with assert. Explain what happens under -O, why it cannot be spotted by reading the file, and what they should use instead.
    7. Stretch. Write a test that generates a hundred random passages and checks the relationship for each. This is property-based testing, and it is the natural conclusion of the third kind of claim — a rule that holds for every input can be checked against inputs nobody thought of.
    Mastery gate — Chapter II.2
    • You can write an assertion, with and without a message, and say what each reports on failure.
    • You can explain why assert must not be used to validate untrusted input, and demonstrate why.
    • You can name the three kinds of claim and give an example of each for a program of your own.
    • You can state the criterion for a test's value, and use it to choose between two candidate tests.
    • You can explain the bug found in this chapter without using the word "punctuation" — that is, in terms of duplicated definitions.
    • You can write a test runner that continues past failures and reports a count.
    • You can explain why a test suite should exit with a status code.
    • You can say what the compiler does to an assertion under -O, and why that is different from skipping it.

    Item five is the one that transfers to every program you will ever write. The bug was not a mistake in any function; it was one concept defined twice. When two parts of a program disagree, look for the duplicate definition before you look for the broken line.

    Volume II · Chapter 3Structures, programs and cost

    Finding the fault

    Debugging as a method rather than a mood: reproduce, narrow, inspect, fix, prove

    Everyone debugs by staring at the code and hoping. It works for small bugs and fails completely for the ones that matter. There is a method instead, and it is closer to science than to cleverness — because a bug is a false belief, and false beliefs are found by experiment.

    Prerequisites

    Chapter I.11 (reading a traceback as the frame stack), Chapter I.9 Unit 6 (repr), Chapter II.2 (tests). Debugging comes immediately after testing because the two are one loop: a test tells you something is wrong, debugging finds where, and a new test makes sure it stays found.

    Unit II.3.1
    Problem

    No error, and the wrong answer

    Something you can feel

    A crash is a gift. It hands you a traceback with a file, a line, and a chain of calls. Chapter I.11 taught you to read it, and half your bugs will surrender to that alone.

    The other half never crash. The program runs, prints something plausible, and is wrong. The report bug in Chapter II.2 was one of these — it would have kept producing sensible-looking numbers forever. There is no traceback because nothing failed. Everything worked exactly as written; what was written was not what you meant.

    Those two kinds of failure need different work, and confusing them wastes time. A crash hands you a location for free: Chapter I.11's traceback names the line and the route to it, so the only question left is why. A wrong answer hands you nothing. The program ran to completion, every line did what it was written to do, and somewhere among them is one whose meaning differs from what its author believed. No instrument points at it, because nothing detectable went wrong.

    That is the situation this chapter is about, and the reason it needs a method rather than a knack. Debugging is often described as a talent, which is both discouraging and false. It is a search problem — the fault is somewhere within a known space — and search problems reward technique over inspiration.

    The reframe that changes how debugging feels

    A bug is not a broken machine. The machine did precisely what it was told. A bug is a false belief you hold about what your program does — and debugging is finding which of your beliefs is the false one.

    That is why staring harder does not work: you would be re-reading the code with the same wrong belief that produced it. You need experiments that can prove a belief false, and that is a method rather than a talent.

    The point deserves stating baldly, because it contradicts what people actually do. If you could see the mistake by reading, you would not have written it: the code says exactly what you thought it should say, which is why you wrote it that way and why re-reading keeps confirming it. Your understanding is the thing that is wrong, and you cannot inspect your understanding by consulting the artefact it produced.

    What breaks the deadlock is evidence from outside your own head — something the program tells you about what it actually did, as opposed to what you believe it does. Every technique in this chapter is a way of obtaining that evidence, and the steps are ordered so that each narrows the space the next must search.

    Unit II.3.2
    Tool

    The five steps

    In this order, every time

    1 · Reproduce
    Make it fail on demand, with the smallest input that still fails. A bug you cannot summon cannot be fixed — only guessed at
    2 · Narrow
    Halve the region it could be in, repeatedly, until it is a few lines. Do not search — bisect
    3 · Inspect
    Look at the actual values at that point, with repr. Do not assume you know what they are — that assumption is the bug, usually
    4 · Fix
    Change one thing, for a reason you can state out loud. Not several things hopefully
    5 · Prove
    Write the test that would have caught it, from Chapter II.2. Now it can never come back unnoticed

    Steps 1 and 5 are the ones people skip, and they are the two that decide whether the bug stays fixed.

    Unit II.3.3
    Tool

    Halving beats searching

    Step 2, and why it is so fast

    A thousand lines of program, and the fault is somewhere in them. Reading from the top means up to a thousand lines of reading. Instead, put one check at the halfway point — is the data still correct here? — and whichever answer you get, half the program is now innocent.

    Do it again on the guilty half. Then again. A thousand lines takes ten halvings to reach a single line, because doubling ten times gets you past a thousand. A million lines takes twenty.

    It is worth noticing why halving beats looking, because the reasoning transfers. Each check eliminates half the remaining space wherever the fault happens to be, so the number of checks grows with the logarithm of the program's size rather than with its size. Doubling the program adds one check. That is the relationship Chapter II.8 calls O(log n), arriving here as a technique for spending your own time rather than the machine's.

    The method has one requirement that is easy to violate: at each midpoint you must be able to say whether things are still correct. That means knowing what correct looks like there — often the hardest part, and the reason a bug in code with no clear intermediate expectations is so much worse than one in code that has them. It is also an argument for Chapter II.2's tests that has nothing to do with catching regressions: a program with checkable intermediate states is a program you can bisect.

    A shape you will meet again

    Halving turns a thousand into ten, and a million into twenty. Searching turns a thousand into a thousand.

    This is the same difference as Chapter II.1's set against list, in another costume — and it is the shape behind binary search, the lookup in a sorted index, and finding a name in a phone book. Chapter II.8 gives it a name and a notation. For now, notice that it applies to your own effort as much as to the machine's.

    The same trick works across time, not just across a file. If the program worked last week and fails today, the bug is in what changed — so bisect the changes: go halfway back, test, and halve again. Version-control tools have this built in for exactly this reason.

    Unit II.3.4
    Break

    Two words that are not the same word

    Step 3, and a bug you cannot see

    Here is a failure that has cost more programmer-hours than almost any other, and it looks like nonsense the first time you meet it.

    Predict

    A dictionary was built with the key 'ada ' — from a file, or a form, or a stray keystroke. You look up 'ada'. The two print identically. What happens, and what would you conclude if you had not seen this before?

    Descend

    Inspect, do not admire

    Earned by the failure

    The false belief is "the key is ada". print cannot disprove it, because print shows what a value looks like. Chapter I.9's second display shows what it is.

    The deeper lesson is about what to distrust. When a program disagrees with you, the temptation is to suspect the machinery — the dictionary, the library, the language — because your own reasoning feels sound. It is almost never the machinery. What is nearly always wrong is an assumption so basic that it was never consciously held: that these two things are the same thing, that this string has no trailing space, that this number is an integer rather than text.

    Such assumptions are invisible precisely because they were never decided. You cannot review a belief you do not know you hold, which is why the productive question while debugging is not "where is the mistake?" but "what am I assuming, and how would I check it?" The instruments below exist to answer the second question, because the first cannot be answered directly.

    The habit to build now

    When you print to inspect rather than to read, always use repr — or {value!r} inside an f-string. Trailing spaces, tabs, a '5' that you thought was a 5, an empty string where you expected nothing at all: all invisible to print, all obvious to repr. It costs one word and removes an entire category of wasted afternoon.

    Unit II.3.5
    Tool

    Printing well, and stopping time

    Two instruments for step 3

    Printing to inspect is not a shameful beginner's technique — professionals do it constantly. It is only bad when done badly. A bare print(x) in a loop gives you a column of numbers with no idea which is which.

    The second instrument stops the program instead of narrating it.

    New Python — breakpoint()

    Put breakpoint() on a line and run the program. Execution pauses there and hands you a prompt inside that frame, with every local name available to inspect. It is the REPL of Chapter I.1, opened in the middle of your running program.

    OS-dependentCPython

    breakpoint() is a language-level function that hands control to whichever debugger is configured; by default that is pdb, which ships with CPython. Editors usually provide a graphical debugger doing the same job with buttons instead of letters. What it can inspect — the locals of a live frame — is exactly what Chapter I.8's slot model says is there.

    Category: standard library; the default debugger and its display are implementation and terminal dependent.

    Ladder · where does a bug live?the honest answer

    1. Human intention — what you meant
    2. Python source text — what you wrote. The bug is the gap between these two rows
    3. Tokens
    4. Syntax tree
    5. Compiler
    6. Code object and bytecode
    7. CPython runtime
    8. Native machine instructions
    9. CPU control logic
    10. Registers and ALU
    11. Caches and RAM
    12. Operating-system services
    13. Device, file, terminal, result

    Eleven floors dark, and that is the point. Everything below floor 2 executed your instructions faithfully. Beginners suspect the language, then the interpreter, then the machine — in almost every case the fault is in the one gap the ladder cannot show you, between what you meant and what you said. Suspect floors 1 and 2 first, and last.

    Unit II.3.6
    Tool

    Say it out loud

    The technique that sounds like a joke

    Explain the failing code, line by line, aloud, to someone who is not listening — a colleague, a pet, a rubber duck on the desk. Programmers have done this for decades and it has a name.

    It works for a precise reason. Reading silently, you skim what you already believe. Speaking forces every line through a different part of your mind, the part that has to make sense to somebody else — and the false belief usually stumbles mid-sentence. People routinely stop halfway and say "oh" without the listener contributing anything at all.

    Retrieval lock

    Reconstruct it without looking

    Close the book

    1. Redraw. Write the five steps from memory, then say which two are most often skipped and what each one costs when it is.
    2. Explain. Why does "stare at the code until you see it" fail so reliably for the bugs that matter? Use the phrase false belief.
    3. Modify. Break Chapter I.12's tidy deliberately — remove the .lower() — then find the fault using only the five steps, without looking at what you changed. Time yourself. Then write the test from step 5.
    4. Transfer. A friend's program reads names from a list and looks each one up in a dictionary. It works for some names and raises KeyError for others, seemingly at random. Give them your first three moves, in order, and say what you expect to find.
    5. Stretch. Put a bug somewhere in a 32-line program, hand it to someone else, and have them bisect it. How many checks did they need? Compare with the halving prediction, and explain any difference — a bad first check is more informative than a good one here.
    Mastery gate — Chapter II.3
    • You can state the five steps in order and explain why the order matters.
    • You can reduce a failure to the smallest input that still reproduces it.
    • You can bisect a program to locate a fault, and say how many checks a given size should need.
    • You can use repr to expose a difference that print hides, and explain the KeyError it caused.
    • You can write an inspection print that says where it is, what the value is called, and exactly what it holds.
    • You can explain why the bug lives between floors 1 and 2 of the ladder, and why suspecting the interpreter is almost always wrong.

    Item six is the attitude the rest of the book depends on. If it is shaky, reread this chapter's ladder — the eleven dark floors are the argument.

    Volume II · Chapter 4Structures, programs and cost

    Rooms in the house

    Modules and packages, what import actually does, and the trap waiting in your own tally program

    You have written import six times in this book without being told what it does. It is not a request for a definition. It finds a file and runs it — and knowing that explains a surprise your own Chapter I.12 listing has been holding in reserve.

    Prerequisites

    Chapter I.8 (functions as objects bound to names), Chapter I.10 (a namespace is a dictionary), Chapter I.12 (the tally program, whose last line is about to cause trouble), Chapter 0.4 (opening a file is a system call). This is the first chapter since Volume I where floor 12 lights for an ordinary statement.

    Unit II.4.1
    Problem

    One file, growing

    Something you can feel

    Your tally program is twenty-six lines and comfortable. Add the tests from Chapter II.2 and it is forty. Add a second program that also wants tidy, and you copy the function across — which is precisely the crime Chapter I.8 opened by condemning, committed at a larger scale.

    You want the same thing you wanted then, one level up: write it once, in one place, and use it from anywhere. Functions divided a file into named jobs. Modules divide a program into named files.

    A module is simply a Python file. That is the whole definition. tally.py is a module called tally, and it became one the moment you saved it.

    The plainness of that definition does real work, and it is worth pausing on, because most languages make modules a separate construct with declarations of their own. In Python there is nothing to declare. Any file is importable, the file's name is the module's name, and there is no manifest, no export list and no ceremony. The consequence is that the distinction between "a script I am running" and "a library I am importing" is not a property of the file at all — it is a property of how the file is being used on this occasion, which is precisely why the guard below is needed.

    Unit II.4.2
    Break

    Importing it made noise

    Deliberate failure, from your own listing

    Here is Chapter I.12's program, unchanged, shortened to fit:

    Predict

    From a new file, or from the prompt, you write import tally because you want to borrow tidy. You have asked for nothing else. What happens?

    Descend

    import executes a file

    Earned by the failure

    This is the sentence to keep:

    What import tally really does

    Find the file. Make a new empty namespace. Run every line of the file, top to bottom, inside it. Wrap that namespace in a module object. Bind the name tally to it.

    Nothing is special-cased. def statements run and bind function objects; assignments run and bind values; and a report(passage) at the bottom runs too, because there is no rule that says it should not.

    That is the sentence to hold on to, and its consequences are larger than they look. If importing means running, then a module's top level is not a declaration section — it is code, executed in order, once, at whatever moment somebody first imports it. A print at the top level prints during the import. A network request at the top level makes a request during the import. An error at the top level surfaces as an import failure at a point in the program that may have nothing obvious to do with the offending line.

    It also explains why order matters within a module in a way it does not inside a function. A function may call something defined further down the file, because the call happens later, when everything exists. A top-level line cannot use something defined below it, because that line runs before the definition has. The rule is not special to modules; it is the ordinary consequence of statements running in order, applied to a whole file.

    Unit II.4.3
    Rebuild

    A file that knows how it was started

    The name guard

    You need the file to behave differently in its two roles: run the program when it is the program, stay quiet when it is being borrowed. Python tells every module which role it is in, through a name it sets automatically.

    New Python — __name__ and the guard

    While a file is running, the name __name__ holds text: the module's own name if it was imported, or '__main__' if it was the file you started Python with. So if __name__ == '__main__': means "only when I am the program, not when I am being borrowed". The double underscores mark it as Python's, not yours.

    Unit II.4.4
    Descend

    A module is an object, and its namespace is a dictionary

    Nothing new, in new clothes

    After the import, tally is a name bound to an object — Chapter I.3's model, unchanged. The object's type is module, and reaching inside it with a dot gets a name from the namespace built in step 2.

    And that namespace is a dictionary: keys are names, values are references to objects. Chapter I.10 is doing the work. When you write tally.tidy, Python looks up the string 'tidy' in that dictionary, hashes it, computes a slot, and hands back the reference it finds — the same mechanism, at the same cost, as any other lookup you have made.

    New Python — three ways to import

    import tally binds one name, the module; you reach through it with a dot. from tally import tidy runs the module exactly as before but binds only tidy in your namespace — the module itself is not bound to any name of yours. import tally as t binds the module under a shorter name.

    What does not exist is a way to import without running the file. There is no such thing.

    Two consequences follow, and both are worth expecting.

    Once only

    The second import is free

    Python keeps every imported module in a cache. A second import tally finds it there and binds the name again — the file is not re-read and not re-run. Editing a file will not change a program that has already imported it.

    Order matters

    Top-level code has consequences

    Anything expensive or noisy at the top level of a module happens at import time, in whatever order the imports happen to run. Keep the top level to definitions, and put actions behind the guard.

    The caching has a second consequence that surprises people at the prompt: editing a module's file and importing it again does not pick up your changes, because the second import finds the cached object and never touches the disk. That is correct behaviour for a running program — a module silently changing underneath code that has already used it would be far worse — and it is a nuisance during exploration, which is why the usual remedy is to restart the interpreter.

    Taken together, the cache and the run-on-import rule give a design guide you can derive rather than memorise. A module's top level should define things and do as little else as possible: definitions are cheap, repeatable and harmless, whereas actions are none of those. Anything that costs time, touches the outside world, or could fail belongs inside a function that somebody chooses to call.

    Ladder · import tallyfloor 12, for once

    1. Human intention — borrow what that file defines
    2. Python source text — two words
    3. Tokens
    4. Syntax tree — an Import node
    5. Compiler — emits IMPORT_NAME and a store
    6. Code object and bytecode
    7. CPython runtime — checks the cache, then searches the import path
    8. Native machine instructions
    9. CPU control logic
    10. Registers and ALU
    11. Caches and RAM — the new namespace and module object, in the heap
    12. Operating-system services — open and read a file: system calls, possibly many
    13. Device, file, terminal, result — bytes off a disk

    Every floor lit — the first time in Volume II. This is why start-up is the slowest part of a small Python program: before your first line runs, dozens of files have been searched for, opened, read and executed. Chapter 0.4's point about the cost of crossing the boundary, arriving where you least expected it.

    Unit II.4.5
    Tool

    Folders full of modules

    Packages, and where imports come from

    When one folder of files is not enough, a folder of folders is a package, and the dots simply follow the folders: import mygame.sound.effects.

    Everything you import comes from one of three places, and telling them apart matters more than it sounds.

    Yours
    Files you wrote, found because they sit beside the program you started
    The standard library
    Ships with Python: os, sys, dis, copy, unittest, pdb and hundreds more. Available on any machine with Python, offline, always
    Third-party
    Written by other people and installed deliberately, usually with pip. Powerful, and someone else's code running with your permissions
    OS-dependentCPython

    Where Python looks, and in what order, is a list of folders in sys.path, assembled at start-up from the interpreter's own location, environment settings and the directory of the program being run. It differs between operating systems and between installations.

    One practical trap this causes: name a file of your own random.py and your folder is searched before the standard library, so every import random in your project quietly gets your file instead. The error that follows will make no sense until you remember this paragraph.

    Category: OS- and installation-dependent. Inspect sys.path on your own machine.
    Retrieval lock

    Reconstruct it without looking

    Close the book

    1. Redraw. Write the five steps of an import from memory and mark which one needs the operating system and which one surprises people.
    2. Explain. Why is there no way to import a module without running it? Answer in terms of where the function objects come from.
    3. Modify. Split your tally into tally.py (the functions, guarded) and run_tally.py (which imports it and reports). Prove the guard works: importing must print nothing, running must print the report. Then move the tests from Chapter II.2 into a third file.
    4. Transfer. A friend's module takes four seconds to import and they cannot see why — nothing they call is slow. Using this chapter, give them the one thing to look at, and the fix.
    5. Stretch. Create a file called copy.py in your project folder containing print('mine'), then in another file in the same folder run import copy and try copy.deepcopy([[1]]) from Chapter I.7. Explain both what happens and why, then delete the file.
    Mastery gate — Chapter II.4
    • You can state what a module is, and what import does in five steps.
    • You can explain why importing a file runs all of it, including code that is not a definition.
    • You can write the __main__ guard and say exactly which situations it distinguishes.
    • You can choose between import x, from x import y and import x as z, and say what each binds.
    • You can explain why a module is only executed once however often it is imported.
    • You can name the three places imports come from, and describe the shadowing trap.

    If item two is shaky, put Figure II.4.1 beside Chapter I.8's point that def is an assignment — the definitions exist because the file ran. Chapter II.5 assumes you can split a program across files.
