    Volume II · Chapter 5Structures, programs and cost

    One at a time

    The protocol behind every for loop, and functions that pause instead of finishing

    Chapter I.5 promised that for works on lists, strings, dictionaries and files because all of them answer the same two questions. This chapter asks those questions by hand — and then builds something that answers them without holding any items at all.

    Prerequisites

    Chapter I.5 (loops, and its Level 3 on FOR_ITER), Chapter I.8 (frames pushed on call, popped on return — a rule this chapter breaks on purpose), Chapter II.1 (comprehensions). No classes are needed and none are used; they arrive in Chapter II.7.

    Unit II.5.1
    Problem

    You wanted one thing and built a million

    Something you can feel

    You want the first square number over a thousand. The obvious approach: build the squares, then look through them. But how many do you build? A hundred is not enough. A million is plenty — and you have just filled memory with 999,968 numbers you never looked at.

    The waste is not only memory. Building the list means doing all the work before you can inspect any of it. If the answer is the thirty-second item, you did a million multiplications to use thirty-two.

    Notice that both costs are paid before the first item is used, and that is what makes them worth attacking. Building the whole list front-loads all the work and all the memory, so a program that stops after ten items has still paid for a million. And if the source is slow — lines arriving from a file or a network — nothing happens at all until the last one has arrived, which for an endless source means nothing happens ever.

    What you want is to produce items only when they are asked for, and to stop the moment you have enough. Python has this everywhere, and you have been using it since Chapter I.5 without noticing.

    Unit II.5.2
    Descend

    Asking the two questions by hand

    The iterator protocol

    New Python — iter and next

    iter(L) asks a container for an iterator: a small object whose only job is to remember how far through you are. next(it) asks that iterator for the next item. When there are none left it raises StopIteration — an error used as a signal rather than a complaint.

    Now Chapter I.5's mystery dissolves. for does not know what a list is. It knows how to ask two questions, and a list, a string, a dictionary and a file all know how to answer them. The loop was never coupled to the container.

    It also explains, exactly, the trap from Chapter I.7 — the loop that skipped an item when you removed one mid-flight. The iterator holds a position, not a copy. Move the items and its position now points at something else.

    Python language

    Anything answering these two questions works with for, and with everything built on it. That includes in, comprehensions, list(), sum(), unpacking, and every function that takes "a sequence of things". Being iterable is not a type — it is a promise about behaviour, and any object that keeps the promise is accepted everywhere.

    Source: Python language reference, the iterator protocol. This is the first protocol in the book; Chapter II.7 shows how to make your own objects keep it.

    One consequence sits in plain sight and is almost always missed:

    The exhaustion is not a limitation that better engineering would remove; it follows from what an iterator is. It holds a position and moves it forward, so once the position has passed the end there is nothing to return it to. An iterator that could restart would have to remember its source and how to begin again, which is exactly what the container already does — and asking the container for a fresh iterator is how you restart. The division of labour is deliberate: the container knows the items, the iterator knows only where it has got to.

    Unit II.5.3
    Tool

    A function that pauses

    yield

    You could write your own iterator. What you actually want is to write the loop that produces the values and have Python handle the bookkeeping. That is what yield does, and it breaks a rule from Chapter I.8 to do it.

    New Python — yield

    Put yield anywhere in a function and it stops being an ordinary function. Calling it runs none of the body; it hands back a generator. Each next runs the body until the next yield, hands that value out, and pauses there — locals intact, position remembered. The next next resumes on the following line. When the function finally ends, StopIteration is raised for you.

    Predict — be exact about when things print

    A function prints "starting", yields 1, prints "resuming", yields 2, prints "finishing". You call it and bind the result. Before calling next, what has been printed?

    Descend

    The frame that refuses to die

    Chapter I.8, amended

    Chapter I.8 was clear: a call pushes a frame, a return pops it, and the locals die with it. Figure I.8.1's third panel showed the parameter ceasing to exist.

    A generator's frame is not popped. It is suspended — set aside, complete with its locals and its exact position in the bytecode — and kept alive by the generator object. Calling next puts that frame back on the stack, runs it to the next yield, and lifts it off again.

    Unit II.5.4
    Tool

    Producing without storing

    Generator expressions, and the payoff

    New Python — the generator expression

    Write a comprehension in round brackets and you get a generator instead of a list: (n * n for n in range(100000)). Same grammar as Chapter II.1, entirely different behaviour — nothing is computed until something asks.

    This is what solves the opening problem. Ask a generator for squares and stop at the first one over a thousand, and the thirty-third is never computed — not skipped, not discarded: never made.

    Use a list

    When you need it more than once

    Or need its length, or an index, or to sort it. A list is a thing that exists.

    Each of those requirements has the same root, and seeing it saves memorising the list. Length, indexing and sorting all need the items to exist together — you cannot count what has not been produced, cannot jump to the fifth of a sequence being made one at a time, and cannot sort without having everything to compare. A generator's economy comes precisely from not holding the items together, so anything needing them all at once is asking it to stop being a generator.

    Use a generator

    When you pass through once

    Especially when the sequence is huge, expensive, or has no end. A generator is a promise to produce.

    Unit II.5.5
    Break

    The second loop found nothing

    Deliberate failure

    Predict

    A generator produces 3, 2, 1. You collect it into a list — then collect it again. What does the second collection give?

    Figure II.5.1 explains it without further help. The frame ran to the end of the function, so it was finally popped for real. There is nothing left to resume. A generator is a single journey through a sequence — and once travelled, it is over.

    The fix is to make a new one: list(countdown(3)) each time, or keep a real list if you need the values twice. Notice that countdown(3) is cheap to call — it runs none of the body.

    Ladder · next(g) on a generatorfloors involved

    1. Human intention — give me the next one
    2. Python source text
    3. Tokens
    4. Syntax tree — a yield anywhere marks the whole function
    5. Compiler — flags the code object as a generator, at compile time
    6. Code object and bytecode — YIELD_VALUE, and a resume point
    7. CPython runtime — push the suspended frame back, run to the next yield, lift it off
    8. Native machine instructions
    9. CPU control logic
    10. Registers and ALU
    11. Caches and RAM — the frame's locals survive in the heap between calls
    12. Operating-system services
    13. Device, file, terminal, result

    Floor 5 decides everything, before the program runs: the compiler sees a yield and marks the whole function as a generator. That is why calling it executes nothing — the decision was made long before the call.

    Level 3 Runtime model — where a suspended frame lives

    Chapter I.8's Level 3 said modern CPython keeps frame data in a contiguous internal stack, which is what made calls cheap. A generator cannot use that arrangement unchanged: its frame must outlive the call that created it, and the stack region only supports last-in-first-out.

    So a generator object carries its frame's storage with it, in the heap, and CPython moves the data on and off the stack as the generator is resumed and suspended. The generator object is an ordinary heap object — reference-counted like everything else in Chapter I.3, and freed, along with its frame, when the last reference to it goes.

    Two practical consequences. Generators cost more per item than a plain loop, because of that moving about — they win on memory and on work avoided, not on raw speed per step. And an abandoned generator holds its locals alive until it is collected, which matters once those locals are files or connections in Volume III.

    CPython

    How frame storage is split between the internal stack and the generator object is a CPython arrangement that changed in 3.11 and may change again. The language guarantees only the behaviour: a generator suspends and resumes with its locals intact.

    Category: CPython implementation. Behaviour: language reference, generator functions.
    Retrieval lock

    Reconstruct it without looking

    Close the book

    1. Redraw. Draw Figure II.5.1 from memory, then use it to explain why calling a generator function prints nothing and why a second pass finds nothing.
    2. Explain. Take a for loop over a string and write out the calls Python actually makes, in order, ending with the exception that stops it.
    3. Modify. Write a generator producing squares forever — no end condition at all. Then use it to find the first square above a thousand, and stop. Explain why the program terminates despite the generator never doing so.
    4. Transfer. A friend's program builds a list of ten million processed records and runs out of memory. They only ever loop over it once, counting matches. Give them the change, and estimate the memory saved using the numbers in this chapter.
    5. Stretch. Rewrite Chapter I.12's count_words so it takes a generator of words rather than text. What does that let you count that the original could not? (Think about a passage too large to fit in memory — the situation Volume III meets for real.)
    Mastery gate — Chapter II.5
    • You can perform a for loop by hand with iter and next, including its ending.
    • You can explain why for works on so many different containers without knowing what any of them are.
    • You can write a generator with yield, and say what a call to it does and does not run.
    • You can explain how a generator's frame differs from an ordinary function's, referring to Figure I.8.1.
    • You can choose between a list and a generator, and justify the choice by how many passes you need.
    • You can explain why a generator is empty the second time, and why nothing warns you.

    If item four is shaky, the whole chapter is shaky — it is the mechanism everything else here follows from. Chapter II.6 pushes on frames from the opposite direction: what happens when too many of them pile up.

    Back · Chapter II.4Rooms in the house Next · Chapter II.6Functions that call themselves
    Volume II · Chapter 6Structures, programs and cost

    Functions that call themselves

    Recursion as a way of thinking, frames piling up, the moment Figure 0.4.1's arrow runs out of room — and how to tell the cases where recursion is right from the ones where it is merely clever

    A function that calls itself sounds like a trick or a mistake. It is neither. It is the natural way to handle data whose shape contains itself, and it works for a reason you can point at in memory: every call gets its own frame, so a function calling itself is not one thing happening twice but two separate workspaces that happen to be running the same instructions. This chapter builds that idea, then measures what it costs and finds the limits.

    Prerequisites

    Chapter I.8 and Figure I.8.1 (frames: what a call creates and destroys), Chapter I.4 (conditions, since every recursion needs one), Chapter I.6 and I.7 (lists, and lists inside lists), Chapter 0.4 and Figure 0.4.1 (the stack region of a process, whose size becomes a real limit here), Chapter I.11 (exceptions), Chapter II.5 (generators, briefly, in the closing unit).

    Unit II.6.1
    Problem

    A shape that contains itself

    Something you can feel

    Chapter I.7 showed lists that hold lists. Suppose one arrives and you must add up every number in it — but you are not told how deeply it is nested. It might be [1, 2, 3]. It might be [1, [2, [3, [4, [5]]]], 6]. It might be nested a hundred deep.

    Try to write it with the loops you have. One loop handles one level. A loop inside a loop handles two. To handle three you need a third, and you must decide how many to write before you have seen the data — which is impossible, because the answer is "as many as it turns out to have".

    That is not a gap in your technique. It is a genuine mismatch between the tool and the problem. A loop repeats a fixed set of steps a variable number of times; what this needs is a variable number of levels, and the two are not the same thing.

    Now describe the task in words, carefully, and notice what happens: to add up a list, add up each of its items; and if an item is itself a list, add that up the same way. The description refers to itself. It is not circular — it does terminate, because each mention is about something smaller — but the rule for the whole is stated in terms of the rule for the parts.

    Why this works, and why it is not a trick

    When a description of a task naturally refers to itself, a function that calls itself is the direct translation of that description into code. The recursion is not being imposed on the problem. It is already in the problem, and the code is merely admitting it.

    That is the test to apply throughout this chapter. If you find yourself contorting a task to make it recursive, it probably should not be. If you find you cannot describe the task without referring to itself, recursion is not a clever choice — it is the honest one.

    Unit II.6.2
    Tool

    Two cases, one of them easy

    The structure every recursion has

    Every recursive function has exactly two parts, and being able to name them turns writing one from a leap of faith into a routine.

    The base case
    A situation simple enough to answer outright, with no further calls. This is where the descent stops
    The recursive case
    Everything else: do a little work, then hand a smaller version of the problem to yourself

    The word "smaller" is carrying the weight. It is what guarantees you eventually reach the base case, and it is the thing to check when a recursion misbehaves. Smaller can mean a lower number, a shorter list, or — as here — one level less deeply nested.

    Notice what is not there. Nothing counts the levels. Nothing decides in advance how deep to go. The function does not know whether it is at the top or fifty levels down, and does not need to — each call sees only its own item and asks the same question about it. That locality is the second reason recursion suits this problem: the rule is genuinely the same at every level, so a function that knows one level knows all of them.

    Unit II.6.3
    Become the machine

    Four frames, then four returns

    What is actually in memory

    The idea is clear; the mechanism is the part people distrust. How can one function be running several times at once without its variables colliding?

    The answer arrived two volumes ago. Chapter I.8 established that a call creates a frame — a private workspace holding that call's parameters, local names, and a record of where to resume when it finishes. Nothing in that description says a function may have only one frame at a time. It says each call gets one.

    So a function calling itself is not one thing happening repeatedly. It is several frames, alive simultaneously, each with its own values, all executing the same instructions. The instructions are shared; the workspaces are not.

    Read the two halves of that figure as two distinct phases, because the second is where the answer is actually produced.

    On the way down, nothing is computed. Each call does a little work, discovers it cannot finish, and calls again — leaving its own frame parked, waiting, holding a partial expression that has nowhere to go yet. The stack grows. No result exists anywhere.

    Then the base case is reached and returns a real value, and the direction reverses. Each waiting frame receives the value it was waiting for, completes its own arithmetic, returns that, and vanishes. The answer is assembled on the way back up, in the reverse of the order the calls were made.

    This explains a puzzle people often have with recursion, which is where the answer is "kept" during all this. It is kept in the parked frames — each holding one multiplication or addition it has not yet been able to perform. There is no accumulator and no shared total. The stack of frames is the workings.

    Unit II.6.4
    Break

    Forgetting to stop

    Deliberate failure

    Since the descent is stopped only by the base case, leaving it out should be interesting. It is, and not in the way most people expect.

    Compare this with Chapter I.5's runaway while loop, which spins forever using no additional memory and must be interrupted by hand. Runaway recursion is different in kind: every call consumes memory that is never released, so it cannot continue indefinitely. Something must give.

    What would give, without protection, is the stack region from Figure 0.4.1 — the part of the process's address space set aside for frames. It has a size fixed when the process starts, and running past its end is not a Python-level event at all. It is a memory fault, and the process would be terminated by the operating system with no traceback, no message from Python, and no chance to clean up.

    So CPython counts. It keeps a limit on how many frames deep Python-level calls may go, and raises before the real boundary is reached.

    The limit is a courtesy, not a wall

    The limit exists so that a clean, catchable Python error arrives instead of an abrupt process death. It is a guard placed in front of the real boundary, and the real boundary is the size of the stack region.

    Which is why raising it with sys.setrecursionlimit is not the innocent fix it looks like. Raising it moves the guard. It does not move the wall — so a limit set far too high simply replaces a tidy RecursionError with a hard crash, which is a strictly worse outcome. If a program needs a depth of ten thousand, the answer is almost never a bigger number.

    Unit II.6.5
    Descend

    Depth is not the same as work

    A distinction that decides which recursions are dangerous

    Recursion has a reputation for being slow, and the reputation confuses two entirely separate things. Separating them is the most practically useful part of this chapter.

    Start by measuring the honest overhead. Factorial can be written either way, so the comparison is fair.

    Now the case that earned the reputation. Fibonacci, written in the obvious recursive way, where each call makes two further calls.

    Predict — before reading on

    Given 242,785 calls, how deep does the stack get? Many people expect something in the tens of thousands, and worry about the recursion limit.

    So the two dangers are entirely separate, and confusing them leads to fixing the wrong one.

    Depth
    How many frames are alive at once. Costs memory, and is what RecursionError guards. Determined by how far the descent goes before a base case
    Number of calls
    How many frames are created in total. Costs time, and nothing guards it. Determined by how many calls each call makes

    A recursion that calls itself once per step, like nest_sum or factorial, has depth equal to its call count, and its danger is depth. A recursion that calls itself twice per step has a call count that doubles at every level while its depth grows by one — so its danger is time, by an enormous margin, and the recursion limit will never warn you.

    Which also locates the defect precisely. The problem with naive Fibonacci is not that it is recursive; it is that it computes the same values over and over, because the two branches overlap. Fix that and the recursion is fine exactly as written.

    Unit II.6.6
    Rebuild

    When to use it, and what to do instead

    Judgement

    Recursion is right when the data or the task is genuinely self-similar: nested structures, trees, directories containing directories, expressions containing expressions. Chapter IV.2 will parse a language with it, and Chapter IV.5 will run it on a machine you have built, at which point the frames stop being a diagram and become a list you can print.

    It is the wrong choice when a loop says the same thing more plainly. A countdown, a total, a search through a flat list — these are not self-similar, and writing them recursively costs frames and clarity for nothing.

    And it is unavailable when the depth may exceed the limit. Here Python differs from some other languages in a way worth knowing rather than discovering.

    When depth is the problem, the reliable answer is not a larger limit but an explicit stack: keep the pending work in a list of your own rather than in frames. The transformation is mechanical, and it is worth doing once because it demystifies what the frames were doing.

    Test both on a structure three thousand levels deep and the difference is decisive: the recursive version raises RecursionError, and the iterative one returns the answer. Same algorithm, same order of work, different place to keep the pending items — and that place is the entire difference between a program that works on real data and one that does not.

    Ladder · a recursive calland the floor where the limit lives

    1. Human intention — do the same thing to each part
    2. Python source text — a function naming itself
    3. Tokens
    4. Syntax tree
    5. Compiler — one code object, used by every depth
    6. Code object and bytecode — a call instruction like any other
    7. CPython runtime — a new frame per call; the depth counter checked here
    8. Native machine instructions
    9. CPU control logic
    10. Registers and ALU
    11. Caches and RAM — the stack region of Figure 0.4.1, filling up
    12. Operating-system services — dark, unless the guard fails and the fault becomes the kernel's business
    13. Device, file, terminal, result

    Floor 5 and floor 11 together are the whole chapter. The compiler produces one code object, shared by every depth — which is why a function can call itself without needing a copy of itself. Floor 11 holds the frames, one per call, which is why the calls do not collide. Shared instructions, private workspaces.

    Retrieval lock

    Reconstruct it without looking

    Close the book

    1. Redraw. Draw the frames for nest_sum([1, [2, [3]]]) at their deepest, showing what each is waiting for. Then draw the returns, marking where each partial total is completed.
    2. Explain. Why can one function have several frames alive at once? Answer using Chapter I.8, and say what is shared between them and what is not.
    3. Explain. Distinguish depth from number of calls. Give one function where they are equal and one where they are wildly different, and say which danger each faces.
    4. Modify. Write a recursive function that counts how many numbers are in a nested list, then a version that finds the largest. Identify the base case and the recursive case in each before you write them.
    5. Modify. Add a counter to fib and confirm the call count for fib(20). Then add lru_cache and count again. Explain the difference in terms of repeated work rather than in terms of recursion.
    6. Transfer. A colleague hits RecursionError and proposes calling sys.setrecursionlimit(100000). Explain what the limit actually guards, what raising it does and does not move, and what you would suggest instead.
    7. Stretch. Convert nest_sum to use an explicit stack, then test both on a structure three thousand levels deep. Explain the difference in terms of Figure 0.4.1's two regions, and say why the heap can take what the stack cannot.
    Mastery gate — Chapter II.6
    • You can recognise a task whose description refers to itself, and say why recursion is the honest translation of it.
    • You can name the base case and the recursive case in any recursive function, and check that the problem really is getting smaller.
    • You can explain how several frames of one function coexist, and what each is waiting for.
    • You can describe both phases — the descent that computes nothing and the return that assembles the answer.
    • You can explain what RecursionError guards, and why raising the limit is usually the wrong response.
    • You can distinguish depth from call count, and say which recursions are limited by which.
    • You can explain why naive Fibonacci is slow without blaming recursion, and fix it without changing the body.
    • You can convert a recursion into a loop with an explicit stack, and say where the pending work now lives.

    If item six is shaky, run the two experiments again: fib(20) makes 21,891 calls and reaches a depth of 20. That single pair of numbers separates the two things people mean when they say recursion is dangerous, and they need entirely different fixes.

    Volume II · Chapter 7Structures, programs and cost

    Types of your own

    Classes, instances, and writing the methods that +, ==, len and for have been looking for all along

    Chapter I.2 said that + follows the left value's type pointer and asks that type how to add. You have believed that for eleven chapters. In this one you write the type, and the method it finds is yours.

    Prerequisites

    Chapter I.2 (the object header and its type pointer — Figure I.2.1 is this chapter's foundation), Chapter I.3 (names, identity, equality), Chapter I.10 (a namespace is a dictionary), Chapter I.8 (the mutable-default trap, which returns in a new costume), Chapter II.5 (the iterator protocol, whose promise is honoured here).

    Unit II.7.1
    Problem

    Data that belongs together, kept apart

    Something you can feel

    A point on a screen is two numbers. You can keep them in a tuple, (3, 4), and everything works — until you have forty of them, and a function that expects (x, y) receives (y, x), and nothing complains because both are tuples of two numbers.

    The deeper problem is that the operations live somewhere else. To add two points you write a function add_points, and to compare them another function, and to print them a third — while +, == and print, which mean exactly those things, sit there refusing to help.

    The symptom is that nothing announces what belongs with what. A dictionary holding two coordinates and a set of functions that expect such a dictionary are related only by your intention, so nothing stops a function receiving a dictionary of the wrong shape, and nothing tells a reader which functions form the set. The knowledge exists, and exists nowhere the program can see.

    What you want is a new type: something that knows what it is, carries its own data, and answers the operators the same way int and str do.

    Unit II.7.2
    Tool

    Making one

    class, __init__ and self

    New Python — class

    class Point: creates a new type. Inside it, def statements create methods — functions that belong to the type. __init__ is special: Python calls it automatically each time you make a new one, to set it up. Every method's first parameter is self, which is the particular object being worked on. self.x = x stores a value on that object.

    Calling the class — Point(3, 4) — builds a new object, called an instance, and runs __init__ on it.

    Descend

    Figure I.2.1, completed

    Where an object's data and its behaviour live

    Chapter I.2 drew a CPython object as a small block: a reference count, a pointer to its type, and a value. The type object at the far end of that pointer, you were told, is "where behaviour lives".

    You have now built both halves. The instance holds the data, in its own dictionary. The type holds the methods, in its dictionary. And p.x and p.distance() are two different searches: the first finds 'x' on the instance, the second fails to find 'distance' there and follows the type pointer to find it on Point.

    The split is worth dwelling on, because it explains a great deal of Python's behaviour at once. Anything varying between instances lives on the instance; anything shared lives on the type, stored once however many instances exist. A million points hold two million numbers between them and exactly one copy of each method.

    It also explains the lookup order you will rely on constantly. Asking for an attribute checks the instance first and the type second, so an instance can shadow something on its class, and a method not found on the instance is found on the type. That single rule accounts for methods working at all, for the mutable-default trap below, and for why assigning to an attribute affects one object while assigning in the class body affects every one.

    Unit II.7.3
    Break

    Two baskets, one basket

    Deliberate failure — an old trap in new clothes

    You want each basket to start empty, so you put an empty list in the class where it looks tidy.

    Predict — you have met this shape twice before

    class Basket: with items = [] written directly in the class body, and an add method doing self.items.append(thing). Make two baskets. Add an apple to the first. What is in the second?

    Descend

    You already know why

    Earned by the failure

    Figure II.7.1 answers it without a new idea. items = [] in the class body runs once, when the class is created, and stores that one list on the type — the shared box on the right. Every instance's lookup for items misses its own dictionary and follows the pointer to the same list.

    This is Chapter I.8's mutable default (box=[] evaluated once, at def) and Chapter I.6's [[0]] * 3 (one object, many references), for the third time. Same rule, three costumes: a mutable object made once and shared is shared by everything that reaches it.

    Unit II.7.4
    Tool

    Answering the operators

    Protocols, and Chapter I.2's promise kept

    Python's operators and built-in functions do not have special knowledge of any type. They look for a method with an agreed name and call it. + looks for __add__; == looks for __eq__; len looks for __len__; for looks for __iter__. Agreed names like these are protocols — and Chapter II.5 already told you that a protocol is a promise about behaviour, not a type.

    So a type of yours becomes a full citizen by keeping promises.

    This is the deepest idea in the chapter and it is worth stating in general form. Python asks objects what they can do rather than what they are. A function that sorts needs only things answering <; a for loop needs only Chapter II.5's two questions; printing needs only a way to produce text. None of them checks a type, so any object keeping the relevant promise works, including one written long after the code that uses it.

    The cost is that a promise not kept is discovered when it is called upon rather than when the object is written, which is Chapter I.2's dynamic checking arriving at the level of your own designs. The benefit is that the set of things your code works with is open-ended by default rather than by anticipation — and Chapter II.10 relies on it, since Python's sort works on your types without ever having heard of them.

    And because iteration is a protocol rather than a type, everything built on it now works, with nothing further written:

    Python language

    Chapter I.2's rule, now visible from both sides. When Python evaluates a + b it follows a's type pointer and calls that type's __add__. There is no built-in addition that types opt into — the method is the addition. For int the method is written in C; for your Vec it is written in Python; the mechanism is identical.

    Two defaults worth knowing. Without __eq__, == falls back to identity, so two separately built points are unequal even with the same numbers — Chapter I.3's distinction, surfacing again. Without __repr__, the prompt shows the type name and a memory address, which is honest but useless.

    Source: Python language reference, data model — special method names.

    Ladder · a + b where a is your Veccompare with Chapter I.2's ladder

    1. Human intention — combine two vectors
    2. Python source text — identical to 5 + 5
    3. Tokens
    4. Syntax tree — the same Add node
    5. Compiler
    6. Code object and bytecode — the same BINARY_OP
    7. CPython runtime — follows the type pointer, finds __add__, and calls your Python function
    8. CPython runtime, again — a new frame for __add__, exactly as Chapter I.8 described
    9. Native machine instructions
    10. CPU control logic
    11. Registers and ALU — two int additions, deep inside your method
    12. Operating-system services
    13. Device, file, terminal, result

    Chapter I.2's ladder for 5 + 5 stopped at floor 7 with "ask the type how to add". This one shows what happens next when the answer is yours: a full function call, frame and all. That is also the honest cost — your + is a Python call, not a machine instruction.

    Level 3 Runtime model — the cost of an instance, and __slots__

    Every instance carrying its own dictionary is flexible — you can attach a new attribute at any moment — and it is not free. A dictionary has the over-allocated table from Chapter I.10's Level 3, per object. Make a million points and you have made a million small hash tables.

    CPython softens this: instances of the same class usually share the keys of their dictionaries, storing only the values per object, because instances of one class almost always have the same attribute names. When a class declares __slots__, the dictionary disappears entirely and attributes become fixed numbered positions — Chapter I.8's STORE_FAST idea applied to objects instead of frames, with the same trade: much smaller and faster, and no adding attributes later.

    The judgement is the same one this whole volume teaches. Reach for it when you have measured a million objects being a problem, not before.

    CPython

    Key-sharing dictionaries, the layout of instance storage, and the exact savings from __slots__ are CPython implementation choices that have changed across versions. Measure with sys.getsizeof on your own build; the language guarantees only that attributes work.

    Category: CPython implementation. Verify per version.
    Unit II.7.5
    Tool

    Borrowing from another type

    Inheritance, briefly and carefully

    class Square(Shape): makes Square borrow everything Shape defines: a lookup that misses on the instance and on Square carries on to Shape. It is one more step along the same arrow Figure II.7.1 already draws.

    It is also the feature beginners over-use, and the reason deserves stating plainly. Inheritance ties two types together permanently, so a change to the parent reaches every child, including the ones written by someone else years later. Protocols achieve most of what people want from it without the tie: your Vec works with for, len, in and unpacking while inheriting from nothing at all.

    A rule of thumb worth keeping

    Ask whether the new type genuinely is a kind of the old one, in every situation the old one is used. If it merely has one, or merely wants a few of its methods, store one inside the other instead. "Has a" is almost always safer than "is a".

    Retrieval lock

    Reconstruct it without looking

    Close the book

    1. Redraw. Draw two instances and their shared type, marking which dictionary holds x and which holds __add__. Then trace p.x and p.__add__ as two different searches.
    2. Explain. Why does items = [] in a class body leak between instances? Give the one sentence that also explains Chapter I.8's box=[] and Chapter I.6's [[0]] * 3.
    3. Modify. Write a Card type with a rank and a suit, giving it __repr__ and __eq__. Then build a list of cards, sort them with the key function from Chapter I.12, and explain why sorting worked without you writing anything about order.
    4. Transfer. A friend's program keeps players as dictionaries: {'name': ..., 'score': ...}. It works, but typos in key names cause silent wrong answers. Say what a class buys them here, and what it costs — the honest answer includes both.
    5. Stretch. Give Vec a __len__ that returns 0 and then test if a: from Chapter I.4. Explain the result using the truthiness rule, and say why a type can accidentally make itself false.
    Mastery gate — Chapter II.7
    • You can define a class with __init__, create instances, and say what self refers to.
    • You can state where an instance's data lives and where its methods live, and what vars(p) shows.
    • You can explain the shared-class-attribute trap and connect it to two earlier traps.
    • You can implement __repr__, __eq__ and __add__, and say what each replaces.
    • You can explain how a protocol differs from a type, and why one __iter__ earned several behaviours.
    • You can say what Chapter I.2 meant by "ask the type how to add", now that you have written the answer.

    Item six is the one this chapter existed for. If it is shaky, read this chapter's ladder against Chapter I.2's — they are the same ladder, and this one carries on past the floor where the other stopped.

    Volume II · Chapter 8Structures, programs and cost

    Counting the cost

    How work grows with input, why the growth matters more than the machine, the notation for saying so — and two pieces of folklore that a measurement refutes

    A program that is fast on ten items and unusable on ten thousand has not become slower. It has been asked to do far more work, in a way its author did not notice, because the work was hidden inside a line that looked like one step. This chapter is about seeing that in advance — and about being careful, because two of the standard warnings turn out not to survive being measured on a current interpreter.

    Prerequisites

    Chapter I.5 (loops), Chapter I.6 (lists and the in test), Chapter II.1 (sets), Chapter I.10 (dictionaries), Chapter II.2 (the discipline of checking claims rather than believing them), Chapter II.11 (reference counting — needed to explain Unit II.8.5's surprise). Chapter II.9 will explain why the structures have the costs this chapter measures; Chapter II.13 turns the analysis into a method.

    Unit II.8.1
    Problem

    Stop guessing and make it count

    Something you can feel

    Two programs solve the same problem. One takes four hundredths of a second and the other three ten-thousandths. That looks like a small difference and a matter of taste. Give both ten times the data and the first takes seventy hundredths while the second takes three thousandths — and the gap has widened from about a hundredfold to about two hundredfold, and will keep widening for ever.

    That is the phenomenon this chapter is about, and the first thing to say is that a stopwatch is the wrong instrument for understanding it. A time measures one program on one machine on one occasion with one input. What you need to know is different and more useful: how does the work change when the input changes?

    The right instrument is a counter. Chapter II.2 argued that a claim should be checked rather than believed; here the claim is about growth, so the check is to count the steps for several sizes and look at the pattern.

    Compare the version that uses a set for the membership test.

    Unit II.8.2
    Tool

    Naming the shape

    Big-O

    Those two patterns have names, and the notation for them is less mysterious than it looks once you know what it deliberately throws away.

    Write O(n) when doubling the input doubles the work: one pass, roughly, over everything. Write O(n2) when doubling quadruples it: for each item, something that looks at all the items. Write O(1) when the work does not depend on the size at all — looking up a dictionary key, reading a list by index. And O(log n) when doubling the input adds only a constant amount, which is what halving repeatedly gives you.

    What the notation discards is as important as what it keeps. It ignores constant factors entirely: a program taking 3n steps and one taking 3000n steps are both O(n). It ignores lower-order terms: n2 + 500n is O(n2), because for large enough n the square dominates however large the 500 is.

    Both omissions are deliberate, and both have a cost worth stating plainly. The benefit is that the answer is a property of the algorithm, independent of machine, language and interpreter — which is why the four ratios above would be identical on any computer ever built. The cost is that big-O says nothing whatever about which of two programs is faster today, on your data. It tells you what happens as the input grows, and that is a different question from what happens now.

    The figure makes the practical point better than the arithmetic does. At small sizes the curves are close together and the choice barely matters. The quadratic curve then leaves the others behind, and no amount of faster hardware brings it back — because a machine twice as fast lets you handle only about 1.4 times as much data when the work grows as the square. The shape wins in the end, always.

    Unit II.8.3
    Descend

    Best, worst, and the question you meant

    One notation, three different claims

    A complexity figure quietly answers a question, and it is worth knowing which. The same operation can do very different amounts of work depending on the data.

    So "O(n)" for list search is a statement about the worst case, and that is the usual convention because the worst case is the one you can rely on. But the distinction matters in both directions.

    It matters when the worst case is rare and catastrophic: a structure with excellent average behaviour and a terrible worst case is fine until somebody sends data chosen to trigger it, which is a real class of attack. And it matters when the worst case is unreachable: an algorithm whose worst case never occurs on your data is being judged on a situation that cannot arise.

    Chapter II.9 will meet a third kind of claim — amortised cost, where a single operation is occasionally expensive but a long run of them averages out cheaply — and having the distinction ready is what will make that argument comprehensible rather than a piece of hand-waving.

    Unit II.8.4
    Break

    The quadratic hiding in one line

    Deliberate failure

    Now the practical skill, which is spotting these before they are measured. The dangerous pattern is a loop whose body contains something that is itself a loop, where the inner loop is invisible because it is written as a single operation.

    Predict

    How does the work grow for this, as the list of names gets longer?

    for name in names:
        if name in banned_list:

    The outer loop runs n times. The membership test on a list is a loop over that list, because a list has no way to find an item except by looking at each one. So the total is n times the length of the banned list, and if the two grow together it is quadratic.

    The correction is one word: make banned_list a set. The membership test becomes O(1) rather than O(n), and the whole thing becomes linear. Nothing else about the program changes.

    Built-in does not mean free

    A single line of Python may contain an unbounded amount of work. in on a list, index, count, remove, max, sum, slicing and sorting all examine many items — and they look exactly like operations that examine one.

    The habit worth building is to ask, of every line inside a loop: does this touch one thing, or all of them? That single question catches most accidental quadratics, and it is a question about meaning rather than about measurement, so it can be asked while writing rather than after profiling.

    Being concrete about which is which matters more than the principle. On a list, append and indexing touch one item; in, index, remove and insert(0, x) touch many. On a dictionary or set, lookup, insertion and removal touch one. Chapter II.9 explains what makes that possible, and until then it is worth taking as a rule with a promised justification.

    Unit II.8.5
    Break

    Two warnings that do not survive measurement

    Second deliberate failure — and it is mine

    Chapter II.2's discipline says a claim should be checked rather than repeated. Applying that to two of the most widely repeated pieces of performance advice produces uncomfortable results, and reporting them is more useful than quietly leaving them out.

    The first is about building strings. The standard warning is that s = s + 'x' in a loop is quadratic, because strings are immutable, so each step must copy the whole string built so far. The reasoning is sound and the conclusion is what this book would have predicted. Measured:

    The explanation is an optimisation in CPython that Chapter II.11 gives you the tools to understand. When a string object has exactly one reference to it, nothing else can observe it changing, so the interpreter may quietly resize it in place instead of building a copy. Immutability is preserved as a promise to the program while being bypassed as an implementation detail, precisely because nobody can tell.

    Which raises the obvious question, and the answer restores the warning in a much more interesting form.

    What to take from this

    The advice — build a list and use ''.join — remains right, but for a better reason than the one usually given. It is not that concatenation in a loop is always quadratic; it is that whether it is quadratic depends on a reference count you are not thinking about, and can change when somebody adds an innocuous line elsewhere. Performance that depends on an invisible property is worse than performance that is merely slower, because it cannot be reasoned about.

    The second warning concerns constant factors, and here the textbook example fails outright. The standard demonstration is that an O(log n) binary search loses to an O(n) linear scan at small sizes, because its constant factor is larger. Measured against Python's own bisect:

    The underlying point survives — constant factors are real and big-O ignores them — but the direction is the opposite of the one the example is meant to teach, and in Python the constant factor that usually dominates is not the algorithm's shape but whether the work happens in interpreted or compiled code. Chapter II.13 makes that the central fact of optimising Python, and here is the evidence arriving early.

    The method, not the numbers

    Two well-known warnings, both with sound reasoning behind them, both refuted by a measurement taking a few seconds. Neither was wrong when it was written; both are stated as facts when they are properties of a particular interpreter at a particular time.

    The transferable lesson is Chapter II.2's, sharpened: a mechanism that predicts a cost is a hypothesis, not a conclusion. Measure it on the interpreter you are actually running, and treat performance advice — including this book's — as dated until re-checked.

    Ladder · where complexity livesand where it does not

    1. Human intention — the algorithm is chosen here, and this is where the growth is decided
    2. Python source text — one line may hide a loop
    3. Tokens
    4. Syntax tree
    5. Compiler
    6. Code object and bytecode — a CONTAINS_OP looks like any other instruction
    7. CPython runtime — where the constant factors live, and the surprise of Unit II.8.5
    8. Native machine instructions
    9. CPU control logic
    10. Registers and ALU
    11. Caches and RAM — where Chapter II.12 shows constants can vary by a further large factor
    12. Operating-system services
    13. Device, file, terminal, result

    Floor 1 and floor 7 divide the chapter. Complexity is decided at floor 1, by you, before any code exists — and no lower floor can repair a bad choice, because faster hardware only shifts a curve rather than bending it. Constant factors live at floor 7 and below, and they are where measurement is indispensable, because nothing about the source predicts them reliably.

    Close the book

    1. Explain. Why is a counter a better instrument than a stopwatch for this question? Say what each measures and which is a property of the algorithm.
    2. Explain. Give the doubling signature of O(n), O(n2) and O(log n), and say how you would identify each from four measurements.
    3. Redraw. For the dedupe example, write out how many comparisons the inner loop performs on the 1st, 2nd and kth item. Sum them and show why the total is about n2/2 — then check against the measured 0.499.

    6. Transfer. Someone says their program is fine because doubling the data only made it a little slower. What would you ask them, and what would you have them measure?

    Mastery gate — Chapter II.8
    • You can instrument a function with a counter and read the growth from the ratios.
    • You can name the common complexity classes and give each one's doubling signature.
    • You can say what big-O discards, why, and what that makes it unable to tell you.
    • You can distinguish best, worst and average case, and say which big-O usually reports.
    • You can spot a hidden quadratic by asking whether a line touches one item or all of them.
    • You can list which list operations are cheap and which are not, and the same for sets and dictionaries.
    • You can explain why s = s + 'x' is sometimes linear and sometimes quadratic, and why that is worse than being reliably slow.
    • You can state why a mechanism that predicts a cost is a hypothesis rather than a conclusion.

    If item five is shaky, go back through a program you have written and mark every line inside a loop as touching one item or many. The exercise takes ten minutes and finds most accidental quadratics before they exist.

    Volume II · Chapter 9Structures, programs and cost

    Under the list and the dict

    Dynamic arrays and hash tables, measured and then rebuilt — the promises from Chapters I.6 and I.10, paid in full

    Two claims have been carrying a lot of weight since Volume I: appending to a list is cheap, and a dictionary lookup is instant. Both were shown to be plausible and neither was proved. This chapter measures them, explains why they are true, and then builds a working hash table out of the parts you already own.

    Prerequisites

    Chapter I.6 and its Level 3 (over-allocation, promised in full here), Chapter I.10 and its Level 3 (collisions and resizing, likewise), Chapter II.7 (classes — you need them to build the thing), Chapter II.8 (shapes and the amortised idea).

    Unit II.9.1
    Problem

    A row of boxes cannot grow

    Something you can feel

    Chapter I.6 established why indexing is instant: slot i is base + i × 8, so the machine calculates rather than searches. But that arithmetic only works if the slots are next to each other in memory — one unbroken block.

    Which raises an awkward question. A block of memory has a fixed size, decided when it was asked for. So how does a list grow? Whatever is immediately after your block belongs to someone else.

    It cannot grow. What actually happens is that a bigger block is requested elsewhere, every existing reference is copied across, and the old block is released — and that copying is O(n). If it happened on every append, building a list of n items would be O(n²), and every program you have written would be quadratic.

    Which raises the obvious objection immediately, and it is the right one. If every append copies the entire list, then building a list of a million items copies a million times, and the total work is proportional to the square of the length — exactly the disaster Chapter II.8 taught you to recognise. Appending would be the most expensive common operation in the language, and it plainly is not.

    So the resolution must be that a bigger block is requested only occasionally, and the question becomes how much bigger. Ask for one extra slot each time and nothing is gained: every append still copies. Ask for a fixed number of extra slots — a hundred, say — and the copying happens a hundred times less often, which sounds sufficient and is not, because a hundredth of a quadratic is still a quadratic. The only arrangement that works is to request an amount proportional to the current size, so the list grows by a fraction of itself rather than by a fixed quantity.

    Unit II.9.2
    Descend

    Length is not capacity

    Measuring the spare room

    A list keeps two numbers: how many slots hold something, and how many it actually owns. len reports the first. sys.getsizeof lets you deduce the second.

    Keep going and the capacities are 4, 8, 16, 24, 32, 40, 52, 64, 76, 92, 108, 128. Notice what that is not: it is not doubling. Each new capacity is roughly the old one plus an eighth — generous when the list is small, thrifty when it is large.

    Why growing by a factor is the whole trick

    Because each move makes the list bigger by a fraction of its size, the moves get further and further apart — so the total copying done over n appends adds up to a multiple of n, not of n². Divide by n appends and the average cost of one is constant.

    That average-over-many is what Chapter II.8 called amortised O(1). It is a genuine promise about totals, not a hopeful one about typical cases. And it fails completely if you grow by a fixed amount instead: adding four slots each time means a move every four appends forever, and the total returns to O(n²).

    The argument is worth following rather than accepting, because "it averages out" is the kind of claim that ought to be checked. Consider growing from empty to n items where the capacity roughly doubles each time. The copies performed have lengths 1, 2, 4, 8 and so on up to about n. That sum is less than 2n — a doubling series always totals under twice its final term — so the total copying across all n appends is proportional to n, and the average per append is constant.

    Notice what the argument does and does not establish. It does not say any particular append is cheap; one in every few is genuinely expensive and copies everything. It says the expensive ones are rare enough, and become rare fast enough, that the average is bounded. That distinction matters when timing is critical rather than merely fast: a program that must respond within a fixed interval cannot rely on an amortised bound, because the occasional expensive append happens whenever it happens.

    Two practical facts follow, and you can now derive both rather than remember them. Appending is cheap. Inserting at the front is not: insert(0, x) must shift every existing reference up one slot to keep the addresses contiguous, which is O(n) every single time.

    CPythonHardware example

    Chapter I.6's Level 3 promise, discharged. The 56-byte header, the 8-byte slots and the exact growth pattern are CPython on a 64-bit build and have changed between versions; measure your own. What is not implementation-specific is the design: this is a dynamic array, the same structure behind Java's ArrayList and C++'s vector, and the factor-growth argument is identical in all of them.

    Category: CPython on 64-bit, verified by measurement. The amortised argument is universal.
    Unit II.9.3
    Descend

    What happens when two keys want one slot

    The dictionary, honestly

    Chapter I.10 said a key's hash is wrapped round the table size to give a slot, and mentioned in passing that two keys can land on the same one. Watch it happen — integers hash to themselves, so the arithmetic is visible.

    You now have every part needed to build one. A list of buckets, a hash, the remainder operator from Chapter II.1, and a class from Chapter II.7.

    And the cost is now visible rather than asserted. Reaching the bucket is O(1) arithmetic. Searching within a bucket is O(its length). So a dictionary is fast exactly as long as buckets stay short — which is what resizing is for.

    It is worth being precise about what that O(1) claims, since it is the most commonly overstated figure in the language. It assumes hashes are well spread, so that keys land in different buckets. If they do not, the chain at a slot must be searched item by item and the lookup degrades towards O(n). The constant-time claim is about the typical case with reasonable hashes, not a guarantee about every case.

    That is not a theoretical caveat. Chapter II.8 noted that a rare catastrophic worst case is an attack surface, and this is the canonical example: an attacker who can choose the keys and predict the hash can force every key into one bucket, turning a fast lookup into a slow scan. Python defends against this by varying string hashing between runs — which is also why the order of a set of strings differs from one run to the next, a security measure whose visible symptom looks like arbitrariness.

    One idea, twice

    Both containers keep spare room, both grow by a factor rather than an amount, and both pay one rare O(n) rebuild to keep every ordinary operation O(1).

    The list buys instant indexing with its spare room. The dictionary buys short buckets. It is the same bargain — memory now, in exchange for time later — and once you see it you will find it everywhere.

    Simplified modelCPython

    What TinyDict gets right: hashing to a slot, collisions being normal, exact-key comparison within a slot, and why short buckets mean fast lookup. What it leaves out: real CPython does not keep a list per slot. It uses open addressing — on a collision it steps to another slot by a repeatable recipe until it finds the key or an empty slot — which touches far less memory, for reasons Chapter II.12 makes clear. It also resizes automatically, keeps a separate compact array to preserve insertion order, and randomises string hashes at start-up. The fuller version is Volume IV, which reads CPython's own implementation.

    Declared simplification. Chapter I.10's Level 3 promise is discharged here; the remaining detail belongs to Volume IV.

    Ladder · L.append(x), the rare expensive onefloors involved

    1. Human intention — add one item
    2. Python source text — identical whether it is cheap or expensive
    3. Tokens
    4. Syntax tree
    5. Compiler
    6. Code object and bytecode — one call, either way
    7. CPython runtime — is there a spare slot? If not, ask for a bigger block and copy
    8. Native machine instructions
    9. CPU control logic
    10. Registers and ALU — one write, or n writes
    11. Caches and RAM — the allocator hands over a new block; the old one is released
    12. Operating-system services — usually dark: CPython keeps its own pool
    13. Device, file, terminal, result

    Floor 12 stays dark even though memory is being acquired, which surprises people. CPython asks the operating system for memory in large chunks and hands out pieces itself, precisely so that ordinary allocation does not cost a system call. Chapter II.11 opens that pool up.

    Retrieval lock

    Reconstruct it without looking

    Close the book

    1. Redraw. Draw a list of capacity 4 with 4 items, then draw what exists immediately after a fifth append. Mark what was copied, what is new, and what is spare.
    2. Explain. Why does growing by a factor give amortised O(1) while growing by a fixed number of slots does not? Answer with totals over n appends.
    3. Modify. Add a load() method to TinyDict returning the length of the longest bucket. Put 20 keys in a table of 8 and report it. Then make the table size 64 and report again — and connect the two numbers to lookup cost.
    4. Transfer. A friend builds a list by inserting each new item at position 0 to keep it newest-first, and it crawls on 50,000 items. Name the shape, give the operation count, and give two fixes — one that changes the algorithm, one that changes the container.
    5. Stretch. Measure a list's size as it grows to 200 and work out each capacity. Where does the extra room come from — roughly what fraction is added each time? Then explain why a small list is given proportionally much more spare room than a large one.
    Mastery gate — Chapter II.9
    • You can distinguish a list's length from its capacity and deduce both from a measurement.
    • You can explain why a list cannot simply grow in place, and what happens instead.
    • You can give the amortised argument for append, and say what breaks it.
    • You can explain why insert(0, x) is O(n) from the address arithmetic, not from a table of costs.
    • You can explain why collisions are inevitable and how a bucket resolves them.
    • You can state what your TinyDict gets right and where CPython's real dictionary differs.

    Item three is the intellectual core of this chapter and it recurs for the rest of your life — every growable structure in every language rests on it. If it is shaky, work out the total copying for 1000 appends both ways, on paper.

    Back · Chapter II.8Counting the cost Next · Chapter II.10Putting things in order
    Volume II · Chapter 10Structures, programs and cost

    Putting things in order

    Why sorting costs what it costs, what stability buys you, why a key function was all Python needed — and watching a real sort notice order that is already there

    Sorting is the best-studied problem in computing, and it is worth your attention for a reason beyond its usefulness: it is the clearest case where thinking differently about a problem changes its cost by a factor that grows without limit. Two methods, both obviously correct, differing by ninety-nine times the work at a thousand items and far more beyond that. This chapter counts both, then looks at what Python actually does, which is cleverer than either.

    Prerequisites

    Chapter II.8 (complexity, counting rather than timing, and the doubling signature), Chapter II.6 (recursion — merge sort is recursive and its shape is the reason it wins), Chapter I.6 (lists and slicing), Chapter II.7 (dunder methods, since __lt__ is what sorting actually uses), Chapter I.7 (mutability, for the difference between sort and sorted).

    Unit II.10.1
    Problem

    The obvious method, counted

    Something you can feel

    Ask somebody to describe how to sort a row of cards and most will describe something like this: look at each neighbouring pair, swap them if they are the wrong way round, and repeat until nothing needs swapping. It is correct, it is easy to believe, and it is called bubble sort because large values rise to the end like bubbles.

    Chapter II.8 established the instrument for judging it: count, do not time.

    The reason for the quadratic is worth stating in words, because it is what the better method attacks. Every comparison in bubble sort settles the relationship of exactly one pair. There are about n2/2 pairs. So a method that learns one pair per comparison and needs to know about all of them cannot do better than n2/2, no matter how it is tidied up.

    To improve, you must find a way for one comparison to settle many pairs at once.

    Unit II.10.2
    Tool

    Halve it instead

    Merge sort

    Here is the idea, and notice that it is the shape of Chapter II.6 rather than a new technique. Sorting a big list is hard. Sorting a list of one item is free, because it is already sorted. And combining two already sorted lists into one sorted list is easy: repeatedly take the smaller of the two front items.

    So: split the list in half, sort each half the same way, then merge. The recursion bottoms out at single items, which need no work.

    The merge step is where the saving happens, and it is worth seeing exactly why. When you compare the front of the left half with the front of the right half and the left one is smaller, you have not only placed that one item — you have established that it precedes every remaining item in the right half, because that half is sorted. One comparison, many pairs settled. That is the property Unit II.10.1 said was necessary.

    The growth is O(n log n), and the two parts of that come from the two parts of the method. The halving can be done about log2n times before reaching single items — ten times for a thousand, twenty for a million. And each level of merging touches every item once, which is the n. Ten levels of a thousand items is ten thousand units of work, against the half-million bubble sort needs.

    It is worth knowing that O(n log n) is not merely the best anyone has found. For sorting by comparisons alone it is provably the best possible, because each comparison has two outcomes and you need enough of them to distinguish every possible arrangement. That is a rare and comfortable thing to know: no cleverer comparison sort is waiting to be discovered.

    Unit II.10.3
    Descend

    Sorting is a protocol, like everything else

    What Python actually calls

    Neither method above says what "smaller" means. Both simply used < or > and left the question to the values — which is precisely Chapter II.7's protocol idea, and it is why Python's sort works on things its authors never anticipated.

    Rather than being handed a comparison function, Python takes a key function: something that turns each item into a value to be sorted by. That choice looks minor and is not.

    That is the whole argument for the design. A key function is less general than a comparison function — there are orderings it cannot express — but it is faster, and it is easier to get right, because you cannot write an inconsistent key whereas you can easily write a comparison that contradicts itself.

    Unit II.10.4
    Tool

    Ties, kept in order

    Stability, and what it makes possible

    When two items compare equal, a sort must put one first, and it may choose either. A sort is stable if it always keeps them in the order they arrived. Python's is, and this is a documented guarantee rather than an accident of implementation.

    Stability sounds like a technicality until you see what it enables. Sorting by several criteria — by score, then alphabetically among equal scores — normally requires writing a combined comparison that handles each criterion in turn. With a stable sort you need no such thing.

    The rule is worth memorising in that form: least significant first. It is the opposite of the order you would say it in English, which is why people get it wrong, and it works only because the sort is stable.

    Two names for one operation

    sorted(x) returns a new list and leaves x alone. x.sort() rearranges x and returns None — which is Chapter I.7's distinction between changing a thing and producing a new one, and the returned None is deliberate: it stops you writing y = x.sort() and believing you have a sorted copy. A method that changes something in place returns nothing, throughout Python, precisely so that the mistake announces itself.

    Unit II.10.5
    Rebuild

    Watch it notice

    What Python actually uses

    Python does not use merge sort as described, nor any of the other classical methods unmodified. It uses an algorithm designed for a specific observation: real data is very often partly ordered already — appended in time order, previously sorted and slightly amended, or assembled from sorted pieces — and an algorithm that notices can do far less work.

    You can watch it notice, using Chapter II.7's protocol to count the comparisons Python itself performs.

    The reversed row is the one that gives the method away. Perfectly reversed data is the worst case for many sorting algorithms and costs 999 comparisons here — the same as already-sorted data. That is because the algorithm looks for runs that are ordered either way, and a descending run is turned round in one pass. It is not detecting sortedness; it is detecting runs, and a reversed list is one enormous run.

    Adaptive, and why that is the right idea

    An algorithm is adaptive when it does less work on input that is closer to the answer. Python's sort finds already-ordered runs, extends short ones, and merges them — so its cost ranges from n−1 on ordered data up to n log n on random data, rather than always paying the worst case.

    The wider lesson is the one worth carrying: the best-known algorithm for a problem in general is not always the best algorithm for the data you actually have. Knowing something about your input — that it is nearly sorted, that it arrives in blocks, that it repeats — is frequently worth more than a better asymptotic bound.

    Python languageCPython

    Guaranteed by the language: that list.sort and sorted are stable, and that sorting uses only <. You may rely on both, including on the two-pass technique of Unit II.10.4.

    CPython's: which algorithm is used, and therefore every comparison count above. The adaptive behaviour is not promised by the language, and the counts will differ between versions and implementations. Run the Counted experiment on your own build rather than quoting these figures.

    Sources: Python language reference on sorting; the sorting how-to in the standard documentation.

    Ladder · sorted(items, key=f)where the work actually happens

    1. Human intention — choosing the algorithm; the growth is decided here
    2. Python source text — one call, hiding n log n comparisons
    3. Tokens
    4. Syntax tree
    5. Compiler
    6. Code object and bytecode — a single call instruction
    7. CPython runtime — the sort runs in C; each comparison may call back into Python
    8. Native machine instructions
    9. CPU control logic
    10. Registers and ALU
    11. Caches and RAM — a new list, or the same one rearranged
    12. Operating-system services
    13. Device, file, terminal, result

    Floor 7 explains why sorting built-in types is so much faster than sorting your own objects. The sort itself is compiled code, but every comparison between Counted instances calls back up into interpreted Python — which is Chapter II.8's finding about the dominant constant factor, and Chapter II.13's advice to stay in compiled code, arriving as a measurable consequence.

    Retrieval lock

    Reconstruct it without looking

    Close the book

    1. Redraw. Sort [5, 2, 8, 1] by hand with merge sort, drawing the splits and the merges. Count your comparisons and check against the formula.
    2. Explain. Why can no method that settles one pair per comparison beat n2/2? Then say what merge sort does differently.
    3. Explain. Where do the two factors in n log n come from? Name which part of the algorithm produces each.
    4. Explain. Why does Python take a key function rather than a comparison function? Give the count that makes the argument.
    5. Modify. Sort a list of records by one field then another using two passes. Then reverse the order of the passes and explain what goes wrong.
    6. Modify. Build the Counted class and reproduce the five arrangements on your own interpreter. Report whether your numbers match, and what you would conclude if they did not.
    7. Transfer. A colleague's log-processing job sorts records that arrive almost in time order, and they are considering a faster sorting library. Using this chapter, say what you would measure before agreeing.
    8. Stretch. Explain why reversed data costs the same as sorted data. Then construct an input of a thousand items that costs more comparisons than the shuffled case, and say what property makes it hard.
    Mastery gate — Chapter II.10
    • You can implement bubble sort and predict its comparison count exactly.
    • You can explain merge sort's method and why one comparison can settle many pairs.
    • You can account for both factors in n log n, and say why no comparison sort can do better.
    • You can explain what sorting requires of the values, and read the TypeError when it is missing.
    • You can define stability and use it to sort by two criteria without writing a combined comparison.
    • You can state the least-significant-first rule and say why it is the reverse of how you would describe it.
    • You can explain what an adaptive sort is, and demonstrate it by counting comparisons.
    • You can say which properties of Python's sort are guaranteed and which are this implementation's.

    If item five is shaky, the two-pass experiment is the fastest cure: sort by name, then by score, and watch the alphabetical order survive inside each score group. That behaviour is the whole of what stability buys.
