    Volume II · Chapter 11Structures, programs and cost

    Who cleans up

    Reference counting, the cycles it cannot see, the collector that finds them, and where memory actually comes from

    Every object in this book so far has appeared when needed and vanished when not, and nothing has ever asked you to arrange the vanishing. That is unusual — many languages require you to free memory by hand, and getting it wrong is the source of a whole family of defects. This chapter is about what is doing the work instead, how you can watch it, and the one situation it cannot handle alone.

    Prerequisites

    Chapter I.3 (names as labels on objects — the whole chapter rests on that image), Chapter I.6 and I.7 (containers holding references), Chapter II.7 (classes and __del__), Chapter I.8 (frames, whose disappearance releases references), Chapter 0.2 and Figure 0.4.1 (memory, and the heap).

    Unit II.11.1
    Problem

    When is an object finished with?

    Something you can feel

    An object occupies memory, and memory is finite. So something must decide when an object is no longer wanted and its memory can be used for something else. The question is who decides, and how they can possibly know.

    Consider what "no longer wanted" means. It cannot mean "the program has finished with it", because no such fact exists anywhere — a program does not announce its intentions. What it can mean is something narrower and checkable: no way remains to reach this object. If nothing refers to it, no future line of code can possibly mention it, so nothing can tell the difference between keeping it and destroying it.

    That gives a workable rule, and the two ways of implementing it are worth naming because Python uses both. You can count the references to each object and free it the moment the count reaches zero. Or you can periodically trace outwards from everything currently reachable and free whatever was not visited. The first is immediate and simple and has one blind spot; the second finds everything and cannot be immediate.

    Unit II.11.2
    Tool

    Counting the labels

    Reference counting, observed

    Chapter I.3 established that a name is a label attached to an object rather than a box containing it. Reference counting is that image with a tally: each object knows how many labels are currently on it, and when the last one comes off, it goes.

    The freeing is immediate, and you can watch it happen — which is worth doing once, because it makes the mechanism concrete in a way the numbers do not.

    It also explains something from earlier in the book that was left as an observation. Chapter III.1 will note that CPython appears to close files you forgot to close; this is why. The file object's count reaches zero when the last reference goes, and closing happens then. And Chapter I.8's frames release everything they held when they are destroyed, which is why local variables do not accumulate.

    Counting has costs, and honesty requires naming them. Every assignment, every argument passed, every container insertion must adjust a count — small work, done constantly. And the counts must be correct even when several threads are running, which is the reason Chapter III.6 gave for the interpreter lock existing at all: unsynchronised increments would corrupt the counts and free objects still in use.

    Unit II.11.3
    Break

    Two objects holding each other up

    Deliberate failure — the blind spot

    The rule is "free it when nothing refers to it". Consider two objects that refer to each other and to which nothing else refers.

    Predict

    Two nodes, each with the other in an attribute. Delete both names. Nothing outside can reach either. What do their counts say?

    Why this is a limitation and not a bug

    Counting asks a purely local question: how many references point at me. That question can be answered without looking at anything else, which is what makes it cheap and immediate. It also cannot detect a group whose only references come from inside the group.

    Answering "is this reachable from the program?" requires tracing from the outside inwards, which is a global question — and global questions cannot be answered incrementally as each assignment happens. The blind spot is the price of the immediacy, not an oversight.

    Cycles are not exotic. A tree whose nodes know their parents contains one for every node. A collection of objects that refer to each other contains many. An exception carries a traceback that refers to frames that refer to the exception. They arise naturally from ordinary designs, so a language that only counted would leak steadily.

    Unit II.11.4
    Rebuild

    The second collector

    Tracing, occasionally

    So CPython runs a second mechanism alongside the first. Periodically it traces outwards from everything the program can definitely reach — names in modules, frames on the stack — and anything not visited is unreachable regardless of what its count says.

    The division of labour is worth stating plainly, because it explains the behaviour you actually observe. The counter handles the overwhelming majority of objects, immediately and cheaply. The tracer handles cycles, occasionally and at some cost, and only examines container objects, since an integer cannot participate in a cycle.

    Two consequences follow. Most objects are freed the instant they become unreachable, so Python's memory use is more predictable than in languages that trace only. But objects in cycles are freed at an unpredictable later time, so anything holding a scarce resource — a file, a connection, a lock — must not rely on being collected. That is the deeper reason Chapter III.1 insists on with: not merely that CPython's tidying is an implementation detail, but that for cyclic objects it is not even prompt.

    Unit II.11.5
    Descend

    Where the memory comes from

    One floor lower

    "Freed" has been used loosely. Freed to whom?

    Chapter 0.4 established that memory comes from the operating system, in pages, on request. Asking for a page is a system call — floor 12 — and Python creates and destroys small objects constantly. A crossing per object would be ruinous.

    So CPython does not ask the kernel for each object. It asks for large blocks and hands out pieces itself, keeping the freed pieces on its own lists for reuse. Most allocation therefore never leaves the process: it is a pointer moved in a structure CPython maintains, at floor 7 rather than floor 12.

    This explains a puzzle people meet when they first watch a Python program's memory. Free a great many objects and the process's memory footprint may not shrink at all, because the memory was returned to CPython's pools rather than to the operating system. The objects are gone and the space is available for new Python objects — but from the outside, nothing was given back.

    CPythonPython language

    The language guarantees only that objects you can no longer reach will eventually be reclaimed. It does not promise when, nor by what method, nor that __del__ runs promptly — which is why relying on it for cleanup is a mistake in any Python.

    CPython's are reference counting, its immediacy, the cycle collector, sys.getrefcount, gc, and the pooled allocator. Other implementations trace only, and there objects can survive far longer after their last use. Code that depends on prompt destruction works on one implementation and quietly holds resources open on another.

    Sources: Python language reference on object lifetime; gc and sys module documentation.

    Ladder · x = Nonewhen it happens to be the last reference

    1. Human intention — done with that
    2. Python source text — a rebinding, or the end of a function
    3. Tokens
    4. Syntax tree
    5. Compiler
    6. Code object and bytecode — a store, which drops the old reference
    7. CPython runtime — count reaches zero; the object is destroyed here and now
    8. Native machine instructions
    9. CPU control logic
    10. Registers and ALU
    11. Caches and RAM — space returns to CPython's pool, not to the system
    12. Operating-system services — dark: this is why allocation is fast
    13. Device, file, terminal, result

    Floor 12 being dark is the point of the whole arrangement. Creating and destroying objects is among the most frequent things a Python program does, and it happens entirely inside the process. The kernel is involved only when CPython's pools run low and it asks for another large block — rarely, and for many objects at once.

    Retrieval lock

    Reconstruct it without looking

    Close the book

    1. Explain. Why is "nothing refers to it" the right definition of finished with, rather than "the program has stopped using it"?
    2. Modify. Use getrefcount to watch a count rise and fall as you add a name, put the object in a list, pass it to a function, and remove each. Predict each number first.
    3. Redraw. Draw two objects in a cycle with no external references, marking each count. Explain why 1 is not 0 and why that is not a bug.
    4. Modify. Build the cycle with __del__ on both, delete the names, and confirm nothing is freed. Then call gc.collect().
    5. Explain. Why can counting not detect cycles? Answer in terms of local versus global questions.
    6. Transfer. A colleague relies on __del__ to close a database connection. Give two separate reasons this is unsafe.
    7. Explain. Why might a program's memory not shrink after freeing many objects? Say where the memory went.
    8. Stretch. Find a cycle in a design of your own. Then look up weak references and explain how they would break it without changing the design.
    Mastery gate — Chapter II.11
    • You can state when an object may be reclaimed, and why that is checkable.
    • You can watch a reference count change and predict it.
    • You can explain why freeing is immediate, and give two things that depend on it.
    • You can construct a cycle and explain why counting alone cannot free it.
    • You can describe the tracing collector and say which objects it examines.
    • You can explain why cleanup must not be left to __del__.
    • You can say where allocated memory actually comes from and why floor 12 is rarely involved.
    • You can separate what the language guarantees from what CPython does.

    If item four is shaky, build the cycle and watch nothing happen. The silence where two messages should be is the most memorable thing in this chapter, and it is the reason the second collector exists at all.

    Volume II · Chapter 12Structures, programs and cost

    Distance costs time

    Caches, cache lines, locality — and why a Python list of numbers gets less benefit from them than you would hope

    Chapter 0.2 treated every memory address as equally far away. That was a declared simplification, and this is where it is corrected. Some addresses are enormously more expensive to reach than others, and which ones depends on what you touched a moment ago.

    Prerequisites

    Chapter 0.2 and 0.3 (memory, addresses, the fetch cycle), Chapter 0.4 (the address space), Chapter I.6 and II.9 (a list holds references, in a contiguous block), Chapter II.8 (shapes, and the fact that constants matter too), Chapter II.11 (objects scattered across the heap). This chapter comes near the end of the volume on purpose: without every one of those, it would be a collection of impressive-sounding numbers.

    Unit II.12.1
    Problem

    Same shape, different speed

    Something you can feel

    Two programs read a million numbers and add them up. Both are O(n). Both do a million additions. One reads them in order; the other jumps about. On a real machine the second can take several times longer.

    Chapter II.8 said complexity is decided at floors 1 and 2, and that everything below buys only a constant factor. That is still true. This chapter is about how large that constant can be — and it turns out to be large enough to matter.

    Unit II.12.2
    Descend

    Memory is not one thing

    The hierarchy

    Chapter 0.3's processor fetched from RAM as though RAM were next door. It is not. A modern processor runs so fast that fetching from RAM leaves it idle for hundreds of cycles — so between the registers and RAM sit several layers of small, fast memory called caches, holding copies of whatever was used recently.

    The reason for the gap is physical rather than a matter of engineering effort, which is why it has not been closed and will not be. Signals travel at a finite speed, and a processor completing several operations per nanosecond performs a great many of them in the time a signal takes to cross a circuit board. Memory that is physically further away is therefore slower in a way no cleverness removes. Fast memory must be small and close; large memory must sit further off and be slower. The hierarchy is not a design compromise but an arrangement forced by geometry.

    Hardware example

    Every number above is a rough figure for one class of desktop processor. Sizes, latencies and the number of levels differ between manufacturers, generations and even between cores on one chip. Treat them as orders of magnitude that explain behaviour — never as facts to quote.

    Category: hardware example. Verify against your own processor's documentation.
    Unit II.12.3
    Tool

    Memory arrives in blocks

    The cache line, and why order matters

    Here is the fact that makes caches predictable rather than mysterious. The processor never fetches one byte. It fetches a whole cache line — commonly 64 bytes — because fetching neighbours is nearly free once you have paid to reach the neighbourhood.

    So reading one address quietly brings its neighbours along. If your next read is one of those neighbours, it is already there and costs almost nothing. If it is somewhere else entirely, you pay the full price again.

    This is the most useful fact in the chapter, because it converts an invisible property into a predictable one. A program's speed depends not only on how many items it touches but on where those items sit relative to each other. Touching a thousand adjacent values costs a fraction of touching a thousand scattered ones, although both are a thousand reads and both look identical in source. Chapter II.8 measured work by counting operations; this is the correction to that model, and it is why two programs of the same complexity can differ by a large constant factor.

    It also names the property worth designing for. Locality means keeping things that are used together close together in memory, and it comes in two forms: using the same item repeatedly while it is still cached, and using neighbouring items in succession so each fetched line serves several accesses. Nearly every cache-related optimisation is one of those two ideas.

    Spatial locality
    Use things that sit near each other. Walking a block in order is the ideal case — one fetch serves many reads
    Temporal locality
    Use the same thing again soon. It is still in cache from last time

    This is why reading in order beats jumping about, even with identical operation counts. It is also why Chapter II.9's contiguous block is worth more than it looked: sixty-four bytes holds eight 8-byte references, so one fetch delivers eight slots.

    Unit II.12.4
    Break

    The Python list is not what you are picturing

    Deliberate correction

    The tempting conclusion is that a Python list of a million numbers is a lovely contiguous block that the cache will love. It is not, and Figure I.6.1 already told you why.

    Predict

    A list of 1000 small integers. The list's own block holds 1000 references, 8 bytes each. But where are the integer objects, and how big is each?

    Why this matters for the cache

    Walking the array touches one contiguous run of memory. Walking the list touches a contiguous run of pointers, and then jumps somewhere else for every single value.

    One 64-byte line holds eight pointers, so the list's own block is read efficiently. But each of those eight pointers then sends the processor to a separate 28-byte object elsewhere in the heap — and those objects were created at different moments, so they are scattered.

    New Python — array and memoryview

    array.array('q', values) stores numbers directly, packed, with no per-item object — 'q' means 8-byte signed integers. It indexes and loops like a list, but can hold only one kind of number, which is the price of the packing.

    memoryview(b) gives a window onto an existing block of bytes without copying it. Slicing a view costs nothing, where slicing a list builds a whole new list.

    Unit II.12.5
    Rebuild

    How much of this can you actually feel?

    The honest answer

    Now the correction that keeps this chapter from misleading you, and the reason it sits here rather than early in the book.

    The honesty is necessary because this material is genuinely true of computers and largely invisible from Python, and presenting it without the caveat would encourage exactly the mistake Chapter II.13 warns against. A reader who takes cache locality as a Python optimisation target will spend effort restructuring data for an effect the interpreter's overhead comfortably swamps.

    So read the chapter as describing a floor you are standing on rather than a lever you are holding. Knowing that memory is a hierarchy explains why compiled numerical libraries are as fast as they are, why they want contiguous arrays rather than lists of references, and why moving work into them helps so much. Those are real decisions available to you. Rearranging a Python list to improve its cache behaviour is not.

    Every operation in ordinary Python carries interpreter overhead: dispatching a bytecode, following a type pointer, building or freeing objects, adjusting reference counts. That overhead is typically much larger than the difference between a cache hit and a cache miss. So in a plain Python loop, cache behaviour is usually hidden beneath the cost of being Python at all.

    Simplified modelHardware example

    What this chapter gets right: the hierarchy, the cache line, locality, and why a list of objects is scattered where an array is packed. All of it is real and all of it explains genuine behaviour. What it leaves out: how much you can measure from Python, which is often far less than the hardware numbers suggest — and how much the processor hides through prefetching and running instructions out of order. The fuller version: measure it, which is Chapter II.13. Do not act on this chapter without a measurement.

    Category: simplified model. Discharged immediately, in Chapter II.13.

    Where it does become visible is precisely where the interpreter steps out of the way: with array, bytes and memoryview; with libraries that do the loop in compiled code over packed data; and when the data is large enough that the caches genuinely cannot hold it. Those are real and common situations — but they are the exception, and reaching for them before measuring is how people make code uglier and no faster.

    Ladder · where the cache livesand where you can reach

    1. Human intention — your choice of container is the only lever you have
    2. Python source text — list of objects, or packed array
    3. Tokens
    4. Syntax tree
    5. Compiler
    6. Code object and bytecode — contains no notion of memory at all
    7. CPython runtime — where the objects were placed, and the overhead that hides the effect
    8. Native machine instructions
    9. CPU control logic
    10. Registers and ALU
    11. Caches and RAM — where the whole effect happens, invisibly
    12. Operating-system services
    13. Device, file, terminal, result

    Three floors lit, and they are far apart. You act at floors 1 and 2; the consequence occurs at floor 11; and nothing between them mentions it. That gap is the reason cache effects feel like magic — and the reason guessing about them is hopeless without measurement.

    Retrieval lock

    Reconstruct it without looking

    Close the book

    1. Redraw. Draw the hierarchy with rough sizes, then draw a list of three ints and an array of three ints, showing which memory each touches when you walk it.
    2. Explain. Why does reading a block in order beat reading it in a scattered order, given both do the same number of reads? Use the phrase cache line.
    3. Modify. Build a list and an array of a million numbers and sum each. Time both several times, note the variation, and report what you find — including if the difference is smaller than you expected. An honest negative result is a real result.
    4. Transfer. A friend has read that Python lists are slow because of cache misses and wants to rewrite their 200-item shopping program with array. Give them the two reasons this is a bad idea, one from this chapter and one from Chapter II.8.
    5. Stretch. A 64-byte line holds eight pointers. Work out how many whole 28-byte int objects fit in one line, then explain why the answer being awkward is itself part of the problem.
    Mastery gate — Chapter II.12
    • You can describe the memory hierarchy and say why it exists.
    • You can explain what a cache line is and why it makes order matter.
    • You can define spatial and temporal locality and give an example of each.
    • You can explain why a Python list of numbers is not a packed block of numbers.
    • You can say what array and memoryview are for, and what they cost you.
    • You can explain why cache effects are often invisible in ordinary Python, and what that implies before you change anything.

    Item six is the one that stops this chapter doing harm. If it is shaky, do not act on anything here until you have read Chapter II.13 and taken a measurement.

    Back · Chapter II.11Who cleans up Next · Chapter II.13Measure, then change
    Volume II · Chapter 13Structures, programs and cost

    Measure, then change

    Profiling, timing honestly, the arithmetic that decides what is worth improving — and the discipline that makes the rest of this volume safe to use

    You now know several ways to make programs faster. This chapter is about the far harder question of whether to, and which part — because the one reliable finding of fifty years of software engineering is that programmers cannot guess where their time goes.

    Prerequisites

    Chapter II.2 (tests — you cannot safely change what you cannot check), Chapter II.8 (shapes), Chapter II.9 to II.12 (the things you might change), and Chapter 0.4 (scheduling, which is why measurements wobble). This chapter is deliberately last: it is the one that tells you when to use the others.

    Unit II.13.1
    Problem

    You are wrong about what is slow

    Something you can feel

    Everyone believes they know which part of their program is slow. Almost everyone is wrong, and the ones who are right have measured. This is not a failing of skill — it is a consequence of how much sits between your source and the machine, as thirteen floors of ladder have shown.

    The failure is expensive twice over. You spend hours making something faster that accounted for two percent of the runtime, and you leave behind code that is harder to read, more likely to be wrong, and no faster in any way anybody notices.

    There is a third cost, less obvious and often larger. The optimised version is nearly always the harder one to read, so every future change to that code is slower and riskier — and you paid that permanent price for a speed-up you never confirmed. Chapter II.2's argument applies directly: without a measurement you have no way to know whether the change helped, and without tests you have no way to know whether it is still correct.

    The reason people optimise the wrong thing so reliably is worth naming, because it is not carelessness. Reading code, attention goes to whatever looks complicated — a dense expression, a clever algorithm, a nested loop. But time is spent where the machine goes most often, and frequency is invisible in source. A three-line function that looks trivial and is called ten million times will dominate a forty-line function called twice, and no amount of careful reading reveals that. The instrument exists precisely because intuition has no access to the relevant fact.

    The discipline, in five steps

    Make it correct. Prove it with tests. Measure to find where the time actually goes. Improve the shape first. Measure again to prove you helped.

    Steps one and two are Chapter II.2, and they come first for a hard reason: an optimisation that breaks the program has not made anything faster. It has made a wrong answer arrive sooner.

    Unit II.13.2
    Tool

    Timing one small thing

    timeit, and why it works the way it does

    New Python — timeit

    timeit.timeit('code', number=1000) runs a snippet a thousand times and returns the total seconds as a float. Use setup= for preparation you do not want timed. The point of running it many times is that a single run is meaningless: your snippet may take a microsecond, and the clock is not that precise.

    Three rules for taking a timing seriously, all of which follow from Chapter 0.4:

    Repeat
    Run the whole measurement several times and take the fastest, not the average. Interruptions can only make a run slower, never faster, so the minimum is the cleanest signal
    Keep setup out
    Building the test data inside the timed code measures the building. Put it in setup=
    Expect wobble
    The scheduler may take your processor away mid-measurement; caches may be warm or cold. A 10% difference between two runs is noise, not a finding
    Unit II.13.3
    Tool

    Finding the hot spot in a whole program

    cProfile

    timeit answers "how long does this line take?". The more useful question is "where does my program spend its time?", and for that you need a profiler: it watches every call and reports how often each function ran and how long it took.

    New Python — cProfile

    cProfile.run('report(passage)') runs your code and prints a table: number of calls, time spent in each function itself, and cumulative time including everything it called. Sort by cumulative time to find where the program lives.

    What profiles almost always reveal is the same shape: a small function called an enormous number of times. Not a slow function — a cheap one, called 4,812 times. Which is Chapter II.8's point arriving as evidence rather than theory: the fix is usually to call it less often, not to make it faster.

    That shape has a name worth knowing, since it recurs across almost every kind of program: the time is concentrated. A handful of places account for most of it and the great majority of your code accounts for almost none. It follows that most of your code should never be optimised at all — not as a concession to readability, but because optimising it cannot produce a measurable result.

    It also explains why the first profile of an unfamiliar program is so often surprising. The hot spot is regularly somewhere nobody would have guessed: a comparison function called by a sort, a repeated conversion inside a loop, a logging call left in from debugging. Being surprised is the normal outcome and a sign the instrument is working.

    OS-dependentCPython

    Profiling changes what it measures: watching every call adds overhead to every call, so profiled code runs slower and functions called very often look relatively worse than they are. Use a profile to find where to look; use timeit, unprofiled, to decide whether a change helped. Timing precision, scheduling behaviour and the profiler's own cost all vary by operating system.

    Category: standard library; measurement behaviour is OS- and implementation-dependent.
    Unit II.13.4
    Break

    The optimisation that gained nothing

    Deliberate failure, in arithmetic

    Predict — commit to a number

    A function accounts for 10% of your program's runtime. You spend a week and make it a hundred times faster. How much faster is the whole program?

    Work it out. The other 90% is untouched, and the 10% becomes 0.1%. So the total is 90.1% of what it was — the program is about 1.11 times faster. A week of work for eleven percent, and the answer would barely have changed if you had made that function infinitely fast: 90% is the floor.

    10% of runtime, 100× faster
    Total gain: 1.11× — and 1.11× is the ceiling, however hard you work
    50% of runtime, 2× faster
    Total gain: 1.33× — from a modest improvement in the right place
    90% of runtime, 100× faster
    Total gain: 9.17× — the same effort, thirty times the payoff
    The rule this arithmetic forces

    Your possible gain is capped by the share of runtime you are working on. Improving something that takes 10% of the time can never make the program more than about 1.11 times faster, no matter how brilliant you are.

    This is why measuring first is not diligence, it is arithmetic. Without a profile you do not know which row of that table you are in — and the difference between the rows is the difference between a wasted week and a real result.

    The same arithmetic runs in the encouraging direction too, and it is the reason profiling pays. A function accounting for eighty per cent of the time, made twice as fast, takes the whole program to sixty per cent of its original duration. Made ten times faster, it takes it to twenty-eight. The identical effort applied to the identical function produces a transformative result or an unmeasurable one depending entirely on a number you can only obtain by measuring.

    The bound has a further implication that is easy to miss: it tells you when to stop. Once the dominant cost has been reduced to a small share, further work on it cannot help however clever it is, and the ceiling is set by everything you have not touched. Knowing that a remaining component fixes an upper limit on your improvement is what turns optimisation from an open-ended activity into one with a defined end.

    Unit II.13.5
    Rebuild

    What to try, in order

    The whole volume, as a checklist

    When the profile has told you where the time goes, work down this list. It is ordered by payoff, and the first two items usually settle it.

    1 · Do less
    Can the work be avoided? Cached? Done once instead of per item? The cheapest operation is the one you removed
    2 · Change the shape
    Chapter II.8. A hidden in on a list, a sort inside a loop, a quadratic that should be linear. This is where the tenfold and thousandfold gains live
    3 · Change the container
    Chapters II.1, II.9. Set instead of list for membership; dictionary instead of paired lists
    4 · Let compiled code do the loop
    sum, sorted, a comprehension, a library. One call instead of a million bytecode dispatches
    5 · Change the layout
    Chapter II.12. array, bytes, memoryview. Real, and rarely the biggest win in Python
    6 · Micro-optimise
    Rearranging lines, avoiding an attribute lookup. Almost never worth the readability, and the first thing beginners reach for
    The comfortable wrong idea

    "Faster code is better code."

    Fast code that nobody can safely change is a liability. Every optimisation costs clarity, and clarity is what lets you fix the next problem. Spend that currency where a measurement says it buys something, and nowhere else. If a change makes the program 3% faster and 30% harder to read, you have made a bad trade with a straight face.

    Ladder · where speed actually comes fromthe whole volume, on one diagram

    1. Human intention — doing less work at all: the largest wins
    2. Python source text — algorithm and container: the reliable wins
    3. Tokens
    4. Syntax tree
    5. Compiler — constant folding, already done for you
    6. Code object and bytecode
    7. CPython runtime — staying in compiled code instead of Python loops
    8. Native machine instructions
    9. CPU control logic
    10. Registers and ALU
    11. Caches and RAM — layout, occasionally, when the data is large
    12. Operating-system services — fewer crossings: buffering, batching. Often the biggest win of all
    13. Device, file, terminal, result

    Four lit floors, and notice where they are: the top of the ladder and the bottom, with the whole middle dark. You cannot make the interpreter faster by trying harder. You can do less work, choose better structures, stay in compiled code, and stop crossing the kernel boundary so often — and that last one is Volume III's opening subject.

    Retrieval lock

    Reconstruct it without looking

    Close the book

    1. Redraw. Write the five steps of the discipline in order, then say what goes wrong if you skip each one.
    2. Explain. A function takes 20% of the runtime and you make it 10× faster. Compute the total gain, then say what the best possible gain would have been.
    3. Modify. Profile Chapter I.12's tally on a large passage. Report which function has the most calls and which has the highest cumulative time, and say which you would attack — and why they are usually different.
    4. Transfer. A friend says their program is slow and they are going to rewrite it in a faster language. Give them the three questions to answer first, and say what each would tell them.
    5. Stretch. Time sum(range(1000)) against a hand-written loop, five times each, and record all ten numbers. How much do repeated runs of the same code vary? Use Chapter 0.4 to explain the variation, then say what that implies about trusting a single measurement.
    Mastery gate — Chapter II.13, and the whole of Volume II
    • You can state the five-step discipline and say why correctness and tests come first.
    • You can time a snippet honestly, keeping setup out and taking the minimum of several runs.
    • You can read a profile's columns and say what a large gap between them means.
    • You can compute the maximum possible gain from improving a given share of the runtime.
    • You can order the six kinds of change by expected payoff and justify the order.
    • You can explain why an optimisation that costs clarity needs a measurement to justify it.

    This gate closes Volume II. Item four is the one that will keep you from wasting weeks; item six is the one that will keep your programs worth reading. If either is shaky, reread Unit II.13.4 — the arithmetic is the argument.

    Where this goes next

    Volume II has been about programs that live entirely inside their own process: containers, structures, cost, memory. The last floor of the ladder above points outward. Volume III is about what happens when a program needs something it does not own — files, the network, other processes, a clock, a disk that might fail halfway through a write. Everything there is floor 12, and everything there is slow, uncertain and genuinely interesting.

    Volume III · Chapter 1The program meets the world

    Opening the world

    Files, the promise that closes them, streaming rather than swallowing — and why text and bytes finally part company at the edge

    Everything in the first two volumes happened inside one process and vanished when it ended. This volume is about leaving. The first thing to leave towards is a file, and opening one turns out to introduce three ideas at once: a resource you must give back, a boundary where text stops being text, and a choice about how much of the world you pull into memory at a time.

    Prerequisites

    Chapter 0.4 (processes, the kernel boundary, and why your program cannot touch a disk itself), Chapter I.9 (strings, code points and encodings — the distinction becomes load-bearing here), Chapter I.11 (exceptions, since the whole of Unit III.1.4 turns on them), Chapter II.5 (iteration and laziness), Chapter II.11 (reference counting, which explains a piece of CPython behaviour you should not rely on).

    Unit III.1.1
    Problem

    Nothing you have made has survived

    Something you can feel

    Every dictionary, list and object you have built in this book has had the same fate. The process ended, the operating system reclaimed its address space, and all of it ceased to exist — completely, immediately, and without any way to get it back.

    That is not a limitation of Python. It is what Chapter 0.4 described as isolation, working exactly as designed: memory belongs to a process, and when the process is gone so is its memory. The isolation that stops other programs corrupting your data also stops your data outliving you.

    So anything that must survive has to be written somewhere that is not your memory. And here the isolation bites from the other side: you cannot write to a disk. Your process runs in user mode, and the disk belongs to the kernel. Every byte that leaves your address space leaves by permission, through a request, across floor 12.

    Which means a file is not really a thing you have. It is an ongoing arrangement with the operating system — one it is keeping track of, one that costs it something, and one you are expected to end when you are done. That framing explains almost everything else in this chapter, including the parts that look like arbitrary Python rules.

    Unit III.1.2
    Tool

    Asking for a file

    What open gives you

    New Python — open

    open(path, mode, encoding=...) asks the operating system for access to a file and returns an object to work through. The mode says what you intend to do; the encoding says how characters are to be turned into bytes, and Unit III.1.5 argues that you should always say it.

    The modes are worth learning properly rather than by trial, because two of them destroy data and the difference is one character.

    'r'
    Read. The default. Fails with FileNotFoundError if the file is not there
    'w'
    Write. Creates the file, and empties it immediately if it already exists — before you have written anything
    'a'
    Append. Creates if needed; otherwise adds to the end, leaving what is there
    'x'
    Create exclusively. Fails with FileExistsError if the file exists — the safe choice when you must not overwrite
    Unit III.1.3
    Descend

    Why a file must be given back

    A resource, not a value

    You have never had to release anything before. Chapter II.11 established that Python objects are freed automatically when nothing refers to them, and that has been true for every object in this book so far. A file is different, and the reason is that the thing being held is not yours.

    When you open a file, the kernel records the arrangement in its own memory: which file, where you have got to, what you are allowed to do. That record is a limited resource, and each process may hold only so many.

    There is a second reason, which matters more often. Chapter III.2 will show that what you write does not go to the disk immediately; it waits in a buffer. Closing is what guarantees the waiting bytes are handed over. A program that writes a file and never closes it can leave the last part of its output simply missing, with no error anywhere.

    The comfortable wrong idea

    "Python closes files for me — I have forgotten before and nothing went wrong."

    In CPython, probably nothing did. Chapter II.11's reference counting frees the file object as soon as the last reference disappears, and closing happens then. That is a property of this implementation's memory management, not a promise of the language, and Python will warn you about it if you ask it to:

    ResourceWarning: unclosed file <_io.TextIOWrapper name='a.txt'>

    An implementation that collects garbage in a different way — and several do — may leave the file open for an unpredictable length of time. Relying on the tidying is relying on an accident of how one interpreter manages memory.

    Unit III.1.4
    Break

    The file you meant to close

    Deliberate failure — and the promise that fixes it

    Knowing that you must close, the obvious approach is to close.

    Predict

    Suppose process(records) raises — a KeyError, say, on one bad record. What happens to the file?

    Chapter I.11 has the answer. The exception abandons the rest of the function, so the third line never runs. The file stays open, its buffered contents unwritten, and the frame that held the only reference to it is destroyed as the exception travels outward.

    This is the difficulty in general form: anything you must do on the way out has to happen on every way out, and there are more ways out than the one you wrote. Normal completion, an early return, a break, and an exception raised anywhere in between — each is a different exit, and a line at the bottom of the block only covers the first.

    You could write it defensively with try and finally, and that works. Python offers something shorter that means exactly the same thing.

    The name for the arrangement is a context manager, and the shape is worth recognising because it recurs: something with a setup and a teardown that must be paired. Chapter III.6's locks use it, Chapter III.9's database transactions use it, and Chapter II.7 showed you how to give your own objects the same behaviour. The guarantee itself rests on finally, whose implementation Chapter IV.6 examines — and which turns out to be the hardest thing in that chapter, precisely because "on every way out" is a demanding promise to keep.

    The practical rule is short: if you are typing open without with, you had better have a specific reason.

    Unit III.1.5
    Descend

    Where text becomes bytes

    The boundary Chapter I.9 prepared you for

    Chapter I.9 established that a Python string is a sequence of code points, not of bytes, and that turning one into the other requires choosing an encoding. Inside your program the distinction can be ignored most of the time. At a file it cannot, because a file is bytes and nothing else.

    When you open a text file without saying which encoding, Python uses a default that depends on the system your program happens to be running on. That is convenient, and it means a file written on one machine may be read incorrectly on another, with nothing in the source of either program to indicate why.

    And "incorrectly" has two very different forms, which is the part that makes this worth a unit rather than a sentence.

    Why the encoding must be stated

    A wrong encoding does not reliably announce itself. Sometimes it raises, and sometimes it hands you plausible-looking rubbish and lets you carry on.

    So encoding='utf-8' is not a formality; it is the difference between a program whose behaviour is a property of its source and one whose behaviour is a property of the machine it happens to run on. Write it every time, including when reading, and including when it seems obvious.

    Text mode does one further thing that surprises people, and it is best met deliberately.

    Which gives the rule for choosing modes. Open in text mode when the file genuinely contains human language and you want characters. Open in binary mode — 'rb', 'wb' — for anything else: images, compressed data, anything whose exact bytes matter. In binary mode nothing is decoded and nothing is translated, and what you get is what is there.

    Unit III.1.6
    Tool

    How much of the world to hold at once

    Streaming

    One decision remains, and it is the one that separates programs that work on real data from programs that work on examples.

    read() returns the entire file as one string. That is simple and fine for a configuration file. For a large file it means the whole thing must fit in memory at once — and Chapter II.5's iterators offer the alternative, because a file object is itself iterable, yielding one line at a time.

    The second version's memory is roughly constant regardless of the file's size, because only one line is held at a time. That is the property that matters: it does not merely use less memory, it uses an amount that does not grow. A program written that way handles a file larger than the machine's memory without noticing.

    Ladder · with open(...) as fthe first time floor 12 is unavoidable

    1. Human intention — keep this, or read what was kept
    2. Python source text — with open(path) as f
    3. Tokens
    4. Syntax tree
    5. Compiler — the with becomes setup, body, and cleanup on every exit path
    6. Code object and bytecode
    7. CPython runtime — builds the wrapper object around a descriptor
    8. Native machine instructions
    9. CPU control logic
    10. Registers and ALU
    11. Caches and RAM — buffers, and the decoded string
    12. Operating-system services — open, read, close: none of it is yours to do
    13. Device, file, terminal, result — the disk, at last

    Volumes I and II filled floors 1 to 11 and left 12 and 13 dark in almost every chapter. This is where they light up, and they will stay lit for most of Volume III. Note also floor 5: the guarantee that with makes is not something the runtime decides at the time — it is arranged by the compiler, which threads the cleanup into every exit path before the program ever runs.

    Retrieval lock

    Reconstruct it without looking

    Close the book

    1. Explain. Why must a file be closed when a list need not be freed? Answer in terms of what is being held and by whom.
    2. Explain. Give four ways execution can leave a block, and say which of them a closing line at the bottom fails to cover.
    3. Redraw. Write out what happens to 'café' between a Python string and five bytes on disk, naming each transformation and where it happens.
    4. Modify. Write a UTF-8 file containing an accented word, then read it three ways: as UTF-8, as ASCII, and as Latin-1. Record which fails loudly, which fails silently, and what each produces.
    5. Modify. Take a program that uses read() and convert it to iterate line by line. Measure both with tracemalloc and report the ratio for a file of your own.
    6. Transfer. A colleague's script sometimes produces a file missing its last few lines, with no error. Give two possible causes from this chapter and say how you would distinguish them.
    7. Transfer. Explain why 'x' mode exists when 'w' already creates files. Give a situation where using 'w' would lose data that 'x' would have protected.
    8. Stretch. Write a file containing Windows line endings, then read it in text mode, in binary mode, and with newline=''. Explain the three results, and say which you would want if you were computing a checksum.
    Mastery gate — Chapter III.1
    • You can open, read and write a file, stating the encoding every time.
    • You can name the four modes and say which two destroy data and when.
    • You can explain why a file is a resource rather than a value, and give two consequences of not closing one.
    • You can explain what with guarantees, and why a closing line at the end of a block does not.
    • You can say why CPython appearing to close files for you is not something to rely on.
    • You can describe both ways a wrong encoding can go wrong, and say which is more dangerous.
    • You can say when to use binary mode rather than text mode, and what text mode does to line endings.
    • You can explain why iterating a file uses roughly constant memory, and when that matters.

    Item six is the one that costs people days. A loud failure is a good outcome; the silent one produces a program that runs perfectly and quietly corrupts every accented character it touches, often into a database where it stays.

    Volume III · Chapter 2The program meets the world

    The cost of speaking

    Buffering, file descriptors, and the layers between your write and the disk — the debt from Chapter I.1, paid

    Chapter I.1 told you that print is expensive because it crosses the kernel boundary, and that the fix is not to make the arithmetic faster. Chapter II.13 closed Volume II by naming fewer crossings as often the biggest win available. This chapter shows you the crossings, lets you watch one not happen, and hands you the controls.

    Prerequisites

    Chapter 0.4 (user mode, kernel mode, the cost of a system call), Chapter I.1 (the cost of print), Chapter III.1 (files), Chapter II.9 (spare room traded for speed — the identical bargain reappears here), Chapter II.13 (measure before you change anything).

    Unit III.2.1
    Break

    You wrote to the file and the file is empty

    Deliberate failure, first

    This chapter opens with the failure, because the failure is the whole subject.

    Predict

    Open a file for writing. Write five characters to it. Without closing it, ask the operating system how big the file is. What do you expect?

    Nothing failed. write did not lie: it accepted your text and promised to deal with it. It simply had not dealt with it yet, and this is deliberate, universal, and the reason file handling works at all.

    The surprise is worth locating precisely, because it is not that the write was slow or unreliable. It is that the word write means something narrower than it appears to. Your program handed the text to the file object; the file object accepted it and returned; and nothing whatever was said about a disk. An operation completing successfully and an operation having taken effect in the world are different events, separated here by an unspecified amount of time.

    That gap is not an oversight and cannot simply be removed, as the rest of the chapter shows. But it explains a class of behaviour that is otherwise baffling: a program that appears to have written a file and has not, output arriving in bursts rather than steadily, and a log file missing its final and most interesting lines precisely when the program has crashed.

    Unit III.2.2
    Descend

    Why waiting is the right thing to do

    The buffer

    Chapter 0.4 established the cost: a system call is on the order of a thousand times an ordinary operation, because the processor must switch mode, the kernel must check permissions, and control must come back. Chapter I.1 used that to explain print.

    Now apply it to a program writing a million short lines. One system call per line is a million boundary crossings for a few megabytes of data — and the crossings, not the data, are the cost.

    So the file object keeps a buffer: a block of memory inside your process where writes accumulate. When it fills — or you flush it, or close the file — the whole block goes across in one call. A million small writes become a few hundred large ones.

    The arrangement is worth stating as a general principle, because it recurs at every level of a computer. When an operation has a large fixed cost and a small cost per item, the answer is to batch: accumulate many items and pay the fixed cost once. A system call costs roughly the same whether it carries one byte or eight thousand, so a buffer of eight thousand bytes turns eight thousand crossings into one.

    Chapter II.9's list is the same idea applied to memory rather than to the kernel: allocation has a large fixed cost, so a list claims room for many items at once and most appends pay nothing. The pattern is identical and so is the trade — both gain enormously in throughput, and both introduce a period during which the work is arranged but not yet done.

    The same bargain as Chapter II.9

    Spend memory now to avoid an expensive operation later, and amortise the expensive operation across many cheap ones.

    A list over-allocates so that most appends need no reallocation. A file buffers so that most writes need no system call. Different problem, identical shape — and in both cases the rare expensive event is what you must understand to predict the behaviour.

    Those layers are not a metaphor. You can look at them.

    Unit III.2.3
    Descend

    What the kernel actually gave you

    File descriptors

    Underneath all three layers is a single small integer. When the kernel grants your process access to a file, it does not hand over anything elaborate — it adds an entry to a table it keeps for your process and gives you the index. That index is a file descriptor.

    New Python — fileno

    f.fileno() reports the descriptor beneath a file object. Every process starts with three already open: 0 standard input, 1 standard output, 2 standard error. Files you open get 3 upwards.

    OS-dependent

    Descriptors as small integers, and the convention that 0, 1 and 2 are standard input, output and error, come from Unix and hold on Linux and macOS. Windows works differently underneath — it has its own handle objects — and Python presents a descriptor-shaped interface over the top. The idea — the kernel keeps the real thing and gives you a token — is universal; the token's form is not.

    Category: operating-system dependent. Verify with fileno() on your own platform.
    Unit III.2.4
    Rebuild

    Three levels of "written"

    And which one you actually need

    Figure III.2.1 has an uncomfortable consequence. When your program says the data is saved, it may be in any of three places — and they fail differently.

    In your buffer
    Lost if the process crashes. Not visible to any other program. This is where write leaves it
    In the kernel's cache
    Survives your process crashing; other programs can read it. Lost if the machine loses power. This is what flush achieves
    On the physical disk
    Survives power loss. Needs os.fsync, and it is genuinely slow — the disk must actually move

    Most programs need the second and reach it by closing the file. Programs that must not lose a transaction — databases, banks, anything where "I told you it was saved" is a promise — need the third, and pay for it. Chapter III.9 is about that price.

    Which gives a rule for when to force the issue, since flushing constantly would surrender everything buffering bought. Ask what happens if the process dies at this instant. For ordinary output the answer is that a little is lost and none of it matters. For a log written so somebody can diagnose a crash, the answer is that precisely the most valuable lines are the ones still sitting in the buffer — which is why logging systems flush more aggressively than performance alone would justify, and why a crash report that stops mid-sentence is such a common frustration.

    Note also that this is only the first of the three boundaries Chapter III.9 identifies. Flushing moves your bytes to the kernel, where they survive your process dying and become visible to other programs. It does not put them on a disk, and a machine losing power will lose them exactly as if they had never been written.

    New Python — controlling the flushing

    f.flush() pushes your buffer across the boundary. print(..., flush=True) does the same for output. open(..., buffering=0) in binary mode turns buffering off entirely — one system call per write, which is almost always a mistake and occasionally exactly right.

    Hardware exampleOS-dependent

    A measurement worth taking yourself. On one representative Linux machine, writing 20,000 short lines one system call at a time took roughly ten times as long as the same 20,000 writes through a normal buffered file. Same data, same disk, same program shape — the difference was entirely the number of boundary crossings.

    Your ratio will differ, possibly by a lot: it depends on the operating system, the storage device and how busy the machine is. Chapter II.13's rules apply — repeat it, take the best, and do not quote a single run.

    Category: hardware and OS example. Approximate, and measured on one machine.
    Unit III.2.5
    Rebuild

    Chapter I.1, settled

    Why the terminal is the slow one

    You now have everything needed to explain the claim Chapter I.1 made on trust.

    print writes to descriptor 1. If that is a file or a pipe, the output is block-buffered like any other file and a million prints cost a few hundred crossings. If it is a terminal, Python switches to line buffering — flushing at every newline — because a program that prints a prompt and then waits silently for you to type would be unusable.

    The answer to the puzzle

    A loop that prints a million lines is slow at the terminal because it makes a million system calls, and the buffering that would prevent that has been deliberately switched off so you can see the output as it happens.

    Redirect the same program to a file and it speeds up enormously — without changing one character of your code. The cost was never in your program. It was in what descriptor 1 happened to be connected to.

    Ladder · one buffered write, and the flush that followstwo different journeys

    1. Human intention — record this line
    2. Python source text
    3. Tokens
    4. Syntax tree
    5. Compiler
    6. Code object and bytecode
    7. CPython runtime — encode, then copy into the buffer. Usually it ends here
    8. Native machine instructions
    9. CPU control logic
    10. Registers and ALU — a memory copy, nothing more
    11. Caches and RAM — the buffer
    12. Operating-system services — dark for most writes; lit on the rare flush
    13. Device, file, terminal, result — and later still, if ever, the disk

    The point of buffering, drawn: floors 12 and 13 are dark for nearly every write your program performs. Buffering exists to keep them dark — and flush is you choosing to light them.

    Retrieval lock

    Reconstruct it without looking

    Close the book

    1. Redraw. Draw the four stops from your text to the disk, marking which are inside your process, where the boundary is, and which step each of write, flush and fsync reaches.
    2. Explain. Why did os.path.getsize report 0 immediately after a successful write? Answer without using the word "bug".
    3. Modify. Reproduce the zero-bytes demonstration yourself. Then do it again with buffering=0 in binary mode and explain the difference in the result.
    4. Transfer. A friend's long-running program prints progress messages, but when they redirect the output to a file the messages appear in bursts, minutes late. Explain exactly what changed, and give them two possible fixes with the trade-off.
    5. Stretch. Time 20,000 writes with and without buffering, following Chapter II.13's rules. Report the ratio you get, then explain why yours differs from the one quoted in this chapter — and why a difference does not mean either measurement is wrong.
    Mastery gate — Chapter III.2
    • You can explain why a successful write may leave the file empty, and demonstrate it.
    • You can name the layers between your text and the disk, and say what each one does.
    • You can explain what a file descriptor is and what 0, 1 and 2 are.
    • You can distinguish the three meanings of "written" and say which failure each survives.
    • You can explain why print to a terminal is slower than print to a file, without changing the program.
    • You can say why buffering is the same bargain as a list's spare capacity.

    Item five is the debt Chapter I.1 opened. If you can now explain it fully — descriptor, buffering mode, crossing count — then the first chapter of Volume I and the second chapter of Volume III have closed a circle.

    Back · Chapter III.1Opening the world Next · Chapter III.3Where things live
    Volume III · Chapter 3The program meets the world

    Where things live

    Paths as structured objects rather than text, the operating-system differences that break programs written by people who forgot, and why a path is a question rather than an answer

    A path looks like a string, and treating it as one works perfectly until the day it does not. This chapter takes paths apart: what they are made of, why two operating systems disagree about them more deeply than the slash suggests, and how a program that joins two paths together can be persuaded to open a file its author never intended. The last part is the sharpest security lesson in this volume, and it rests on a single line of behaviour you can verify in ten seconds.

    Prerequisites

    Chapter III.1 (opening files, and the with statement), Chapter III.2 (file descriptors and what the kernel actually holds), Chapter I.9 (strings, code points and encodings — needed in earnest for Unit III.3.6), Chapter 0.4 (processes, since one thing in this chapter belongs to the process rather than to your code), Chapter I.7 (mutability, for why paths are built rather than modified).

    Unit III.3.1
    Problem

    Two machines disagree about a slash

    Something you can feel

    You write open('data/' + filename) and it works. It works on your machine every time you run it, for months. Then a colleague runs it on Windows and it fails, or worse, it does not fail and opens something else.

    The obvious diagnosis is the separator: Windows writes \ where Unix writes /. That is real, and it is the least of it. If it were the only difference, a single replacement would fix everything and this chapter would be a paragraph.

    The deeper problem is that 'data/' + filename treats a path as text, and a path is not text. It is a structured description of a location that happens to be written down as text, in the same way that a date is a structured thing that happens to be written as 2026-08-04. You would not add two dates together as strings and expect a sensible answer. Paths deserve the same suspicion, and for the same reason: the notation is a rendering of the structure, not the structure itself.

    Once you look, the disagreements multiply. Windows paths may begin with a drive letter, and Unix paths never do — so "the beginning of the path" means different things. Windows compares path names without regard to case, so Notes.txt and notes.txt are the same file; most Unix filesystems treat them as two different files, and a program that assumes either way will corrupt data on the other. Windows reserves certain names entirely, so a file called con cannot exist there and can on Unix. And a path may contain elements that do not name anything at all, like .., which means "go back up" and is not a directory.

    None of that is fixable by replacing one character with another. What is needed is to stop pretending the string is the thing.

    Unit III.3.2
    Tool

    A path has parts

    Structure, made visible

    New Python — pathlib

    from pathlib import Path gives you a type that represents a location as a structured object. Path('a') / 'b' joins two paths using the correct separator for the system you are on — the / operator has been given a meaning for paths, exactly as Chapter II.7 showed you could give operators meanings for your own types.

    Start by asking what a path is made of. The answer is not "characters".

    Predict — before reading on

    Given that suffix is '.gz', what do you expect p.stem to be? Most people say 'diary'.

    This is worth more than the minute it takes. The definition is perfectly reasonable — suffix and stem are complementary, and together they always reassemble name — and it is still not what you assumed. Whenever a library gives you something that is nearly what you meant, the gap is where the defects live, and the way to find it is to check the surprising case rather than the obvious one.

    Unit III.3.3
    Tool

    Seeing both systems from one machine

    The pure path types

    You cannot test Windows behaviour by running on Unix — except that you can, because pathlib provides pure path types that do the arithmetic of a system without touching any disk. PureWindowsPath reasons about Windows paths on any machine at all, which makes the differences inspectable rather than theoretical.

    That last result deserves a moment, because it is a design decision rather than an accident. It would have been easy to make the comparison string-based and let 'a/b' equal 'a/b' regardless of flavour. Refusing to do so means a program that mixes the two gets an early, loud disagreement instead of a late, quiet one — the same principle Chapter II.2 argued for in tests, applied to a library's design.

    Unit III.3.4
    Break

    The join that threw your path away

    Deliberate failure — and a security lesson

    Now the behaviour this chapter exists for. Imagine a program that stores uploaded files in /srv/uploads and lets somebody ask for one by name. The natural implementation joins the base directory to the requested name.

    Predict

    What is PurePosixPath('/srv/uploads') / '/etc/passwd'?

    The rule is that joining an absolute path replaces everything before it, which is entirely logical: an absolute path already says where it starts, so anything to its left is meaningless. Every path library behaves this way, and it is the correct behaviour.

    It is also, in a program that joins a base directory to something a stranger supplied, a way of handing over your entire filesystem. The attacker does not need to escape your directory. They need only give you a name beginning with a slash, and your own join will politely delete the restriction.

    There is a second route, which survives even if you check for a leading slash.

    Why this is worse than an ordinary bug

    The program is not broken. It does exactly what it was told, and every individual step is correct. The defect is in the assumption that the string came from a friend.

    Chapter III.5 will show the same shape with a shell command, Chapter III.8 with a network stream, and Chapter III.9 with a database query. Four different technologies, one mistake: letting somebody else's text decide the structure of something you build. Chapter III.10 gathers all four and shows that they have a single fix.

    Unit III.3.5
    Rebuild

    Asking the disk, rather than the string

    Resolving, and checking containment

    The pure paths of Unit III.3.3 are pure precisely because they never touch the disk, and that is exactly why they cannot answer the question we now need answered. Where does .. lead? That depends on what is really there.

    It must ask, because of symbolic links. A link is a filesystem entry that points at another location, and a path passing through one does not lead where its text suggests.

    Which gives the correct way to check that a requested path stays inside a directory. Resolve both, then ask whether one is beneath the other — and let the failure be an exception rather than a boolean you might forget to test.

    The order matters and is easy to get wrong. Resolve first, then compare. Comparing the unresolved paths would accept /srv/uploads/../../etc/passwd, since it does begin with the base as text. The whole point is that text is not where the answer lives.

    The comfortable wrong idea

    "I check whether the file exists first, so I know it is safe to open."

    Checking and opening are two separate requests to the kernel, with a gap between them. In that gap, anything can happen: another process — possibly one that wants to — can delete the file and put a symbolic link in its place. Your check told you the truth about a moment that has passed.

    This shape of defect has a name, time of check to time of use, and it applies to every "look, then act" pair. The fix is to stop asking and start doing: attempt the open, and handle the failure. One request cannot be interfered with halfway, because the kernel performs it as a unit — which is precisely the guarantee Chapter III.9 will build on for renaming files.

    Unit III.3.6
    Descend

    What a filename actually is

    Bytes, text, and the gap between

    One more layer, because it explains a class of failure that otherwise looks like magic.

    Chapter I.9 established the distinction between text and bytes, and Chapter III.1 applied it to file contents. It applies to file names too, and here the situation is worse, because on a typical Unix filesystem a filename is a sequence of bytes with no declared encoding at all. The kernel stores whatever bytes it was given. Nothing records what they were meant to mean.

    Python presents filenames as text, which requires decoding bytes that may not be valid in any encoding. Something must happen to the undecodable ones, and simply failing would be intolerable — a single strange filename would make a directory unlistable.

    The practical consequence is that such a string is fine for opening the file and dangerous for almost anything else. Print it and you may get an error; put it in a JSON document and the encoder will refuse; send it over a network and Chapter III.8's rules apply with a vengeance. If you handle other people's filenames, the safe assumption is that at least one of them is not valid text, and the safe operation is to pass it straight back to the filesystem rather than through anything that expects real text.

    Unit III.3.7
    Descend

    The invisible first component

    A relative path is a question with a hidden argument

    Every relative path in your program has a component you did not write. Path('data/notes.txt') does not identify a file; it identifies a file relative to wherever the process happens to be, and that location is not a property of your code.

    The working directory belongs to the process — it is part of the state Chapter 0.4 described the kernel keeping for each one — and that has two consequences worth carrying.

    It is set by whoever started your program, not by you. A script that works when run from its own folder and fails when run from elsewhere is not suffering a mysterious fault; it is reading a relative path against a working directory it did not anticipate. The robust habit is to derive paths from something fixed, such as the location of the file being executed, rather than from wherever the user's shell happened to be.

    And because it belongs to the process, changing it changes it for everything in that process. Chapter III.6's threads all share one working directory, so a thread that changes it has changed it under every other thread, with no warning and no way for them to notice. That makes chdir one of the few operations in this book that is essentially incompatible with concurrency, and the reason to prefer absolute paths is not tidiness but safety.

    Ladder · two kinds of path operationand the floor that separates them

    1. Human intention — the file over there
    2. Python source text — base / name
    3. Tokens
    4. Syntax tree
    5. Compiler
    6. Code object and bytecode — BINARY_OP /, dispatched to the path type
    7. CPython runtime — pure joining happens entirely here: object arithmetic, no kernel
    8. Native machine instructions
    9. CPU control logic
    10. Registers and ALU
    11. Caches and RAM — new path objects in the heap
    12. Operating-system services — dark for joining; lit for resolve, exists and open
    13. Device, file, terminal, result — dark until something is actually read

    This is the distinction the chapter turns on, drawn as a ladder. Building a path is arithmetic on objects and costs nothing but memory; you may do it a million times in a loop. Asking what a path means crosses to floor 12 and cannot be answered without the kernel, which is why resolve is slow, why it can fail, and why it is the only operation that can tell you the truth about .. and links.

    Close the book

    1. Redraw. Write out parts, parent, name, stem and suffix for /var/log/app.2026.log by hand, then check. Explain the value of stem.
    2. Explain. Give three ways Windows and Unix paths differ beyond the separator, and for each say what a program that ignored it would do wrong.
    3. Explain. Why does joining an absolute path discard the base? Argue that the behaviour is correct, then explain why correct behaviour still produces a security hole.
    4. Modify. Write a function that takes a base directory and an untrusted name and returns a safe path or raises. Test it with report.txt, /etc/passwd, ../../etc/passwd and a name containing a symbolic link. Explain why resolving before comparing is essential.
    5. Transfer. A colleague's code calls exists and then open. Explain what can happen in between, name the class of defect, and give the fix in one sentence.
    6. Transfer. A script works when run from its own directory and fails from elsewhere. Diagnose it without seeing the code, and say what you would change.
    7. Stretch. Create a file whose name is not valid UTF-8, then try to list the directory, print the name, and write it into a JSON file. Explain each result using Chapter I.9's distinction between bytes and text, and say which operations are safe.
    Mastery gate — Chapter III.3
    • You can explain why a path is not a string, and take one apart into its structural pieces.
    • You can name at least three ways two operating systems disagree about paths, and demonstrate them from one machine.
    • You can predict what joining an absolute path does, and explain why that is both correct and dangerous.
    • You can write a containment check that resolves before comparing, and say why the order is not negotiable.
    • You can explain why purely textual reasoning about paths can never be made safe, using symbolic links.
    • You can state the time-of-check-to-time-of-use problem and give its fix.
    • You can explain what a filename really is on a POSIX filesystem, and what Python does about names that are not valid text.
    • You can say which path operations touch the kernel and which do not, and why that distinction matters for both speed and truth.

    If item three is shaky, run the two-line join experiment again and watch the base disappear. That single behaviour is the seed of one of the most common security defects in real software, and Chapter III.10 will show you it wearing three other disguises.
