    Volume III · Chapter 4The program meets the world

    Memory that isn’t there

    Pages, page faults and memory mapping — how a program reads a file larger than its memory by pretending the file is memory

    Chapter 0.4 said addresses are virtual and translated in blocks called pages, and promised the fuller account later. This is later. The mechanism turns out to do something stranger than protecting programs from each other: it lets memory contain things that are not in memory at all.

    Prerequisites

    Chapter 0.4 (virtual addresses, pages, the kernel boundary — the declared simplification made there is discharged here), Chapter 0.3 (the fetch cycle), Chapter III.1 and III.2 (files and buffering), Chapter II.12 (the memory hierarchy). Chapter II.9's amortised bargain appears once more, in its largest form.

    Unit III.4.1
    Problem

    A file bigger than your memory

    Something you can feel

    Ten gigabytes of data, eight gigabytes of RAM. Chapter III.1 gave you two options and neither is good enough. read() would need all ten at once. Looping over lines works, but only forwards, one line at a time — and you want the record at byte nine billion.

    What you want is to treat the file as though it were an enormous list of bytes you can index into. Which sounds like it requires having it all in memory, and does not.

    Notice how odd that wish is, stated plainly. You are asking to use a thing far larger than your memory as though it were in memory. The obvious objection is that it cannot be, and the obvious workaround — read a chunk, process it, read the next — means writing code that is about bookkeeping rather than about the problem. Every access must first ask which chunk holds the byte you want, whether that chunk is loaded, and what to discard to make room.

    That bookkeeping is real work and it is also, suspiciously, work somebody has already done. Chapter 0.4 described a mechanism that presents an address space larger and more convenient than the memory actually installed, keeping track of what is present and fetching what is not. The question this chapter answers is whether that machinery can be pointed at a file, and the answer turns out to be that it was always doing something very close to it.

    Unit III.4.2
    Descend

    The page, and the lie the hardware tells

    Chapter 0.4, finished

    Chapter 0.4 established that your addresses are virtual, translated by hardware, in blocks. That block is a page, and Python will tell you its size.

    Now the part Chapter 0.4 held back. A page table entry does not have to say "this page is at that physical address". It can also say this page is not in memory at all.

    When your program reads such an address, the hardware cannot translate it, and instead of failing it traps — control jumps to the kernel, exactly as in a system call, except you did not ask. The kernel finds the missing page, puts it in physical memory, updates the table, and restarts your instruction. Your program resumes with no idea anything happened.

    The most misleading name in computing

    That trap is called a page fault. It is not an error, not a bug, and not a sign of trouble. It is the normal, designed way memory gets filled — the mechanism working, not failing.

    Every program you have ever run began with a burst of them: the code was not loaded, it was mapped, and each page arrived the first time it was executed.

    The consequence is worth stating because it inverts the usual understanding of what starting a program means. A program is not loaded and then run. It is declared and then run, with the loading happening piecemeal, in response to the program actually touching things. A large application whose user never opens the printing dialogue may never load the code for printing at all — not because anybody arranged that, but because nothing ever caused the fault that would have fetched it.

    This also explains a measurement that otherwise looks impossible: a program can report a virtual size far larger than the machine's memory and be perfectly healthy. Virtual size counts what has been declared; the number that matters is how much is actually resident, and the gap between them is everything the program has arranged for and not yet needed.

    Unit III.4.3
    Tool

    Making a file into memory

    Memory mapping

    Now the payoff. If a page table entry can point at a page that lives on disk, there is no reason that disk page has to belong to your program's own storage. It can be a page of an ordinary file.

    New Python — mmap

    mmap.mmap(f.fileno(), 0, access=mmap.ACCESS_READ) maps an open file into your address space. The 0 means the whole file. What comes back behaves like a bytes: index it, slice it, search it, take its length. Nothing is read until you touch it.

    What has actually happened here

    You did not read a file. You told the kernel that a region of your address space is that file, and then read memory. The reading happened underneath you, one page at a time, only where you looked.

    A ten-gigabyte file on an eight-gigabyte machine is now unremarkable: your address space is enormous and mostly absent, and only the pages you touch are ever resident.

    Two properties make this more than a convenience. The first is that the operating system, not your program, decides what to keep — and it has information your program does not, such as what every other process is doing and how much memory remains. A hand-written caching scheme optimises in ignorance of all that; the kernel's does not.

    The second is that pages read from a file and not modified need no writing back when they are evicted, because an identical copy already exists on disk. Discarding them is free. That is why reading a large file this way can be cheaper than reading it conventionally: the conventional route copies bytes from the kernel's cache into your process's memory, so the same data occupies space twice, whereas a mapping lets your program look directly at the pages the kernel already has.

    OS-dependentHardware example

    Mapping is a service of the operating system with hardware support, and the details differ: 4096-byte pages are usual on x86-64 and ARM64, but larger pages exist and are used for large mappings; Windows and POSIX systems offer the facility with different names and options; and how aggressively the kernel reads ahead, or evicts pages under pressure, is a policy that varies by system and by version.

    The costs deserve equal billing, because mapping is presented as a trick often enough that its limits get skipped. Accessing a byte may take microseconds or nanoseconds depending on whether its page happens to be resident, and nothing in the source distinguishes the two — so performance becomes unpredictable in a way ordinary reads are not. A file being changed by somebody else while you have it mapped gives you a moving picture rather than a snapshot. And on a thirty-two-bit system the address space itself is too small for a large file, which is a hard limit rather than a slow one.

    The honest summary is that mapping suits large files accessed unpredictably, and conventional reading suits files consumed from beginning to end — which Chapter III.1's line-by-line loop already handles in constant memory. Reaching for a mapping to read a file sequentially adds complexity and buys nothing.

    Category: OS- and hardware-dependent. mmap.PAGESIZE reports your own.
    Unit III.4.4
    Rebuild

    The same trick, three more times

    Where else this is happening

    Once you can see demand paging, you notice it is holding up most of the system.

    Starting a program
    Chapter 0.5 said the kernel maps CPython's code into the new process. Maps, not loads — which is why a large program can start before most of it has been read
    Sharing code
    Twenty Python processes map the same interpreter file. One copy in physical memory, twenty page tables pointing at it
    Copy-on-write
    When a process is duplicated, pages are shared and marked read-only. The copy is made only if one side writes — a page fault, again, doing the work at the last possible moment
    Running out of memory
    Pages not used recently can be written back to disk and marked absent. Touch one and it faults back in, slowly. This is what a machine that has started "thrashing" is doing
    Simplified model

    Chapter 0.4's declared simplification, discharged. You were told addresses are translated per process in blocks, and that multi-level tables, the translation cache, page faults and swapping were left out. Faults and swapping are now covered. What remains outside this book: page tables are themselves a tree several levels deep, and the processor keeps a small cache of recent translations without which every memory access would need several extra memory accesses. Those belong to a book about processors.

    Declared simplification from Chapter 0.4, discharged as promised.

    Ladder · touching an absent pagea shape you have not seen before

    1. Human intention — read one byte
    2. Python source text — an ordinary index
    3. Tokens
    4. Syntax tree
    5. Compiler
    6. Code object and bytecode — a subscript, like any list
    7. CPython runtime — computes an address and reads it
    8. Native machine instructions — one ordinary load instruction
    9. CPU control logic — translation fails; the hardware traps mid-instruction
    10. Registers and ALU
    11. Caches and RAM — the page arrives here
    12. Operating-system services — entered without being called
    13. Device, file, terminal, result — a disk read, then the instruction runs again

    Every ladder so far has run downwards, with floor 12 reached deliberately from floor 7. This one is different: floor 9 jumps to floor 12, in the middle of a single machine instruction, and then hands control back so that instruction can be retried. Nothing in your Python asked for any of it — which is exactly why an ordinary-looking line can occasionally take a hundred thousand times longer than usual.

    What this means for judging speed

    Chapter II.13 warned that measurements wobble. Here is one of the largest reasons. The first pass over mapped data pays a fault per page; the second pass finds everything resident and is dramatically faster. Time a loop twice and you may be measuring the page cache rather than your code — so warm it deliberately, or say plainly which of the two you are reporting.

    Close the book

    2. Explain. Why is "page fault" a misleading name? Say what actually happens and why it is a normal event.
    3. Modify. Make a file of a few megabytes, map it, and find a marker you placed near the end. Then read the same file with read() and compare the memory your process uses. Explain the difference.
    4. Transfer. A colleague reports that a program is fast on the second run and slow on the first, every time, on identical data. Give two explanations from this book — one from this chapter, one from Chapter II.12 — and say how you would tell them apart.
    5. Stretch. A machine with plenty of free memory suddenly becomes unusable when a program allocates slightly more than exists. Using swapping and faults, explain why performance collapses so sharply rather than degrading gently.
    Mastery gate — Chapter III.4
    • You can state what a page is and report its size on your machine.
    • You can explain a page fault as a mechanism rather than an error.
    • You can explain how a program reads a file larger than its memory.
    • You can say what memory mapping does that read() does not.
    • You can give two other places demand paging is at work, including copy-on-write.
    • You can explain why this ladder enters floor 12 from floor 9 rather than floor 7.

    Item six is the one that shows you have understood rather than memorised. If it is shaky, reread the ladder note beside Figure III.4.1 — the difference is between asking and being interrupted.

    Volume III · Chapter 5The program meets the world

    Programs starting programs

    Spawning a child process, reading its exit status, connecting two children with a pipe — and the one argument that turns a convenience into a vulnerability

    Sometimes the right answer is that somebody has already written it. Python can start another program, wait for it, and collect what it produced. Doing so means creating a genuine second process, with everything Chapter 0.4 said about processes applying in full — and it means meeting a piece of API design that has caused more real-world breaches than almost anything else in this book.

    Prerequisites

    Chapter 0.4 (processes, address spaces, the kernel boundary and process identity), Chapter III.2 (file descriptors 0, 1 and 2, and buffering), Chapter III.3 (the absolute-join trap, which this chapter repeats in a different technology), Chapter I.6 (lists), Chapter I.11 (exceptions), Chapter I.9 (bytes against text, which decides one keyword argument here).

    Unit III.5.1
    Problem

    Somebody has already written it

    Something you can feel

    You need to know the size of a video file in frames, or convert an image, or list what a directory contains on a machine you do not control. Somebody has written a program that does each of those, and it is already installed. Rewriting it in Python would be foolish; what you want is to run it and take the answer.

    This is a different kind of reuse from Chapter II.4's import, and the difference matters. An import brings code into your process, where it shares your memory, your names and your interpreter. Starting a program creates a separate process, with its own address space, which shares nothing with yours and might not even be written in Python.

    That separation is the whole point, and it has consequences in both directions. The child cannot corrupt your data, because it cannot reach your data — Chapter 0.4's isolation, working for you. But you also cannot simply hand it an object or read its variables. Everything that passes between you must be converted into something that survives the boundary: arguments, an exit number, and streams of bytes.

    So the question the chapter has to answer is: what exactly can cross, and in what form?

    Unit III.5.2
    Tool

    A list of strings, not a line of text

    The interface between processes

    New Python — subprocess.run

    subprocess.run(args) starts a program, waits for it to finish, and hands back an object describing what happened. Passing capture_output=True collects what the child wrote; passing text=True decodes those bytes into strings, which is Chapter I.9's distinction appearing as a keyword argument — without it you get bytes, because that is what actually crossed.

    The list is not a stylistic preference. It reflects what a process actually receives, and understanding that is the key to the whole chapter.

    When the operating system starts a program, it hands it an argument vector: an array of separate strings. Not a line of text to be interpreted — an array, already divided, in which each element is one argument and no element needs any further splitting. The child does not parse anything. It is simply given the pieces.

    So a list is the honest representation, and any single string is a lie that must be converted back. That conversion is where the trouble comes from.

    Unit III.5.3
    Break

    The convenience that opens your machine

    Deliberate failure — shell=True

    subprocess.run accepts shell=True, which lets you pass a single string instead of a list. It looks friendlier, it resembles what you would type, and it is the single most dangerous argument covered in this book.

    With it, Python does not start your program at all. It starts a shell, and gives the shell your string to interpret. The shell is a full programming language whose entire purpose is to find meaning in punctuation, and it will find meaning in yours.

    Begin with something that is merely wrong rather than dangerous, because it shows the mechanism cleanly. Suppose a file is called my report.txt.

    Now notice how much else the shell will interpret. Every one of these is a character that means something to a shell and nothing to your program.

    That third row is already the vulnerability, and the classic form makes it unmistakable. Suppose the filename comes from somewhere you do not control.

    The same mistake, wearing its second disguise

    Chapter III.3 showed a base directory being erased by a leading slash. This is the same defect: text from outside was allowed to determine the structure of something you were building, rather than being placed inside a structure you had already fixed.

    There the structure was a path and the dangerous character was /. Here the structure is a command line and the dangerous characters are ;, |, &, $, backticks and several more. Chapter III.8 will show it in a network stream and Chapter III.9 in a database query, and Chapter III.10 will show that all four have one fix.

    The comfortable wrong idea

    "I will escape the dangerous characters, and then shell=True is safe."

    Python does provide shlex.quote for this, and used correctly on every interpolated value it does work — the earlier example, quoted, yields the single harmless argument ['notes.txt; echo PWNED']. But consider what you are now relying on: that you have identified every place a value enters the string, that you have quoted each one, that you will remember to quote the next one somebody adds, and that the quoting rules of the shell that actually runs match the ones the function assumed. Windows uses a different shell with different rules entirely.

    The list form needs none of that. It is not a stricter version of the same approach — it removes the parser rather than trying to outwit it. Prefer the design that cannot go wrong over the discipline that must not be forgotten.

    There is one honest reason to use shell=True: when you genuinely want shell features — wildcards expanded, or several commands chained. Even then, the rule is that the string must be one you wrote entirely, with nothing interpolated into it from anywhere else. If any part of it came from a file, a form, a filename or a network, use the list.

    Unit III.5.4
    Tool

    The number that means "fine"

    Exit status, and how failure arrives

    A child process reports its outcome as a single small integer, by convention zero for success and anything else for a problem. That is the whole vocabulary — one number — which is why programs also write explanatory text to their error stream.

    This is the return-code design that Chapter IV.6 examines as an alternative to exceptions, appearing here as a genuine constraint rather than a choice. A process boundary can carry an integer; it cannot carry a Python exception object, because the child may not be a Python program at all. So the outcome must be checked, and forgetting to check it is exactly the failure mode that design has.

    Python offers a way to convert the convention into an exception at your boundary, which is usually what you want:

    One value does not fit the convention and is worth recognising, because it looks like nonsense until you know:

    Unit III.5.5
    Tool

    Joining two children together

    Pipes, without a shell

    A common reason people reach for shell=True is that they want a pipeline — the output of one program becoming the input of another. That can be done directly, and doing it once removes the last excuse.

    The third line looks like tidiness and is not optional. A pipe is a file descriptor, and Chapter III.2 established that descriptors are duplicated when a process is created. So after the second process starts, two processes hold the reading end: the sorter, and you. The sorter finishes only when every writer has closed — and it cannot know that you are not going to write. Leave your copy open and it waits forever. Closing it is how you say: nothing more is coming from me.

    That is a small, concrete instance of a general truth about concurrency, and Chapter III.6 will meet it again in a different form: when several parties hold a resource, finishing requires all of them to let go, and the one who forgets causes a hang rather than an error.

    Unit III.5.6
    Descend

    What the operating system actually does

    Underneath run

    Chapter 0.4 said a process is created by the kernel and that a process cannot make another by itself. Here is that machinery being used, and it is worth seeing because it explains several behaviours at once.

    Trace · subprocess.run(['sort'])

    1. cpythonPython builds the argument vector and, if pipes were requested, asks the kernel for them first — each is a pair of descriptors.
    2. syscallPython asks the kernel to create a new process. Floor 12.
    3. kernelThe new process begins as a near-copy of yours, and inherits your open descriptors — which is why the child can write to your terminal without being told how, and why the pipe ends need closing.
    4. kernelThe child then asks to be replaced by the requested program: its address space is discarded and rebuilt from the new executable. The process survives; its contents do not.
    5. kernelIf the program cannot be found, this is where it fails — which is why a missing command raises FileNotFoundError in the parent rather than producing an exit code.
    6. bothBoth processes now run, competing for the processor exactly as Chapter 0.4 described. Neither can see the other's memory.
    7. syscallYour process asks to wait until the child finishes. While waiting it is not scheduled at all, so it costs nothing.
    8. kernelThe child ends. The kernel keeps its exit status until you collect it, then removes the last trace of it.

    Two details in that trace explain things you would otherwise have to memorise.

    Inheritance is why the child can already talk. You did not tell sort where the terminal is. It inherited descriptors 1 and 2 from you, which it received because a new process starts as a copy. Redirecting output is therefore not a matter of instructing the child at all — it is a matter of arranging which descriptors it inherits, which is what stdout=subprocess.PIPE does.

    The environment is inherited too, and can be replaced. That is how a program's behaviour can be configured without touching its arguments — and it is why Chapter III.10 recommends passing secrets through the environment rather than on the command line, since arguments are visible to anyone who can list the processes on the machine and the environment is not.

    Ladder · starting a childone of the few operations that reaches every floor

    1. Human intention — let that program do it
    2. Python source text — subprocess.run([...])
    3. Tokens
    4. Syntax tree
    5. Compiler
    6. Code object and bytecode — build a list, then call
    7. CPython runtime — assembles the argument vector
    8. Native machine instructions
    9. CPU control logic
    10. Registers and ALU
    11. Caches and RAM — and then a second address space, which is new
    12. Operating-system services — create, replace, wait: only the kernel can do any of it
    13. Device, file, terminal, result — inherited descriptors, or a pipe you supplied

    Floor 11 is doing something no previous chapter needed: there are now two address spaces, and nothing in one can reach the other. Every earlier ladder in this book described work inside a single process. This is the first that leaves it — and the isolation that makes a child safe is the same isolation that means everything crossing must be reduced to arguments, bytes and one small integer.

    1. Redraw. Draw two processes with a pipe between them, marking which descriptors each holds and which one you must close. Say what happens if you do not.
    2. Explain. Why is a list the honest way to pass arguments? Answer in terms of what the operating system hands a starting program.
    3. Explain. Give three characters that mean something to a shell and nothing to an ordinary program, and say what each does to an argument containing it.
    4. Modify. Write a function that runs a command with a filename supplied by somebody else, safely. Then write the unsafe version, test it with notes.txt; echo PWNED, and confirm both behaviours.
    5. Explain. Somebody proposes making shell=True safe with shlex.quote. Give the argument against — not that it fails, but what it requires you to keep getting right.
    6. Transfer. Put this chapter's defect beside Chapter III.3's absolute-join trap and state the one sentence that covers both. Then predict what the same mistake will look like in a database query.
    7. Stretch. Run a child that writes a great deal to a pipe you never read from, and observe what happens. Explain it using Chapter III.2's account of buffers, and then find the documented advice about which method to use instead.
    Mastery gate — Chapter III.5
    • You can start another program, capture what it wrote, and check whether it succeeded.
    • You can explain why arguments are a list rather than a line, in terms of the argument vector.
    • You can demonstrate shell injection and explain precisely which component does the interpreting.
    • You can say when shell=True is legitimate and state the rule that makes it so.
    • You can explain why failure arrives as a number rather than an exception, and how to convert it.
    • You can interpret a negative return code.
    • You can build a pipeline without a shell and explain why the parent must close its copy of the pipe.
    • You can describe what the kernel does to create a child, and use inheritance to explain redirection.

    Item three is the one that matters outside this book. If it is shaky, run the two versions with the semicolon again and watch the second command execute — then read Chapter III.10, which shows the same shape three more times.

    Volume III · Chapter 6The program meets the world

    Two things at once

    Threads, the global interpreter lock, races, and the difference between overlapping and going faster

    Chapter 0.4 said that "at the same time" usually means "taking turns very fast". Threads are that idea inside a single process — and in CPython they buy you something quite different from what most people expect, for a reason worth understanding exactly.

    Prerequisites

    Chapter 0.4 (scheduling, context switching, the illusion of simultaneity), Chapter I.8 (frames — each thread needs its own stack of them), Chapter II.11 (reference counts, adjusted on every operation), Chapter II.13 (measure, do not assume), Chapter III.2 (waiting for the outside world).

    Unit III.6.1
    Problem

    Most of a program's life is waiting

    Something you can feel

    Download three files one after another and you spend nearly all of the time doing nothing — your processor idle, waiting for a network that answers when it feels like it. Chapter III.2 established the shape: crossing to the outside world is slow, and while you wait, you are not computing.

    A thread is a second sequence of execution inside the same process. Same heap, same objects, same address space — but its own stack of frames, so it can be somewhere else in the program while the first thread waits.

    The phrase inside the same process carries the weight, and it is worth unpacking against Chapter 0.4's picture. Two processes have separate address spaces and share nothing; two threads share one address space entirely. Every object, every module-level name and every open file is visible to both. That is what makes threads cheap to create and to communicate between — there is no copying and no message-passing, because they are already looking at the same memory — and it is precisely what makes them dangerous, since either can modify what the other is reading.

    What each thread has of its own is small: a program counter and a stack of frames. That is enough for two of them to be at different points in different functions, which is the entire point, and it means everything Chapter I.8 said about frames applies per thread rather than per program. The heap, where Chapter II.11's objects live, is shared without qualification.

    New Python — threading

    threading.Thread(target=f, args=(x,)) makes a thread that will run f(x). .start() sets it going and returns immediately; .join() waits for it to finish. Nothing runs until you start it, and your program will not end tidily until you join it.

    Unit III.6.2
    Break

    The same trick on real work

    Deliberate failure

    Predict

    That worked beautifully for waiting. Now replace the nap with actual computation — a loop adding several million numbers — and run two of them in threads on a machine with several cores. How much faster?

    Descend

    One lock, and a good reason for it

    The GIL

    Standard CPython has a global interpreter lock: a single lock that a thread must hold to execute Python bytecode. One thread runs Python at a time, however many cores you own. Threads take turns — Chapter 0.4's illusion again, now inside one process.

    The reason is Chapter II.11. Every operation in CPython adjusts reference counts, constantly, on objects that all threads share. If two threads adjusted the same count at once, a count could be lost and an object freed while still in use — a crash of the worst kind. Making every count adjustment individually safe would slow down single-threaded code, which is nearly all code. So CPython took one big lock instead of a million small ones.

    It is worth resisting the common description of the lock as a design mistake, because the trade it represents is a real one. Reference counting gives CPython the immediate, predictable freeing Chapter II.11 demonstrated, and every increment and decrement must be correct even when several threads touch the same object. Making each count individually safe would mean an atomic operation on nearly every action the interpreter performs, and that cost would be paid by every program — including the overwhelming majority that use a single thread. One coarse lock imposes no such cost and makes all of it safe at once.

    The result is a language that is fast for single-threaded work and cannot use several processors for computation. That is a defensible position rather than an oversight, and it is not a permanent one: the free-threaded build described below removes the lock and pays the cost the other way round, which is exactly why it exists as a separate build rather than as a replacement.

    What threads are and are not for

    Threads let waiting overlap, not computing. A thread releases the lock whenever it waits for the outside world — a file, a network, a sleep — so other threads run while it does nothing.

    For work that is genuinely computation, threads in a standard build cannot help. Use separate processes instead, which Chapter III.5 showed how to create: separate processes have separate interpreters and separate locks, and genuinely run at once.

    Unit III.6.3
    Break

    The bug that will not reproduce

    Second deliberate failure, and an honest one

    A tempting conclusion: if only one thread runs at a time, shared data must be safe. It is not, and the reason is visible in bytecode.

    That is a race condition: the result depends on which thread got there first. Now the honest part, which matters more than a staged demonstration would.

    The mechanism deserves spelling out, because "the threads interfered" is not an explanation. The disassembly shows that counter += 1 is not one action but three: read the current value, add one, write the result back. A thread can lose the processor between any two of them, because the switch is imposed by the scheduler and can fall anywhere. So two threads can both read 5, both compute 6, and both write 6. Two increments happened and the count rose by one. Nothing was corrupted and no rule was broken — each thread did exactly what it was told, using a value that was true when it read it and stale by the time it wrote.

    Notice what this implies about the interpreter lock. Holding it guarantees that only one thread executes bytecode at a time; it says nothing about a thread keeping the processor for the duration of a statement. The lock is released and reacquired periodically, at boundaries that have nothing to do with your source lines. A single line of Python is therefore not indivisible, and the mental model in which the lock makes shared data safe is exactly backwards: it makes the interpreter's own bookkeeping safe and leaves yours entirely to you.

    An experiment that did not do what it was supposed to

    Preparing this chapter, the classic demonstration — four threads each incrementing a shared counter two hundred thousand times — was run repeatedly on a current CPython. No updates were lost. The total was correct every time, even with the thread switch interval forced to its smallest setting.

    Modern CPython's specialised handling of common operations makes this particular race very hard to observe. The danger is entirely real; the demonstration is not reliable. And that is worse, not better: a bug you cannot reproduce on demand is a bug you will meet in production, on a busier machine, months later.

    So the rule cannot rest on having seen it fail. It rests on the bytecode above: if two threads can touch the same mutable thing, and one of them writes, you need a lock — whether or not you have managed to make it break.

    New Python — Lock

    lock = threading.Lock(), then with lock: around the lines that must not be interrupted. Only one thread can be inside that block at a time; the others wait. It is Chapter III.1's with again, releasing the lock however you leave — including by exception.

    A lock works by making the region it guards indivisible from the point of view of everyone who respects it, and that last clause is the crucial one. A lock does not attach to data and cannot prevent access to it. It is a convention: every piece of code touching the shared thing must acquire the same lock first, and one place that forgets defeats the arrangement entirely while leaving the rest looking correct. This is why locks are difficult in practice rather than in principle — the discipline must hold everywhere, including in code written later by somebody who never knew the rule existed.

    Two further costs follow. A lock serialises the work it protects, so holding one longer than necessary removes the very concurrency you were trying to gain; hold it for the smallest region that must not be interrupted. And a program using more than one lock can reach a state where each thread holds one and waits for another, so that none can proceed and none can be interrupted — a deadlock, which produces a program that is not slow but permanently still. Chapter III.7 offers a model in which this class of problem cannot arise, at the price of a different discipline.

    Ladder · a thread waiting on the outside worldwhy this one helps

    1. Human intention — do something else while I wait
    2. Python source text
    3. Tokens
    4. Syntax tree
    5. Compiler
    6. Code object and bytecode
    7. CPython runtime — releases the interpreter lock before waiting, reacquires it after
    8. Native machine instructions
    9. CPU control logic
    10. Registers and ALU
    11. Caches and RAM — one heap, shared by every thread; one stack each
    12. Operating-system services — the kernel parks this thread and schedules another
    13. Device, file, terminal, result — the slow thing, finally answering

    Floor 7 is the whole story. The lock is released before the wait and taken again afterwards, which is why waiting overlaps and computing does not — a thread doing arithmetic never lets go.

    Level 4 Expert microscope — the free-threaded build

    The lock is not part of the Python language. It is a property of the standard CPython build, and other implementations have never had one.

    Since Python 3.13 an official free-threaded build has existed without the global lock, and with 3.14 it became a fully supported configuration rather than an experiment. In it, threads can execute Python bytecode genuinely simultaneously on several cores — which required making reference counting itself safe under concurrency, exactly the problem the lock was avoiding.

    Two cautions. Single-threaded code can be somewhat slower there, because the safety is no longer free. And every race condition in this chapter becomes far easier to hit, since threads really do run at the same instant. Code that was accidentally safe may stop being so.

    CPython

    This book's reference is the standard build with the lock. Which build you have determines whether CPU-bound threads help, so check rather than assume — and treat any measurement of threaded performance as specific to the build it was taken on.

    Category: CPython build configuration; see PEP 703 and PEP 779 for the free-threaded build's status.

    Reconstruct it without looking

    Close the book

    1. Redraw. Draw two threads sharing a heap but holding separate stacks of frames. Mark what they share and what they do not.
    2. Explain. Why does the interpreter lock exist? Answer with reference counting, not with "to make threads safe".
    3. Modify. Reproduce both measurements: three sleeps in threads, and two CPU loops in threads. Report your own numbers and say which matched the prediction.
    4. Transfer. A colleague adds threads to speed up an image-processing program and it gets slower. Diagnose it, and say what they should use instead and why that works.
    5. Stretch. Try to make the shared-counter race actually lose an update on your machine. If you fail, say what that tells you about relying on testing to find concurrency bugs — and connect it to Chapter II.2.
    Mastery gate — Chapter III.6
    • You can start threads and wait for them, and say what each owns separately.
    • You can explain what the interpreter lock is and the reference-counting reason for it.
    • You can say which kind of work threads help with and which they do not.
    • You can explain, from bytecode, why x += 1 is not safe between threads.
    • You can use a lock correctly and say what over-locking costs.
    • You can explain why a race that will not reproduce is more dangerous than one that will.

    Item six is the lesson this chapter was most reluctant to teach and most needed to. If it is shaky, reread the experiment box — the finding there is a real negative result, not a rhetorical device.

    Volume III · Chapter 7The program meets the world

    Waiting without stopping

    Cooperative concurrency, the discovery that you built its machinery in Chapter II.5, and the one mistake that undoes all of it

    Chapter III.6 showed that threads make waiting overlap and computing not. This chapter shows a second way to overlap waiting, one that needs no threads at all — and it turns out to be built from something you already have. The price is a rule that must be obeyed everywhere at once, and a single line breaking it costs you everything the technique was for.

    Prerequisites

    Chapter III.6 (threads, the GIL, and what waiting costs), Chapter II.5 (generators — a suspended frame that resumes where it stopped, which is the whole mechanism here), Chapter I.8 (frames), Chapter III.2 (why a read waits at all), Chapter I.11 (exceptions, since cancellation is one). Chapter IV.6 builds the underlying machinery from scratch and is the fuller account.

    Unit III.7.1
    Problem

    A thread each is a lot of machinery

    Something you can feel

    Chapter III.6 established the useful half of threading: when work is spent waiting, threads let the waits overlap, and three tenths of a second of naps happened in three tenths rather than nine. That is genuine and it is the right tool for a handful of concurrent operations.

    Now consider ten thousand. A web server holding ten thousand connections is, almost all of the time, doing nothing at all — waiting for bytes that have not arrived. Giving each connection a thread means asking the operating system for ten thousand independently scheduled entities, each with its own stack of the kind Figure 0.4.1 showed, each a thing the kernel must consider when deciding who runs next.

    The memory alone is prohibitive: stacks are sized in megabytes because a thread might recurse deeply, and ten thousand of them is a serious quantity of memory reserved for programs that are asleep. And the scheduler's work grows with the number of threads, so a large fraction of the machine's effort goes into deciding which of ten thousand idle things should wake up.

    Which suggests the question this chapter answers. If the threads are only waiting, and waiting requires nothing but remembering where you had got to — do you need a thread at all? Or is there a cheaper way to remember?

    Unit III.7.2
    Descend

    You have already built this

    The mechanism, recognised

    What a waiting thread is actually holding is small: which line it had reached, and what its local variables were. Everything else — the stack, the scheduling, the kernel's bookkeeping — is overhead for a job that is essentially "keep this frame until something happens".

    Chapter II.5 built exactly that. A generator suspends at a yield, keeps its frame intact with locals and position preserved, and resumes later from where it stopped — and it is an ordinary heap object, costing what an object costs rather than what a thread costs.

    The whole idea, in one sentence

    If a suspended frame can be an object, then "a task that is waiting" can be an object too — and one program can hold a hundred thousand of them, in one thread, resuming whichever one has become ready.

    That is what async and await are. Not a new kind of parallelism, and not threads with better syntax: a suspendable frame, plus a scheduler that decides which suspended frame to continue.

    New Python — async, await, asyncio

    async def defines a coroutine function. Calling it runs none of the body and returns a coroutine object — exactly as calling a generator function returns a generator. await marks a point where the coroutine may suspend and let something else run. asyncio.run(...) starts the scheduler, called the event loop; asyncio.gather(...) runs several coroutines concurrently and waits for all of them.

    Unit III.7.3
    Run and observe

    The log that proves interleaving

    One thread, three overlapping waits

    The timing alone would not settle what is happening, since three concurrent naps and one clever nap would both take three tenths of a second. The order of the printing settles it.

    Two things in that output are worth pausing on.

    There are no locks. Chapter III.6 needed one because a thread could be interrupted anywhere — between the read and the write of a single increment, as its disassembly showed. Here a coroutine can only be suspended at an await, and nowhere else. So between two awaits your code runs without interruption, and the whole class of race conditions from that chapter cannot occur.

    That is a genuine simplification and worth the trade. It also means the suspension points are visible in the source: every await is a place where the world may change beneath you, and every line without one is not. Chapter III.6's races were invisible; here they are spelled.

    And the scale is different in kind. The point of the technique is not three tasks but very many.

    Unit III.7.4
    Break

    The task that would not step aside

    Deliberate failure

    Everything above depends on a promise: that a coroutine reaches an await reasonably soon and lets the loop run something else. Nothing enforces this. The concurrency is cooperative, meaning it works only if every participant cooperates.

    Predict

    Change one line. Instead of await asyncio.sleep(0.3), use time.sleep(0.3) — the ordinary blocking sleep from Chapter III.6, with no await. What happens to the elapsed time and to the log?

    The reason is exactly the cooperative bargain. time.sleep blocks the thread, and there is only one thread, and the event loop is running in it. While A sleeps, the loop is not running, so it cannot start B. A has not merely delayed itself; it has stopped the scheduler that was to give everyone else their turn.

    One task can hold the whole world still

    In a threaded program a badly behaved thread slows things down, because the operating system will interrupt it and run somebody else regardless. In a cooperative program a badly behaved task stops everything, because nothing can take control away from it.

    So the rule is absolute and applies to every line of every coroutine: never block. Any call that waits without being awaited — a file read, a database query, an ordinary network request, a long computation — freezes every other task in the program.

    This is the real cost of the technique, and it is a cost in discipline rather than in speed. It applies transitively: a library you call must also never block, so an async program generally needs async versions of everything it touches. That is why adopting it is a decision about a whole program rather than a part of one.

    When you must call something blocking, hand it to a thread — which is Chapter III.6's tool used deliberately for the one job it is good at.

    Unit III.7.5
    Descend

    Stopping something that is waiting

    Cancellation

    One capability distinguishes this model sharply from threads, and it follows directly from the frames being objects.

    A thread cannot be stopped from outside. There is no safe way to interrupt one, because it might be holding a lock or half-way through modifying something, and killing it would leave the program in a state nobody designed. Threaded programs therefore ask politely, with a flag the thread checks.

    A coroutine can be cancelled, because its suspension points are known and an exception can be delivered into it at one.

    This is Chapter III.1's with guarantee mattering more than usual. A cancelled coroutine may be stopped at any of its awaits, so anything it holds must be released by finally rather than by a line at the end of the block — because for a cancelled task, the end of the block is one of the exits that never happens.

    Level 3 Runtime model — how close to a generator is a coroutine?

    Closer than an analogy. The event loop drives a coroutine using the same protocol that drives a generator, and you can do it by hand.

    An event loop is therefore less mysterious than it sounds: keep a collection of coroutines, ask the operating system which of the things they are waiting for has become ready, and send into the corresponding one. The clever part is the asking, which uses a system call that can watch thousands of descriptors at once — the piece of kernel machinery that makes the whole model viable, and the reason this is a chapter in Volume III rather than Volume II.

    CPythonOS-dependent

    Coroutines and generators have overlapping internals in CPython and the details have been reorganised more than once. Which mechanism the event loop uses to watch many descriptors differs by operating system, and its scaling behaviour differs with it. The model is stable; the implementation is not.

    Category: CPython implementation and OS facilities. See PEP 492 for coroutines and the asyncio documentation for event-loop implementations.
    Three tools, one rule

    Chapter III.6 and this one now give you the complete picture, and the choice is decided by what the work is doing rather than by preference.

    Waiting, a few at a time — threads. Simple, and the operating system handles the switching.
    Waiting, very many at a time — coroutines. Cheap enough for tens of thousands, provided nothing blocks.
    Computing — neither. Chapter III.6 measured threads making CPU work slower, and coroutines cannot help at all, because a computation never reaches an await. Separate processes are the answer, and Chapter III.5 built them.

    Ladder · await asyncio.sleep(0.3)and what is not happening

    1. Human intention — wait, but let others work
    2. Python source text — await
    3. Tokens
    4. Syntax tree
    5. Compiler — an await anywhere marks the whole function as a coroutine, at floor 5
    6. Code object and bytecode — a suspend point, and a resume point after it
    7. CPython runtime — the frame is set aside intact; the loop drives another
    8. Native machine instructions
    9. CPU control logic
    10. Registers and ALU — almost idle: this is waiting, not computing
    11. Caches and RAM — suspended frames, in the heap, one per task
    12. Operating-system services — the kernel is asked to watch many things at once
    13. Device, file, terminal, result — whatever is being waited for

    Compare this with Chapter III.6's ladder for threads. There the kernel schedules; here it only reports, and the scheduling happens at floor 7 in Python. That is the whole difference between the two models: who decides what runs next. It is also why a coroutine is cheap — floor 11 holds an object rather than a stack, and floor 12 is asked one question about thousands of tasks rather than thousands of questions.

    Close the book

    1. Explain. Why does a waiting thread cost so much more than a waiting coroutine? Name what each one holds.
    2. Explain. Why does the log order prove interleaving where the elapsed time would not?
    3. Modify. Write three coroutines that sleep for different durations and gather them. Predict the log order before running, then explain any difference.
    4. Modify. Replace one await asyncio.sleep with time.sleep and measure. Report both the time and the log, then fix it with to_thread.

    6. Transfer. A colleague's async web service becomes unresponsive whenever one particular endpoint is called. Give the most likely cause and how you would confirm it.

    Mastery gate — Chapter III.7
    • You can write coroutines, run them concurrently, and read the log to confirm they interleaved.
    • You can explain what a coroutine is in terms of Chapter II.5's suspended frame.
    • You can say why calling a coroutine function runs none of the body.
    • You can explain why no locks are needed, and identify exactly where suspension can occur.
    • You can describe what one blocking call does, and demonstrate it.
    • You can explain why cancellation is possible here and not with threads.
    • You can choose correctly between threads, coroutines and processes given a description of the work.
    • You can say who does the scheduling in each model, and what that costs.

    Item five is what decides whether an async program works. If it is shaky, run the one-word change again and look at the log rather than the clock — strict sequence, no overlap, no warning of any kind.

    Volume III · Chapter 8The program meets the world

    Talking to strangers

    Sockets, byte streams without boundaries, the two ways to put the boundaries back — and why every assumption you make about a network is wrong

    A network connection looks like a file you can write to and read from, and that resemblance is genuine and useful. It is also the source of the single most common defect in network code, because a file has one property a connection does not: when you write a thing to it, the thing stays a thing. Over a connection, what you send and what arrives are related only by their bytes.

    Prerequisites

    Chapter III.1 (files, and the resource that must be closed), Chapter III.2 (file descriptors and buffering — a socket is another descriptor), Chapter I.9 (bytes against text, which is not optional here), Chapter III.6 (threads, used to run both ends at once), Chapter I.11 (exceptions), Chapter III.3 (the trap of letting a stranger's text decide your structure — this chapter is its third appearance).

    Unit III.8.1
    Problem

    The other end is a stranger

    Something you can feel

    Everything in this volume so far has involved things the operating system controls but that are nonetheless local: your disk, your memory, your child process. A network connection is different in a way worth naming precisely, because it changes what can be assumed rather than merely what can go wrong.

    The other end is a program you did not write, on a machine you do not control, possibly written in a language you have never used, run by somebody whose interests may not match yours, reachable only through equipment that can fail. Every property you have relied on so far is now negotiable.

    Consider what that removes. You cannot assume the peer is running: it may have crashed between one message and the next. You cannot assume it is honest: it may send anything at all, including things designed to break you. You cannot assume it is quick, so any read may wait indefinitely. And you cannot assume the connection survives, because the network sits between you and it can stop at any moment, in the middle of anything.

    What remains, given all that, is remarkably little — and knowing exactly what remains is the whole of writing network code that works.

    New Python — socket

    A socket is an endpoint of a connection. socket.create_connection((host, port)) connects to a listener; on the other side, a socket is bound to a port, told to listen, and then accept waits for somebody to arrive and returns a second socket for that particular conversation.

    Unit III.8.2
    Break

    Three messages arrived as one

    Deliberate failure

    Here is the code almost everybody writes first. One side sends three separate messages; the other reads.

    Predict

    Three calls to sendall, with b'MSG1', b'MSG2' and b'MSG3'. On the other end, one call to recv. What comes back?

    The natural response is that this is a quirk of small messages, or of a fast local connection, and that real messages would stay separate. The opposite experiment settles it.

    A stream has no messages in it

    What a connection carries is an ordered sequence of bytes. Order is guaranteed — byte five arrives before byte six, always. Grouping is not guaranteed, because grouping was never part of what was sent.

    Your calls to sendall are not units of transmission. They are additions to a stream. The network divides that stream into packets according to its own concerns — how much room is in a buffer, how large a packet the path allows, how much has been acknowledged — and the receiver sees the results of those decisions, not yours.

    This is why recv(4096) does not mean "read 4096 bytes". It means "give me up to 4096 bytes, however many happen to be available now". It may return one byte. It will not return zero unless something significant has happened, which is the subject of Unit III.8.4.

    And it explains why the mistake survives testing so reliably. On one machine, with small messages, the bytes usually do arrive in the groups they were sent in — not always, but often enough that a program built on the assumption passes every test its author runs. It fails later, under load, over a real network, with larger messages, intermittently. Chapter II.2's warning about tests that cannot distinguish, in its most expensive form.

    Unit III.8.3
    Rebuild

    Putting the boundaries back

    Framing

    If the stream will not carry your message boundaries, you must send them yourself, as part of the bytes. That is called framing, and there are two designs worth knowing. Every network protocol you have ever used chooses one of them.

    A delimiter. Agree on a byte that cannot appear inside a message — a newline, typically — and read until you see one. This is simple, it is what most text protocols do, and it has one hard requirement: the delimiter must be impossible inside the data. If it can appear, it must be escaped, and now you have invented an escaping scheme with all the awkwardness Chapter IV.1's tokenizer met around quotes.

    A length prefix. Send the size first, in a fixed number of bytes, then exactly that many bytes of message. This works for any data at all, including data containing the length bytes themselves, because the reader never has to search for anything.

    New Python — struct

    struct.pack('!I', n) turns an integer into a fixed number of bytes; struct.unpack reverses it. The I means an unsigned four-byte integer, and the ! means network byte order — a fixed convention for which end of the number comes first, so that two machines that disagree internally still agree on the wire.

    The reader now needs something the socket does not provide — the ability to read exactly a given number of bytes — and building it is the point at which everything in this chapter becomes concrete.

    The comfortable wrong idea

    "I will just trust the length the sender gives me and allocate that much."

    The sender is a stranger. A four-byte length can say four billion, and a program that reads it and prepares to receive four billion bytes has been told by a stranger to exhaust its memory — a complete denial of service, using one well-formed message and no cleverness at all.

    So the length must be checked against a maximum you decide before any space is committed. This is the same lesson as Chapter III.3's path and Chapter III.5's command, in its third costume: a value from outside was allowed to determine something structural about your program. There it was which file, and which command. Here it is how much memory.

    Unit III.8.4
    Descend

    Everything that can go wrong

    The failure modes, and what each looks like

    Network code is dominated by failure handling, and the failures are worth meeting individually because they arrive as different exceptions and demand different responses.

    Nothing is listening. The most common failure, and the friendliest, because it is immediate and unambiguous.

    The peer closed. This one is easy to misread, because it does not raise.

    The connection broke. Distinct from a clean close: the peer vanished, or the network failed, and this surfaces as a ConnectionResetError or a write that fails. It can happen at any point, including halfway through a message, which is why recv_exactly raises rather than returning a partial result.

    Nothing happens at all. The peer is running, the connection is fine, and it simply does not reply — because it is overloaded, or waiting for you, or wedged. Without a timeout your program waits indefinitely, and Chapter III.7's account of waiting applies: the process is not consuming processor time, which makes this failure invisible from outside. A hung network read looks exactly like a program doing nothing, and every socket in production should have a timeout for this reason.

    What actually remains true

    Bytes that arrive, arrive in order. That is very nearly the whole list.

    Not that they arrive in groups. Not that they arrive at all. Not that the peer is still there, or was ever what it claimed. A connection guarantees ordering and, while it lasts, delivery — and every other property your program needs must be built on top by you, in the bytes, deliberately.

    One last consequence, which Chapter I.9 makes obvious in retrospect. Everything crossing a socket is bytes; there is no text on a network. If two programs are to exchange text they must agree on an encoding, and that agreement is part of the protocol just as much as the framing is. Sending message.encode('utf-8') and receiving data.decode('utf-8') is not a formality — it is the second half of a contract, and Chapter III.1's demonstration of what a wrong encoding does applies here with a stranger supplying the bytes.

    Ladder · sock.sendall(data)and the floor beyond floor 13

    1. Human intention — tell the other program something
    2. Python source text — sock.sendall(payload)
    3. Tokens
    4. Syntax tree
    5. Compiler
    6. Code object and bytecode
    7. CPython runtime — loops until every byte has been handed over
    8. Native machine instructions
    9. CPU control logic
    10. Registers and ALU
    11. Caches and RAM — your bytes, copied into a kernel buffer
    12. Operating-system services — the kernel decides when and in what pieces to transmit
    13. Device, file, terminal, result — a network card, and then somebody else's machine entirely

    Floor 12 is where your message boundaries are lost, and it is worth being precise that this is not carelessness. The kernel is doing its job: it batches, it waits for acknowledgements, it fits packets to what the path allows. Your three sendall calls are three additions to a buffer, and what leaves that buffer is decided by conditions you cannot see and should not have to. Floor 13 goes further than in any other chapter — past your own hardware entirely, to a machine whose behaviour is not yours to reason about.

    Retrieval lock

    Reconstruct it without looking

    Close the book

    1. Explain. Why did three sendall calls arrive as one recv? Answer in terms of what a connection actually carries, not in terms of a bug.
    2. Explain. Give the two framing designs, one requirement each, and say which you would choose for sending arbitrary binary data and why.
    3. Redraw. Write out the exact bytes on the wire for send_message(sock, b'hi'). Then say what the reader does with each one.
    4. Modify. Implement delimiter framing with newlines, then find an input that breaks it. Fix it by escaping, and note how much complexity that added compared with the length prefix.
    5. Modify. Add a maximum message size to recv_message and make it reject anything larger before allocating. Explain what attack this prevents.
    6. Explain. Why must recv_exactly loop? Give the exact circumstance where a single recv would return less than asked, and say what a version without the loop would do.
    7. Transfer. A colleague's server occasionally uses 100% of one processor while apparently doing nothing. Given this chapter, give the most likely cause and the one-line fix.
    8. Stretch. Put this chapter's untrusted length beside Chapter III.3's path and Chapter III.5's command. State the single sentence covering all three, then predict the fourth form before reading Chapter III.9.
    Mastery gate — Chapter III.8
    • You can open a connection, send bytes, and read a reply.
    • You can explain why message boundaries do not survive, and demonstrate the failure in both directions.
    • You can implement length-prefix framing, including a function that reads exactly n bytes.
    • You can say why that function must loop and why it must treat an empty result as an error.
    • You can name four network failure modes and say how each appears in Python.
    • You can explain what an empty recv means, and what happens to a program that misreads it.
    • You can state exactly what a connection guarantees, and list what it does not.
    • You can explain why an untrusted length must be bounded, and connect it to two earlier chapters.

    Item two is the one that decides whether your network code works in production. If it is shaky, run the million-byte experiment and look at the sizes of the pieces — 63,973 and 29,696 correspond to nothing you wrote, which is exactly the point.

    Back · Chapter III.7Waiting without stopping Next · Chapter III.9Making it stick
    Volume III · Chapter 9The program meets the world

    Making it last

    Durability, the torn file, the rename that cannot half-happen, and what a database is actually for

    Chapter III.1 showed how to write a file, and quietly left a question unanswered: what happens if the machine stops in the middle? The answer is worse than losing the write, because the file can be left in a state that never existed as a whole — half old and half new, and valid enough that nothing notices. This chapter is about arranging that this cannot happen.

    Prerequisites

    Chapter III.1 (writing files, and the with guarantee), Chapter III.2 (buffering, and the three layers between your string and the disk), Chapter III.3 (paths, and that renaming is a filesystem operation), Chapter 0.4 (the kernel does the work, not you), Chapter I.11 (exceptions), Chapter III.10 (which assembles this chapter's injection lesson with three others).

    Unit III.9.1
    Problem

    The file that is half old and half new

    Something you can feel

    You have a configuration file, and your program updates it. The obvious way is to open it for writing and write the new contents over the old. It works every time you test it, and it contains a failure mode that testing will not find.

    Recall from Chapter III.1 that opening for writing empties the file immediately. So between that moment and the completion of your write, the file is short, or empty, or partly filled. If the machine loses power there, or the process is killed, or the disk fills up, what remains is whatever had been written by then.

    Compare the two failure modes honestly. A file that is missing announces itself: the next read raises, you notice, you restore a backup. A file that is half-written may parse successfully, may load, may be acted upon, and may propagate its damage into everything downstream before anybody looks. Chapter II.2 argued that a confident wrong answer is worse than a crash; here is the same principle at the level of stored data.

    Unit III.9.2
    Descend

    Three things "written" can mean

    Why you do not know when it is safe

    Chapter III.2 established that there are layers between your string and the disk. Durability is where those layers stop being an efficiency detail and start being the whole question, because each one has its own idea of what "written" means.

    after write
    In your process's memory. Lost if the process dies. Invisible to everyone
    after flush or close
    In the kernel's cache. Survives your process dying; visible to other programs. Lost if the machine loses power
    after fsync
    On the device. Survives power loss — which is the only meaning of durable

    The middle row is the one that surprises people, and it explains why "I closed the file" is not the reassurance it sounds like. Closing guarantees the bytes reached the kernel. The kernel then writes them out when convenient, because batching writes is enormously faster than performing each immediately, and that convenience may be seconds away.

    So fsync is the only way to know, and it is slow — it must wait for hardware. That is the trade at the heart of this chapter: durability costs time, always, and a program that calls fsync after every small write will be far slower than one that does not. The skill is knowing which writes deserve it.

    Unit III.9.3
    Rebuild

    Never write over the thing you care about

    The atomic rename

    Given that a write can be interrupted, the fix is not to make writing safer. It is to arrange that the file you care about is never in a partial state — by never writing into it at all.

    The filesystem provides one operation that cannot half-happen: renaming a file onto another. Either the name refers to the old file or it refers to the new one; there is no moment at which it refers to something in between, and no interruption can create one. That operation is the entire technique.

    Three details make the difference between this working and appearing to work.

    The temporary file must be on the same filesystem as the target, which is why it is placed beside it rather than in a system temporary directory. A rename across filesystems is not a rename at all — it is a copy followed by a delete, and a copy can be interrupted.

    os.replace rather than os.rename, because the behaviour when the target already exists differs between operating systems for the latter, and replacing is exactly what you mean.

    And the fsync must come before the rename, not after. Otherwise the rename may reach the disk before the contents do, and a crash in that window leaves the name pointing at a file whose data never arrived — which is the original problem with an extra step.

    Unit III.9.4
    Problem

    When one file is not enough

    Transactions

    The rename trick protects one file. It does nothing for a change that must touch several things together — and those are common. Moving money between two accounts is the standard example precisely because its requirement is so stark: subtracting from one and adding to the other must both happen or neither must.

    Two renames cannot express that, because between them is a moment when one has happened and the other has not. What is needed is a way to group changes so that the group is all-or-nothing, and that is what a transaction is.

    New Python — sqlite3

    sqlite3 is a complete database in the standard library, storing everything in one ordinary file. Used as a context manager — with con: — it commits on success and rolls back if an exception leaves the block, which is Chapter III.1's with guarantee applied to a group of changes rather than to a file handle.

    That is worth restating, because it is the property that makes databases worth their complexity. The rollback did not happen because the program was careful. It happened because the change had not been committed, and an uncommitted change is not a change — it is a proposal that expires.

    A database gives you this, plus the durability of Unit III.9.2 without your having to think about fsync, plus a way for several programs to make changes at once without corrupting each other. That last is the one hardest to build yourself, and it is usually the real reason to stop hand-rolling files.

    When a file is enough, and when it is not

    Use a file with the atomic-rename pattern when the whole state is small, changes are infrequent, and one program at a time is writing.

    Use a database when several things must change together, when several programs may write at once, when the data is too large to rewrite entirely, or when you need to find things without loading everything. Each of those is a reason on its own.

    Unit III.9.5
    Break

    The most famous injection of all

    Deliberate failure

    A query is text, and the natural way to build text containing a value is to interpolate it. Chapter III.3 and Chapter III.5 have both trained you to distrust that sentence, and here it produces the best-known vulnerability in the industry.

    Consider building a query with an f-string, and a name supplied by somebody else: x'); DROP TABLE users; --. The quotation mark ends the value early; everything after it is read as query structure; the trailing dashes comment out whatever your code appended. One string, one destroyed table.

    The fix is a placeholder, and its mechanism is the point rather than the syntax.

    The comfortable wrong idea

    "I escape the quotation marks, so my f-string queries are safe."

    Escaping requires knowing every construct the database's parser treats as structure, in every context, for every version — and getting it right every single time, including in the query somebody adds next year. Placeholders require nothing of you. The parser never sees the value, so there is nothing for a clever value to be clever at.

    This is Chapter III.5's argument against shlex.quote, in a different technology, with the same conclusion: prefer the design that cannot go wrong to the discipline that must not lapse. Chapter III.10 shows that these are two of four.

    Ladder · os.replace(tmp, target)a promise only the kernel can make

    1. Human intention — this must not be seen half-done
    2. Python source text — os.replace(...)
    3. Tokens
    4. Syntax tree
    5. Compiler
    6. Code object and bytecode
    7. CPython runtime — a thin wrapper; it does none of the work
    8. Native machine instructions
    9. CPU control logic
    10. Registers and ALU
    11. Caches and RAM — the kernel's cache, which is where "written" often stops
    12. Operating-system services — only the kernel can make a change indivisible
    13. Device, file, terminal, result — and only fsync reaches this floor

    The two lit floors at the bottom are the chapter. Atomicity is a property the kernel provides and that no amount of careful Python can construct — you cannot make two operations indivisible from above. And durability lives one floor lower still: everything short of floor 13 is a cache that a power cut empties.

    Retrieval lock

    Reconstruct it without looking

    Close the book

    1. Explain. Why is a half-written file more dangerous than a missing one? Connect it to Chapter II.2's argument about confident wrong answers.
    2. Explain. Give the three meanings of "written" and say which failure each survives.
    3. Modify. Write a save_atomically(path, text) function using the full pattern. Explain each of its three easily-omitted details.
    4. Explain. Why must the temporary file be on the same filesystem? What is a cross-filesystem rename actually doing?
    5. Modify. Build the two-account transfer and interrupt it. Confirm the rollback, then remove the with and observe what changes.
    6. Explain. Why does a placeholder defeat injection when escaping is fragile? Answer in terms of when parsing happens.
    7. Transfer. Give three questions you would ask to decide between a file and a database for a program of your own.
