    Mastery gate — Chapter III.9
    • You can describe a torn write and say why it is worse than losing data.
    • You can distinguish buffered, flushed and synced, and say what each survives.
    • You can implement the atomic-rename pattern, including all three details.
    • You can explain why atomicity must come from the kernel.
    • You can use a transaction and explain why an uncommitted change is not a change.
    • You can list the reasons to prefer a database over a file.
    • You can explain why placeholders are safe and escaping is not.
    • You can say why durability is inherently slow.

    If item three is shaky, write the function and then delete the fsync. The code will pass every test you can write, and the defect it reintroduces only appears when the machine loses power — which is the definition of a failure you cannot test your way out of.

    Back · Chapter III.8Talking to strangers Next · Chapter III.10Who is allowed
    Volume III · Chapter 10The program meets the world

    Who is allowed

    Permissions, trust boundaries, secrets, least privilege — and the single idea that unifies every security failure in this volume

    Four chapters of this volume each contained an attack, and they looked like four different problems belonging to four different technologies. They are one problem. This closing chapter names it, shows that all four have the same fix, and then asks the question that matters more than any individual defence: given that you will sometimes get it wrong, how much should a mistake be allowed to cost?

    Prerequisites

    Chapter III.3 (the absolute-join trap), Chapter III.5 (shell injection), Chapter III.8 (the untrusted length), Chapter III.9 (SQL placeholders) — this chapter assembles all four. Also Chapter 0.4 (processes, user and kernel mode, and what a process is permitted to do) and Chapter III.1 (files as an arrangement with the operating system).

    Unit III.10.1
    Problem

    Your program has more power than you think

    Something you can feel

    Chapter 0.4 established that your process runs in user mode and cannot do whatever it likes with the machine. That is true and it is a much weaker guarantee than it sounds, because the boundary it enforces is between your program and the kernel — not between your program and your own files.

    Inside that boundary, your program can do everything you can. It can read every file you can read, delete every file you can delete, start any program you can start, and open any network connection you are permitted. The operating system will not stop it, because as far as the operating system is concerned it is you: it runs as your user, with your privileges, and every request it makes is indistinguishable from one you made deliberately.

    So when this volume showed a filename causing the wrong file to be opened, or a string causing an extra command to run, the machinery was never subverted. Nothing was broken into. The program asked for exactly what it asked for, and the operating system obliged, because the request was legitimate and came from someone entitled to make it.

    The reframe this chapter turns on

    Security failures in ordinary programs are almost never a matter of defeating a protection. They are a matter of a program being persuaded to use its own legitimate power on the attacker's behalf.

    Which is why the fixes in this chapter are not about adding barriers. They are about being precise where a program was vague — and about arranging that the power available to be misused is as small as the job allows.

    Unit III.10.2
    Tool

    Who may touch a file

    Permissions

    The operating system records, for every file, who may do what with it. On a POSIX system this is three groups — the owner, the owner's group, everybody else — and three permissions each: read, write, execute. Nine bits, conventionally written as three octal digits.

    Two things about permissions are worth knowing beyond the mechanics.

    They belong to the file, not to your program. They persist after your process ends, they apply to every program that touches the file afterwards, and they are the only part of your program's security that outlives it. That makes them the most durable defence available and the easiest to forget.

    And they are coarse. Three categories and three permissions cannot express most of what you actually want — "this program may read this file but not that one" is not expressible at all, because permissions describe who a user is rather than what a program is allowed. That gap is precisely why the rest of this chapter matters: the operating system's protection stops at the user boundary, and everything inside it is your responsibility.

    Unit III.10.3
    Rebuild

    The one idea behind four attacks

    The volume, assembled

    Put the four side by side. Each appeared in a different chapter, in a different technology, with a different-looking symptom.

    Chapter III.3 · paths
    A leading slash in a filename discarded the base directory, so a request for one file opened another
    Chapter III.5 · commands
    A semicolon in an argument became a command separator, so a second program ran
    Chapter III.8 · streams
    A length field from the network was believed, so a stranger decided how much memory to allocate
    Chapter III.9 · queries
    A quotation mark in a value ended the value early, so the rest was read as query structure

    Now describe what happened in each without naming the technology. A program took text from outside, placed it into something it was building, and the text was allowed to determine that thing's structure rather than merely occupying a place in it.

    The sentence that covers all four

    Data from outside must never be allowed to become part of the structure of a command. It must occupy a slot in a structure you fixed in advance.

    Every one of the four fixes is the same manoeuvre: build the structure first, out of things you wrote, and put the foreign data into it as a value that nothing will parse.

    The database case is the clearest demonstration that this works even when the data is designed to be structural.

    The comfortable wrong idea

    "I will scan the input for dangerous characters and reject anything suspicious."

    This is called blocklisting, and it loses. You must enumerate every dangerous construct, in every context, for every version of every component that will parse the text — and the attacker needs to find only one you missed. Chapter III.5's list of shell characters is long and incomplete; encodings, alternative quotings and nesting expand it further.

    The structural fix does not require you to know what is dangerous. It removes the parser from the path entirely, so there is nothing for a clever input to be clever at. Prefer the design that cannot go wrong to the vigilance that must not lapse — the same argument Chapter III.5 made against escaping, generalised.

    The complementary practice is validation, and it is worth distinguishing from blocklisting because they are often confused. Blocklisting asks "does this contain anything bad?" Validation asks "is this one of the things I accept?" — a filename matching a pattern you specified, a number within a range, a choice from a fixed set. Validation is an allowlist, it fails safely when something unexpected arrives, and it belongs in addition to the structural fix rather than instead of it.

    Unit III.10.4
    Tool

    Keeping secrets out of the program

    And being honest about how well that works

    A password or key written into source code is exposed by every copy of that source: in the repository, in its whole history, on every machine that has ever checked it out, in every backup. Removing it later does not remove it from the history, which is why leaked credentials are usually old ones.

    The usual advice is to pass secrets through the environment instead, and it is good advice for a reason more precise than "the environment is hidden" — because it is not hidden.

    So the ranking is: never in source; not in command-line arguments, because those are public; the environment or a file with mode 0o600 for ordinary purposes; and a dedicated secret-management system when the stakes justify it. Each step reduces the audience rather than eliminating it, and knowing which is which is more useful than believing any of them makes a secret safe.

    Unit III.10.5
    Descend

    Assume you will get it wrong

    Least privilege

    Everything so far assumes you can identify the trust boundaries and defend each one. Over a large program, written over years, by several people, that assumption is optimistic. The final idea is the one that survives being wrong.

    Least privilege means giving each part of a system only the power its job requires, so that a mistake in it cannot cost more than that. It does not prevent failures. It bounds them — which is a different and more achievable goal.

    The principle scales beyond these two examples, and the same reasoning applies at each level. A program that only reads should open files for reading. A program that needs one directory should not be started somewhere it can reach others. A service that never needs administrative rights should not run with them, because Unit III.10.1's observation cuts both ways: a program can do everything its user can, so running as a user who can do less is the single most effective thing you can do about a defect you have not found.

    And the reason to think this way is uncomfortable and worth stating plainly. Chapter II.2 argued that you cannot test your way to certainty about correctness. The same is true of security, more so, because the inputs are chosen by somebody trying to find what you missed. Least privilege is the acknowledgement built into the design: something will be wrong, and the question is what it will cost.

    Ladder · where a trust boundary sitsand who enforces what

    1. Human intention — the boundary is identified here, or not at all
    2. Python source text — a list, a placeholder, a bound
    3. Tokens
    4. Syntax tree
    5. Compiler
    6. Code object and bytecode
    7. CPython runtime — builds the structure; the data never touches a parser
    8. Native machine instructions
    9. CPU control logic
    10. Registers and ALU
    11. Caches and RAM
    12. Operating-system services — enforces permissions and process identity, and nothing above that
    13. Device, file, terminal, result — the thing that was or was not protected

    Floors 1 and 12 hold the entire subject, and the gap between them is the point. The kernel enforces a real boundary, and it is about identity: which user, which process, which permissions. It knows nothing about which filename you meant to allow or which query you meant to run. Every boundary that concerns meaning rather than identity exists only at floor 1, in the design, enforced by nobody but you.

    What Volume III was for

    You began this volume able to write programs that computed. You can now write programs that persist data, survive crashes, run other programs, speak to strangers over a network, and do several things at once — and, more importantly, you know where each of those touches something you do not control.

    The recurring lesson has been the same in every chapter, and it is worth carrying out of this volume in one form: the moment a program stops being alone is the moment its assumptions have to become explicit. Inside one process, an assumption that goes unstated is usually harmless. At a boundary, an assumption that goes unstated is a defect waiting for the input that finds it.

    Retrieval lock

    Reconstruct it without looking

    Close the book

    1. Explain. Why is it misleading to say a program was "broken into" in any of this volume's four attacks? Say what actually happened instead.
    2. Redraw. Write out the four attacks as a table: technology, the character or value that did the damage, and the structural fix. Then write the single sentence covering all four.
    3. Explain. Distinguish blocklisting from validation. Say why the first loses, and why the second is not a substitute for the structural fix.
    4. Modify. Take a program of your own that touches the outside world. Mark every point where data crosses in, and check each against the four fixes.
    5. Explain. Why is passing a secret in the environment better than in a command-line argument? Give the precise reason, and say what it does not protect against.
    6. Modify. Open a file read-only and try to write to it; open a database read-only and try to insert. Explain what each buys you that a careful programmer would not already have.
    7. Transfer. A colleague proposes rejecting any input containing a semicolon. Give three reasons this is the wrong approach, and what you would do instead.
    8. Stretch. Predict what the same defect looks like in a technology this book has not covered — building HTML, or a filename for a template. Describe the attack and the structural fix before looking anything up.
    Mastery gate — Chapter III.10 and the whole of Volume III
    • You can explain what your program is permitted to do, and why the kernel boundary does not protect your own files from it.
    • You can read and set POSIX permission bits, and say why the default is world-readable.
    • You can state the single idea behind all four of this volume's attacks, without naming any technology.
    • You can give the structural fix for each of the four, and say what they have in common.
    • You can explain why blocklisting loses and what validation adds.
    • You can rank the places to keep a secret, and say what each rank actually changes.
    • You can define least privilege and give two examples in ordinary Python.
    • You can say which trust boundaries the operating system enforces and which exist only in your design.

    Item three is what makes the rest transferable. If you can state it without mentioning paths, shells, streams or SQL, you will recognise the same defect in technologies this book never mentions — which is the only form of security knowledge that stays useful.

    Volume IV · Chapter 1The interpreter laid open

    Chopping text into tokens

    Building the first stage of Figure 0.5.2, discovering the decisions hidden inside it, and checking the result against the tokenizer inside Python

    Since Chapter 0.5 you have been told what happens between the source text you type and the program that runs. You have seen it named, diagrammed and referred back to a dozen times, always from outside. This volume builds it. Four stages, one per chapter, in the same staged way you built the processor in Volume 0 — and by Chapter IV.4 you will have a working interpreter for a small language of your own, which you can extend, break and measure.

    Prerequisites

    Chapter 0.5 (the four stages and Figure 0.5.2, which this volume constructs), Chapter I.1 (what quotation marks do to a tokenizer — a claim you are about to be able to verify), Chapter I.9 (strings, characters and code points), Chapter I.12 (your word tally, which had this shape without being told so), Chapter I.11 (raising errors). Nothing beyond Volume I is required, which is one reason this volume comes last rather than first: it can be built entirely out of things already earned.

    Unit IV.1.1
    Problem

    The character is the wrong unit of meaning

    Something you can feel

    Take the source line x = 2 + 3 * 4. It is thirteen characters. Now ask what it consists of, in the sense of the parts you would name if somebody asked you to describe it, and the answer is seven things: a name, an equals sign, a number, a plus, a number, a times, a number. Neither count is wrong. They are counts of different things.

    The gap between thirteen and seven is the whole of this chapter. Something must get from one to the other, and the getting involves genuine decisions rather than mere transcription. Where does a number end? Is total five separate letters or one name? The two spaces around the plus sign — do they mean anything, and if not, at what precise moment do they stop meaning anything? If a language had both = and ==, how would you know which one you were looking at when you had read only the first character?

    None of those questions has an obvious answer that requires no thought, and each has a wrong answer that produces a plausible-looking tokenizer that fails on real input. That is why this stage exists as a stage at all. It would be conceivable to write a parser that worked directly on characters — and every parser written that way spends most of its effort re-deriving these answers over and over, in every rule, which is precisely the duplication Chapter I.8 identified as a truth problem rather than a typing problem.

    So we separate the concerns. One pass over the text answers the question what are the units, once and for all, and hands on a sequence of units to a stage that never has to think about characters again. The unit is called a token, and the stage is called a tokenizer or a lexer — two names for the same thing, which you will meet in both forms elsewhere.

    Chapter I.12 ended by observing that your word tally had the shape of a tokenizer without your having been told so: a stream in, meaningful units out, the meaningless discarded, the survivors normalised. This chapter builds the real thing, and the familiarity is not a coincidence. Splitting a stream into meaningful pieces is one of the small number of genuinely recurring shapes in computing.

    The language we are going to implement

    Small enough to hold entirely in your head, and large enough to be interesting: whole numbers, names, the four arithmetic operators, brackets, and assignment. That is exactly the language of Figure 0.5.2, whose worked example was x = 2 + 3 — so at the end of this volume you will be able to put your own four stages beside that figure and check them line by line.

    Everything omitted is omitted deliberately and will be named as we go, because knowing what a small implementation leaves out is most of knowing what a large one is doing.

    Unit IV.1.2
    Descend

    Choosing how to recognise things

    The design space, before the code

    There is more than one respectable way to write a tokenizer, and it is worth knowing the alternatives, because the one we will use is not obviously the best until you see what it buys.

    The first approach is a table of patterns. Describe each kind of token as a regular expression — digits for a number, letters for a name, and so on — and repeatedly try each pattern at the current position, taking whichever matches. This is compact, it is what many production tokenizers do, and Python's own tokenize module is built substantially this way. Its weakness is that the pattern language becomes a second thing to be fluent in, and that the awkward cases — nested quotes, escapes, indentation — tend to escape what patterns can express and need special-casing anyway.

    The second is a formal state machine. Define states such as "in the middle of a number" and "in the middle of a name", with transitions for each character. This is the approach a tool would generate for you, it is provably correct in a way hand-written code is not, and it is genuinely how some compilers do it. Its weakness for our purposes is that the mechanism obscures the ideas: you end up reading a transition table rather than a description of the language.

    The third is a hand-written loop with an explicit position, deciding at each step what kind of thing is starting and consuming as much of it as belongs together. It is longer than the first, less rigorous than the second, and it is what most real language implementations actually use — including CPython's own C tokenizer — because it copes with awkward cases by simply having code for them, and because it is readable by someone who has never met the other two approaches.

    We will write the third, and the reason is pedagogical as much as practical: every decision will be visible as a line of code you wrote, rather than encoded in a pattern or a table where it can be applied without being understood.

    Unit IV.1.3
    Tool

    One pass, one position

    The tokenizer

    The algorithm is a loop with a position in it. Look at the character at that position. Decide what kind of thing is starting. Consume as much of it as belongs together, advancing the position. Record what you found. Repeat until the text runs out.

    Notice the structure of the branches, because it is not arbitrary. Each branch is chosen by looking at a single character — the one at the current position — and that single character is sufficient to decide what kind of token is beginning. A digit can only begin a number. A letter can only begin a name. That property is what makes this a simple loop rather than something that must try alternatives and back up, and a language designer who breaks it makes every implementation of the language harder for ever.

    Unit IV.1.4
    Descend

    Three decisions, and what each one costs

    Reading the code as design

    Three choices are embedded in those twenty lines. Each is a real decision, each has an alternative, and each has consequences that reach far beyond this stage.

    The first is greed. Once a number has started, the inner while consumes digits as long as they keep coming. This is what makes 1234 a single token rather than four, and stated that way it sounds obvious. The general form of the rule is not obvious and has a name: maximal munch, meaning that at each point the tokenizer takes the longest thing that could be a token, rather than the shortest or any intermediate length.

    Why the longest? Because the alternative is unusable. If the tokenizer took the shortest match, 1234 would be four numbers and total five names, and no language could be written. There is no third option that is coherent: any rule other than "longest" requires the tokenizer to know what the parser wants, which is exactly the coupling this stage exists to prevent.

    The second is discarding. When the character is a space, the position advances and nothing is recorded. This is the moment — the exact line of code — at which whitespace stops existing. Everything downstream is permanently unable to know how the source was spaced, because the information is not merely ignored but never captured.

    The third is conversion. Look carefully at what the number branch records: int(src[start:i]), the integer 2, not the character '2'. Chapter I.2 spent a chapter on that distinction and here is where it is settled, once, for the whole implementation. Every later stage receives a number that is already a number and never has to ask.

    This one is a genuine judgement rather than a necessity. A tokenizer could perfectly well hand on the text and let a later stage convert. Doing it here has a cost: the token no longer records exactly what was written, so 007 and 7 become indistinguishable, and an error message that wanted to quote the source could not. Real implementations often keep both the text and the value for precisely that reason. We convert early because our language has one kind of number and no need to quote the source back — a simplification that is worth noticing as a simplification.

    Unit IV.1.5
    Break

    A character it has never heard of

    Deliberate failure, and the limits of this stage

    Notice also what it reports: a position. That is the reason a tokenizer tracks more than it appears to need. Every "line 7, column 12" you have ever seen in an error message exists because this stage kept count as it went, and passed the count onward attached to each token. Our tokenizer keeps a position and reports it in errors but does not attach it to tokens, which is why the later stages of this volume will produce error messages that say what is wrong and not where — a limitation worth feeling.

    Now the more interesting question: what can this stage not catch?

    The division of labour, which explains a great deal about error messages

    This stage catches exactly one kind of mistake: characters that cannot begin any token. It cannot catch bad arrangements, because it does not know about arrangement. It cannot catch undefined names, because it does not know what a name means.

    Being clear about which stage catches what is most of understanding why compilers say what they say — and why an error is sometimes reported at a position surprisingly far from the mistake. If you forget a closing bracket on line 10, the tokenizer is content, and the parser only notices when it reaches something that cannot follow, which may be line 40.

    Unit IV.1.6
    Break

    The character that is not enough

    Second deliberate failure — where one character stops deciding

    Our language has = for assignment. Suppose we add == for comparison, as almost every language does. The single-character rule breaks immediately: seeing = no longer tells you which token you are looking at, because you might be one character into a two-character token.

    The fix is to look ahead before committing, and to check the longer possibility first.

    The order of those two branches is the entire point, and getting it wrong produces a bug that is easy to write and slightly baffling to diagnose. Put the single-character test first and it will match the first = of a ==, emit an assignment token, and leave the second = to be emitted as another assignment token — producing two tokens where there should be one, with no error anywhere.

    That is maximal munch again, and now you can see why it must be a rule rather than a habit: with more than one token sharing a prefix, the longest must be tried first, always, or the shorter one silently wins. Real languages have long chains of these — <, <=, <<, <<= — and every one must be ordered correctly.

    You can watch Python obey the same rule, and watch a single space change the answer:

    Unit IV.1.7
    Rebuild

    Now look at Python's

    The comparison

    Python's own tokenizer is available to you as a module, and running it on the same line is the first real check on whether what you have built resembles the real thing.

    One difference in that output is worth chasing rather than skipping, because it corrects a natural assumption. Python's NUMBER token holds the string '2', not the integer 2. Python's tokenizer makes the opposite choice to ours on the third decision of Unit IV.1.4 — it keeps the text and lets a later stage convert — and it does so for exactly the reason given there: Python has many kinds of numeric literal, and the tokenizer's job is to say where the literal ends, not what it means.

    A second surprise in the same direction: Python's tokenizer does not know what a keyword is.

    This is a genuinely instructive division. It would have been easy to have the tokenizer check each name against a list of keywords and emit a different kind — and some languages' tokenizers do. Leaving it out keeps this stage completely ignorant of the language's vocabulary, which means adding a keyword to Python requires no change here at all.

    Unit IV.1.8
    Descend

    What a real tokenizer must do that ours does not

    The omissions, named

    Four jobs separate our twenty lines from a production tokenizer. Each is a genuine difficulty rather than mere bulk, and knowing them is knowing what the extra thousands of lines are for.

    Position tracking. Real tokens carry the line and column where they start and end. This is not decoration: it is what allows a traceback in Chapter I.11 to point at a line, what allows an editor to underline the offending characters, and what allows a formatting tool to put things back. It means the tokenizer must count newlines as it goes and reset a column counter, which is bookkeeping on every single character.

    Strings, comments and escapes. Chapter I.1 claimed that quotation marks act on the tokenizer, sealing everything until the closing quote into a single unit, and that this is why '2 + 2' never becomes arithmetic. You are now in a position to see that this is genuinely a tokenizer-level fact and not a later one. It is also where the hardest cases live: escapes mean the closing quote can be preceded by a backslash and not be closing; triple quotes mean a string can contain newlines; and an unterminated string is one of the few errors a tokenizer can detect on its own.

    Indentation. This is the largest structural difference, and it explains something about Python that is otherwise arbitrary. Our tokenizer throws whitespace away because our language has no blocks. Python's blocks are indentation, so its tokenizer cannot — it must emit tokens where the indentation changes.

    This forces a property our tokenizer does not have. To know whether indentation has changed, the tokenizer must remember the indentation levels currently open — a stack of them, since blocks nest. It is therefore stateful: what it emits depends not only on the character at the position but on the history of the file so far. Ours is stateless, which is why it is simple, and Python's cannot be.

    It also explains why mixing tabs and spaces in Python is an error rather than a matter of taste. The tokenizer must compare indentation levels for equality, and if a tab is sometimes eight columns and sometimes one, two lines that look identical may or may not be at the same level. The ambiguity is not resolvable at this stage, so the language forbids the situation instead.

    Unicode. Our LETTERS is twenty-six characters. Python allows names in any alphabet, so its equivalent of "is this a letter?" is a Unicode property question rather than a membership test — Chapter I.9's code points arriving in a place you would not expect them.

    CPythonPython language

    What the language specifies: the lexical structure — which character sequences form which tokens, how indentation is interpreted, what a valid identifier is. Any implementation must agree, and it is written down in the language reference.

    What is CPython's: that there is a tokenizer stage at all, and that there are two of them — the tokenize module you have just used is written in Python and serves tools, while the compiler uses a separate one written in C. They agree about the language and differ in their internals. Chapter 0.5's claim holds: tokens are an implementation's chosen route, not a promise Python makes to you.

    Sources: Python language reference, lexical analysis; tokenize module documentation.

    Every ladder until now described what happened to your program. Chapter 0.5's stacked interpreters, with you now occupying one of the layers.

    Retrieval lock

    Reconstruct it without looking

    Close the book

    1. Redraw. Write the token stream for total = (a + 12) * 3 by hand, then check with the code. Mark on the source where each token begins and ends, and which characters produced nothing.
    2. Explain. State the maximal-munch rule and give two reasons the alternative is unworkable — one from numbers, one from two-character operators.
    3. Explain. Whitespace is discarded, yet a space changes the meaning of x==y. Reconcile those two statements precisely.
    4. Modify. Add support for <, <=, > and >=. Get the branch order wrong on purpose first, and record exactly what token stream the bug produces before you fix it.
    5. Modify. Add numbers with a decimal point. Then decide what 1.2.3 should do — and notice that you have moved from implementing a language to designing one, since there is no right answer, only a choice with consequences.
    6. Transfer. Your tokenizer is stateless; Python's cannot be. Explain why, using indentation, and then explain why Python forbids mixing tabs and spaces rather than defining a conversion.
    7. Stretch. Add position tracking: give every token the index at which it started, then make the parser's error messages in Chapter IV.2 say where the problem is. This is a small change with a large effect on how the finished thing feels to use.
    Mastery gate — Chapter IV.1
    • You can write a tokenizer for a small language starting from a blank file.
    • You can state the maximal-munch rule, justify it, and order overlapping branches correctly.
    • You can identify the exact line at which whitespace stops existing, and say what follows from that for the rest of the implementation.
    • You can say which errors this stage can catch and which it structurally cannot, and give an example of each.
    • You can explain why an error is sometimes reported far from the mistake that caused it.
    • You can name four things a real tokenizer does that yours does not, and say why each is genuinely difficult rather than merely lengthy.
    • You can explain why Python's tokenizer must be stateful and yours need not be.

    If item four is shaky, run tokenize_tiny('2 + * 3') and observe that it succeeds. Chapter IV.2 is the stage that rejects it, and understanding why the rejection belongs there rather than here is the foundation of everything that follows.

    Volume IV · Chapter 2The interpreter laid open

    Shape from a straight line

    The parser: where precedence and associativity actually live, and why a tree is the only honest way to hold a program

    A token stream is flat. But 2 + 3 * 4 is fourteen and not twenty, so something must know that the multiplication binds more tightly. This chapter builds the stage that knows — and the answer to where that knowledge is stored turns out to be surprising, elegant, and impossible to forget once you have seen it.

    Prerequisites

    Chapter IV.1 (the token stream this consumes), Chapter II.6 (recursion — the parser is recursive, and its shape mirrors the language's own), Chapter I.7 (nested structures), Chapter II.7 (classes), Chapter I.11 (raising errors). Figure 0.5.2's third stage is what you are building.

    Before you start

    This chapter consumes what the last one produced, so tokenize_tiny must still be defined. If you have started a fresh session, put it back — or better, save it in a file and import it, which is what Chapter II.4 was for.

    Unit IV.2.1
    Problem

    A flat list cannot say which goes first

    Something you can feel

    Your tokens for 2 + 3 * 4 are a straight sequence: number, plus, number, times, number. Read them left to right, doing each operation as you meet it, and you get 2 + 3 = 5, times 4, twenty. Which is wrong; every schoolchild knows the answer is fourteen.

    Ask where the correctness has to come from. It cannot come from the tokens themselves, because they are identical in both readings — the same five items in the same order. It cannot come from their positions, because the multiplication sign is to the right of the plus and yet must act first, so position and priority point in opposite directions.

    What is missing is a way to say belongs together. 3 * 4 is a single thing, and it is one of the two things being added; the sequence has no way to express that, because a sequence has only one relationship available — comes before — and this is a different relationship entirely.

    So you need a structure that can hold a thing inside another thing, to arbitrary depth, because expressions nest arbitrarily. That structure is a tree: a node holding other nodes. Chapter II.6 taught you to walk data nested to unknown depth, and observed that recursion earns its place when data has that form. A program has exactly that form — which is not a happy accident but the reason programming languages look the way they do.

    What a tree buys, stated precisely

    In a tree, "inside" means "must be finished first". The * node sits inside the + node, so the multiplication must produce a value before the addition can use it. Precedence stops being a rule you apply and becomes a fact about the shape.

    That is why every serious language implementation builds one, and why the intermediate form is worth its cost. A rule can be applied wrongly. A shape cannot.

    Unit IV.2.2
    Descend

    Choosing how to build it

    The design space

    As with the tokenizer, there is more than one respectable method, and knowing the alternatives makes the choice meaningful rather than arbitrary.

    A precedence table. Give every operator a number, then scan the tokens, using a stack and comparing numbers to decide when to combine. This is compact and handles a large operator set without new code per operator — adding an operator means adding a row to a table. Its weakness is that the algorithm is not obviously correct on reading, and the correspondence between the table and the language you meant is something you must take on trust.

    A generated parser. Write the grammar in a formal notation and let a tool produce the parser from it. This is what large compilers often do, it is rigorous, and it catches ambiguities in the grammar automatically. Its weakness for us is that the generated code is not meant to be read, so the ideas are hidden inside a tool.

    Recursive descent. Write one function per grammatical layer, each calling the layer below. The grammar is not written in a separate notation; the functions are the grammar. It is what CPython's own parser does, and what most hand-written parsers do, and it has the property this volume needs above all others: every rule of the language is visible as a line of code you wrote.

    We will write the third. And its central property — the one that makes it worth the chapter — is that the thing you would expect to need a table for is expressed instead by which function calls which.

    Unit IV.2.3
    Tool

    The language, written as three functions

    The grammar as layers

    Describe the language in layers, weakest binding at the top:

    an expression
    is a term, followed by any number of + or - each followed by another term
    a term
    is an atom, followed by any number of * or / each followed by another atom
    an atom
    is a number, or a name, or a bracketed expression

    Read those three lines carefully, because they contain the whole design. Each layer is defined in terms of the layer below it, so anything the lower layer can match is automatically available to the higher one. And the last line closes the circle: an atom may be a whole expression in brackets, which is what allows nesting to any depth.

    Now write one function per layer. That is the entire method.

    Unit IV.2.4
    Descend

    Where precedence actually lives

    The chapter's central claim

    Search that parser for a precedence table. There is none. Search it for a comparison of priorities, a number attached to an operator, any statement anywhere that multiplication outranks addition. There is nothing of the kind.

    The answer

    Multiplication binds more tightly than addition because expr calls term, and term calls atom. The order of the calls is the order of the binding.

    Work through why that produces the right result, because seeing the mechanism is better than accepting the claim. When expr begins parsing 2 + 3 * 4, its first act is to call term to get its left-hand side. term parses the 2, looks at the next token, sees a + which is not one of its operators, and returns just the 2. So expr now has 2, sees the +, takes it, and calls term again for the right-hand side.

    That second call to term is where it happens. term parses the 3, looks ahead, sees * — which is one of its operators — and greedily consumes the multiplication, returning the whole 3 * 4 node. expr receives that node as a single right-hand side and wraps it in the addition.

    The tighter-binding operator wins because its function is called deeper, and a deeper function returns before the shallower one can act. Precedence is not consulted; it is structural.

    Two practical consequences follow immediately, and both are the kind of thing that makes a language implementer's life easier or harder for years. Adding a new level of precedence means adding a new function between two existing ones — not editing a table that other rules also depend on. And a language's precedence can be read off the shape of its grammar without running anything, which is why language references present grammars in exactly this layered form.

    Unit IV.2.5
    Descend

    Two more properties nobody wrote down

    Brackets and associativity

    The same code, without another line being added, settles two further questions.

    Brackets work because atom calls expr. That single line sends the recursion back to the top of the grammar, so anything the language can express may appear inside brackets, including further brackets, to any depth. The recursion in "recursive descent" is precisely this: the layers do not merely descend, they can loop back, and that loop is what makes the language infinite rather than a fixed set of shapes.

    Associativity comes from the loop. Look at the line inside expr: node = ('binop', op, node, self.term()). The node it already has becomes the left child of the new node. So parsing 2 - 3 - 4 first builds (2 - 3), then wraps that whole thing as the left side of the second subtraction. Each iteration buries the previous result one layer deeper on the left, which is exactly left-associativity.

    Nobody wrote "subtraction is left-associative" anywhere. It is a consequence of accumulating into node inside a while loop, and it would be very difficult to get wrong by accident — which is a good property for a mechanism to have.

    And when you want the other direction

    Some operators group rightwards. In Python, ** is the notable one: 2 ** 3 ** 2 is 512, meaning 2(32), and not 64, which is what leftward grouping would give. Mathematics agrees, which is why the language does.

    A loop cannot produce that, because a loop always buries the accumulated result on the left. Right-associativity requires the function to call itself for the right-hand side, so that the deeper call finishes first and ends up nested on the right. The difference is one keyword, and it is worth doing once to see it.

    Unit IV.2.6
    Descend

    The glance forward

    Lookahead, and how much is enough

    One method in the parser does something the others do not, and it is worth isolating.

    Why is one not enough? Because a statement beginning with a name might be an assignment, x = 3, or it might be an expression, x + 1, or simply x. Seeing the name tells you nothing; the deciding token is the second one. So the parser must look at it without consuming anything, then commit.

    This is lookahead, and how much a grammar requires is one of the standard ways of classifying languages. A grammar decidable with one token of lookahead is easier to parse and, not coincidentally, tends to be easier for people to read, because a human reader is also deciding what they are looking at as they go. Ours needs two in exactly one place, which is a very mild requirement.

    Some constructs need more, and a few need something stronger than any fixed number: the parser must try one interpretation, and if it fails, back up and try another. That is more powerful and costs more, since work can be thrown away. It matters here because it is what CPython now does — a point Unit IV.2.8 returns to.

    Unit IV.2.7
    Break

    The errors this stage catches

    Deliberate failure

    Chapter IV.1 ended by noting that 2 + * 3 tokenizes perfectly. Here is where it stops.

    The two failures are different in kind, and the difference is instructive. In the first, atom was called to produce a value, took the next token, found an operator, and had no branch for it: the token exists but cannot appear here. In the second, atom consumed the opening bracket, recursed to parse the inner expression, and then looked for a closing bracket — and take returned the harmless (None, None) from past the end of the list, which is not ('OP', ')'), so the check failed. Running out of input is detected as a mismatch rather than as a special case, which is what the sentinel bought us.

    Three stages, three kinds of wrong

    @ is rejected by the tokenizer: not a legal character. 2 + * 3 is rejected by the parser: legal tokens in an impossible shape. And y + 1 where y was never defined passes both and fails only when it runs.

    That third one is not laziness on the parser's part. Whether a name exists is not a property of the program at all — it is a property of the program together with a particular state, and that pairing does not exist until run time. This is why Python has SyntaxError and NameError as different things, one reported before your program starts and the other during it.

    Unit IV.2.8
    Rebuild

    Python's tree, for the same line

    The comparison

    New Python — ast

    ast.parse(source) gives you Python's own syntax tree as objects, and ast.dump(tree, indent=2) prints it readably. This is the real stage three of Figure 0.5.2, available for inspection whenever you like.

    The extra parts are each a job your language does not have, and naming them is naming the distance between a small implementation and a real one.

    Module wraps a list of statements, because a real program is many. ctx=Store() records that this particular x is being written rather than read — the same node type serves both, distinguished by context, which is how a later stage knows to emit a store rather than a load. And every real node carries line and column numbers, start and end, which is how the traceback in Chapter I.11 could point at a line and how an editor can underline exactly the offending characters.

    Two features of Python's grammar are worth meeting, because both show a parser doing something more than a straightforward layered descent.

    Python languageCPython

    What the language specifies: the grammar. Which programs are legal, and what shape each legal program has, is written down in the language reference, and every implementation must agree. Precedence and associativity are part of that specification, not of any implementation.

    What is CPython's: the tree itself. The ast module's node classes are an implementation detail — there are over a hundred and thirty of them — and they have changed between versions, which is why tools built on ast need updating when Python moves. So is the parsing technique: CPython replaced a long-standing table-driven parser with a hand-written one able to back up and retry, which allowed grammar constructs the older technique could not express.

    Sources: Python language reference, full grammar specification; ast module documentation; PEP 617 on the parser change.

    The tree is the last stage at which a program still resembles something a person wrote. From Chapter IV.3 onwards it becomes a flat list of instructions and this shape is discarded — having done its job, which was to decide what belongs to what. It is also the stage tools work at: formatters, linters and type checkers all read this tree, because it is the last form that still knows the program's structure.

    Retrieval lock

    Reconstruct it without looking

    Close the book

    1. Redraw. Draw the tree for 1 + 2 * 3 - 4 as boxes inside boxes, then check with parse. Say which operation must happen first and why the drawing makes it unarguable.
    2. Explain. Where does precedence live in this parser? Answer without using the word "table", and trace the calls for 2 + 3 * 4 to show the mechanism rather than assert it.
    3. Explain. Distinguish precedence from associativity, giving an example where each decides the answer. Then say which one a while loop produces and which needs recursion.
    4. Modify. Add exponentiation with ^, binding more tightly than *, as a new layer between term and atom. Make it right-associative and confirm that 2 ^ 3 ^ 2 gives 512. Then change the recursion to a loop and confirm it gives 64.
    5. Modify. Make the parser reject trailing rubbish: parse('2 + 3 )') currently succeeds, ignoring the stray bracket. Add a check that all tokens were consumed, and say why the omission was easy to miss.
    6. Transfer. Explain to somebody why 2 + * 3 is reported before the program runs while dividing by a variable that happens to be zero is not. Use all three stages, and be precise about why the third case could not be caught earlier even in principle.
    7. Stretch. Use ast.parse on a program of your own and walk the tree with a recursive function from Chapter II.6, printing each node's type and line number. You have written a program that reads programs, which is how linters and formatters work — and you now know why they operate on the tree rather than on the text.
    Mastery gate — Chapter IV.2
    • You can write a recursive descent parser for a small expression language from a blank file.
    • You can explain why a flat token list cannot express precedence, in terms of what relationships a sequence can hold.
    • You can say where precedence comes from in the code, and trace the calls that produce it.
    • You can say where associativity comes from, and produce either direction deliberately.
    • You can explain what brackets do to the recursion, and why that makes the language infinite.
    • You can explain what lookahead is, identify where this parser needs two tokens, and say why one is not enough there.
    • You can say which errors belong to the tokenizer, which to the parser, and which cannot be found until run time.
    • You can read ast.dump output, match it to your own tree, and name three things a real tree carries that yours does not.

    Item three is the chapter. If it is shaky, delete the term layer so that expr calls atom directly, and see what 2 + 3 * 4 becomes — the parser will still run, and will be confidently wrong, which is the most instructive way to learn where the knowledge was living.

    Volume IV · Chapter 3The interpreter laid open

    Flattening the tree

    The compiler: turning shape into order, choosing a machine to target, and discovering that CPython does exactly the same thing

    You have a tree. No machine can run a tree — Chapter 0.3 established that a processor does one instruction after another, in a line. This chapter throws the shape away, carefully, in the one order that preserves its meaning. Along the way it makes a decision that every language implementation has to make and that nobody tells you about, and it discovers that a compiler does not merely translate: it reasons.

    Prerequisites

    Chapter IV.2 (the tree this consumes — keep it in the same session), Chapter II.6 (recursion, which does the walking), Chapter 0.3 (a machine runs a flat sequence, and your toy processor's nine opcodes), Chapter 0.5 Unit 4 (where you first saw a constant folded and were told it would be explained), Chapter I.8 (numbered local slots, whose origin is here).

    Keeping the pieces

    Each chapter of this volume feeds the next, so tokenize_tiny and parse must still be defined. Either stay in the same session, or do what Chapter II.4 was for: save them in tiny.py and from tiny import tokenize_tiny, parse. By Chapter IV.4 you will have four stages to keep together, and the file is much the easier way.

    Unit IV.3.1
    Problem

    Which part do you write down first?

    Something you can feel

    Your tree for 2 + 3 * 4 is an addition whose right-hand side is a multiplication. To run it you must produce a list of instructions, and a list has a first item, so something has to go first. The question sounds trivial and turns out to generate the entire chapter.

    It cannot be the addition. You cannot add two things before you know what the second one is, and the second one is a multiplication that has not happened yet. Nor can it be the multiplication's result, since that does not exist until the multiplication runs. So the deepest, innermost part of the tree must be written down first, and the operations that combine things must come after the things they combine.

    That single observation is the whole compiler, and everything below is working out its consequences carefully.

    But notice what the observation does not settle. It tells you the order in which operations must happen. It says nothing about where the intermediate values live while they wait — and there is no way to avoid that question, because 3 * 4 produces a 12 that must be somewhere until the addition consumes it. Every compiler must decide what "somewhere" means, and the decision shapes everything downstream.

    Unit IV.3.2
    Descend

    Choosing a machine to aim at

    The decision nobody mentions

    There are two established answers, and they lead to genuinely different instruction sets. It is worth understanding both, because the choice explains a great deal about why real bytecode looks the way it does.

    A register machine gives every intermediate value a numbered place, and every instruction says explicitly where its inputs are and where its output goes. An addition becomes something like "add the contents of place 3 to the contents of place 4 and put the result in place 5". Real processors work this way, and so do some language implementations.

    Its advantage is that each instruction is self-contained and the machine executes fewer of them, because nothing is spent on moving values into position — the instruction names its operands wherever they happen to be. Its cost is that the compiler must now decide which value goes in which place and reuse places when values die, a job called register allocation that is one of the harder parts of a serious compiler. Instructions are also larger, since each carries three place-numbers.

    A stack machine gives intermediate values no names at all. Instructions take their inputs from the top of a stack and leave their results there. An addition becomes simply "add", with no operands whatever, because both inputs are implied.

    Its advantage is that the compiler becomes almost trivial: emit the parts in the right order and the stack takes care of itself, with no allocation decisions to make. Instructions are small, since most carry no operands. Its cost is more instructions executed, because values must be pushed into position before use, and a certain amount of shuffling that a register machine would not need.

    Why the stack machine wins here, and in CPython

    Two properties decide it. The stack discipline matches the tree exactly — the innermost sub-expression is started last and finished first, which is precisely the order a stack returns things — so no allocation problem exists to be solved. And the compiler becomes short enough to read.

    CPython made the same choice for related reasons, and it is a defensible one for an interpreter: when every instruction already costs a dispatch through the evaluation loop, saving a few instructions matters less than keeping the compiler simple and the code objects small. For a compiler targeting real hardware the trade goes the other way, which is why processors are register machines.

    So: a stack machine, and the rule from Unit IV.3.1 becomes concrete.

    The emit rule

    For an operation node: emit the left branch, then the right branch, then the operation itself. Apply it to every node, all the way down.

    This has a name in the study of trees. Visiting a node's children before the node itself is a post-order traversal, and the fact that post-order is exactly what a stack machine needs is not a coincidence — both are expressions of the same idea, that a thing must be complete before whatever uses it.

    Unit IV.3.3
    Tool

    Six instructions is enough

    The compiler

    Our instruction set, in the same spirit as Volume 0's nine opcodes and for the same reason: small enough to hold in your head, large enough to be a real machine.

    PUSH n
    Put the number n on the stack. The only instruction that carries a value
    LOAD name
    Look the name up and push what it is bound to
    STORE name
    Pop a value and bind the name to it
    ADD SUB MUL DIV
    Pop two values, combine them, push the result. No operands — both inputs are implied by the stack
    PRINT
    Pop a value and show it

    Two things about that code are worth making explicit, because both are choices rather than necessities.

    The first is that the walk is depth-first. Each branch is fully compiled before the next begins, so all of the left subtree's instructions appear before any of the right subtree's. That is what makes the output correct, and it falls out of the recursion naturally — you would have to work quite hard to get it wrong.

    The second is that assign and expr nodes emit their child first and their own instruction second, exactly like binop. That is not a coincidence but the same rule applied: a STORE needs a value already on the stack, so the thing producing the value must come first. The rule is not about arithmetic; it is about anything that consumes.

    Unit IV.3.4
    Run and observe

    Where the brackets went

    Shape becoming order

    Now compile two programs that differ only in bracketing, and read them side by side.

    There are no brackets in either output, and there is nowhere for brackets to be. This is worth sitting with rather than nodding at, because it explains something people commonly get wrong about performance.

    A bracket is not a thing the machine does. Its entire meaning was "this operation happens before that one", and that meaning has now been expressed by position — which instruction appears earlier in the list. Once expressed that way, the bracket has nothing left to contribute and simply does not exist. Both programs execute exactly six instructions. Brackets can never make a program slower, and adding them for clarity is free.

    The same is true of everything else about how the source was written. Spacing vanished at Chapter IV.1's tokenizer. The tree vanished here. What survives into the instruction list is only what the program means, which is the precise sense in which Chapter II.3 could say that a bug lives between floors 1 and 2: by floor 6 there is nothing left of how you wrote it.

    Something the compiler gets for free

    Compare how deep the stack gets in each version. The unbracketed one holds 2, then 2 and 3, then 2 and 3 and 4 — three values at once. The bracketed one never holds more than two, because the addition consumes its operands before the 4 arrives.

    A compiler can work that number out while emitting, by tracking how each instruction changes the depth and remembering the largest value seen. It matters because a real machine must know how much room to reserve for the stack before it starts. Figure IV.4.1 draws these two traces; Unit IV.3.6 shows CPython recording exactly this number.

    Unit IV.3.5
    Rebuild

    Now look at CPython's

    The comparison, and it is exact

    Use names rather than numbers, so that nothing can be worked out in advance, and disassemble the same two shapes.

    One difference is worth noticing rather than passing over. CPython uses a single BINARY_OP instruction with the operator as an operand, where we used four separate instructions. That is a real design decision with a real trade: one instruction with an operand keeps the instruction set smaller and the evaluation loop's dispatch table shorter, at the cost of an extra decision inside the instruction. CPython made the opposite choice until version 3.11, when a family of separate arithmetic opcodes was merged into BINARY_OP — which is a useful reminder that these are engineering judgements, revisited as circumstances change, rather than facts about how compilers must be.

    Unit IV.3.6
    Descend

    A compiler does not merely translate

    Constant folding, and its limits

    Chapter 0.5 showed you something without explaining it, and promised that this volume would. Compile the version with numbers rather than names, and look at what CPython stored.

    This is constant folding, and it is the smallest possible example of what an optimising compiler does: notice something that cannot change between now and run time, and settle it now. The reasoning is simple and completely general. The expression 2 + 3 * 4 contains no names, so nothing in it can differ from one run to the next; therefore its value is the same every time; therefore computing it once, now, is safe and computing it repeatedly, later, is waste.

    It also explains, in retrospect, why Figure 0.5.2's fourth panel showed a single constant where you might have expected three numbers and an addition. That was not a simplification for a Volume 0 reader. It was exactly what happens.

    Now the more interesting question, and the one that shows folding is a judgement rather than a rule: when does CPython decline to fold?

    The first two refusals are about size. CPython could certainly compute a twenty-thousand-character string or a three-hundred-digit number at compile time. It declines because the result would have to be stored in the code object, and the code object is loaded into memory whenever the module is imported, and kept for as long as it lives. Folding trades run-time work for permanent memory, and past a certain size that trade stops being worth making. There is a threshold, and it is a judgement rather than a principle.

    The third refusal is about something more fundamental. A list is mutable, and Chapter I.7 established what that means: if the same list object were handed out every time the code ran, a program that appended to it once would find the change still there on the next run. A constant must be safe to share, and only immutable things are. So tuples fold and lists do not — which is the same rule that decides what may be a dictionary key in Chapter I.10, appearing in a place you would not have expected it.

    The comfortable wrong idea

    "Constant folding means I should not worry about writing wasteful expressions, because the compiler will clean up after me."

    It will do very little of that. Folding requires the compiler to know the values, which means literals only. The moment a name is involved — and almost everything in a real program involves a name — the compiler must assume the value could be anything, because in Python it genuinely could: the name might be rebound, the object might have a custom __add__ from Chapter II.7, or the module might be reloaded. Python's dynamism is exactly what prevents the aggressive compile-time reasoning that languages with fixed types can perform, and it is a real cost paid for a real benefit.

    Unit IV.3.7
    Descend

    What a code object really is

    Chapter I.8's promise, completed

    Your compiler returns a plain list of tuples. CPython bundles rather more together, and every part of the bundle is something this book has already explained from another direction.

    the bytecode
    The instruction sequence, as bytes rather than tuples — compact, because a module may hold a great many
    the constants
    Every literal value the code needs, including anything folded
    the names
    Every global name referred to, as text. The instructions hold an index into this list rather than the text itself
    the local names
    Chapter I.8's numbered slots, assigned here, at compile time. This is where they come from
    the stack size
    How much room the machine must reserve before running it
    the exception table
    Chapter I.11's map from instruction ranges to handlers, built in Chapter IV.6
    line numbers
    How a traceback knows which line of source an instruction came from

    Two properties of that bundle matter, and each explains something asserted earlier.

    A code object is immutable. Try to change one and you get a refusal:

    And a code object holds no values. Look at what is in the list above: instructions, constants, and the names of things. There is nowhere in it for a variable's current value to live, because a variable's current value is not a property of the code — it is a property of a particular execution. The values live in a frame, built fresh for each call, which is why Chapter I.8 could say that one code object serves every depth of recursion and Chapter IV.5 could demonstrate it with a single shared list.

    That separation — code that describes what to do, frames that hold what is being done to — is the most important structural idea in this volume, and it is the reason the two halves fit together at all.

    Ladder · four floors builtone to go before it runs

    1. Human intention
    2. Python source text — a string in your program
    3. Tokens — Chapter IV.1
    4. Syntax tree — Chapter IV.2
    5. Compiler — this chapter: the walk that flattens it
    6. Code object and bytecode — this chapter: the list it produces
    7. CPython runtime — Chapter IV.4, where it finally runs
    8. Native machine instructions
    9. CPU control logic
    10. Registers and ALU
    11. Caches and RAM
    12. Operating-system services
    13. Device, file, terminal, result

    Everything so far has been translation, and nothing has been executed. Your instruction list is data: tuples in a list, sitting in memory, meaning nothing until something reads them and acts. Which is the keystone of this whole book arriving from the inside — and Chapter IV.4 supplies the something.

    Level 3 Runtime model — what else a compiler could target

    Bytecode for a stack machine is one destination among several, and knowing the alternatives puts CPython's choice in context.

    A compiler can emit machine instructions directly, which is what C compilers do. The result runs at hardware speed with no interpretation layer at all — Chapter IV.4 measures what that layer costs — but the output only runs on one kind of processor, and the compiler must do register allocation and a great deal else. It also cannot easily support a language where a name's type is unknown until run time, because it has to commit to an instruction before it knows what kind of addition is meant.

    A compiler can emit bytecode for a register machine, which some languages do, and which typically executes fewer instructions for the same work at the cost of a more complicated compiler and larger instructions.

    Or it can emit bytecode and then, while the program runs, translate the parts that turn out to be hot into machine instructions — a just-in-time compiler. This gets the flexibility of bytecode with much of the speed of native code, at the cost of considerable complexity and memory, and of a warm-up period during which the program is slow. Several Python implementations do this, and CPython has been adding pieces of the machinery.

    There is a further, subtler point. A JIT can do something no ahead-of-time compiler can: it can observe that a particular addition has only ever been given integers, emit fast integer code, and keep a check that reverts if a float ever arrives. That is optimisation based on facts that are true so far rather than true always — and it is the natural answer to the difficulty raised in Unit IV.3.6, that Python's dynamism prevents compile-time reasoning. If you cannot know in advance, watch and find out.

    CPython

    Which optimisations CPython performs, and where, has changed substantially across recent versions and continues to. The adaptive specialisation of 3.11 is exactly the watch-and-find-out idea applied within the interpreter rather than by generating machine code. Treat any specific claim in this area as dated, and check the release notes for the version you use.

    Category: CPython implementation. See PEP 659 for adaptive specialisation.

    Reconstruct it without looking

    Close the book

    1. Redraw. Compile 1 + 2 * 3 - 4 by hand into the six-instruction set, then check with the code. Track what is on the stack after each instruction, and state the maximum depth.
    2. Explain. Why must an operation come after both its operands? Answer in terms of the stack, then say what a register machine would do instead and what it would cost.
    3. Explain. Where did the brackets go? Use the two instruction listings, and say what follows for anyone worried that brackets slow a program down.
    4. Modify. Add constant folding to your own compiler: when a binop node has two num children, compute the value and emit a single PUSH. Test it on 2 + 3 * 4 and count the instructions saved. Then explain why your version cannot fold x * 0.
    5. Modify. Have your compiler compute the maximum stack depth as it emits, and return it alongside the instructions. Check your answer against co_stacksize for the equivalent Python expression.
    6. Transfer. Someone claims that 'ab' * 10000 is folded away at compile time and therefore free. Using Unit IV.3.6, explain why it is not, and what the compiler is trading.
    7. Stretch. Your machine has a stack; Chapter 0.3's toy processor had one accumulator and no stack. Try to compile 2 + 3 * 4 for that processor, using memory locations to hold intermediates. Write down the instructions, then say precisely what the stack saved you and what a register machine would have needed you to decide.
    Mastery gate — Chapter IV.3
    • You can compile a small tree into stack-machine instructions by hand and in code.
    • You can state the emit rule, name it as a post-order traversal, and explain why that order is forced.
    • You can describe the stack-machine and register-machine alternatives, and give the trade-off in both directions.
    • You can explain how brackets disappear into instruction order, and what follows about their cost.
    • You can match your instruction listing to CPython's disassembly, instruction for instruction.
    • You can explain constant folding, identify it in co_consts, and give two reasons a compiler might decline to fold something.
    • You can list what a code object holds, and explain why it can be shared across every call and every depth.

    If item four is shaky, compile the two bracketed versions again and read them side by side until the swap is obvious — nothing else in this chapter matters as much. If item seven is shaky, the reason is worth chasing: it is the separation between code and frames, and Chapters IV.4 and IV.5 both depend on it entirely.
