    Volume IV · Chapter 4The interpreter laid open

    The loop that runs it

    Building a machine that obeys instructions — and the moment three machines turn out to be one machine

    You have a list of instructions and nothing that obeys them. This chapter writes the twenty lines that do. It is the shortest program in this volume and the most consequential, because when you finish it and look at what you have written, it is the loop from Chapter 0.3, which is the loop from Chapter 0.5, which is the loop the processor beneath your fingers is running at this moment. The keystone this book asked you to accept forty chapters ago becomes something you can check from the inside.

    Prerequisites

    Chapter IV.3 (the instruction list this executes), Chapter 0.3 Stages 6 to 10 (the program counter, the instruction register, the decoder, and the fetch–decode–execute loop you built by hand), Chapter 0.5 Unit 4 (CPython's evaluation loop, placed beside your toy processor's), Chapter I.10 (dictionaries, which will hold the names), Chapter I.11 (raising errors), Chapter II.13 (measuring rather than assuming, which the last unit does).

    Unit IV.4.1
    Problem

    A list that means nothing at all

    Something you can feel

    At the end of Chapter IV.3 your compiler produced this: [('PUSH', 2), ('PUSH', 3), ('PUSH', 4), ('MUL', None), ('ADD', None), ('STORE', 'x')]. Six tuples in a list. It computes nothing. It will sit in memory unchanged for as long as the program that made it survives, and then be collected by the machinery of Chapter II.11 without ever having done anything.

    It is tempting to say that this list "is a program", and worth resisting the temptation for a moment, because the resistance is where the chapter's central idea lives. Nothing about that list distinguishes it from any other list of tuples. Nothing in it is special. Chapter 0.1 established the principle in its very first pages and it has held ever since: a pattern in memory carries no information about what it means. The word 'PUSH' does not push. It is five characters that happen to spell an English word, and if you renamed the opcode to 'FLUMPH' throughout, nothing whatever would change.

    What makes that list a program is the existence of something that reads it and acts. Until then it is data. The moment such a thing exists, the same bytes become instructions — and they become instructions relative to that reader and to no other. Give your list to a different interpreter with a different idea of what 'PUSH' means and it would do something different, or nothing, or fail. Meaning does not live in the data; it lives in the relationship between the data and its reader.

    This is not a philosophical aside. It is the precise reason the keystone sentence of this book is true, and by the end of this chapter you will have built the reader and can therefore verify the claim rather than accept it.

    Unit IV.4.2
    Descend

    What such a reader must keep track of

    Deriving the state before writing the code

    Before writing anything, work out what the machine must remember between one instruction and the next. Do it by asking what would go wrong if each piece were missing, because that is how you can be sure the list is complete and not merely plausible.

    It must know where it is. Instructions come in a definite order, and after finishing one the machine must know which is next. Without that there is no "next" at all — the machine could not distinguish the beginning from the middle. Chapter 0.3 built exactly this and gave it a name: the program counter. That it is now a Python integer rather than a physical register changes nothing about its role.

    It must have somewhere to leave values for later instructions. Consider PUSH 2 followed by PUSH 3 followed by ADD. The ADD needs two numbers that it did not itself produce; they were produced by instructions that finished before it started. So there must be a place those instructions could put them and this one can find them.

    The natural next question is what shape that place should be, and the answer is worth deriving rather than assuming, because it is the one design decision in this machine that could plausibly have gone another way. Chapter 0.3's toy processor used a single accumulator — one value, in one register. Would that serve here?

    It would not, and the reason is nesting. Work through 2 + 3 * 4. The machine must hold the 2 while it works out 3 * 4, because the addition cannot happen until the multiplication is done. So at one moment two values are in flight simultaneously. Deepen the expression — 1 + 2 * (3 + 4 * 5) — and three are, then four. There is no fixed number of holding places that suffices for expressions of arbitrary depth, and expressions of arbitrary depth are exactly what Chapter IV.2's recursive parser accepts.

    What the structure needs is the property that values are finished with in the reverse of the order they were created: the innermost sub-expression is started last and completed first. A structure whose last item in is the first item out is a stack, and Python's list with append and pop is one. That is not a convenience; it is a match between the shape of the data structure and the shape of the problem, and it is why nearly every language implementation in the world uses a stack for expression evaluation.

    And it must remember names. STORE 'x' must put something where a later LOAD 'x' can find it, by name. A mapping from names to values is a dictionary, which Chapter I.10 built and Chapter II.7 revealed to be what a namespace is made of. Nothing new is required.

    The three pieces, and nothing else

    A position, a stack, and a dictionary of names. That is the complete state of the machine you are about to write — and, with more of each, the complete state of the machine CPython runs.

    It is worth noticing how short that list is. A great deal of apparent complexity in programming languages turns out to rest on very little at the bottom, and the reason it feels complex from above is that the layers accumulate, not that any single layer is intricate.

    Unit IV.4.3
    Tool

    Fetch, decode, execute

    The machine, line by line

    The loop has the shape Chapter 0.3 established for the toy processor, and it will help to name the phases as you read, because they are the same four every processor has performed since the 1940s. Fetch the instruction at the current position. Advance the position. Decode the opcode to work out what is being asked. Execute it.

    Four details in that code are worth examining, because each is a decision rather than an inevitability, and three of them are places where a plausible-looking alternative would be wrong.

    The counter advances before the instruction executes. pc += 1 sits immediately after the fetch and before any of the work. This looks like an arbitrary placement and is not. Chapter 0.3 made the same choice in the toy processor for the same reason: an instruction that changes the flow of control must be able to overwrite the counter, and it can only do that if the ordinary advance has already happened. With the increment afterwards, a jump would set the counter and then the increment would immediately spoil it. Our six-instruction set contains no jumps yet, so nothing here depends on it — but Chapter IV.5 adds them, and the machine is already correctly shaped for it.

    The default argument is None, not {}. Chapter I.8 spent a whole unit on why: a default value is built once, when def runs, so a mutable default is shared by every call that omits the argument. Had this been written names={}, every program run would have inherited the names of every previous program run, in an entirely invisible way. Here the trap is being avoided rather than demonstrated, which is what the earlier chapter was for.

    Unknown opcodes raise rather than being ignored. A machine that quietly skips instructions it does not recognise would run a corrupted program to completion and produce an answer. Chapter II.2's argument applies exactly: a wrong answer arriving confidently is worse than a crash, because the crash tells you something and the answer does not. This is also, incidentally, what Chapter 0.3's fourth failure experiment demonstrated on the toy processor.

    And right is popped before left. This is the subtlest of the four and deserves its own unit.

    Unit IV.4.4
    Break

    The bug that half your tests would miss

    Deliberate failure — pop order

    Why must the right operand come off the stack first? Trace it against what the compiler emitted. Chapter IV.3's rule was: emit the left branch, then the right branch, then the operation. So the left operand was pushed first and the right operand second — and a stack returns items in the reverse of the order they arrived. The last thing on is the right operand, so the first thing off is the right operand.

    Get it backwards and the machine still runs, still produces numbers, and is wrong. But not always wrong, which is the interesting part.

    Predict — before reading on

    Suppose you write left = stack.pop() first and right = stack.pop() second, swapping them. Which of your four arithmetic operations would give incorrect answers, and which would appear to work perfectly?

    Addition and multiplication would appear to work perfectly, because they are commutative: 10 + 3 and 3 + 10 are both 13, so swapping the operands is undetectable. Subtraction and division are not commutative, and would silently give the wrong answer — 10 - 3 would come out as −7.

    Why this is worth more than the bug it prevents

    A test suite that exercised only addition and multiplication would pass completely on a machine with this bug. The defect is real, present in every run, and invisible to a plausible set of tests.

    This is the concrete form of a warning Chapter II.2 gave in the abstract: choosing what to test is a skill, and the choice that matters is not "more cases" but cases that can distinguish. Two tests of commutative operations carry almost no information about operand order. One test of subtraction carries all of it. When you next write tests, ask not how many you have but which wrong implementations each one would catch.

    Unit IV.4.5
    Run and observe

    Watching the stack

    The machine, traced

    Run the two bracketings from Chapter IV.3 and follow the stack after each instruction. This is the clearest demonstration in the volume that the tree's shape survived into the instruction order, because you can watch the two programs diverge and reconverge.

    Now run them, and keep the same names dictionary between lines so that you have a session rather than a series of unrelated programs — which is exactly what Chapter I.1's interactive prompt is.

    The second line is worth a moment. y = x * 2 worked because x was still in the dictionary from the first line — a value produced by one program, stored under a name, and found by another program run later. That is what makes a session a session, and it is why Chapter I.1's prompt can remember what you told it.

    Unit IV.4.6
    Break

    Two ways to be wrong at run time

    Completing the three-stage story

    Chapter IV.2 promised a three-way division of errors and could only demonstrate two of them. Here is the third, and with it the full picture.

    Consider why z + 1 cannot be caught at compile time, since the reason is more interesting than it first appears. It is not that the compiler is lazy or that the check would be expensive. It is that the question is genuinely unanswerable then: whether z exists depends on what has run before, and the same instruction list can be run against different name dictionaries with different answers. Run it after z = 5 and it succeeds. The error is not a property of the program; it is a property of the program together with a particular state, and that pairing does not exist until run time.

    The two errors also differ from each other in a way worth noticing. Your machine detects the NameError deliberately — there is an explicit check in the LOAD branch. It does not detect the ZeroDivisionError at all. That one was raised by Python's own // operator, deep inside the execution of your DIV branch, and your loop simply did not catch it, so it travelled outwards through your machine and out to the user. Chapter I.11's unwinding passed straight through your interpreter without your interpreter participating — which is a small illustration of a large fact: an error in a program being interpreted and an error in the interpreter itself are, without deliberate effort, indistinguishable. Chapter IV.6 is about making that distinction properly.

    A third kind of wrong, which your machine does not survive

    There is a further category that neither the compiler nor a well-formed program can produce, but a malformed instruction list can. Hand your machine [('PUSH', 2), ('ADD', None)] — an ADD with only one value available — and it fails with IndexError: pop from empty list, an error about Python's lists rather than about your language.

    Your compiler cannot produce such a list, because the emit rule guarantees each operation is preceded by its operands. But a real implementation reading bytecode from a file cannot make that assumption, which is why CPython's code objects record the maximum stack depth their instructions require and why feeding it hand-edited bytecode is a documented way to crash the interpreter outright. Figure IV.4.1's "deepest point" is that number.

    Unit IV.4.7
    Rebuild

    Three machines, one shape

    The circle closes

    Now put your new loop beside the two you have already met in this book. Read them as three columns of one thing rather than three different things.

    The differences are real and worth enumerating precisely, because knowing which differences are superficial is as valuable as knowing what is shared.

    Where the instructions live
    Numbers in a Python list; tuples in a Python list; bytes inside a code object. All three are data structures in somebody's memory
    How wide an instruction is
    Two cells, so the toy advances by 2; one tuple, so yours advances by 1; a variable number of bytes, so CPython's pointer advances by the size of what it read
    Where values are held
    One accumulator; a stack; a stack. The toy's single register is the only genuinely limiting difference, and it is why the toy could not evaluate a nested expression without using memory as scratch
    How many opcodes
    Nine; six; around a hundred and forty on this build. A larger set means more can be done in one instruction, which is the main reason CPython's loop is faster than yours by more than the language difference alone would suggest
    What runs the loop
    CPython runs the toy; CPython runs yours; the processor runs CPython. Only the last is executed by hardware
    The keystone, arriving from the inside

    Your instruction list is data to the Python program that reads it. Python's bytecode is data to the C program that reads it. The C program's machine code is what the processor actually executes — and it is the only thing in this entire arrangement that the silicon has ever seen.

    Chapter 0.5 asked you to accept this on the strength of an argument. You have now written one of the layers, so you can check it directly: point to any line of your run function and ask what is executing it. The answer is CPython. Ask what is executing CPython. The answer is the processor. There is no line anywhere at which the machine looks at 'PUSH' and understands it.

    It is worth pushing on this once more, because it is the point at which people usually feel they have understood and have not. A natural response is: "yes, but at the bottom the computer really does run something, and that thing is machine code — so machine code is the real language and the rest is pretence." That is half right and the wrong half is instructive.

    The processor's own behaviour is also a matter of interpretation, just implemented in silicon rather than in software. A modern x86 processor does not execute its documented instructions directly either; it decodes them into narrower internal operations and executes those, which is precisely the same relationship one layer further down. What makes the bottom layer feel different is not that it escapes interpretation but that its interpreter is made of transistors and cannot be changed by you. The chain does not terminate in something self-evidently meaningful; it terminates in something physically fixed, which is a different property.

    Unit IV.4.8
    Descend

    What each layer costs

    Measured, not asserted

    Chapter II.13 insisted that claims about speed be measured. This chapter makes a claim about speed — that layers of interpretation cost something — so it should be measured too, and it can be, because you have a layer you built yourself and can remove.

    Take one line of arithmetic, total = total + i * 2, and run it two hundred thousand times two ways: as ordinary Python, and as six instructions through your machine. Both compute the same result.

    Where does the factor of ten go? Not into the arithmetic: the additions and multiplications are identical in both versions, performed by the same CPython on the same objects. It goes into everything around the arithmetic. For each of your instructions, CPython must index a list, unpack a tuple, compare a string against several candidates until one matches, and call a list method — and only then perform the operation the instruction names. Six of your instructions, each costing perhaps eight of CPython's bytecodes, is roughly fifty bytecodes to do what Python did in eight.

    That accounting also explains something Chapter II.13 asserted without demonstration: why staying in compiled code is so effective. Every layer multiplies. Your language is roughly ten times slower than Python; Python is perhaps fifty times slower than C for the same loop; and the product is the distance between your toy machine and a compiled language. None of the layers is badly built. They are simply stacked, and stacking is expensive.

    And it explains, finally, why CPython works so hard on the details of its own dispatch — the topic of the depth section below — and why the advice "let compiled code do the loop" appears fourth on Chapter II.13's list rather than last. Removing a layer is worth more than optimising within one.

    Ladder · your interpreter running one lineevery floor accounted for

    1. Human intention — somebody's tiny program
    2. Python source text — their source, which to you is a string
    3. Tokens — yours, Chapter IV.1
    4. Syntax tree — yours, Chapter IV.2
    5. Compiler — yours, Chapter IV.3
    6. Code object and bytecode — yours: a list of tuples
    7. CPython runtime — your run loop — itself Python bytecode, interpreted by CPython
    8. Native machine instructions — CPython's compiled C: the only real instructions here
    9. CPU control logic — fetch, decode, execute, in silicon
    10. Registers and ALU — where left + right finally becomes an addition
    11. Caches and RAM — your stack, your names and your program: all heap objects
    12. Operating-system services — dark; nothing here needs the kernel
    13. Device, file, terminal, result — dark until something is printed

    Floor 7 now contains two interpreters stacked on one another, yours running inside CPython's, and that stacking is the ten-fold factor measured above made visible as a diagram. Note also floors 12 and 13: an entire language implementation, and not one system call. Everything in this chapter happens inside a single process, which is why it is fast enough to be worth doing at all.

    Level 3 Runtime model — how a real interpreter makes dispatch cheap

    Your machine decides what to do by comparing a string against candidates in order. 'STORE' is checked against 'PUSH', then 'LOAD', and so on. That means later opcodes cost more than earlier ones, which is an accidental property of the order you happened to write the branches in — and with well over a hundred opcodes it would be intolerable.

    The first improvement is to make the opcode a small number rather than a string, so the comparison is integer equality rather than string comparison. Chapter 0.3's toy processor already did this; your machine used strings only because they are readable, and the readability cost real speed.

    The second is to stop comparing at all. With numbered opcodes, the machine can use the opcode as an index — jump straight to the code for that opcode without testing anything, which is Chapter I.6's base-plus-offset arithmetic applied to code instead of data. In C this is what a switch over a dense range of values compiles into: a jump table.

    The third is subtler and specific to interpreters. With one central switch, every instruction returns to the same place before dispatching the next, and the processor's branch predictor — which learns patterns in where jumps go — sees one branch that goes everywhere and can predict nothing. The technique known as computed-goto dispatch gives each opcode's code its own copy of the dispatch jump at the end, so the predictor sees many branches each with its own history, and can learn that a comparison is usually followed by a jump. The instruction count barely changes; the misprediction rate falls substantially, which Chapter II.12's discussion of the cost of getting things wrong at the hardware level should make plausible.

    The fourth goes further still: notice that an instruction is being executed repeatedly with the same kinds of operands, and replace it with a specialised version that skips the checks it has learned are unnecessary — reverting if the assumption ever fails. This is what recent CPython versions do adaptively while your program runs, and it is why the disassembly of a function can differ before and after it has been called many times.

    CPythonHardware example

    Which dispatch technique CPython uses depends on the version and on how it was compiled — computed goto requires a compiler extension and is not available everywhere. Adaptive specialisation arrived in 3.11 and has been extended since. The benefit of each is genuinely hardware-dependent, since it turns on branch prediction behaviour that differs between processors. Measure on your own machine before quoting a figure, and expect any figure to age.

    Category: CPython implementation and processor behaviour. See PEP 659 for adaptive specialisation.
    What you have actually made

    Roughly eighty lines, across three chapters: a tokenizer, a parser, a compiler and a virtual machine. That is a complete language implementation. It is small, and it is not a toy in the dishonest sense — it has the same architecture as CPython, the same stages in the same order, producing the same kind of artefact at each boundary, and the differences are of scale rather than of kind. Someone who understands these eighty lines can read a real implementation and recognise what they are looking at, which is not something that could be said before this volume began.

    Retrieval lock

    Reconstruct it without looking

    Close the book

    1. Redraw. Trace (2 + 3) * 4 through your machine instruction by instruction, writing the stack after each. Six rows. Then do the same for 2 + 3 * 4 and say at which row the two diverge and at which they reconverge.
    2. Explain. Derive the three pieces of state a stack machine needs, saying for each what would become impossible without it. Then justify the choice of a stack over a fixed number of registers, using an expression of your own devising.
    3. Explain. Why must right be popped before left? Say which operations would still appear to work if you swapped them, and what that implies about choosing test cases.
    4. Modify. Add a DUP instruction that duplicates the value on top of the stack, then use it to compile x * x without loading x twice. Check the instruction count before and after.
    5. Modify. Replace the string opcodes with integers and re-run your timing. Report the improvement, and say what you gave up.
    6. Transfer. Explain to somebody why "the computer runs Python" is wrong, using both of the machines you have built and being precise about what the processor does execute. Then anticipate their objection that machine code must be the real language, and answer it.
    7. Stretch. Add a JUMP_IF_ZERO instruction and a while statement to your language, changing all four stages. You know the shape from Chapter I.5: a conditional jump out and an unconditional jump back. When it works, you will have built loops from nothing but a counter you can assign to — and you will understand why the increment had to come before the execute.
    Mastery gate — Chapter IV.4
    • You can write a stack-machine interpreter loop from a blank file.
    • You can name the three pieces of state it needs and derive each from what would otherwise be impossible.
    • You can justify a stack rather than registers, from the structure of nested expressions.
    • You can trace a program by hand, tracking the stack, and state its maximum depth.
    • You can explain why some errors can only appear at run time, and why that is a fact about the question rather than about the compiler.
    • You can put your loop, the toy CPU's loop and CPython's loop side by side, name the shared skeleton, and enumerate the real differences.
    • You can explain, from a measurement you have taken, why each layer of interpretation costs, and where the cost goes.

    Item six is what the whole book has been building towards. If you can state it in your own words without looking, Volume 0's keystone has stopped being something you were told and become something you have verified from the inside — which is the difference this book exists to make.

    Volume IV · Chapter 5The interpreter laid open

    Frames, calls and closures

    Giving your machine functions, watching Figure I.8.1 become a list you can print, and finding out where a name actually lives

    Your interpreter has one stack, one dictionary of names, and no way to call anything. Adding functions turns out to force exactly the structure Chapter I.8 drew for you seven volumes-worth of pages ago: a stack of frames, each with its own workspace. This time you build it rather than being shown it — and then you discover the one thing that structure cannot do, which is where closures come from.

    Prerequisites

    Chapter IV.4 (the machine this extends — you will need it in the same session), Chapter I.8 and Figure I.8.1 (frames pushed and popped, and the UnboundLocalError sting, which this chapter finally explains from the other side), Chapter II.6 and Figure II.6.1 (recursion piling frames up), Chapter I.5 (loops as jumps, since you need a conditional jump here), Chapter II.7 (classes), Chapter II.11 (reference counting, which decides when a cell dies), Chapter II.13 (measuring rather than assuming, which one unit does at some length).

    Unit IV.5.1
    Problem

    One set of names is not enough

    Something you can feel

    Your machine keeps names in a single dictionary. That was sufficient while there was one program, and it stops being sufficient the instant there are two pieces of code that might use the same name for different things — which is to say, the instant you have functions.

    Make the failure concrete. Suppose a function called double uses a variable n, and it is called from a function that also uses n. With one shared dictionary, the moment double executes STORE 'n' it overwrites the caller's value. When it returns, the caller carries on using n and finds something it did not put there. Nothing raises; the program simply computes the wrong answer.

    And notice this is not a problem you can avoid by being careful with names. Recursion makes it structural rather than accidental: factorial calling factorial uses the same name n by definition, because it is the same function. There is no naming discipline that helps, because there is only one function and it is honestly using its own parameter.

    So each call needs its own set of names. And they must nest correctly: the inner call finishes, its names disappear, and the outer call resumes finding everything exactly as it left it. That is a stack of workspaces — and Chapter I.8 called such a workspace a frame. You are now going to build the thing that chapter drew, and print it.

    Unit IV.5.2
    Descend

    What a call must actually arrange

    Four obligations, derived

    Before writing code, work out what CALL must do, by asking what would be broken if each part were left out. There are four things, and the fourth is the one people forget.

    It must create a new namespace and bind the arguments into it. This is the requirement Unit IV.5.1 established. The values come from the caller's stack, because that is where the caller's instructions put them, and they are bound to the callee's parameter names.

    It must record where to resume in the caller. When the callee finishes, execution has to continue in the caller at the instruction after the call — not at the beginning, not somewhere else. So the caller's position must survive the call, untouched, for however long the callee runs.

    It must arrange for the returned value to reach the caller. The callee produces a value; the caller's next instruction expects to find it. Since the caller's instructions were compiled by Chapter IV.3's rule — operands then operation — they expect it on the caller's value stack, exactly where a PUSH would have left it.

    And it must give the callee its own value stack. This is the one that looks optional and is not. Consider a call happening part-way through evaluating an expression: 2 + factorial(3) leaves the 2 sitting on the stack while the call runs. If the callee used the same stack, its own pushes and pops would sit on top of the caller's partial results — which would work, as long as the callee were perfectly balanced and left the stack exactly as it found it plus one value. That is a real technique and some machines use it. But a callee that goes wrong then corrupts its caller's data rather than only its own, and debugging that is miserable. Giving each frame its own stack makes the failure local.

    Put those four together and a frame is exactly: a set of local names, a program counter, a value stack, and knowledge of which code it is running. Which is the list Chapter I.8 gave and Chapter IV.4 derived for the machine as a whole — now needed once per call rather than once per machine.

    The shape this forces

    Calls nest strictly: the callee always finishes before the caller does. A structure whose items are removed in the reverse of the order they were added is a stack — so the frames go on a stack, for the same structural reason the values did in Chapter IV.4, but about workspaces rather than about numbers.

    Hold on to the word "strictly", because Chapter IV.6 is about the two features that break it, and everything difficult in that chapter follows from the break.

    Extending the instruction set

    Four new instructions. CALL name pops an argument and starts a new frame running that function. RETURN pops a value from the current frame, discards the frame, and pushes the value onto the caller's stack. JUMP_IF_ZERO n pops a value and sets the counter to n if it was zero — Chapter 0.3's opcode 7 returning, and needed here because a recursive function without a base case is a function that never stops. And LOAD and STORE now act on the current frame's locals rather than on one global dictionary.

    Unit IV.5.3
    Tool

    A frame is an object with four things in it

    The machine, rebuilt

    The line f = frames[-1] deserves more attention than its length suggests, because it is doing something subtle. It is re-fetched at the top of every iteration, not once before the loop. That is what makes calls and returns work: after a CALL pushes a frame, the next iteration picks up a different f, and after a RETURN pops one, the iteration after that picks up the caller again. The machine does not need any explicit notion of "switching context". Switching context is re-reading which frame is on top.

    And each frame having its own pc is what makes returning land in the right place. When CALL runs, the caller's pc has already been advanced past the call instruction — that is Chapter IV.4's decision to increment before executing, arriving with a purpose. The caller's counter then sits untouched, pointing at the instruction after the call, while an arbitrary amount of other work happens. When the callee finally returns, the caller resumes at exactly the right instruction without anyone having stored a return address anywhere: the frame is the return address.

    Unit IV.5.4
    Tool

    Recursion, in a language you wrote

    Assembling a function by hand

    Your parser cannot yet express function definitions, so write the instructions directly. This is worth doing even once you have syntax, because it is the only way to see the jump targets as the plain numbers they are.

    Instruction 2 is the one worth tracing, because it is where the stack discipline earns its keep. It loads n and leaves it sitting on the frame's stack — and then instructions 3 to 6 do an entire recursive call, of arbitrary depth, before instruction 7 multiplies. For fact(5) that value waits while five further calls happen. It survives because it is on this frame's stack, and every one of those calls got its own.

    What this demonstrates about recursion

    Recursion needs no special support whatever. There is one code object, shared by every depth — the expression functions[a] hands back the same list every time. There is one frame per call, each with its own locals, stack and counter. And there is a base case that stops the descent.

    Chapter II.6 asserted that the code is shared and the frames are not. Here is the line that shares it, and here are the frames that are not shared, countable.

    The same machine also explains RecursionError exactly. Remove instruction 1 — the base case test — and frames grows by one on every call and is never popped. It does not loop forever in the manner of Chapter I.5's runaway while, because each pass consumes memory that is never returned; it grows until the list can no longer be extended. Python places a counter in front of that, so it can raise a clean, catchable error while there is still stack left to build a traceback with. The limit is a courtesy, not a limitation.

    Unit IV.5.5
    Break

    The thing this structure cannot do

    Deliberate failure — a frame that outlives its call

    Your frames vanish on RETURN. That is correct, it is what makes the stack discipline work, and it makes one thing impossible.

    Predict — reason from your machine

    A function defines another function inside itself, one that uses the outer function's parameter, and returns it. The outer function then finishes. Later, somebody calls the inner one. Where does it get the value?

    A function that keeps hold of names from the place it was defined is a closure. The name refers to the whole arrangement: the function together with the captured environment, "closed over" the names it needs.

    Something must survive the frame, and it must be reachable from the inner function. CPython will show you precisely what it is.

    The cell is the answer to "what survives". It is an ordinary heap object, so Chapter II.11's reference counting keeps it alive exactly as long as something points at it — and the inner function object points at it. The frame dies on schedule; the cell does not, because its lifetime is governed by references rather than by the stack discipline. This is the first time in the book that those two lifetimes have come apart, and it will happen again, more dramatically, in Chapter IV.6.

    Unit IV.5.6
    Descend

    Three places a name can live

    And a compiler that decides which, in advance

    Your machine has one way to find a name: look it up in f.local. Python has three, and which one is used is settled at compile time by where the name was bound. A single function can use all three in one expression.

    The three differ in what they cost, at least in principle. A local is an index into an array — Chapter I.6's base-plus-offset arithmetic, the cheapest lookup there is. A cell is one extra hop: read the cell, then read its contents. A global is a dictionary lookup by name — Chapter I.10's hash, mask and probe — and if the name is not found there, a second lookup in the built-ins.

    Which invites a natural conclusion, and a piece of advice that has circulated for decades: hoist globals into locals inside hot loops, because local access is faster. Chapter II.13 insists that such claims be measured rather than repeated, so measure it.

    An honest negative result

    The measurement does not show what the mechanism predicts, and the discrepancy is worth explaining rather than hiding. Recent CPython specialises LOAD_GLOBAL adaptively: after the instruction has run a few times and found the name in the same place, it rewrites itself into a version that checks a cached pointer instead of performing the full lookup. The dictionary hash is skipped in the common case, so the mechanism's cost is real and is no longer paid.

    Two lessons, both of which this book has argued for before. Chapter II.13's discipline is vindicated: an optimisation justified by a plausible mechanism turned out, when measured, to buy nothing on a current interpreter — and would have cost readability for free. And the finding is version-specific rather than eternal: on an older Python the advice was sound, which is why it exists. Measure on the interpreter you are actually running, and treat performance folklore as dated until re-checked.

    Unit IV.5.7
    Break

    Three functions that all say the same thing

    Second deliberate failure

    Predict

    A loop runs three times. Each pass defines a function returning the loop variable, and appends it to a list. Calling all three afterwards gives what?

    Figure IV.5.1 explains it without any new idea. There is one i in one scope, therefore one cell. All three functions close over that cell. The loop changed what the cell held; the functions read it when called, which was afterwards; and by then it held 2.

    They did not capture a value. They captured a place — which is Chapter I.3's distinction, arriving for the last time and in its most consequential form. A closure keeps hold of the label, not of what the label was pointing at when the function was written. Everything about this trap follows from that one sentence, and nothing about it is peculiar to loops: two functions defined anywhere in the same scope share the same cells for the same reasons.

    Notice also that the behaviour is not a defect to be worked around. It is exactly what you want in the ordinary case, which is what makes the trap a trap. A closure that captured values would be useless for a counter, because the count could never change; the whole point of nonlocal, below, is that the shared place can be written through.

    The cell can also be written through, deliberately, which is what makes closures more than a curiosity.

    Unit IV.5.8
    Rebuild

    The sting from Chapter I.8, explained from the other side

    A debt paid

    Chapter I.8 showed a function whose first line printed x and whose second line assigned to it, and observed that this raises UnboundLocalError on the first line — the reading line — even though a global x existed. The explanation given there was that the compiler had already decided x was local. You can now see that decision being made and see why it must be made that way.

    The compiler must choose, for every name in a function body, which of the three instructions from Figure IV.5.1 to emit. It has to choose once, at compile time, because the instruction is fixed in the code object and will be executed possibly millions of times. So it examines the whole body and asks: is this name assigned anywhere in this function? If yes, it is local, and every reference to it becomes LOAD_FAST — including references on lines above the assignment, because a slot number is a property of the function, not of a position within it.

    The slot therefore exists from the function's first instruction and holds nothing until the assignment runs. Reading an empty slot is precisely what UnboundLocalError reports, and its wording — a local variable "not associated with a value" — is exact rather than obscure once you know there is a slot to be unassociated.

    The alternative design is worth considering, because rejecting it shows why Python is arranged this way. The compiler could emit a general instruction that searched locals, then enclosing cells, then globals, at run time, for every name. That would make the sting impossible: x would simply be found in globals until the local existed. It would also make every single name access a chain of lookups instead of an array index, and would mean the same line of source behaved differently depending on what had run before it. Python trades a confusing error in a rare situation for fast, predictable name access everywhere — and this book's position is that stating the trade is more useful than defending the outcome.

    Ladder · where a name livesdecided at floor 5, every time

    1. Human intention — use that name here
    2. Python source text
    3. Tokens
    4. Syntax tree — where each name is bound becomes visible
    5. Compiler — decides: numbered slot, cell, or global lookup
    6. Code object and bytecode — LOAD_FAST, LOAD_DEREF or LOAD_GLOBAL
    7. CPython runtime — an array index, one hop through a cell, or a dictionary lookup
    8. Native machine instructions
    9. CPU control logic
    10. Registers and ALU
    11. Caches and RAM — frames on the stack; cells and module dictionaries in the heap
    12. Operating-system services
    13. Device, file, terminal, result

    Floor 5 is doing the interesting work, and floor 11 shows why it matters: the three mechanisms reach three regions with three different lifetimes. A slot dies with its frame. A cell dies when nothing references it. A module dictionary lives as long as the module. Scope is not an abstract rule about visibility — it is a claim about where a value is stored and therefore about how long it lasts.

    Retrieval lock

    Reconstruct it without looking

    Close the book

    1. Redraw. Draw the frame stack at the deepest point of fact(3), showing each frame's n, its pc, and what is waiting on its value stack. Then say what each frame is waiting for.
    2. Explain. Give the four things a CALL must arrange, and for each say what breaks if it is omitted. Then explain why a callee having its own value stack is a choice rather than a necessity.
    3. Explain. Why can a closure's variable not live in the frame? Name what holds it instead, and say what governs its lifetime.
    4. Modify. Add a fib function to your machine, hand-assembled, and report the deepest frame count for fib(10). Explain why it is far smaller than the number of calls, using the shape of the recursion.
    5. Modify. Delete instruction 1 from fact and run it. Describe exactly how it fails, and relate that to RecursionError and to Figure 0.4.1's stack region.
    6. Transfer. A colleague builds a list of functions in a loop and finds they all behave identically. Diagnose it in terms of places rather than values, then give both fixes and say why each works.
    7. Transfer. Someone shows you a blog post recommending that you copy globals into locals for speed. Using this chapter, say what the mechanism predicts, what the measurement shows, why they disagree, and what you would tell them to do.
    8. Stretch. Give your machine closures: make CALL able to carry a dictionary of captured cells that the new frame can read through but does not own. What did you have to add, where does the captured value now live, and when can it be freed?
    Mastery gate — Chapter IV.5
    • You can extend a stack machine with frames, calls and returns.
    • You can derive the four obligations of a call, and say why frames form a stack.
    • You can explain why each frame needs its own program counter, and why that removes the need for a stored return address.
    • You can run recursion on your own machine, report the frame depth, and derive RecursionError from the structure.
    • You can define a closure, say what a cell is, and explain what governs its lifetime.
    • You can name the three name-resolution mechanisms, say what each costs in principle, and report what measurement shows.
    • You can explain the late-binding trap as capturing a place rather than a value, and say why the behaviour is desirable in the ordinary case.
    • You can explain the UnboundLocalError sting from the compiler's side, and state the trade Python made in accepting it.

    Item seven is the one people carry wrong for years, and item six is the one that will keep you honest for the rest of your career. If either is shaky, reread Unit IV.5.6 and Unit IV.5.7 together — both turn on the same fact, that a name is a place and not a value.

    Volume IV · Chapter 6The interpreter laid open

    Errors and pausing

    Exceptions and generators, built from first principles — and the discovery that they are two answers to one question

    Chapter I.11 gave you exceptions and Chapter II.5 gave you generators, and nothing in either suggested they had anything to do with each other. One is about failure; the other is about laziness. Yet when you try to build them, both run into the same wall in the same place, and both get past it by the same trick. This chapter builds both, discovers the connection by hitting it, and then shows you the line in CPython where the connection is made explicit.

    Prerequisites

    Chapter IV.5 (frames, calls and returns in your own machine — this chapter modifies that machine), Chapter I.11 (exceptions, tracebacks, unwinding), Chapter II.5 and Figure II.5.1 (generators and the suspended frame), Chapter I.8 and Figure I.8.1 (the ordinary frame lifecycle these two features both violate), Chapter II.11 (reference counting, which turns out to decide when a suspended frame is finally released).

    Unit IV.6.1
    Problem

    Two features that will not fit the machine you built

    Something you can feel

    Your interpreter from Chapter IV.5 can do a great deal. It has functions, it has frames, it does recursion, and it correctly gives every call its own workspace. It has exactly one way in and exactly one way out: CALL pushes a frame, RETURN pops it and hands a value back. That single pathway is clean, and it is about to be the problem.

    Consider what has to happen when something goes wrong five frames deep. A function fails; it cannot produce the value it promised; and the code that can do something sensible about the failure is not its caller, nor its caller's caller, but somebody much further up. With only RETURN available, that is impossible to express. RETURN goes exactly one frame outwards and it must carry a value. A failure has no value to carry, and it needs to travel an unknown distance.

    Now consider the opposite difficulty. A generator produces a value and stops, and later somebody asks for the next one and it carries on from where it stopped, with its local variables exactly as it left them. Again RETURN is the wrong instrument, and this time for the opposite reason: RETURN destroys the frame, and here the frame must survive. The value goes out; the workspace must stay.

    Set those two next to each other and a shape appears. In both cases control needs to leave a frame in a way ordinary return cannot express. In one case it must leave further than a return goes; in the other it must leave less permanently than a return does. Both are what a compiler writer calls non-local control flow — movement of control that the plain call-and-return discipline cannot describe — and building either one forces the same structural change on your machine. That change, and the fact that it is the same change, is the subject of this chapter.

    We will take them in the order that reveals the connection. Exceptions first, because they are the more constrained problem and their solution turns out to be reusable; generators second, because once the machinery exists they need surprisingly little that is new. And at the end, the two will turn out to be joined not merely by analogy but by an actual mechanism: in Python, the way a generator announces that it has finished is by raising an exception.

    Unit IV.6.2
    Descend

    What an exception is obliged to do

    Deriving the requirements before writing any code

    It is worth being precise about the job before choosing a mechanism, because the obvious mechanisms fail in instructive ways. Strip away the syntax and an exception has exactly three obligations.

    First, it must abandon work in progress. When a function raises, the rest of that function does not run. Neither does the rest of its caller, unless the caller was prepared. This is not merely a convenience; it is the entire point. If the remaining statements ran anyway, they would run on the assumption that the failed operation had succeeded, and would produce results that look plausible and are wrong — which Chapter II.2 identified as the most dangerous class of defect there is.

    Second, it must search for somebody willing to deal with the problem. The search is dynamic, meaning it depends on who called whom at run time rather than on how the source is laid out. The same function might be called from a place that catches its errors and from a place that does not, and it cannot know which. So the search has to walk the frames that actually exist at the moment of failure, outwards, until it finds a handler or runs out of frames.

    Third, it must carry information. Something has to reach the handler describing what went wrong — in Chapter I.11's terms, an error object with a type and a message. And, because the frames it passes through are about to be destroyed, it must also record what they were, or the traceback that made those errors so useful would be lost.

    Those three obligations are the whole specification. Everything that follows is an argument about how to satisfy them cheaply.

    Break

    The design that seems obvious and is not chosen

    Return codes, examined honestly

    Before building anything, it is worth taking seriously the design that most people invent first, because it is not stupid and because several respected languages use it.

    The idea: do not add a mechanism at all. Let every function that might fail return two things — a result and an indication of whether it worked — and have every caller check. Nothing about the machine changes. RETURN already carries a value; make it carry a pair.

    This works, in the sense that programs written that way are correct. It also has genuine virtues that deserve stating rather than dismissing. Failure becomes visible in the source: you can see, at every call site, that this operation might not have worked, because the check is right there. There is no invisible control flow, so reading the code tells you the truth about where execution can go. And the cost is exactly the cost of the checks, with no machinery hiding anywhere.

    The difficulty is what happens as the distance grows. Suppose the failure happens five frames down and the code that can respond is at the top. Every one of the four intermediate functions — none of which cares about this failure, none of which can do anything useful about it — must nevertheless check for it, and pass it on, and be written to have somewhere to pass it to. Their signatures change to accommodate an error they merely transport. Their bodies fill with checks that do nothing but forward. And the cost is paid on every call, including the overwhelming majority that succeed.

    Worse, the checks are optional in the sense that forgetting one is not detected. A caller that ignores the failure indication compiles perfectly and runs perfectly and is wrong. The mechanism relies on discipline exactly where discipline is hardest to maintain, which is in code nobody is thinking about because it is not where the interesting work happens.

    Being fair to the alternative

    This is a genuine design trade rather than a solved question, and reasonable languages land on both sides. Languages that use return values for errors gain explicitness and lose brevity; languages that use exceptions gain brevity and lose explicitness about where control can go. Python chose exceptions, and this book explains that choice rather than defending it as the only possibility. What follows is how the choice is implemented — and the implementation, it turns out, removes the cost objection almost entirely, which is a large part of why the choice is defensible.

    Unit IV.6.3
    Break

    The first implementation anybody writes, and why it is wrong

    A cost argument, done properly

    Given the three obligations, here is the implementation that suggests itself immediately. Add a flag to the machine: am I currently carrying an error? After each instruction, check it. If the flag is set, stop executing normally, look for a handler in this frame, and if there is none, pop the frame and check the next one.

    It satisfies the specification completely. It is also a bad design, and the reason is arithmetic rather than taste.

    Consider what fraction of instructions execute during a failure. A program running for one second executes perhaps hundreds of millions of instructions. It might raise, say, a hundred exceptions in that time — a generous estimate for most programs, since exceptions are for exceptional things. So the flag is set during a vanishingly small proportion of instruction executions, and clear during essentially all of them. Yet this design checks it after every single one. You have added a cost to the common path in order to serve the rare path, which is precisely backwards.

    Chapter II.13 gave the arithmetic for judging this. If checking adds even a small percentage to every instruction, and instructions are what your program spends its time on, then you have made the entire program slower to make failure handling simpler. The correct instinct is the opposite: make the rare path bear the cost, however expensive that makes it, and leave the common path untouched.

    Which raises the design question this chapter actually turns on. If the machine does not check for errors as it goes, how does it know, at the moment an error appears, where the handler is?

    Unit IV.6.4
    Tool

    Write it down in advance

    The handler table

    The answer is one you have seen before in a different costume. Chapter IV.3 established that the compiler knows things at compile time that the running program would otherwise have to work out. Constant folding was the small example. This is the large one.

    When you write a try block, the compiler knows exactly which instructions are inside it, because it is the thing generating them. It knows precisely where the handler's instructions start. Neither fact can change while the program runs. So the compiler writes down a table, stored alongside the code and never consulted unless something goes wrong: for instructions in this range, the handler is at that position.

    The consequence is the important part, and it deserves stating explicitly because it is counter-intuitive: entering a try block executes no instructions at all. There is nothing to execute. The protection is not something the program does; it is something the compiler recorded about a region of code. The program runs through a protected region exactly as it would run through an unprotected one, at exactly the same speed, and the table sits there unread.

    Only when an error is actually raised does anything consult it — and at that moment the machine can afford to do real work, because it is a moment that happens rarely and something has already gone wrong.

    Extending the machine — handlers and RAISE

    Each function now comes as a pair: its instructions, and a tuple of handler entries. Each entry is (start, end, target), meaning that if an error occurs while executing an instruction at a position from start up to but not including end, control should jump to target. That half-open range is the same convention as range and slicing from Chapters I.5 and I.6, used here for the same reason: it makes adjacent ranges join without gaps or overlaps.

    The machine changes in three places, and only three. The instruction loop is wrapped in a try of its own — we are, after all, implementing exceptions in a language that has them, which is a convenience worth noticing rather than hiding. A ToyError class carries the error value. And when one is caught, an unwinding loop walks the frame stack outwards.

    Three details in that code repay attention, because each corresponds to something Chapter I.11 described from the outside.

    The line frames.pop() is where a traceback entry would be produced. The frame is about to cease to exist, and everything it knew — which function it was running, which line it had reached — is about to be lost. Chapter I.11 said the traceback is built from the wreckage as the unwinding proceeds; this is the instruction at which each piece of wreckage would be recorded.

    The line top.stack.append(error.value) is as e. The handler needs the error object, and the natural place to leave it is on the stack, where the handler's first instructions will expect to find it. Nothing more elaborate is required.

    And top.pc = target is the whole of "control transfers to the handler". It is an assignment to a program counter — the same operation that Chapter I.4 revealed underneath if, and Chapter I.5 underneath loops. Every control structure in every language, at the bottom, is a number being written into a register. Exceptions look like the most magical control flow in Python, and they reduce to the same single assignment.

    Unit IV.6.5
    Run and observe

    Watching an error cross a frame boundary

    The machine, tested

    Now assemble two functions to exercise it. The inner one divides by zero and has no handler at all. The outer one calls it, and does have a handler covering the instruction at which the call happens.

    Remove the handler and the difference is exactly the difference between a caught error and a crash.

    And the case that matters most for the cost argument: a program that raises nothing runs through the same machine with the handler table completely unread.

    Unit IV.6.6
    Rebuild

    The same design, in CPython

    The comparison, and a misconception corrected

    Chapter I.11's Level 3 asserted that modern CPython uses zero-cost exceptions and that entering a try executes no extra bytecode. You now have the machinery to check that claim rather than believe it.

    The twelve bytes of co_exceptiontable are the table: the same information as our tuple of (start, end, target) entries, compressed into a byte format for space. The instructions after RETURN_VALUE are the handler, sitting in the code object and never executed unless the table sends control there.

    Two of those handler instructions are worth naming, because they do jobs our toy machine skipped. CHECK_EXC_MATCH tests whether the error that arrived is of the type this handler claims to catch — our machine's handlers catch everything, which is Chapter I.11's bare except:, and now you can see that catching by type costs one extra instruction on the failure path and nothing at all otherwise. And RERAISE is what happens when the type does not match: the search resumes outwards, exactly as if this frame had had no handler.

    The comfortable wrong idea

    "try blocks are slow, so wrap as little as possible in them."

    This was true once and has not been for years. Older CPython pushed a small setup instruction on entering a try and popped it on leaving, so there genuinely was a per-entry cost, and the advice made sense. The exception-table design removed it. Wrapping a loop in try rather than wrapping each iteration is still worth doing — but for clarity, not for speed.

    What does cost is raising. Building the error object, unwinding the frames, searching the tables and constructing a traceback are all real work. So the modern guidance is precise: protecting code is free, and failing is not. Which is why exceptions are for exceptional things, and why using them as ordinary control flow — to leave a loop, say — is a genuine performance mistake as well as a readability one.

    Unit IV.6.7
    Descend

    The obligation that makes this hard

    finally, and why it complicates everything

    Everything so far handles try/except. Chapter I.11 mentioned a third clause in passing, promising it would matter later, and this is later. finally is where the design earns its complexity.

    A finally block must run on the way out of its region however that exit happens. Enumerate the ways and the difficulty appears. Execution can reach the end of the block normally. It can leave via return. It can leave via break or continue. An exception can be raised and caught further out. An exception can be raised and never caught at all, terminating the program. Each of those is a different path through the machine, and every one of them must be made to pass through the finally instructions on its way.

    This is why a compiler cannot treat finally as just another handler. A handler is a destination: control arrives and stays. A finally is a detour: control must pass through it and then continue to wherever it was already going — and where it was going differs by path. If an exception was travelling outwards, it must resume travelling outwards afterwards, still carrying the same error. If a return was in progress, the return must complete afterwards, still carrying the same value.

    Implementations solve this in two broad ways, and both are legitimate. One is to duplicate the finally instructions into every exit path, so each path has its own copy and simply falls through. This is fast and makes the code object larger. The other is to keep one copy and record, before jumping to it, why control is passing through — so that the end of the finally can dispatch back to the right continuation. This is compact and requires the machine to carry that "why" somewhere.

    You do not need to know which CPython does to write correct Python. You do need to know why it is harder than it looks, because it explains an otherwise puzzling piece of advice: a return inside a finally block silently discards any exception that was travelling through, since the return is a new decision about where control goes, and it overrides the old one. That is not a quirk. It falls directly out of the detour-with-a-continuation design, and once you have seen the design it is the only thing that could happen.

    Where you have already relied on this

    Chapter III.1's with statement is built on exactly this guarantee. When it closes a file however you leave the block — normally, by return, or by exception — it is using the machinery just described. Chapter III.6's lock release is the same. Every resource that is reliably cleaned up in Python rests on finally being genuinely unavoidable, which rests on the compiler having threaded it into every exit path.

    Unit IV.6.8
    Problem

    Now the other half: a frame that must not die

    Generators, derived

    Turn to the second feature, and approach it the same way — by asking what it is obliged to do before asking how to do it.

    Chapter II.5 established the behaviour. A generator function, when called, runs none of its body and hands back an object. Each next runs the body until the next yield, hands out that value, and stops there. The following next resumes on the line after the yield, with every local variable exactly as it was left. When the body finally ends, StopIteration is raised.

    Ask what must be preserved between one next and the next, and the answer is short and exact. The local variables must survive, or resuming would find them gone. The position must survive, or the machine would not know which instruction comes next. And the value stack must survive, because a yield can occur part-way through evaluating a larger expression, with partial results waiting on it.

    Compare that list against the contents of a frame. Locals, program counter, value stack — that is a frame, exactly and completely. So the requirement is not "save some information about the function"; it is keep the frame alive after control has left it.

    And there is the wall from Unit IV.6.1, hit from the other direction. Your machine keeps frames in a Python list used as a stack, and RETURN pops and discards. A structure where the only way out destroys the thing you need to keep cannot express generators at all. The frame must stop being a stack entry and become an object that something else can hold a reference to.

    Unit IV.6.9
    Tool

    A generator is an object holding a frame

    Building it

    Once the requirement is stated that way, the implementation is almost forced. Make a class whose instances hold a Frame. Give it a method that runs that frame until a YIELD instruction, and returns the yielded value without discarding the frame. The next call picks the same frame up and carries on, because the frame's own pc is still pointing at the instruction after the yield.

    Hand-assemble the countdown from Chapter II.5 and run it.

    Run it once more and the picture completes: the fourth resume continues from instruction 4, decrements n to 0, jumps back to the test, finds zero, falls off the end, and raises. Only then does n reach 0 — and only then is the generator finished.

    Notice also what happens at instruction 3 across those three calls. The first time, control arrives there having come from instruction 2. The second time, control starts at instruction 4 — the machine did not begin at the top and fast-forward, and it did not recompute anything. It simply continued from a saved position, which is why Chapter II.5 said a generator is not slower for having paused.

    Unit IV.6.10
    Rebuild

    The join

    Where the two halves of this chapter meet

    Look again at the last line of resume. When the instructions run out, the generator sets a flag and raises. It does not return a special value meaning "no more"; it does not return None; it raises an exception.

    That choice was not made for the convenience of this chapter. It is Python's, and you can watch it in the real thing.

    This is the connection promised at the start, and it is a mechanism rather than an analogy. The reason the design is right rather than merely convenient is worth spelling out. A generator's values can be anything at all — any object, including None, including False, including whatever sentinel you might have chosen. So there is no value that can safely mean "finished", because any value you pick is one the generator might legitimately want to yield. The end of a sequence has to be signalled outside the channel that carries values, and an exception is exactly a channel that runs outside the ordinary flow of values. Chapter II.5 called StopIteration "an error used as a signal rather than a complaint"; now you can see why nothing else would do.

    The design also lets the ending carry information, which a sentinel could not.

    And the traffic runs both ways. Because a suspended frame is a real object that something else holds, an exception can be delivered into it, raised at the point where it is paused.

    Which finally explains a detail from Chapter III.7 that was stated there without justification. Closing a generator raises GeneratorExit inside it, so that any finally block gets its chance to run. That is how an abandoned generator holding a file manages to close it — and it works only because a suspended frame can receive an exception, which works only because the frame is an object rather than a stack entry.

    Unit IV.6.11
    Descend

    What CPython had to do about this

    Frames as objects, and the cost of it

    Chapter I.8's Level 3 said that CPython keeps frame data in a contiguous internal stack, because that makes calls cheap, and Chapter II.5's Level 3 said a generator's frame cannot use that arrangement unchanged. You now have the reason stated precisely: an ordinary frame's lifetime is exactly nested within its caller's, which is what makes a stack the right structure, and a generator's frame is not nested within anything.

    CPython's answer is visible from Python. A generator object holds its frame, and you can look at it while it is suspended.

    That last line has a practical consequence worth carrying away. A generator that has run to completion holds nothing; a generator that has been abandoned part-way holds its entire frame, including every object its local variables refer to, until the generator object itself is collected. Chapter II.5's Level 3 warned that an abandoned generator keeps its locals alive, and Chapter III.1 warned about files not being closed. Those are the same warning, and this is the mechanism underneath both.

    The bytecode shows the other half of the arrangement.

    CPythonPython language

    What the language guarantees: that a try block's handlers catch by type; that finally runs on every exit path; that a generator suspends at yield with its state intact and raises StopIteration when it ends, carrying any return value. All of that you may rely on in any Python.

    What is CPython's: the exception table's byte format and its existence at all; every opcode name above; where frame storage lives and when it is moved; and the attributes gi_frame, gi_suspended and co_exceptiontable, which are introspection conveniences rather than promises. All have changed between versions and will change again. Run dis on your own build before quoting any of it.

    Sources: Python language reference on the try statement and on yield expressions; CPython 3.11 release notes for zero-cost exceptions; the dis and inspect module documentation.

    Ladder · an exception, and a yieldtwo shapes on one diagram

    1. Human intention — give up here; or pause here
    2. Python source text — raise, or yield
    3. Tokens
    4. Syntax tree — a Raise or Yield node; a yield anywhere marks the whole function
    5. Compiler — writes the handler table; flags the code object as a generator
    6. Code object and bytecode — a table beside the code; a suspend point inside it
    7. CPython runtime — unwind frames and search tables; or set a frame aside intact
    8. Native machine instructions
    9. CPU control logic — in both cases, ultimately an assignment to a program counter
    10. Registers and ALU
    11. Caches and RAM — frames destroyed, or frames kept alive in the heap
    12. Operating-system services — dark; neither feature touches the kernel
    13. Device, file, terminal, result — dark, until a traceback is printed

    Floor 5 is where both features are actually decided, before the program runs: the table is written, and the function is marked. Floor 7 is where they diverge, and the divergence is exactly one word — destroy the frame, or keep it. Everything else about these two apparently unrelated features is shared, which is why one chapter can hold both.

    Level 4 Expert microscope — what this makes possible next

    Once frames are objects that can be suspended, resumed and thrown into, a family of features becomes available that would otherwise each need their own machinery.

    yield from delegates to another generator, forwarding values outwards and exceptions inwards, which is only expressible because both directions of travel exist. Chapter III.7's coroutines are the same suspend-and-resume mechanism with an event loop deciding who resumes; await is a suspend point of exactly the kind yield is, and the compiler marks an async def function at floor 5 in the same way and for the same reason. Context managers combine with generators through a decorator that turns a single-yield generator into a with-compatible object, using the throw mechanism to deliver exceptions into the block's cleanup.

    None of those is a separate invention. Each is a use of the two capabilities this chapter built — leave a frame without destroying it, and transfer control non-locally with a value attached — which is a good illustration of why it is worth understanding mechanisms rather than memorising features. Learn the two, and a dozen features stop needing to be learned separately.

    CPython

    How much of this is shared implementation rather than merely shared idea varies by version; coroutines and generators have had overlapping internals since async was introduced, and the details have been reorganised more than once. The conceptual relationship is stable; the code is not.

    Category: CPython implementation. See PEP 380 for yield from and PEP 492 for coroutines.
    Retrieval lock

    Reconstruct it without looking

    Close the book

    1. Redraw. Draw three frames with an error raised in the innermost and a handler only in the outermost. Number the steps of the unwinding, and mark at which step each traceback line would be recorded.
    2. Explain. State the three obligations of an exception, then explain why the handler table satisfies all three while costing nothing on the ordinary path. Then explain why the flag-checking design satisfies them too and is still wrong.
    3. Explain. Why can no ordinary value signal the end of a generator? Give the argument, not the rule, and say what it implies about any sequence protocol you design yourself.
    4. Modify. Give your toy handler entries a type, so that a handler catches only errors of a kind it names, and add a re-raise when the type does not match. Then verify that an unmatched error still unwinds to an outer handler. You have implemented CHECK_EXC_MATCH and RERAISE.
    5. Modify. Make ToyGenerator.resume accept a value that becomes the result of the paused YIELD, so that the caller can send information inwards. Then use it to write a running-total generator. You have implemented send, and therefore most of what a coroutine needs.
    6. Transfer. A colleague uses exceptions to leave a deeply nested loop, arguing that it is cleaner than flags. Give the case for and the case against, using this chapter's cost analysis rather than taste — and say what measurement would settle it.
    7. Stretch. Combine both halves: give your machine a YIELD that can occur inside a protected range, then throw an error into a suspended generator and make its handler catch it. Then explain why this is impossible in a machine whose frames live only on a stack.
    Mastery gate — Chapter IV.6
    • You can state the three obligations of an exception and evaluate a proposed implementation against them.
    • You can explain the return-code alternative fairly, including its genuine advantages, and say what Python traded away by not choosing it.
    • You can explain why checking a flag after every instruction is the wrong shape, using the arithmetic rather than an appeal to authority.
    • You can implement a handler table and cross-frame unwinding, and say which line of your code corresponds to each part of a traceback.
    • You can explain why entering a try costs nothing and raising costs a great deal, and give the practical advice that follows.
    • You can say why finally is harder to implement than except, and what that explains about returning from inside one.
    • You can derive, from what must be preserved, that a generator requires the frame itself to survive.
    • You can explain why StopIteration is an exception rather than a sentinel value, and what it can carry that a sentinel could not.
    • You can explain why gi_frame becomes None and what an abandoned generator holds until it does not.

    Items three, seven and eight are the ones that will still be useful in ten years, in whatever language you are then writing. They are arguments about design rather than facts about Python, and each one generalises: rare paths should carry their own costs; a feature's requirements determine its data structures; and a channel that carries values cannot also carry the news that there are no more values.
